  that uses a table, an indirect call, a passive segment, a start function, a
  global other than its stack pointer and the zero memory/table bases of
  position-independent code, an absolute linker symbol (such as
  `__heap_base`) or a 64-bit, TLS or location-relative memory relocation is
  not linkable. Linking is deterministic, and a program without a linked
  import is emitted byte for byte as before.
- **Memory: the intrinsic region of memory 0.** A linked module has exactly
  one memory (owner decision: no multi-memory, so Safari and embedded engines
  run it). Emission sizes the module's intrinsic region
  ([static region](#multi-page-static-region-program_limits), `m` pages after
  the static extension, declared by `varta.intrinsics`) from the operations
  it links, before code is emitted, so the heap base, the allocator, the
  collector and the memory minimum already account for it. The region holds:
  - `[base, base + abi::INTRINSIC_STACK_BYTES)`: the library's shadow stack.
    Its stack pointer starts at the top, and every `global.set` of it in
    linked code is replaced by a call of one synthesized check that traps
    when the new value is below `base`, so a deep linked call can never
    overwrite the static extension or the root stack below the region;
  - from `base + abi::INTRINSIC_STACK_BYTES`: the data segments the linked
    functions reach, in library order, each at the next offset of its own
    `WASM_SEGMENT_INFO` alignment (zero-initialized `.bss` segments
    included);
  - then, 16-byte aligned, the reserved arena of `abi::INTRINSIC_ARENA_BYTES`
    that ends the region. Nothing else is placed there.

  Both sizes are measured (`linked_footprint_tests`): the stack and reserved
  arena are painted before `_start` and scanned afterwards, over adversarial
  inputs of every linked family (every Math function at extreme arguments,
  Number text of the largest, smallest-normal and subnormal Numbers with 100
  digits and every radix, long parse prefixes, `BigInt(Number.MAX_VALUE)`,
  case mapping of 2^16 expanding units, 100,000-digit parses, BigInt
  multiplication, division, widths and text of 300,000-bit operands, and
  serialization and logged text of 5,000 nesting levels and 2,000 records).
  The maximum stack depth is 5,372 bytes (serialization) and the largest
  bounded scratch (the
  operations whose inputs are Numbers or bounded prefixes) 6,984 bytes; both
  constants are 16 KiB, at least twice the measurement, and the test fails
  when a rebuilt library needs more than half of either or when bounded
  scratch leaves the reserved arena. A region is one page for every measured
  closure (two to three pages with the earlier 64 KiB stack and 32 KiB
  arena).
- **Relocation.** The library is linked once, at its own placeholder
  addresses, with relocations kept (`--emit-relocs`, one data segment per
  input section). Linking moves each reached segment to its region address
  and rewrites every memory address that names it: the padded LEB/SLEB
  immediates of `R_WASM_MEMORY_ADDR_LEB`/`SLEB` and of
  `R_WASM_MEMORY_ADDR_REL_SLEB` (position-independent code from the
  `wasm32-wasip2` standard library adds them to `__memory_base`, which the
  library links as 0, so they are absolute and the base stays 0) in code, and
  the `R_WASM_MEMORY_ADDR_I32` words in data. Each new value is the placed
  segment address plus the symbol offset and addend from the `linking`
  symbol table; the old value in the bytes must equal the library address the
  relocation names, or linking fails. No absolute address is assumed.
- **Arena and accessors.** The per-call arena of an allocating export starts
  in the region's reserved arena (committed with the region, so a call with
  bounded scratch needs no memory growth, even when the guest heap fills the
  memory budget). An allocation that no longer fits continues at the guest
  heap's end (the allocator's bump pointer, read by the synthesized
  `arena_base` accessor; the heap base for a module without a managed heap)
  and grows memory 0 within its maximum and the memory budget. The arena is
  a bump allocator that returns the newest block to the bump pointer and
  keeps other freed blocks in size-class free lists (first fit within a
  class, else the smallest larger nonempty class), so the out-of-order
  temporaries of big-integer text and arithmetic reuse their bytes within a
  call. When the memory budget cannot hold an allocation, linked code stores
  `limits::Resource::Memory` and the requested bytes in the module's
  `resource_failure`/`resource_request` exports (every module with an
  intrinsic region exports them) and traps, so the runtime reports the typed
  `RuntimeError::Resource` (memory budget exhausted, with the request) of the
  [data limits](#data-limits-data_limits), never a bare trap. The arena's
  memory, reserved or grown, counts against the memory budget like any guest
  memory. Linked code calls the guest allocator (which may collect) only for
  its owned result, after its arena scratch is complete and with the text in
  the reserved arena or staged in the result buffer, so nothing else writes
  above the heap end while arena data lives there; afterwards the guest
  allocator uses those bytes as fresh heap space (it initializes every block
  it hands out, as it does for reused blocks).
- **Arguments in place.** String arguments and string cells are read in
  place in guest memory after their bounds, limit and UTF-16 length checks
  (`memory::Memory::borrow`), so an operation never copies its input per
  call; only results are copied (`charAt` on 1,024 non-ASCII units: 24,533
  fuel per call with the earlier copy, 738 now, and the same on 2,048
  units). A range at address 0 (a Rust slice cannot start at null) or
  overlapping the result buffer (which linked code writes) is copied. The
  pinned fuel checks (`linked_string_operations_read_their_input_in_place`)
  fail when an operation that reads a bounded prefix costs more on a longer
  input or case mapping exceeds its measured cost per unit.
- **Accessors.** The library reaches guest values and the result globals
  only through synthesized accessors: bounds-checked `memory.copy` within
  memory 0 in each direction, setting the exported `env_result_len`,
  `arena_base`, the reserved arena's bounds (`arena_reserved`,
  `arena_reserved_end`), `resource_failure` and the module's static
  extension pages (`static_pages`, a constant: the static region of the
  linked value readers, whose other bounds are the v38 limits); words and
  ranges outside the result buffer are read in place; string results are
  owned guest strings from the `allocate` accessor (BigInt payloads still
  use the result buffer, and so does text staged while an arena continued
  above the heap). Each allocating export resets the arena on entry and
  traps on a nested entry, so no pointer or state survives a call; linked
  code allocates guest heap values only for its owned results, linked JSON
  and linked serialization, and roots what it reads across an allocation.
- **Validation.** A v38 module that imports a linked operation is rejected
  before instantiation ("pure intrinsic must be linked"). Every module has at
  most one memory. The library's data segments are the only ones a v38 module
  may place outside its static region, and only inside its declared
  intrinsic region; linked functions and signatures count against v38's own
  structural limits (the Wasm limits of
  [program limits](#program-limits-program_limits)). The region is part of
  memory 0, so the store limits cover it with no extra memory, and
  instantiation, which is not charged to the guest, with no extra fuel.
- **Semantics and budgets.** Results equal the host implementation's on the
  same inputs, with two documented differences: Math and `**` use the portable
  `libm` backend (bit-identical on every host, faithful but not always
  correctly rounded; earlier profiles keep the platform library), and a fatal
  failure (a noncanonical argument, a linked stack overflow) is a trap
  instead of a host error message, and an exhausted memory budget is the
  typed resource failure above. Linked BigInt multiplication and decimal
  text of operands near a million bits exhaust the 8 MiB budget in linked
  code where the host import (native allocator) succeeds. Linked calls
  consume fuel and no host-call budget; their data segments are initialized
  without guest fuel like every data segment, and the region
  takes `m` pages of the memory budget. Integral `Number.prototype.toString(radix)`
  arguments below 2^53 take an exact integer-digit path instead of the
  big-integer interval search. Production budgets are unchanged. Linked
  string intrinsics read strings within the v38 data limit, and every
  linked operation that returns text returns an owned guest string
  ([owned text results](#owned-text-results-v38)), so case mapping,
  serialization and the logged text of a value beyond the 1 MiB result
  buffer succeed within the memory budget, and an exhausted budget is the
  typed resource failure. `String(x)` of a string cell is that string itself
  (the fast path). Linked conversions read string cells
  within the v38 data limit (the host imports of earlier profiles keep the
  frozen 1 MiB), so `Number(s)` of a longer string parses. The fuel of the
  general linked paths (fractional Number text, parsing a non-digit string,
  comparisons with a large BigInt) is their instructions: several thousand
  per call where the host import charged none
  ([measurements](development-plan.md#wave-3-conversions-and-readers-measurement-v38)).

#### Owned text results (v38)

- **Every linked text result is an owned guest string.** Number text
  (`number_to_string`, `number_to_fixed`, `number_to_exponential`,
  `number_to_precision`, `primitive_to_string`, `primitive_to_string_v6`),
  `string_char_at16`, case mapping (`string_to_upper_case16`,
  `string_to_lower_case16`), `value_typeof_v11`, BigInt text
  (`bigint_to_string`, `bigint_to_string_v2`) and `value_format_v12` return
  a fresh string from the guest allocator (`varta-intrinsics-wasm` `text`):
  its pointer (0 for the empty string) with its byte length in
  `env_result_len`, the registry signature unchanged. The call site
  (`link::owned_text`, `strings::owned_text`, the fast-path helpers
  included) packs the two into the string handle instead of copying the
  text out of the result buffer; like a snapshot's result the block is
  unrooted and consumed before any later allocation.
- **Allocation.** An operation computes its text in the reserved arena and
  allocates the result last; what it reads after allocating is rooted for
  the call (case mapping roots its input). When an arena allocation
  continued above the heap end, where the allocator places blocks, the text
  is staged in the result buffer first (the texts of this path are bounded
  by it).
- **Case mapping** streams over its input in place (`string::map_case`):
  one pass sizes the result and keeps up to 4,096 units of it in the
  reserved arena; a longer result is mapped again directly into its owned
  string, so nothing proportional to the input is allocated besides the
  result. `Final_Sigma` is decided from the characters around a capital
  sigma within its well-formed run, as `str::to_lowercase` decides it;
  `string::convert_case`, which host imports keep, is the reference of a
  differential test over every BMP unit, sigma contexts and random mixes.
- **Limits.** A result within the v38 string limit and the memory budget
  succeeds; beyond the budget it is the guest allocator's typed
  `RuntimeError::Resource` (memory budget exhausted, with the request),
  beyond the string limit `Resource::ValueSize`. BigInt text keeps its bound
  (a text longer than the result buffer is the `RangeError` it always was).

#### Linked serialization and logging (v38)

- **One encoder.** `varta_intrinsics::json` serializes value layout 18 for
  `JSON.stringify` (`stringify`, private state hidden as by
  `json_stringify_v17`) and for the text of a logged value (`format`, the
  notation of `value_log_v12`: BigInts with `n`, functions as
  `[Function (anonymous)]`, promises as `Promise { … }`, private state shown;
  scalars, strings and Error objects as that host import shows them). It is
  the host serializer's behavior: the same output, the same order of checks
  over the graph and the same failures. Aggregates are read by the shared
  readers (`read_record_with` over a descriptor validated once per call,
  `Vector::read_in`, `Dictionary::read_in`, `ErrorObject::read_in`; a union
  cell by its header, `ReferenceBox::read_envelope`, since the member's own
  reader validates it next), and a noncanonical layout traps. The traversal
  is iterative (a frame stack; the cycle path is scanned while short and
  kept in a set beyond 32 aggregates), so nesting up to
  `limits::V38_MAX_JSON_DEPTH` needs no native stack; the UTF-8 bytes of the
  output are counted against the host's output limits (the memory budget
  for JSON, the result buffer for a logged aggregate). Numbers use an exact
  fast path (`number::Shortest`: integers below 2^53, decimals of at most
  six fraction digits and fifteen significant digits, checked by the
  correctly rounded quotient) and `ryu-js` otherwise; the text equals
  `canonical_display` (a random differential test).
- **Failures.** A BigInt inside `JSON.stringify` is the recoverable
  `TypeError` after the whole graph was validated (the export sets the sign
  bit with the class, and the adapter yields `(0, class)`). A cycle, the
  depth limit (`JSON.stringify`: "nesting exceeds the host depth ceiling of
  10000"; logged text: "depth or node limit"), the output limit and a
  callable `toJSON` field store `EncodeError::linked_code` (above the
  `JsonInputLimit` codes; the request word carries the ceiling) and trap,
  and the runtime reports `EncodeError`, whose messages are the host
  serializer's. The execution deadline is the engine's for linked code (the
  host import checked it every 1,024 values).
- **Memory.** Both run in a scratch entry (rooted guest blocks, as linked
  JSON) with the serialized value rooted. The first pass counts the output
  and keeps up to 16,384 units (the first 32 in place) to copy into the
  result, allocated at its exact length; a longer output is written by a
  second pass into the result, which stays rooted while that pass
  allocates scratch. The result is exactly as long as the host's, so the
  memory budget admits the same values. `json_stringify_owned` retains its
  result, as the host import does; `value_format_v12` returns an unrooted
  owned text, and a string cell's own string without a copy.
- **Logging.** V38 lowers `console.log` of anything but one string to
  `log_string16(value_format_v12(cell))`, where `cell` holds the `unknown[]`
  argument list and the text is Node's ([console
  notation](#console-notation-node_console)), so a v38 module imports no value
  renderer: `LanguageProfile::host_operation` maps the logging operations to
  `value_format_v12`, and no profile admits `value_log_v12` (the runtime
  keeps it for the compiler's `host_import_test_hook`). Under v38
  `log_string16` reads its argument within the module's string limit
  (earlier profiles: the frozen 1 MiB), and the output budget bounds what is
  logged. The logged text lives in guest memory until the effect reads it:
  logging a value whose text needs more memory than the budget has left is
  the typed memory failure where the host renderer, working in host memory,
  succeeded; an Error message beyond the frozen 1 MiB, which the host
  renderer rejected, is logged.
- **Fuel.** Linked serialization costs its instructions
  ([measurement](development-plan.md#linked-serialization-measurement-v38)).
  `JSON_STRINGIFY_VALUE` is calibrated against it by the published method
  (the largest per-value fuel of the linked encoder beyond the old charge on
  the measured shapes, rounded up), so the host import of an earlier profile
  rated at the v38 rates, or of a test build that imports serialization,
  never costs less than the linked encoder; since v38 links serialization
  the rate only documents that cost. The like-with-like corpus check
  compares a program's guest instructions through its build that imports
  serialization; `linked_serialization_stays_within_its_measured_cost`
  requires the linked encoder to stay within the fair charge on every
  measured shape.
  The host's value logging, under the test-only rating of earlier profiles,
  is charged the serialization rates (values visited, output units).

#### Shared checked JSON decoder and linked JSON (wave 3)

- **One decoder (implementation unified, output unchanged).** Every
  recoverable checked parse (`json_parse_v13` to `json_parse_v19`, profiles
  v10 to v38) runs `varta_common::json::scan`, a `no_std`
  decoder over the guest's UTF-16LE text read in place (no UTF-8
  transcoding), iterative at any depth. It produces a tape (every value in
  document order, completely checked) before any guest allocator call. Its
  outcome is exactly the earlier host classification over the input's UTF-8
  transcoding (`text::json_input_limited` followed by
  `JsonSchema::parse_json_classified`, kept as the reference the
  differential tests compare against): the transcoding's byte limit and its
  lone-surrogate syntax errors first (in transcoding order), then
  `serde_json`'s strict grammar over the whole input, then the whole-input
  budgets in document order (depth, visited values, array elements, string
  units), then the schema in document order (a mismatch, or the
  schema-only budgets: dictionary entries, and the values missing optional
  fields add). Numbers convert as `serde_json` (`float_roundtrip`)
  converts them: correctly rounded (an exact path for at most 15 significant
  digits and decimal exponents within 22, `core` otherwise), an infinite
  result a mismatch, `-0` a binary64 negative zero; strings keep their exact
  units, lone surrogates included; record keys must be well-formed UTF-16.
  Syntax positions are diagnostics only (no guest-visible message changes).
  The host turns the tape into the existing `JsonValue` tree for the
  child-first builder of v10 to v37; under v38 (`data_limits`) the tape is
  built by the shared top-down builder `varta_common::json::build` through a
  `Heap` (the host's checks the guest allocator's every block as before).
  The static descriptor check is the shared
  `JsonSchema::check_descriptors`; the non-recoverable imports of earlier
  profiles keep their `serde_json` decoder.
- **Schema reader.** `JsonSchema::read` is a `no_std` reader that accepts
  and rejects exactly what the strict `serde` reader does (object or
  sequence forms of structs, unit variants ignoring other members, numbers
  in range), with a fast path for the compact form `to_bytes` writes;
  `validate_bounded` validates within `SchemaBounds` (`SchemaBounds::WASM`
  for v38). Neither formats through `core::fmt` (linked code cannot link the
  function tables it dispatches through).
- **Linked JSON.** V38 links `json_parse_v19`: `varta-intrinsics-wasm`
  exports it with the host import's checks and outcomes: the input
  byte limit, an empty and canonical exception channel (v9), the schema in
  the static region read and validated within `SchemaBounds::WASM`, schema
  version 18 and its descriptors, then the shared decoder and builder.
  `SyntaxError`/`TypeError` are thrown through the exception channel with
  the host's messages (message string, error object and cell each retained,
  `env_result_len` zero, the channel root slot, value and pending flag set);
  an input limit stores `JsonInputLimit::linked_code` (above every
  `limits::Resource` code) in `resource_failure` and traps, and the runtime
  reports the host import's `JsonDecodeError::Limit`, word for word; any
  other failure (a malformed schema, descriptor or channel) is a trap.
  The runtime keeps the host import (a v38 module importing it is rejected);
  the compiler's test switch `host_json_test_hook` compiles v38 modules
  that import it, so tests compare both paths. The linked decoder's fuel is
  in the [measurement](development-plan.md#linked-json-measurement-v38).
  Under [compiled decoders](#compiled-json-decoders-json_decoders) a parse
  calls the linked decoder only as its fallback.
  `json_stringify_owned` is linked too
  ([linked serialization](#linked-serialization-and-logging-v38)).
- **Rooted scratch blocks.** Linked JSON's scratch (tape, frames, key sets)
  is not a reserved gap: the library's allocator, inside a JSON entry
  (`arena::scratch`), takes ordinary guest heap blocks from the guest
  allocator (linker accessor `allocate` = the module's `Allocate` helper),
  stamps each an edge-free block and pushes it on the guest root stack
  (accessor `retain` = the `RootPush` helper). Blocks up to 64 KiB double
  from 4 KiB and are shared; a larger request gets a block of its own. A
  block whose allocations are all freed loses its root (its root-stack slot
  is zeroed, which the collector skips), so a growing tape holds at most its
  old and new capacity. The input string's handle is pushed too, so the
  text the builder copies strings from survives every collection the
  builder's allocations run. On return the root-stack top (accessors
  `roots`/`set_roots`) is reset to its entry value and only the result is
  retained, as the host retains it. The guest's memory budget, collector
  and resource failures govern the scratch like any other block; linked
  JSON writes nothing above the heap end. The value accessors trap in a
  module without a managed heap (only linked JSON reaches them at run
  time); `exception_version`, `exception_pending`, `exception_value`,
  `raise` and `static_pages` read and write the exported channel globals and
  return the static region's pages.
- **Construction.** The builder publishes every container (zero slots) into
  its reachable parent slot, or retains it at the root, before allocating
  its children; a record's presence and order words and the `undefined`
  cells of missing optional union fields are written when the record is
  complete. Record storage slots remain canonical, but their enumeration trailer
  follows input order for ordinary names, with array-index names first in numeric
  order (`4294967295` and noncanonical numeric strings are ordinary names).
  Missing optional fields do not acquire enumeration positions; deleting and
  re-adding a field uses the ordinary record insertion rules. Dictionary entries
  take their own-key positions (array-index
  keys ascending, then input order); value18 dictionaries are built
  unindexed (zero holes, zero table). A failed parse throws before the
  first value allocation, so no partial result exists.

#### Compiled JSON decoders (`json_decoders`)

Selector `json_decoders()` (v38 only) compiles every checked parse of a
static target type (`JSON.parse(text) as T`, `varta.json.parse<T>`, the
untyped `JSON.parse(text)` at `unknown`, and the preludes' parses such as
`Response.json()` and the network head) to a decoder the compiler emits for
that type. It changes no host ABI, value layout, schema version or import:
ordinary targets still link `json_parse_v19` and embed schema 18 for their
fallback. Literal-constrained assertions use the private attempt described
below and retain their original checked conversion as fallback. KV
decodes (`kv_key`, `kv_value`) stay host imports. Contract:

- **Same outcome.** For every input the result is the one the shared
  decoder produces: the same value graph (layouts, presence and order words,
  `undefined` cells of missing fields, own-key order, unindexed value18
  dictionaries), or the same `SyntaxError`/`TypeError` with the same message,
  or the same typed input limit. The decoder accepts an input only when it
  is certain to agree; every failure, and the inputs it leaves alone (keys
  with escapes, dictionary keys starting with a digit, more than 64
  dictionary entries, nesting deeper than 128 containers, records of more
  than 64 fields, numbers whose leading digit's decimal exponent reaches 308,
  BigInt targets, inputs longer than a quarter of the byte limit), go to the
  linked decoder unchanged, which then decides alone. No message, limit or
  error class is produced by compiled code.
- **Check, then build.** The entry roots the input string, takes one tape
  block from the guest allocator (rooted; edge-free; it doubles while it
  fills, the old block rooted until copied), and runs the node checkers over
  the whole input: grammar, shape, duplicates, required fields and the v38
  limits, allocating no value. Only an input accepted to its end is built:
  the node builders read the tape and build top-down exactly as
  `varta_common::json::build` does (each container published into its
  reachable parent, or retained at the root, before any child is
  allocated; the same allocation sequence). On return the root-stack top is
  reset to its entry value and only a reference result is retained;
  `env_result_len` is zero. Before a fallback the entry resets the root
  stack too, so the linked decoder starts from the caller's state.
- **Literal-constrained assertions.** Eligible `JSON.parse(text) as T` targets
  containing literals (records, discriminated reference unions and their arrays)
  keep a compiler-only semantic graph captured before literal erasure. Targets
  must satisfy the existing checked-conversion admission; object views, tuples,
  nominal collections and other non-schema types keep their original path. Scalar
  checkers validate string, number and boolean literal sets. For unions with
  multiple record members, a required literal field must prove each alternative
  disjoint from every other alternative; a tag probe skips preceding values on
  the tape, selects one member, then validates the complete record once. Tags
  are scanned once per field/scalar kind and their decoded tape entry is reused
  across the candidate tests. No intermediate guest `unknown` value graph is
  built on success; fields declared `unknown` still build their required values. Escaped tags,
  slow numeric tags, unproven/overlapping choices and all other misses retain the
  original unknown parse followed by checked assertion, including its errors.
  The input expression runs once, also across `await`. Private attempts return
  zero only internally on a miss: roots are released first, the caller inspects
  the address, and fallback completes before any language value is exposed.
  Successful structured values always have nonzero allocated handles. No public
  schema drops literal constraints; `varta.json.parse<T>` with literal-bearing
  types remains unsupported. Host/schema/value ABIs and older profiles stay fixed.
  Tape rewinds use offsets from the current block base after growth or collection.
- **Record key order.** Each field slot is appended to the record's order words
  as its tape entry is consumed. After building, present integer-named fields
  move to the front in numeric order with stable rotations; named fields retain
  document order. This changes no descriptor, physical field slot or ABI. The
  shared fallback sorts its recorded input slots by the same own-key rule;
  wide records and escaped input keys therefore preserve the same order.
- **Schema at compile time.** The checkers and builders are generated from
  the target's schema nodes (one graph per module; every node is one value
  type, shared by all call sites and targets reaching it): field names as
  UTF-16 constants compared by length and then eight bytes at a time,
  union members selected from the value's first unit as the shared decoder
  selects them (the first member of that value kind; an object also selects
  a dictionary member), required-field masks, record lengths, link masks,
  presence and order words, and the static descriptors of records and
  dictionary storage. The descriptors are the module's static data, as for
  every record the guest builds; the linked fallback still checks the
  schema and its descriptors on every call it makes.
- **Numbers.** A literal is checked in the strict grammar; within 15
  significant digits and a decimal exponent within 22 it converts exactly
  (one correctly rounded multiplication or division by a power of ten, from
  a 23-entry static table), otherwise the builder converts its text with the
  linked `primitive_to_number` through a string cell (correctly rounded,
  like the shared decoder's `core` path). Both give the shared decoder's
  bits, `-0` included.
- **Vectorised scanning (`simd128`).** Selector `simd128()` (v38 only)
  admits fixed-width WebAssembly SIMD (WebAssembly 2.0) in the module, and
  the decoders use it in three shared functions; their contract above is
  unchanged. Each step loads sixteen UTF-16 units (two `v128.load`s) and
  narrows them to one signed-saturated byte per unit
  (`i8x16.narrow_i16x8_s`): an ASCII unit stays itself and every other unit
  becomes `0x7f` or `0x80`, neither special to JSON, so the narrowed bytes
  classify every unit exactly and non-ASCII text needs no scalar step. The
  string scanner finds the first quote, backslash or control character of a
  step (`(b ^ 0x02) <u 0x21`, or `b == 0x5c`, then `i8x16.bitmask` and
  `i32.ctz`) and hands exactly that unit to the scalar path, which checks
  it as before (an escape is validated against a two-word bit set of the
  simple escapes); the whitespace skipper skips sixteen whitespace units per
  step (an `i8x16.swizzle` table of `\t`, `\n`, `\r` and a comparison with
  the space) after the first unit of a run, so a single space costs one
  scalar test more; the builder of an escaped string copies sixteen units
  per step up to the next backslash (both `v128` stores land before the
  string's end and the scalar decoder overwrites what follows the
  backslash; a letter escape maps through a nibble table). A step runs only
  while its sixteen units lie inside the input (the string's decoded end for
  the builder); the units near the input's end take the scalar path, so
  every outcome, position, error, limit and fallback is the scalar
  scanner's. SIMD instructions are ordinary operators: one fuel unit each,
  deterministic on every host and metered identically by the browser
  transform. Runtime validation admits `v128` types, locals and
  instructions only in modules of a `simd128()` profile and the engine
  disables relaxed SIMD for every module
  ([embedding validation step 10](embedding.md#module-validation)), so a v38
  host must support `simd128`; earlier profiles emit and admit no SIMD and
  stay byte-for-byte unchanged. The compiler's test switch
  `json_decoder_test_hook::scalar` builds the same decoders with the scalar
  scanner, the reference of `json_simd_tests`.
- **Resources.** The decoders' recursion is bounded by their depth limit;
  their scratch is the rooted tape (eight bytes per entry: a container count,
  field slot, union member, string span, number or boolean; the first block
  `min(4·len + 8, 4096)` bytes; the shared decoder's tape takes sixteen bytes
  per node) and their work is paid as guest fuel. Five mutable i32
  globals (input end, tape cursor, base, end and root slot) follow the
  module's other globals; the decoder functions follow every other
  function. Nothing survives a call.
- **Tests.** `varta-runtime` `json_decoder_tests` compares the decoders with
  the linked decoder alone (the compiler's test switch
  `json_decoder_test_hook::compile_generic`) and with the host import on the
  case corpus, a hand corpus, seeded random schemas, inputs and mutations,
  wide unions, deep nesting to the limit, dictionaries around 64 entries,
  wide records and the data-limit cases, and runs decoders that collect
  before every block they allocate (`compile_collecting`); the compiler's
  `emit::decoders::tests` validates the modules in Wasmtime and checks that
  decoders are shared per type and absent before v38. `direct_json_tests`
  compares private attempts with `compile_assertions_reference` (only direct
  assertion decoding disabled), generic/host decoding and forced collection,
  including recursive/array targets, literal failures, seeded mutations,
  relocated tape blocks, single evaluation and default production budgets.
  Source-free CLI cases include imported union types. Measured last-tag cases
  use 69,707 vs 102,176 fuel (2 variants/128 numbers), 71,660 vs 105,810
  (32/128), 297,330 vs 407,976 (32/512) and 81,307 vs 125,167 (200/128).
  Existing dispatch ceilings pass unchanged (12 vs 7 fuel per preceding candidate
  for 24 vs 200 members). These are selected regression measurements, not a
  general throughput or allocation benchmark.

#### Fair host fuel (`fair_fuel`)

Under v38 every host import charges the module's fuel for its work at the
fixed rates of `varta_common::fuel`, part of the host-operation contract and
published in the [embedding contract](embedding.md#fair-host-fuel-v38)
(generated, drift-tested): `CALL` per call, `BYTE` per byte of a string
argument read (through `host::input` and the UTF-16 readers) or of a string
result written (`host::result*`), and for checked JSON `JSON_PARSE_UNIT` per
input unit, `JSON_SCHEMA_TYPE` per schema type, `JSON_SCHEMA_FIELD` per
record field or union member and `JSON_PARSE_VALUE` per decoded value,
`JSON_STRINGIFY_VALUE` per value visited and `JSON_STRINGIFY_UNIT` per
output unit. The call charge is taken by a store call hook (`CallingHost`)
before the import runs; argument charges before the effect; result and JSON
charges before the result is published (the parse charge before the first
guest allocation). A charge the remaining fuel cannot cover sets the fuel to
zero and fails with Wasmtime's out-of-fuel trap, which the turn reports as
the ordinary typed fuel-budget error; a host failure caused by a charge is
that error too, never a logged host status. Fuel the import's guest
callbacks consume (allocator, retention helper) is guest fuel. Fuel-profile
probes refund their call charge. Profiles before v38 charge nothing; a
test-only switch (`Execution::rate_host_work`) charges an earlier profile at
the same rates so fuel comparisons are like with like.

KV storage ([`kv`](#kv-storage-kv)) adds three rates: `KV_OPERATION` per
`kv_open`, `kv_read` and `kv_commit` (after the grant check, before the file
is opened, the read runs or the commit is submitted), `KV_BYTE` per key or
value byte encoded by `kv_stage` (before it is kept), written by a commit
(with the operation charge) and returned by a read, and `KV_ENTRY` per entry
a read returns (with its bytes, before the entry count reaches the guest).
A decode (`kv_key`, `kv_value`) pays `JSON_SCHEMA_TYPE`,
`JSON_SCHEMA_FIELD` and `JSON_PARSE_VALUE` for its schema and the values it
decodes, before the first guest allocation, as checked JSON does; a failed
decode pays them before its `TypeError` is thrown. A charge the fuel cannot
cover is the typed fuel-budget error before the operation's effect: an
unaffordable commit is never submitted. KV has no linked equivalent, so its
rates are calibrated against guest time instead
([KV fair fuel](development-plan.md#kv-fair-fuel-v38)): the host time of each
operation (wall time minus its guest fuel at the measured guest fuel rate),
fitted to a fixed part, a part per byte and a part per entry and converted at
the guest's fuel rate, then rounded up. The JSON rates are calibrated against
the linked equivalents
([fair host fuel](development-plan.md#fair-host-fuel-v38)): `CALL` the
cheapest linked call, `BYTE` Wasmtime's `memory.copy` rate, the JSON rates
the fitted upper bound of the linked decoder's and encoder's fuel per unit,
value and schema node, so a host import never costs less than its linked
equivalent.

#### Web bytes (`web_bytes`)

Wave 2 of v38 admits byte bodies and the Web types around them under
`web_bytes()`, with three host imports at minimum host ABI 34; v37 and
earlier profiles keep their bytes, preludes and diagnostics (v37 rejects
`Blob`, `FormData`, `ArrayBuffer`, `ReadableStream<Uint8Array>` and
`globalThis`). No value tag or layout is added; the wave-3
[bytes stream](#bytes-held-by-unknown-byte_values) later gives a
`Uint8Array` a value tag of its own.

- **Byte bodies.** Under v38 the `fetch` prelude is
  `<varta>/web/fetch.ts` with the source `prelude/fetch_bytes.ts` (the
  `extended` text of the v37 module). `ReadableStream<R extends Uint8Array =
  Uint8Array>`, `ReadableStreamDefaultReader<R>`,
  `ReadableStreamReadResult<R>`, `ReadableStreamDefaultController<R>` and
  `UnderlyingSource<R>` carry `Uint8Array` chunks; the type parameter exists
  for TypeScript's spelling and must be `Uint8Array` (another argument fails
  its constraint). `read()` returns `{ done, value }` with an empty
  `Uint8Array` once done (WHATWG: `undefined`). `Response` adds
  `arrayBuffer()`, `bytes()` and `blob()` (its type the lowercased
  `content-type`, or empty); `text()` and `json()` of a network body keep the
  v37 host-decoded UTF-8 path, every other consumption reads bytes. A
  `BodyInit` is `string | URLSearchParams | Blob | ArrayBuffer | Uint8Array |
  FormData` for `Request`, `RequestInit.body` and `new Response(body)` (which
  also takes a `ReadableStream<Uint8Array>`); a string body defaults its
  content type to `text/plain;charset=UTF-8`, `URLSearchParams` to the form
  type, a `Blob` to its non-empty type and `FormData` to
  `multipart/form-data; boundary=…`. Bytes travel as byte strings (one
  UTF-16 code unit 0..=0xFF per byte); `varta.text.units` (an engine
  intrinsic of the preludes, the inverse of `varta.text.fromUnits`) turns one
  into a `number[]` reserved at its final length.
- **Imports.** `net_request_start_v2 (ptr:i32, len:i32) -> f64` is
  `net_request_start` for request descriptor version 2
  (`net::DESCRIPTOR_VERSION_BYTES`), whose body flag is `0` (none), `1` (text,
  sent as UTF-8) or `2` (`net::DESCRIPTOR_BYTES`: bytes, a code unit above
  0xFF is a fatal malformed descriptor); same `net.request` check before any
  effect, host-call budget and recoverable denial. V38 maps
  `net_request_start` to it (`LanguageProfile::host_operation`), so a v38
  module never imports the v1 start and validation rejects one that does;
  each import accepts only its own descriptor version.
  `net_body_read_bytes (id:f64) -> ()` arms the next chunk like
  `net_body_read` but delivers its bytes undecoded (bytes a text read kept for
  an unfinished UTF-8 sequence come first); it is bookkeeping (no
  capability, no host-call charge, the deadline observed). A v38 read
  delivers at most `net::MAX_READ_DELIVERY_BYTES` (v37 chunks keep
  `net::MAX_CHUNK_BYTES`); `net::MAX_RESPONSE_BODY_BYTES` bounds what one read
  receives ([long-lived transfers](#long-lived-transfers-and-host-owned-headers-v38));
  a byte request body is at most half of `net::MAX_REQUEST_BYTES`
  ([values](embedding.md#network-request-limits-v37)).
  `env_snapshot (ptr:i32, len:i32) -> i32` is below.
- **Declared response headers and the canonical head.** Under v38 the
  `net.request` grant gains an optional `responseHeaders` list (manifest
  `{"id": "net.request", "patterns": [...], "responseHeaders": [...]}`,
  project form `"net": {"request": {"urls": [...], "methods": [...],
  "responseHeaders": [...]}}`), admitted only from host ABI 34
  (`abi::PROGRAM_LIMITS_VERSION`), so an earlier manifest that names it is
  rejected. Each entry is an exact lowercase RFC 9110 token, listed once,
  within `net::MAX_GRANT_RESPONSE_HEADERS` names of at most
  `net::MAX_RESPONSE_HEADER_NAME_BYTES`; `net::FORBIDDEN_RESPONSE_HEADERS`
  (`set-cookie`, `set-cookie2`, in any case) are never declarable and fail
  validation with a diagnostic naming the header. The request's visible set
  is the declared list, or `net::SAFELISTED_RESPONSE_HEADERS` (the
  CORS-safelisted response-header names a browser always exposes) when the
  grant declares none; `[]` shows nothing. A host ceiling may declare the
  field too, and the visible set is then the intersection of both sides'
  sets, each computed the same way (a ceiling without the field admits only
  the safelisted names; a ceiling never adds a name). The runtime builds the
  head record of a `net_request_start_v2` request in the canonical form
  (`net::HeadForm::Canonical`): undeclared and forbidden fields are dropped
  before the record exists, every remaining name appears once in byte order
  of the lowercase names, and repeated values are combined with
  `net::COMBINE_SEPARATOR` in arrival order. Fair host fuel charges the
  record's bytes, so a dropped field costs nothing. `Response.headers`
  therefore holds only visible names, `get()` of any other name is `null`
  on every host, and `getSetCookie()` of a network response is empty; a
  `Blob` from `blob()` has an empty type when `content-type` is not
  visible. `location` stays a separate head member used only to follow
  redirects (each hop is checked again). `net_request_start` (v37) ignores
  the field and keeps its frozen record (every field, in arrival grouping).
  The normative rule, the examples and the browser note
  (`Access-Control-Expose-Headers` is deployment configuration) are in
  [Canonical head](embedding.md#canonical-head-v38).
- <a id="long-lived-transfers-and-host-owned-headers-v38"></a>**Long-lived
  transfers and host-owned headers.** A typed SDK's session stream
  (server-sent events) runs for minutes and may carry any total, and an
  unmodified SDK sets `User-Agent` on every request; `net_request_start_v2`
  therefore differs from the frozen v37 start in five ways, identically on
  every host. (1) **Inactivity, not an end-to-end deadline:** the head must
  arrive within one window of the start and each wait of an armed body read
  lasts at most one window, where the window is the network's own
  `net::READ_INACTIVITY_SECONDS` (owner decision 2026-11-06; until then the
  per-turn deadline, which cut every live stream quiet for five seconds and
  made clients reconnect in a loop); a host may lower it
  (`RunOptions::network_idle`). Receiving bytes ends a
  wait, so every chunk renews the window; no window runs while no read is
  armed; and no wait passes the instance's bound (the embedder's lifetime of
  a long-lived instance, none without one, or the execution deadline of a
  bounded run, where the rule therefore changes nothing). Expiry fails the
  head with `request timed out` or the read with `response body timed out`,
  recoverably (`TypeError: fetch failed` / `terminated`). (2) **Per-read body
  bound:** `net::MAX_RESPONSE_BODY_BYTES` bounds the bytes the host receives
  while serving one read (`net::BodyBound::Read`), not the body; there is no
  total byte bound. A body is bounded in time by the window and the
  instance lifetime, in host memory by the per-read cap plus one received
  transport chunk beyond it and a held-back split sequence (the transfer receives only while the guest has a
  read armed), and what the guest keeps by its memory budget (the v37
  rationale, one string value of `abi::MAX_STRING_BYTES`, does not hold under
  the v38 data limits). (3) **Host-owned request headers**
  (`net::HOST_REQUEST_HEADERS`: `accept-encoding`, `user-agent`): a guest
  value is checked like any header, then ignored and never sent, because a
  browser always sends its own; the native reference host sends no
  `user-agent`. (4) **Content codings:** the native host decompresses nothing,
  so it sends `accept-encoding: identity` (`net::NATIVE_ACCEPT_ENCODING`) and
  fails a response that names another coding before its head
  (`RequestFailure::Encoding`); a browser host admits a body Fetch decoded and
  shows neither `content-encoding` nor `content-length` for it. (5) **Per-read delivery cap** (owner decision, over
  documenting the fatal outcome): one read delivers at most
  `net::MAX_READ_DELIVERY_BYTES`, held-back bytes included, and larger
  received data is split across successive reads. Each read is one event
  turn, and the guest byte path costs about `net::READ_BYTE_FUEL` fuel per
  delivered byte (measured), so a read of `net::MAX_CHUNK_BYTES` would
  exhaust `budget::TURN_FUEL` and terminate a well-behaved instance during a
  burst; the cap keeps that path within one `net::READ_FUEL_SHARE`-th of the
  turn fuel (a compile-time assertion in `varta_common::net`); a guest
  `TextDecoder` over every read measured about two thirds of a turn. Further per-byte application work
  (line splitting, `JSON.parse` per event) is not guaranteed to fit and is the
  application's budget. No production budget changed. Other headers
  a browser controls (cookie, origin, referer, `sec-*`, `proxy-*`, …) are not
  host-owned: the native host sends them, a browser host refuses them (owner
  decision: accepted as documented, like the native fail-closed rule for
  codings). `net_request_start` (v37) keeps one end-to-end deadline, its
  chunk bytes, the whole-body bound and every header as given. The wire
  rules, failure texts and the browser hosts' obligations are in
  [Transfer timing](embedding.md#transfer-timing-v38),
  [Per-read delivery cap](embedding.md#per-read-delivery-cap-v38) and
  [Host-owned headers](embedding.md#host-owned-headers-and-content-codings-v38).
- **`ArrayBuffer`, `Blob`, `FormData`** (`<varta>/web/blob.ts`, guest code,
  no host import, loaded when a module names one of them). `ArrayBuffer`
  (`new ArrayBuffer(n)`, `byteLength`, `slice`, `ArrayBuffer.isView`) owns
  the `number[]` storage that `new Uint8Array(buffer)` views (shared, so
  writes through the view are seen by the buffer; there are no offsets).
  `ArrayBufferView` is `Uint8Array` (no other typed array exists), so
  `ArrayBuffer.isView(value)` is `value instanceof Uint8Array`, which tests
  the byte-array tag of an `unknown` cell
  ([bytes](#bytes-held-by-unknown-byte_values)). `Blob` (parts of
  `string`, `Blob`, `ArrayBuffer` or `Uint8Array`, strings as UTF-8 with lone
  surrogates as U+FFFD; `type` normalized as WHATWG; `size`, `slice`,
  `arrayBuffer`, `bytes`, `text`) is immutable and holds a byte string, so
  `response.blob()` and blob request bodies copy no byte one at a time; there
  is no `stream()`, no `File` and no `endings`. `FormData` (`append`, `set`,
  `delete`, `get`, `getAll`, `has`, and snapshot `keys`/`values`/`entries`
  arrays instead of iterators) keeps string and `Blob` entries with their file
  names (`blob` by default; `get` returns the `Blob`, not a `File`); a file
  name with a string value is a `TypeError`. As a body it serializes in
  Node's layout (CR/LF normalization, `%0A`/`%0D`/`%22` escapes,
  `application/octet-stream` for untyped blobs) with a deterministic boundary:
  `----formdata-varta-` and the first 11-digit counter, from 0, whose
  boundary occurs in no part (Node draws a random one).
- **Typed `globalThis`** (`<varta>/web/global.ts`). Unless a module binds the
  name, `globalThis` is an instance of the prelude's `GlobalObject`, whose
  getters are `globalThis`, `crypto` (a `Crypto` with `getRandomValues` and
  `randomUUID`) and `process` (a `Process` with `env`); any other member is a
  compile error, never `any`. `globalThis.fetch`, `globalThis.encodeURIComponent`
  and `globalThis.encodeURI` are the global functions themselves (the module
  scanner rewrites the member into the name before implicit imports, unless
  the module binds it). `typeof x.m` of a class method is `"function"`, so
  `typeof c.randomUUID === 'function'` feature detection compiles.
  `typeof NAME` of an *engine global* that no binding, function or generic
  function of the program shadows is a constant string that evaluates
  nothing and loads no prelude for the operand (`instanceof` and other uses load
  as usual): `"function"` for the class and function exports of the preludes
  the profile admits (except `RegExpExecArray`, `RegExpMatchArray` and
  `ViewEvent`, whose instances only engine APIs create), the error classes,
  `Map`/`Set`/`Uint8Array`, `Number`, `String`, `Boolean`, `BigInt`,
  `Object`, `Array`, `Promise`, `parseInt`, `parseFloat`, `isNaN`,
  `isFinite` and the timers; `"object"` for `Math`, `JSON`, `console` and
  the members of `GlobalObject` (`globalThis`, `crypto`, `process`), the
  values Node 24 reports. A shadowed name keeps its binding's `typeof`; any
  other identifier stays `unknown identifier`, never `"undefined"`. The
  folded `typeof process` does not make a bare `process` readable: the
  environment is still `globalThis.process`.
  `globalThis as T` (any `x as T` to a wider object type) is the structural
  view an assignment makes, and `f as F` (or `F | undefined`) of a named
  function whose parameters accept `F`'s is a fresh adapter function of `F`'s
  signature (not `===` to `f`).
- **`process.env`** names variables exactly; the environment is never
  enumerated. `env_snapshot (ptr:i32, len:i32) -> i32` (capability `env.get`,
  one host call) takes a UTF-16 name:
  - With the empty name it returns, in the host result buffer, a JSON object
    (in name order) of the set variables whose names appear *exactly* (no
    `*` or `?`) in the package's `env.get` patterns and, when there is a host
    ceiling, also exactly in the ceiling's, each passing the check `env_get`
    makes. `process.env` read as a value is this snapshot, a fresh
    `Record<string, string | undefined>` per read, so a dynamic key,
    `Object.keys(process.env)` and spreads see only exactly granted names. A
    wildcard pattern lists nothing.
  - With a name it returns `{"NAME": value}`, or `{}` when the variable is
    unset, after the same check as `env_get` (any matching pattern, package
    and ceiling); a denial is the recoverable `env.get` denial (failed status,
    logged), checked before any read. `process.env.NAME` and
    `process.env['NAME']` with a static key compile to this read
    (`environmentValue`), so a wildcard grant reads a variable by name when
    the read runs. A denied or unset variable is `undefined`.
  Values that are not Unicode are skipped; a result beyond the host result
  buffer fails recoverably and reads as `{}`. Writes change only the
  snapshot.
- **`Promise.race` over differently typed promises.** An array literal of
  promises of different value types races into `Promise<T0 | T1 | …>` (one
  job per element, in index order, as for one type); `await
  Promise.race([...])` assigned or declared at a union type takes it as
  context. Promise values erase literal types (`new Promise<'timeout'>` is a
  `Promise<string>`), so an element whose value is the base of a literal
  member of the context fulfills through a checked assertion (`TypeError`
  for another value). `Promise.all`, `allSettled` and `any` still take one
  promise type.
- **Strict conversions to record unions without a discriminant.** A checked
  conversion (`unknown as T`, `JSON.parse(text) as T`, checked declared
  reads) to a union with several record members of which some has no literal
  discriminant: a cell that already holds one member (exact) is that member;
  otherwise every member is built from the JSON object in member order. Each
  build is strict (an unknown key, a missing required field or a mistyped
  value fails it; builds have no effect). Exactly one successful build is the
  result; none throws the conversion's `TypeError`, and more than one throws
  `TypeError("checked conversion to T is ambiguous: the value matches more
  than one member")`. Member order never decides. `JSON.parse(text) as T`
  with such a union anywhere in `T` parses to `unknown` first, since the
  host's schema parser cannot select the member. Unions whose members all
  have discriminants keep the v37 selection. A literal field is never disjoint
  from a corresponding `unknown` field: unknown admits every scalar. Such
  overlapping alternatives require strict matching, retaining valid alternatives
  and rejecting multiple successful matches rather than choosing by member order.
- **Unions and `unknown` with bytes.** `x as U` from a union to a union of
  some of its members (a `BodyInit` to a `BlobPart`) tests the cell against
  `U`'s members, `TypeError` otherwise; `o.p instanceof C ? o.p : y` narrows
  the property of a record or dictionary in the consequent. A record, array
  or dictionary whose fields reach a `Uint8Array` (and no `Map`, `Set` or
  opaque builtin) may enter `unknown` or `object` as it is. How `unknown`
  holds the `Uint8Array` itself and what its readers and the JSON-object view
  do with it is the wave-3
  [bytes stream](#bytes-held-by-unknown-byte_values).
- **Classes merged with an interface.** `interface C extends A, B { … }` and
  `class C` in one module merge: the interface's members (own and inherited,
  optional ones as `T | undefined`) become ordinary public instance fields of
  `C`; a method member is a function field whose value comes from the
  assigned object. The constructor must contain exactly one top-level
  `Object.assign(this, X)`; it is rewritten into `const t: interface C = X`
  followed by `this.m = t.m` for every merged member, so the ordinary checks
  prove every member provided with a compatible type (a mismatch names both
  types and each missing or mismatched member) and the constructor
  discipline proves that no use of `this` before it can observe a merged
  member (only already assigned declared fields may be read; no method call,
  no escape). Without the call, with a second one, or with a merged member
  the class also declares, compilation fails naming the members. Members of
  `X` that the interface does not declare are not copied (they are not
  visible through `C`'s type). Both `export interface C` and `export class C`
  export the one class. Generic merged classes and interfaces are rejected;
  v37 keeps rejecting every class and interface merging.
- **Cost.** A byte read converts its chunk with one guest loop
  (`varta.text.units`), and `TextDecoder`/`TextEncoder` and multipart
  serialization run per byte in guest code; network `text()` keeps the host
  decoder. Production budgets are unchanged.

#### SDK paths (`sdk_paths`)

Wave-2 additions to v38 for the multipart, query and error paths of the pinned
uarp-sdk 0.13.2, under the selector `LanguageProfile::sdk_paths()`. No host
import, value layout or ABI changes; v1–v37 keep rejecting every form below.

- **Error causes.** `error.cause` reads a native error, an Error subclass
  instance or a union of both after `instanceof Error`: the instance's
  `cause` slot, and `undefined` for a native error. `new Error(message,
  options)` (and `new TypeError(…)` and the other native families) builds
  an instance of the family's synthetic Error root, the class an Error
  subclass extends, with `message`, the family's `name` and `options.cause`
  installed exactly as `super(message, options)` does. Its static type is
  that root class, so it passes `instanceof` of its family and of `Error`,
  is reported like a subclass instance when uncaught and serializes as `{}`,
  as in JavaScript; like a subclass instance it is not assignable to a
  parameter annotated `Error` (the native error union). Native error values
  never own a `cause`, so the `undefined` read is exact. Before any body is
  lowered, `link` creates the root of every family that some module
  constructs with two arguments, so catch unions and `unknown` analyses see
  the class from the start. Any other argument list (more than two
  arguments, an argument spread, type arguments) fails with `error
  constructor arguments other than (message?, options?)`. `"cause" in` an
  Error-class instance (an Error root or subclass instance) is refused:
  JavaScript defines the own `cause` only when the options object has one
  (`'cause' in new Error('m', {})` is false), and the instance's `cause`
  slot records no presence. `"message" in` and `"name" in` stay true, as
  the prototype provides both.
- **Generic method calls on element receivers.** `xs[i].m<T>()` reaches a
  function field of the element type like `x.m<T>()` of a binding does: the
  element is read once (an absent element fails with `TypeError` when the
  field is read) and the erased generic call checks its result. Only a
  computed key other than a string literal is an element read, as in member
  lowering: `xs['length']` stays the length, so a `switch` over it is never
  exhaustive over the element type.
- **`instanceof Map`, `Set` and `Uint8Array`.** Of a closed union, the test
  is a member tag test and narrows the union both ways; of any other closed
  type it is a constant (the operand is still evaluated). A map or set has
  no value tag of its own (it shares the record tag), so `instanceof Map`
  and `instanceof Set` are refused for an `unknown` or `object` operand,
  which never holds one, and for a union whose other members share the
  selected member's tag. `instanceof Uint8Array` of an `unknown` or
  `object` operand, and of a closed union, tests the byte-array tag of the
  wave-3 [bytes stream](#bytes-held-by-unknown-byte_values). Union formation
  refuses two members with one tag (a `Map` or `Set` with another map, set,
  record or class instance) and keeps the wave-2 rule that counts a
  `Uint8Array` as an array member, so `Uint8Array | T[]` stays refused even
  though the cells carry different tags: telling the two apart in a closed
  union is not implemented. A
  `Uint8Array` with records or class instances (`Blob | ArrayBuffer |
  Uint8Array | string`) and a `Map` or `Set` with primitives or arrays are
  admitted.
- **`File` and `FormData` entries.** The blob prelude's `File` is a `Blob`
  with a `name` (a USVString). `FormData.append`/`set` take `string | Blob`
  and follow WHATWG "create an entry": a `Blob` that is no `File` becomes a
  `File` named `blob` with the same bytes and type, a given file name makes
  a new `File` of that name, and a `File` without one stays the same object.
  `FormDataEntryValue` is `string | File`, so `get`, `getAll`, iteration and
  the multipart `filename` (the entry's `File` name) agree with Node. The
  entry test is `instanceof File` and the name the `File` field; a
  program's subclass cannot override an engine-internal member of a prelude
  class (`override of the engine-internal member byteString of Blob`).
  `lastModified` is not declared: its default is the wall-clock time, which
  needs a clock grant, so reading it is a compile error. `for (const [name,
  value] of form)` iterates the snapshot `FormData.prototype.entries()`
  returns.
- **Spreads and enumeration through views.** A record spread (into a record
  or a dictionary context) and an own-key enumeration (`Object.keys`,
  `Object.values`, `Object.entries`, an `Object.assign` source, `for...in`)
  whose source type is a view of a wider object type, one with other field
  names or another field order, fail when `resolve` sees the view: the
  lowering would copy or list the view's declared fields in the view's
  order, where JavaScript takes every own property in the object's own key
  order. A view whose sources declare exactly its fields in its order (the
  SDK's `{ ...spec, headers, query }` passed back as a `RequestSpec`) is
  admitted, as are dictionary spreads (`{ ...spec.query, ...options.query }`
  merges and serializes byte for byte as Node does).
- **Not admitted.** `A[] | B[]` of records, `Blob.stream()`,
  `Response`/`Request` `formData()` and the `FormData`
  `keys()`/`values()`/`entries()` iterator objects (they return array
  snapshots) stay as they were. A `Uint8Array` held by `unknown` and the
  SDK's byte parts are the wave-3
  [bytes stream](#bytes-held-by-unknown-byte_values).

#### Iteration protocol (`iteration_protocol`)

Additions to v38 (2026-11-06) that make program classes iterable and let
array literals, `Array.from` and generators consume every synchronous
iterable the checked subset has, under the selector
`LanguageProfile::iteration_protocol()`. No host import, value layout, frame
catalog, scheduler or ABI changes: the forms below lower to guest code over
the existing generator frames, so the native runtime and every JavaScript
host run them unchanged. V1–v37 keep rejecting every form below with their
old diagnostics (`computed or numeric class member name`, `generator method`,
`array spread`, `yield* delegation`, `Array.from of a value other than a Map,
Set, Uint8Array or their iterators`). No `Symbol` value exists: `Symbol.iterator`
and `Symbol.asyncIterator` are recognized only as the spelled-out computed
keys below.

- **Iterable classes.** An instance method declared with the computed key
  `[Symbol.iterator]` (a generator method `*[Symbol.iterator]()` or a plain
  method returning a generator object) makes the class's instances
  iterable, inherited and overridden like any other method (an override
  dispatches through the root's dispatcher). `for...of`, an array literal
  spread, `Array.from` and `yield*` call it once and iterate the generator
  it returns; the method must have no parameters, must not be a getter and
  must return a synchronous generator (`unsupported … over a class
  instance: [Symbol.iterator]() must be a method without parameters
  returning a synchronous generator`), and a class instance without one is
  refused by name (`… the class declares no [Symbol.iterator]() method`).
  `x[Symbol.iterator]()` and `x[Symbol.asyncIterator]()` call the methods
  explicitly. A static or string-keyed `[Symbol.iterator]` and other
  computed keys stay refused. `RegExp` match arrays, `Headers`, `FormData`
  and collections keep their own iteration.
- **Generator methods.** Every synchronous generator instance method is
  admitted (`*entries(from: number): Generator<…>`): the method keeps its
  index, receiver and shape and returns the object of a receiver-free
  generator body that takes the receiver as its first parameter, so the
  frames, liveness and resume rules of [synchronous
  generators](#synchronous-generators-generators) apply unchanged. Optional
  and rest parameters stay refused (`generator method with optional or rest
  parameters`).
- **Annotations.** `Iterator<T, TReturn?, TNext?>` and
  `IterableIterator<T, TReturn?, TNext?>` denote synchronous generator
  objects with `Generator`'s defaults, as the async iteration interfaces
  denote async generator objects. `implements Iterable<T, TReturn?, TNext?>`
  checks that the class declares a `[Symbol.iterator]()` method without
  parameters returning a synchronous generator that yields exactly `T` (and
  has the given `TReturn` and `TNext`). `Iterable<T>` as a value annotation
  is refused by name: an iterable parameter would also have to accept
  arrays, which a generator type does not.
- **Array literal spreads.** `[a, ...xs, b, ...source]` spreads checked
  arrays and tuples, strings (their code points, as the String iterator
  yields them: a surrogate pair is one element, a lone surrogate one
  element of its own), synchronous generators (whose `TNext` accepts
  `undefined`), `Map`, `Set` and `Uint8Array` values and their
  `keys()`/`values()`/`entries()` iterators, and iterable class instances.
  Elements and sources evaluate in source order, and each source is iterated
  to completion where it appears, before the next element is evaluated; a
  generator source is resumed with `undefined` until it completes and is
  never closed (no abrupt exit can leave a spread). An array source is read
  at its live length; a hole of an element type without `undefined` throws
  `TypeError: array element is a hole`, as in `for...of`, and reads as
  `undefined` when the element type includes it. The result is a fresh
  array whose element type is the context's array element type, or else the
  union of every element and source element type. A hole beside a spread
  element and async generators are refused by name. The v37 form
  `[...collection]` keeps its own lowering.
- **`Array.from(source)`.** One argument: the same fresh array as
  `[...source]` for every source above, besides the v37 collection forms. A
  map function, more arguments or a spread argument stay refused.
- **`yield*`.** In a synchronous generator body, `yield* source` over a
  generator, an array (or tuple, string, collection or `RegExp` match array)
  or an iterable class instance yields each value the source produces (widened to
  this generator's `T`). The delegating point observes how this generator is
  resumed instead of throwing or returning at it (`Suspend::observe`):
  `next(v)` resumes a generator source with `v` (the first resumption sends
  `undefined`, so the source's `TNext` accepts `undefined` and this
  generator's `TNext` converts to it), `throw(e)` is forwarded to the
  source's `throw` (a not-started or completed source rethrows `e`), and
  `return(v)` to its `return`: a completed source makes this generator return
  the source's completion value, a source that yields again from a `finally`
  block keeps the delegation going. An array source has no `throw` or
  `return` method: a forwarded `throw` throws `TypeError: The iterator does
  not provide a 'throw' method.` and a forwarded `return(v)` returns `v`
  from this generator. The expression's value is the source generator's
  return value (`undefined` for an array). Conversions are checked at
  compile time (`yield* source yields …`, `yield* forwards what this
  generator receives from return() to its source`); a generator whose
  `TReturn` is `void` returns `undefined` after a forwarded `return()`, and
  closes a source whose `TReturn` excludes `undefined` with a placeholder
  the source cannot observe. This is the one deviation: if the source's
  `finally` block returns a value of its own, JavaScript would return that
  value from this `void` generator; Varta returns `undefined`. Async
  generators keep their own `yield*` rules.
- **Not admitted.** Iterator helpers, `Symbol()` values and symbol-keyed
  properties, `Array.from` with a map function or an array-like, and
  `Iterable<T>` value annotations. Hand-written iterator objects behind
  `[Symbol.iterator]()` and destructuring of generators, strings,
  collections and iterable instances are admitted by the [expression
  forms](#expression-forms-expression_forms) stream.

#### Expression forms (`expression_forms`)

Additions to v38 (2026-11-06, K9 track C: expressions and functions) under
the selector `LanguageProfile::expression_forms()`. No host import, value
layout, frame catalog, scheduler or ABI changes: every form lowers to guest
code over existing IR, so the native runtime and every JavaScript host run
it unchanged. V1–v37 keep rejecting every form with its old diagnostic.
Node 24 is the reference for every output below.

- **`await` in every operand position.** In an async function `await`
  may appear in call and `new` arguments, operands of every operator,
  template substitutions, conditions, object and array literals (optional
  fields included), member and index targets, compound and logical
  assignments and optional chains. Normalization splits every intrinsic
  value block around the suspension point: the block's roots become the
  statement's frame-saved temporaries and its statements keep their order,
  so operands evaluated before an `await` are materialized first and a
  short-circuited operand (`a?.f(await x)`, `a || await b`) never awaits.
  `await` in a `switch` case test and a `do...while` condition stays
  refused (`await inside switch case test`). Top-level `await` in module
  initializers follows [module evaluation](#module-evaluation-module_evaluation).
- **Operators and statements.** The comma operator evaluates every operand
  in order and yields the last. `new.target === C` (`!==`, either order) in
  a class constructor tests the class of the instance under construction
  exactly; `new.target === undefined` is `false` there and `true` in a
  function; other operands and comparisons inside constructor closures are
  refused by name. Iterator results are created as `{ value, done }`, the
  CreateIterResultObject order, so `JSON.stringify` and `Object.keys` of a
  generator result match JavaScript.
- **Tagged templates.** ``tag`a${x}b` `` calls `tag` with the site's
  template object followed by the substitutions, like `tag(strings, x)`;
  the substitutions are checked against the tag's parameters as call
  arguments. The template object is GetTemplateObject's: one
  `TemplateStringsArray` per site (a `string[]` array type of its own whose
  values only sites create) holding the cooked strings, and its `raw`
  property is the site's array of raw strings (line terminators normalized
  to LF). Every evaluation of a site, in every call and every
  instantiation of a generic function, passes the same two arrays: they
  are built once per instance by a synthesized initializer, which runs
  before the module initializers, into two permanent root slots behind the
  module constants, and `strings.raw` finds the site whose cooked array
  `strings` is (a strings array no site created throws `TypeError`).
  Everywhere else a `TemplateStringsArray` is the `string[]` it is: array
  methods, `string[]` parameters (`readonly string[]` in TypeScript) and
  identity comparisons see the same array. ``String.raw`…` `` joins the
  raw text with the ToString of each substitution. Refused: assigning
  `raw`, a part whose cooked string is `undefined` (an invalid escape),
  type arguments on a tagged template and `String.raw(strings, …values)`
  called as a function. Deviation: the arrays are not frozen (Varta has no
  integrity levels), so a write through a `string[]` alias changes the
  site's array where JavaScript throws `TypeError`.
- **Spreads into fixed parameters.** A spread argument whose length is
  static expands in place: an array literal spreads its elements and a
  binding of a fixed-length tuple type spreads its elements (`f(...pair)`,
  `new P(...pair)`, `Math.max(...[a, b])`). Other spreads keep the
  array-snapshot path of rest parameters (and the standard library's
  `Math.max(...xs)`), and a constructor spread of an
  array whose length is not static keeps its refusal (`spread to a class
  constructor`).
- **Receivers.** A field `m` holding a function with an explicit `this`
  parameter is called as `o.m(...)` with `o` as the receiver when `o` is a
  binding or `this` (other bases are refused by name). A class field
  without an annotation initialized by an arrow or function expression has
  that function's type: annotated parameters (a default makes one
  optional) and the annotated return type, or, without one, the type the
  body's outermost operator fixes (arithmetic, comparisons, `!`, literals,
  templates, `String(…)`, `+` with a string operand); other bodies need a
  return annotation. A field initializer may read and capture `this.f` for
  the fields initialized before it, as a constructor statement may.
- **Object-literal methods that use `this`.** A method sees the receiver
  it is called on, as in JavaScript: `o.m()` passes `o`, a spread copy
  passes the copy, a method assigned to another object passes that object
  and an extracted method called alone passes `undefined` (reading a
  property of that `this` throws `TypeError`). Function values have no
  receiver parameter, so a program with such methods passes receivers
  through a register, one permanent root slot behind the module constants:
  every function-value call stores the object of `o.m(...)` (evaluated
  once into a local) or nothing (`undefined`) right before the dispatch,
  and the method, a closure over a hidden `this` binding, takes and clears
  it first, before its parameter defaults. Programs without such methods
  keep their code. The object's type is its contextual closed object type,
  or the record of its literal or binding field values and annotated
  methods; the receiver must be an object of that type or of a type viewed
  as it ([structural subtyping](#structural-subtyping-structural_subtyping)),
  otherwise the call throws `TypeError: object literal method called on an
  object that is not of its literal type` (deviation: JavaScript would read
  the other object's properties; a spread copy with more fields than the
  literal is such an object). Spreads, `Object.assign` and own-key
  enumeration of such objects are admitted. Generator methods that use
  `this` and a spread in a literal whose methods use `this` stay refused by
  name.
- **Object-literal getters and setters.** `get p() {…}` and `set p(v) {…}`
  define accessor properties (owner decision 2026-11-06): reading `o.p`
  calls the getter and assigning it calls the setter, with the object as
  `this` (the receiver register above); compound and logical assignments
  read through the getter and write through the setter; an assignment to a
  getter-only property throws `TypeError: Cannot set property p of
  #<Object> which has only a getter`; `in` and `Object.hasOwn` report the
  property; spreads, `Object.keys`/`values`/`entries`, `Object.assign`
  sources and `for...in` read through the getter, so a spread copy has a
  data property. The literal's type is its contextual record type, or the
  record of its data fields, annotated methods and annotated accessors (a
  getter's return or a setter's parameter type). The object has a physical
  shape of its own: its data fields and, per accessor, the getter and
  setter closures in fields with reserved private names, and the literal's
  value is a [structural view](#structural-subtyping-structural_subtyping)
  of that shape as its type, so member accesses select the layout by the
  object's descriptor and call the accessor functions. No value layout or
  host ABI changes (the owner had accepted a new value ABI version; none is
  needed): hosts read records as data and skip private fields, so the
  compiler never lets an object with accessors reach a host read silently.
  `JSON.stringify` of a record or array that may hold such an object
  serializes a copy made by a synthesized materializer, which reads every
  property through its getter (nested records and arrays included); every
  other host operation (`varta.kv`, logging of objects, HTTP bodies) of a
  value that may hold one, and an `unknown` cell that may hold one, is
  refused by name. Deviations: the own keys of an object with accessors,
  and of the objects a `JSON.stringify` materializer copies, are in the
  order of the type's members (sorted by name) rather than creation order,
  and a cyclic graph of such objects exhausts the materializer instead of
  throwing JavaScript's `TypeError`. Refused: a setter without a getter, a
  spread in a literal with accessors, a `this` parameter of a setter, an
  optional member in a type whose objects `JSON.stringify` copies, and
  accessors in an `unknown` or other non-record context.
- **Computed keys.** `{ [k]: v }` with a constant key — a string or number
  literal, a template without substitutions, or a `const` binding or
  module constant initialized by such a literal — names a closed record
  field, the ToString of the constant; `o[k]` reads it. Keys known only at
  run time need an index-signature context and symbol keys stay refused.
- **Destructuring everywhere.** Tuple parameter patterns, nested object and
  array patterns with defaults and rest in the parameters of arrows,
  functions, methods and callbacks (array methods, iterator helpers),
  declarations, assignment patterns and `for...of` heads; the rest of a tuple
  pattern is a tuple of the remaining element types (an empty array when
  none remain; refused over optional elements); an array rest has the source's
  element type (a hole throws `TypeError: array element is a hole`). An
  array pattern over a non-array source iterates it as `for...of` does
  (strings by code point, `Map`/`Set`, iterable class instances,
  generators): a generator is stepped once per element named and closed
  with `return()` when the pattern has no rest element and the generator
  is not done. Deviation: the elements are taken before the pattern's
  defaults and targets run (JavaScript interleaves them).
- **Hand-written iterators.** A non-generator class method
  `[Symbol.iterator](): Iterator<T>` returning `{ next(): IteratorResult<T> }`
  becomes the generator that calls `next()` once per element until a
  result's `done` is true, so every iteration-protocol consumer drives it.
  Deviations: the method body runs at the first `next()` rather than when
  `[Symbol.iterator]()` is called, and the object's `return`/`throw`
  members are not called.
- **`using` and `await using`.** A block's `using x = e;` binds `x` like
  `const`; the rest of the block runs in a `try` whose `finally` calls
  `x[Symbol.dispose]()` (`await x[Symbol.asyncDispose]()`), one nested
  `try` per declarator, so disposal runs in reverse order on normal
  completion, `return`, `break`, `continue` and throws. Classes declare
  `[Symbol.dispose]()`/`[Symbol.asyncDispose]()` and may `implements
  Disposable`/`AsyncDisposable`. Deviation: when the block and a disposal
  both throw, the disposal's error propagates instead of a
  `SuppressedError`. `using` in a `for` head or at module top level stays
  refused.
- **Structural thenables.** `await t` and `Promise.resolve(t)` of a value
  whose static type has a callable `then` (a closed object field or a class
  method taking `(onFulfilled[, onRejected])`) resolve as PromiseResolve
  does: a new promise whose resolving functions `then` receives one job
  later (NewPromiseResolveThenableJob), so jobs interleave as in Node. A
  thenable reached through a union or `unknown` keeps the runtime
  `TypeError` of the [promise rules](#promise-values-promise_values).
- **Not admitted.** Hand-written iterator objects (`{ next() {…} }`),
  `Symbol()` values and symbol-keyed properties, destructuring of
  generators, strings and iterable instances, and `Iterable<T>` value
  annotations. Iterator helpers and `Array.from` with a map function or an
  array-like are admitted by the [standard library](#standard-library-standard_library).

#### Standard library (`standard_library`)

Additions to v38 (K9 D, 2026-11-06) that complete the ECMAScript 2025
library forms typed npm code uses most, under the selector
`LanguageProfile::standard_library()`. Everything is typed guest code of the
engine preludes (`<varta>/builtins/standard.ts`, `<varta>/builtins/aggregate.ts`,
the v38 collections prelude and the v38 date prelude) called by
`lower::standard`, so there is no host import, value layout, frame catalog
or ABI change, and the native runtime and every JavaScript host run the same
Wasm. V1–v37 keep rejecting every form below with their old diagnostics; the
prelude loads only for programs that name one of its methods
(`modules::engine::STANDARD_LOADS`).

- **Sorting.** `array.sort(compare?)` and `array.toSorted(compare?)`
  (§23.1.3.30, §23.1.3.34) run V8's TimSort (`array-sort.tq`, CPython's
  listsort: run detection, binary insertion below the minimum run, galloping
  merges with the adaptive `minGallop`), so every comparator is called with
  the same arguments in the same order as in Node and an inconsistent
  comparator leaves V8's order. A comparator result of NaN counts as 0.
  Holes and `undefined` are taken out first; the sorted values, then the
  `undefined`s, then the holes are written back (`sort` returns its
  receiver). Without a comparator the elements' String forms compare by
  code units; elements other than primitives are refused by name
  (object-to-string conversion is not modelled). A readonly (`as const`)
  receiver is refused for `sort`, `splice`, `copyWithin`, `shift` and
  `unshift`.
