- **Copying and mutating methods.** `toReversed`, `with` (`RangeError:
  Invalid index : n` outside the array), `toSpliced`, `splice` (the argument
  count decides the delete count, as in §23.1.3.31), `copyWithin`,
  `shift`, `unshift`, `concat` (an argument of the receiver's array type
  spreads, one of its element type is appended; holes stay holes; a receiver
  whose elements are arrays only takes arguments of its own type, since
  JavaScript spreads every array argument), `keys`, `values` and `entries`
  (live generators that read the length at every step) and `at` on strings.
  Mutations keep holes as holes (`Object.hasOwn`/`delete` semantics). A
  copying method that reads a hole of an element type without `undefined`
  throws `TypeError` (`array element is missing`), as `for...of` does,
  because such an array cannot hold the `undefined` JavaScript would copy;
  with `undefined` in the element type the hole reads as `undefined`.
- **Flattening.** `flat(depth?)` with a number literal, `Infinity` or no
  depth (the result type depends on it): each level flattens `T[][]` or
  `(T | T[])[]`, skipping holes; depth 0 is a hole-free copy.
  `flatMap(callback)` flattens a callback returning arrays one level, maps
  one returning other values, and refuses a callback returning both.
- **Constructors.** `Array.of(...)` (the same fresh array as the literal,
  `Array.of<T>()` typed by its argument), `Array.from(source, map)` (the
  source is collected as one-argument `Array.from` collects it, then mapped
  with `(value, index)`), `Array.from({ length: n }, map)` (ToLength, then
  `RangeError: Invalid array length` above 2³²−1).
- **Iterator helpers.** On a synchronous generator that returns `void` and
  takes no `next` input (every built-in iterator: array, `Map` and `Set`
  `keys`/`values`/`entries`, and the helpers themselves): `map`, `filter`,
  `take`, `drop`, `flatMap` (array results), `reduce` (with or without an
  initial value: `TypeError: Reduce of a done iterator with no initial
  value`), `toArray`, `forEach`, `some`, `every`, `find`, and
  `Iterator.from` of a generator, array, `Set` or `Map`. Helpers are lazy
  guest generators over the source; `take`/`drop` validate their limit when
  the helper is created (`RangeError: -1 must be positive`), a `break` or
  `return()` closes the source through the helper's `for...of`, and
  `take(0)` closes it without pulling. The one difference: `return()` on a
  helper that has not started does not close the source (a JavaScript
  helper does; a generator body that never ran has nothing to close).
- **Sets and grouping.** `union`, `intersection`, `difference`,
  `symmetricDifference`, `isSubsetOf`, `isSupersetOf`, `isDisjointFrom`
  (§24.2.4) of two `Set`s with the same element type, iterating the receiver
  or the argument exactly as the specification chooses by size; other
  set-like arguments are refused. `Map.groupBy(items, callback)`,
  `Object.groupBy(items, callback)` (string and number keys, a dictionary in
  JavaScript key order) and `Object.fromEntries` of `[key, value]` tuples or
  a `Map`. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` of a record or dictionary is its
  `Object.keys`; `value.hasOwnProperty(key)` is `Object.hasOwn(value, key)`.
- **JSON.** `JSON.stringify(value, replacer, space)` with a `null` or
  `undefined` replacer or a property list (an array of strings and numbers,
  deduplicated, selecting and ordering every object's members), and a number
  (clamped to 10 spaces) or string (its first 10 code units) `space`: both
  are deterministic rewrites of the compact text the engine serializer
  produces. Replacer functions are refused (the host serializer cannot call
  guest code). The replacer and space arguments must be free of effects
  (literals, bindings, field reads), since they are evaluated after the
  value is serialized.
- **Errors and promises.** `AggregateError(errors, message?, { cause })`
  is an `Error` subclass of typed guest code (`errors: unknown[]`,
  `instanceof`, `cause`, `toString`). `Promise.all`/`allSettled`/`any`/`race`
  over an array literal that mixes `Promise.reject(...)` with promises of one
  type give the rejections that type (TypeScript's `Promise<never>`).
  `Promise.any` rejects with an `AggregateError` whose `errors` are the
  elements' reasons in input order (ECMA-262 §27.2.4.3; the aggregate
  prelude's `anyRejection`, loaded by `Promise.any`), and with an empty
  one for an empty array (K9 D1, 2026-11-06). V37 keeps its `Error`.
- **Math and strings.** `Math.max(...xs)`/`Math.min(...xs)` with spread
  `number[]` arguments (NaN wins, +0 above −0). `String.prototype.at`,
  `substr` (Annex B), `isWellFormed`, `toWellFormed` and locale-free
  `toLocaleUpperCase`/`toLocaleLowerCase`. `String.prototype.normalize`
  (`NFC` by default, `NFD`, `NFKC`, `NFKD`; any other form throws
  `RangeError`) through the linked `string_normalize16` (pure, never
  imported; form word `text::NormalizationForm`) with ICU4X's compiled
  normalization data (`icu_normalizer` 2.4.0, already locked through the
  text stack). A lone surrogate is a normalization boundary kept as it is,
  as V8 keeps it; the Unicode version is ICU4X's, which may differ from
  Node's ICU for characters assigned after it.
- **Date.** The v38 date prelude replaces the v37 class with the complete
  `Date` (§21.4): `Date.UTC`, the component constructor (local time,
  years 0–99 as 1900–1999), every local and UTC getter and setter (with
  rest parameters, so an omitted argument and an explicit `undefined` never
  meet), `getTimezoneOffset`, `getYear`, `toString`, `toDateString`,
  `toTimeString`, `toUTCString`/`toGMTString`, `toJSON`, `valueOf`, and
  `Date.parse` of the forms `toString`, `toDateString`, `toUTCString` and
  `toISOString` produce. The time zone is a recorded host input; without a
  host-granted zone (none is defined yet, an owner decision) it is UTC, so
  every output equals Node's with `TZ=UTC`. `toString`, `valueOf` and
  `toJSON` are prelude functions the compiler calls for `Date` receivers (a
  class cannot declare them); `JSON.stringify` of a `Date`, `String(date)`
  and the `toLocale*String` forms stay refused.
- **Refused by name.** `Symbol()`/`Symbol.for`/`Symbol.keyFor`, `WeakMap`,
  `WeakSet`, `WeakRef`, `FinalizationRegistry`, `Proxy`, `Reflect.*`,
  `structuredClone`, `Object.freeze`/`seal`/`preventExtensions` and their
  predicates, descriptor and prototype functions, and `Intl` fail with the
  missing value-model part in the diagnostic.

#### Full RegExp (`full_regexp`)

K9 D3 (2026-11-06), under the selector `LanguageProfile::full_regexp()`: the
whole ECMAScript 2025 pattern language (§22.2) replaces the v37
[linear-time subset](#regexp-regexp) in v38. Patterns are still compiled
only ahead of time (literals and `new RegExp` with constant arguments, as in
v37); V37 keeps its subset, its program format 1, its emitted Pike VM and
its diagnostics and bytes unchanged.

- **Admitted syntax.** Everything v37 admits, plus numbered and named
  backreferences (`\1`, `\k<name>`, forward references match empty),
  lookahead and lookbehind (`(?=…)`, `(?!…)`, `(?<=…)`, `(?<!…)`; Annex B
  quantified lookahead without `u`), pattern modifiers `(?ims-ims:…)`
  (ES2025), duplicate named groups in different alternatives (ES2025
  MightBothParticipate), `\u` escapes in group names, Unicode property
  escapes `\p{…}`/`\P{…}` (`General_Category`/`gc` values and groups,
  `Script`/`sc`, `Script_Extensions`/`scx`, the binary properties of
  ECMA-262's table, `Any`, `ASCII`, `Assigned`), the `d` (`hasIndices`) and
  `v` (`unicodeSets`) flags, and under `v` the class set notation: nested
  classes, `&&`, `--`, `\q{…|…}` and the emoji properties of strings
  (`Basic_Emoji`, `Emoji_Keycap_Sequence`, `RGI_Emoji_Modifier_Sequence`,
  `RGI_Emoji_Flag_Sequence`, `RGI_Emoji_Tag_Sequence`,
  `RGI_Emoji_ZWJ_Sequence`, `RGI_Emoji`). Early errors are compile-time
  `invalid` diagnostics with V8's text (`Duplicate capture group name`,
  `Invalid named capture referenced`, `Repeated flag in flag group`,
  `Invalid property name`, `Invalid set operation in character class`,
  `Negated character class may contain strings`, …); `u` with `v` is
  `Invalid flags supplied to RegExp constructor 'uv'`. Flags print in
  `dgimsuvy` order.
- **Property data.** Code point properties come from the ICU4X 2.4 compiled
  data (`icu_properties`, already locked; strict name matching as the
  specification requires), resolved at compile time into class ranges; the
  properties of strings come from the Unicode Emoji 17.0 data
  (`regexp/emoji_sequences.txt`, from `emoji-sequences.txt` and
  `emoji-zwj-sequences.txt`). Node 24.20.0 ships ICU 78.3 with Unicode 17.0,
  and every case pinned against it agrees.
- **Programs (format 2).** The compiler (`regexp::backtrack`) emits a
  backtracking program, a static string of UTF-16 code units shared with the
  matcher through `varta_common::regexp`: a header (format version 2,
  `UNICODE`/`ANCHORED`/`PREFILTER` flags, capture and register counts, the
  code offset and an ASCII first-unit prefilter), variable-length
  instructions (`MATCH`, `CHAR`, `CHAR32`, `ANY`, `CLASS`, `JUMP`, `SPLIT`,
  `SAVE`, `RESET`, `ASSERT`, `BACKREF`, `LOOK`, `LOOK_END`, `REPEAT_INIT`,
  `REPEAT`, `ENTER`, `REPEAT_END`, `STAR`) whose consuming instructions and
  backreferences carry a backward bit inside lookbehind, and sorted class
  range tables. Offsets are single code units, so a program has at most
  65 535 units (`RegExp program larger than 65535 code units` beyond);
  counted repetitions use counters and are not expanded (`a{100000}` is
  small). Case-insensitive characters and classes are widened at compile
  time as in v37 (under `v` with `i`, operands are folded with simple case
  folding before set operations and complemented among the folded
  characters, MaybeSimpleCaseFolding); only case-insensitive
  backreferences compare by Canonicalize at run time.
- **Matcher.** `regexp_exec` is a linked intrinsic (`HostOperation::RegExpExec`,
  pure, capability-free, linked in every v38 module and imported by no
  profile, see the [linked intrinsics table](embedding.md)): the backtracking interpreter
  `varta_intrinsics::regexp`, one implementation compiled into the guest.
  It follows §22.2.2 as a continuation machine: `SPLIT` and quantifiers push
  choice points, every capture and register write is undone when matching
  backtracks past it, `REPEAT` counts iterations (RepeatMatcher: the
  minimum without choice, then greedy or lazy priority, captures cleared per
  iteration, an optional iteration that consumes nothing fails), `STAR`
  runs a quantified single character without captures without
  per-iteration state, lookarounds are atomic (a positive one keeps its
  captures and drops its choice points, a negative one undoes its body) and
  lookbehind bodies read backward with their captures recorded end first.
  Under `u` or `v` the matcher reads code points, a start inside a surrogate
  pair backs up to the pair, and the search advances by code point.
- **Work is fuel.** Matching may take time exponential in the input, as in
  every backtracking engine. Because the matcher is guest code, every step
  is metered as ordinary fuel and its backtracking stack is arena memory
  under the memory budget: a catastrophic pattern (`/^(a+)+$/` on 64 `a`s
  and `!`) ends with the turn's typed `BudgetExhausted` fuel error, the same
  on every run, instead of hanging, and an exhausted memory budget is the
  typed memory failure. Browser hosts run the same Wasm, so the official
  metered browser bundle charges matching like any guest code. Measured under the
  production budgets (`full_regexp_tests`): about 3 700 fuel of fixed work
  per run including the RegExp object (v37: about 3 000), about 33 fuel per
  skipped input unit for a search led by a literal or a class (the prefilter
  skips units without a run), and about 160 fuel per unit for `/^(a+)+$/`
  on a matching input (v37: about 1 450). Production budgets are unchanged.
- **Prelude.** V38 compiles `prelude/regexp_v38.ts` in place of the v37
  prelude (`Prelude::lifted`): `hasIndices` and `unicodeSets` reflect their
  flags; `exec`, `match` without `g`, `matchAll` and replacer match arrays
  carry `indices` (a `RegExpIndicesArray` of `[start, end]` pairs or
  `undefined`, with `groups`, when the RegExp has `d`, otherwise
  `undefined`); a groups object holds one key per name in first-group order
  whose value is the group that took part; `$<name>` substitutes the
  participating group of a shared name; AdvanceStringIndex is by code point
  under `u` or `v`. A replacer's groups parameter is the (defined) groups
  object. Match arrays and indices arrays are read like v37 match arrays
  (index, destructuring, `for…of`).
- **Deviations.** Patterns are compiled ahead of time only (a run-time
  pattern, `new RegExp(regexp)`, `RegExp(…)` without `new`, `RegExp.escape`
  and Annex B `compile` stay compile-time errors: a run-time pattern would
  need the pattern compiler in the guest); `matchAll` returns an array;
  match arrays have no array methods; `split` throws for a capture that did
  not take part (its result is `string[]`); `Symbol.match`/`matchAll`/
  `replace`/`search`/`split` protocols wait for symbol values; legacy static
  properties are not modelled. Behaviour is pinned against Node 24.20.0
  (`varta-runtime` `full_regexp_cases`, including a 600-pattern
  differential corpus) and conformance cases `regexp-*`.

#### Type level (`type_level`)

K9 track A (2026-11-06), under the selector `LanguageProfile::type_level()`:
TypeScript's type-level language, with tsc 5.x as the reference and the
[TypeScript Handbook](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/) as the
cited source. Varta monomorphizes: every type parameter is bound to a
resolved type before a type expression is lowered, so each operator below is
evaluated at compile time over resolved types and yields an existing closed
type (record, dictionary, literal set, tuple, union, function type). No host
import, value tag, value layout, frame catalog or ABI changes; nothing generic
or deferred reaches emission. V1–v37 keep rejecting every form below with
their earlier diagnostics. A construct without a sound static layout is
refused with an `unsupported …` diagnostic that names it (list below).

- **Conditional types** `C extends E ? T : F` ([Conditional
  Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/conditional-types.html)):
  the check type is resolved, so only the selected branch is evaluated. A
  naked type parameter bound to a union distributes over its members (the
  values of a literal set and `true | false` of `boolean` included); `never`
  yields `never`; `[T] extends [U]` does not distribute. `infer X` and
  `infer X extends C` bind the matched part of the check type in array,
  `Array`/`ReadonlyArray`, `Promise`/`PromiseLike`, tuple (one rest position,
  `[infer H, ...infer R]`, `[...infer I, infer L]`), function and construct
  (`(...args: infer P) => infer R`; parameters contravariant, `never[]`
  accepts every list), object (`{ k: infer V }`) and template literal
  patterns; two candidates of one name join into a union. The assignability
  relation of the condition, of generic constraints and of predicates is
  TypeScript's over closed types: unions distribute on the source, literal
  sets are subsets of their base, tuples and arrays are covariant, object
  types are structural with width subtyping and optional properties, a record
  is assignable to a string index signature when every property is, function
  types are contravariant in parameters and covariant in their result, `{}`
  admits every non-nullish value and `object` the object kinds.
- **Recursive aliases.** A generic alias may refer to itself with other type
  arguments (`type Reverse<T> = T extends [infer H, ...infer R] ?
  [...Reverse<R>, H] : []`), up to `type_level::MAX_TYPE_DEPTH` (64) nested
  instantiations and evaluations; the same instantiation inside itself, and
  non-generic cycles, keep the earlier rules.
- **Mapped types** `{ [K in C as N]: V }` with `+/-readonly` and `+/-?`
  ([Mapped Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/mapped-types.html)):
  the key set must resolve to string or number literals (a closed record) or
  to `string` (a dictionary); `K` is bound to each key's singleton literal.
  Over `keyof T` the mapped type is homomorphic: it keeps each property's
  optionality, maps a tuple element-wise (`K` is `"0"`, `"1"`, …) and an
  array element-wise, distributes over a union bound to a naked `T` and maps
  a primitive to itself. `?`/`+?` adds `undefined` to an optional property,
  `-?` removes it; `readonly` modifiers are accepted and, like `Readonly<T>`,
  binding-level intent (the closed type is the same). An `as` clause renames
  or (`never`) drops keys; keys renamed onto one name union their values.
- **Template literal types** and `Uppercase`/`Lowercase`/`Capitalize`/
  `Uncapitalize` ([Template Literal
  Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/template-literal-types.html)):
  placeholders of string, number (ECMAScript `Number::toString`), boolean,
  `null` and `undefined` literal sets expand to the string literal set of
  every combination, at most `literals::MAX_LITERAL_MEMBERS`. The intrinsic
  types map each member with JavaScript's `toUpperCase`/`toLowerCase` (the
  first code unit for (Un)capitalize). As an `extends` pattern a template
  matches string literals: a placeholder followed by text takes the text up
  to its first occurrence, one followed by another placeholder one code unit,
  the last the rest; `${string}` matches any text, `${number}` round-tripping
  numeric text, and `infer N extends number` converts such text to its number
  literal (TypeScript 4.8).
- **Utility types** ([Utility
  Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/utility-types.html)):
  `Partial`, `Required`, `Readonly`, `Pick`, `Omit`, `Record`, `Exclude`,
  `Extract`, `NonNullable`, `ReturnType`, `Parameters` (optional parameters
  are optional elements, a rest parameter the rest element),
  `ConstructorParameters`, `InstanceType`, `ThisParameterType`,
  `OmitThisParameter`, `Awaited`, `NoInfer` and the intrinsic string types,
  each evaluated as its `lib.es5.d.ts` definition would be; `Partial` and
  `Required` distribute over unions and apply to tuples and arrays. A module
  declaration of the same name shadows the built-in.
- **`keyof` and indexed access.** `keyof` of a record is its key literal set
  (`never` when empty), of a dictionary `string | number`, of a union the
  keys every member has, of `unknown` `never`. `T[K]` distributes over both
  members: record properties, class data fields, tuple positions (`"0"` or
  `0`), `T[number]` of tuples and arrays, `["length"]` of a tuple (the number
  literal set of its admitted lengths), dictionary values and string
  `length`/indexes. A computed read `obj[k]` whose key has a string literal
  type of the record's fields has the precise type `T[K]` (the union of
  those fields' types, read through a checked narrowing).
- **Type queries.** `typeof x` gives module values a type-level identity: a
  module constant is typed by its annotation or by TypeScript's declaration
  type of its initializer (a `const` primitive literal keeps its literal
  type; object and array literals widen theirs; `as const` keeps every
  literal and makes readonly tuples; `as T` is `T`; a call of a module
  function its result); a function by its signature; a class by its
  constructor type. `typeof a.b` indexes the result, and queries follow value
  imports.
- **Intersections** ([Intersection
  Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html#intersection-types)):
  object types merge their properties (a property in both intersects its
  types; it is optional only if optional in both), literal sets intersect
  their base, disjoint primitives give `never`, `unknown` is the identity, a
  union distributes, and a type assignable to the other is the result.
- **Call and construct signatures, constructor types.** An object type or
  interface whose only member is one call signature is that function type;
  one construct signature, `new (…) => T` and `abstract new (…) => T` are a
  construct type: a function type marked `construct` (`FunctionType::construct`),
  physically the closure that constructs. A class named where a construct
  type is expected (an annotated binding, an argument, `typeof C`, a generic
  argument inferring from `typeof C`) becomes `(a0, …) => new C(a0, …)`;
  only `new c(…)` invokes such a value (calling it is a type error).
- **Tuples.** Named members, optional elements (`[name: string, age?:
  number]`), one trailing rest element (`[number, ...number[]]`, stored in
  `TupleType::rest`), the empty tuple `[]` (physically an empty array) and
  variadic spreads of resolved tuples and arrays (`[...A, ...B]`), which
  flatten at compile time.
- **Type predicates and assertion functions.** A top-level or generic
  function returning `x is T` returns `boolean`; `asserts x is T` and
  `asserts x` return `void`. A call used as a condition narrows the argument
  binding in each branch (union members assignable to `T` and the others;
  a primitive `T` for `unknown`); an assertion call statement narrows it for
  the rest of the block. TypeScript trusts a predicate's body; Varta reads a
  predicate-narrowed binding holding a reference member through a run-time
  member test that throws `TypeError` when the value holds another member,
  so a lying predicate cannot confuse layouts.
- **`satisfies`** (TypeScript 4.9): the expression keeps its own type when
  that type is assignable to the target; otherwise the target is its
  contextual type (literal properties, function literal parameters) and the
  expression takes it. A failure is a type error naming both types.
- **Polymorphic `this`.** `this` in a class method's signature is the class;
  a method returning `this` has the receiver's class at each call (also in
  call chains), and every return in its body must be `this`.
- **`never` exhaustiveness.** Excluding the last value of a literal set
  narrows to `never`, so a `default` clause or final `else` can assign the
  discriminant to `never`.
- **Literal inference** ([Literal
  Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html#literal-types)):
  an unannotated `const` initialized by a string, number or boolean literal
  has that literal type (a widening literal type); a `let`/`var` initialized
  by a literal or by such a binding widens to the base primitive, while
  annotated and `as const` literal types are kept; `x as const` gives readonly
  tuples and records of literal types. The [build-time Tailwind
  scanner](#build-time-tailwind-stylesheets-k8-t1) reads these types, so
  `` `text-${size}` `` with `const size = "sm"` is enumerated without an
  annotation.

- **Step 2 admissions (2026-11-06, owner decisions).**
  - *Branded primitives*: `string & { __brand: "Id" }` (any primitive or
    literal set intersected with an object type) is the primitive; the object
    type is a phantom brand with no run-time property.
  - *`typeof` of local bindings*: a query in a function body sees the
    bindings in scope at its statement (declared or inferred types; inner
    scopes shadow module values); an annotated declaration whose annotation
    queries a local resolves when the declaration is reached. A module-level
    declaration never sees a function's locals.
  - *Overloads*: an object type or interface with several call (or several
    construct) signatures, and an intersection of function types, is an
    overloaded function type: the function type whose parameters and result
    are the unions of the overloads' (`FunctionType::overloads`). A call
    selects the first overload whose parameters accept the arguments' static
    types, checks the arguments against it and reads the result as that
    overload's result through a run-time member test. A value converts to the
    overloaded type when its own signature is the merged one (typically
    `fn as Overloaded`).
  - *Generic call signatures* (`<T>(x: T) => T`, `{ <T>(xs: T[]): T[] }`):
    the erased signature of generic method signatures; a call instantiates
    the type parameters from explicit arguments, from whole-parameter (`x: T`)
    and element (`xs: T[]`) arguments, then defaults, then `unknown`, and
    checks the result back to the instantiated type. A function literal
    lowered against the erased type takes it.
  - *`this` in object types*: in an interface or object type alias, `this` is
    the declared type itself (through the recursive-type reservation); a
    generic declaration's `this` stays refused.
  - *`keyof` and mapped types over every closed type*: a class instance's
    public fields, getters and methods (methods as function types without a
    receiver; `C["m"]` is that type, and `Partial<C>`/`Pick<C, K>`/mapped
    types map them); an array's and tuple's `number`, positions and
    `Array.prototype` string keys; a primitive's prototype string keys
    (`number` for strings). Symbol-keyed members have no key type here.
  - *Pattern template literal types* (`` `on${string}` ``, `` `${number}px` ``,
    `` `id-${bigint}` ``) and the intrinsic string types over `string`
    (`Uppercase<string>`, and over a pattern: `` Uppercase<`on${string}`> ``
    is `` `ON${Uppercase<string>}` ``) are checked as in tsc (step 3,
    2026-11-06). A pattern is a member of a string literal set
    (`LiteralValue::Pattern`), physically a string like every literal type.
    A string literal is assignable to it when it matches (TypeScript's
    inference from a literal to a template: a placeholder followed by text
    takes the text up to that text's first occurrence, the last one the
    rest; `${number}` takes a non-empty text whose ECMAScript `ToNumber` is
    finite, `${bigint}` a bigint literal's text, `${Uppercase<string>}` a
    text the mapping leaves unchanged); a pattern is assignable to another
    when every string it describes matches the other; `string` is
    assignable to none. A template literal expression where a string
    literal type is expected takes the template type of its parts
    (`` `on${name}` `` with `name: string` is `` `on${string}` ``). A union
    drops the string literals its patterns match, and `` `${string}` `` is
    `string`. `Record` and mapped types over a pattern key type are string
    index signatures (their keys are not checked against the pattern), and
    `Omit` drops the keys a pattern matches. Refused by name: a checked
    assertion (`x as T`, `JSON.parse(text) as T`) to a type with a pattern,
    which has no run-time test, `Pick` with pattern keys, and an intrinsic
    type over a pattern with a `number`, `bigint` or other mapped
    placeholder.
  - *`infer`* inside a declared generic type's arguments (`Box<infer U>`: the
    declaration body with its parameters as inference positions), in a union
    pattern with one inferring member (`infer U | undefined`) and over
    optional tuple elements (`[unknown, (infer S)?]` binds the declared type).
  - *Elements after a rest element* (`[...string[], number]`,
    `TupleType::trailing`): literal positions are typed from the end, a read
    at a literal index past the leading elements has the union of the rest
    and trailing types.
  - *Narrowing*: a predicate narrows a class instance to a subclass (the read
    tests the descriptor) and `unknown` to an object type (the read is the
    checked assertion of `x as T`); `this is T` method predicates narrow the
    receiver of `x.isT()`.
  - *Class subtyping in containers*: a subclass instance is accepted wherever
    an ancestor is expected in arrays (`push`, literals, element writes),
    tuples, records, `Map`/`Set` values and unions.
- **Shared class arrays (step 3, owner decision of 2026-11-06).** An array
  whose elements are class instances, or a union of classes with `null` or
  `undefined`, converts to an array type whose element type admits every
  one of them (`B[]` and `(B | C)[]` to `A[]`, `(B | null)[]` to `(A |
  null)[]`) without a copy, as in JavaScript: both names hold one array, so
  every write through one is seen through the other. The compiler joins the
  array types that such conversions connect into components
  (`type_level::covariance`) and gives every array type of a component one
  element representation, so no element is converted: instance handles
  (the arrays of unions of classes hold the instances, boxing on read and
  unboxing on write) or, when a union of the component admits `null` or
  `undefined`, union cells (the arrays of one class box on write and unbox
  on read). Both are existing canonical array layouts (element kind Record
  or ReferenceUnion), so no value layout, value ABI or host import changes.
  TypeScript's array covariance is unsound: through the wider name an
  `A` (or `null`) may be stored that a narrower name does not admit. Every
  element read (`xs[i]`, `at`, `pop`, iteration, callbacks, destructuring,
  library methods) through an array type of a component whose element type
  does not admit every value stored through the component's other types
  tests the element (the class descriptor against the admitted classes and
  their subclasses; `null`/`undefined` against the element union) and
  throws `TypeError` (`array element is not a value of the array's element
  type`) on a mismatch, consistent with the checked predicate reads.
  Programs without such conversions keep their code. A collection whose
  key vector is an array type with a changed representation is refused by
  name.
- **Intentional deviations from Node.** (1) A type predicate that lies
  (narrows to a member the value does not hold) throws `TypeError` at the
  narrowed read (`value does not have the type its type predicate
  asserted`), consistent with the checked `as` assertions; Node continues
  with the mistyped value. (2) An element of a shared class array that the
  read's element type does not admit (an `A` stored through `A[]` and read
  through `B[]`) throws `TypeError` at the read; Node continues with the
  mistyped value.

- **Step 3 admissions (2026-11-06).** `infer` inside an intersection pattern
  (`T extends { a: infer A } & { b: infer B }`: the check type matches
  every member, sharing the bindings; a name inferred twice joins its
  candidates). `this` in a generic interface or object type alias is the
  instantiation being resolved, and a generic declaration may refer to the
  same instantiation of itself (`interface Link<T> { next: Link<T> | null
  }`): the recursive reservation is kept per type argument list. An
  `asserts this` or `asserts this is T` method narrows the receiver binding
  of its call statement for the rest of the block (a subclass narrowing
  reads through the descriptor test, `TypeError` when the method lied). An
  overload set with a rest parameter merges into one rest parameter of the
  union of every parameter type (`{ (...parts: string[]): string; (n:
  number): string }` is `(...args: (string | number)[]) => string`); the
  call selects the first overload whose parameters (rest elements
  included) accept the arguments.

Still refused, each by name: `unique symbol` (no Symbol values in this
profile; track D's Symbol values are not in this profile yet), `import("…")`
types, callable objects with properties (a call signature together with
other members: no closed layout holds a function value and fields),
overloads with a `this` parameter or type parameters, generic construct
signatures and constructor types (a monomorphized class has one layout per
instantiation, so one constructor value cannot build every instantiation),
intersections of object types whose shared property has no common type,
mapped types over `number` or symbol key sets, `keyof never`, `typeof` of a
generic function or class and of a module initializer whose type would need
lowering, and `infer` in a union with several inferring members.

#### Declarations and classes (`declaration_forms`)

Additions to v38 (2026-11-06, K9 track B) under the selector
`LanguageProfile::declaration_forms()`: TypeScript's declaration forms and
the remaining class member forms. No host import, value layout, frame
catalog, scheduler or ABI changes: every form lowers to the checked subset
before or during type checking, so the native runtime and every
JavaScript host run it unchanged. V1–v37 keep rejecting every form below
with their old diagnostics (`top-level declaration`, `abstract class`,
`function body is required`, `class setter`, `static class field`,
`function or class in a module constant initializer`, `class auto-accessor`;
`@` stays a syntax error). Generated declarations are named
`__vartaDecl$…`; program identifiers may not start with `__vartaDecl`. A
class declared under a generated name shows its own declared name at run
time (`new.target.name`, an Error subclass's `name`).

- **Enums.** `enum` and `const enum`, numeric (auto-increment from 0 or
  from the previous numeric member), string and heterogeneous. Member
  initializers are TypeScript's constant enum expressions, evaluated by
  the compiler with ECMAScript number semantics: numeric and string
  literals, no-substitution templates, references to earlier members (bare
  or qualified) and to members of other enums, parentheses, unary `+ - ~`,
  binary `+ - * / % ** << >> >>> & | ^`, string concatenation and the
  `length` of a string literal. The enum type is the union of its member
  literal types; `E.X` (and `E['X']`) is the member's literal, and the
  member type `E.X` its literal type, so enum members narrow and
  discriminate unions like literals. Assignability follows tsc 5: the
  numeric part of an enum type accepts any `number` value but a numeric
  literal only if it is a member value (it stays a literal type for
  narrowing and exhaustive `switch`; an out-of-domain value read from a
  `number` falls to `default`), and the string part is nominal: only the
  enum's members (`E.X`, `'x' as E`) are assignable, never a bare string
  literal (`lower::literals::LiteralKind`). An unannotated `let`/`var`, parameter
  default or mutable class field initialized with a member gets the enum
  type, as TypeScript widens it. The reverse mapping `E[k]` of a non-const
  enum with numeric members is the member name for a constant key, and
  otherwise a call of a generated function typed
  `(value: number) => string | undefined` that returns the name of the last
  member with that value or `undefined`. TypeScript types it `string`; this
  is the intended deviation (owner decision, 2026-11-06): it equals tsc
  under `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` and keeps a missing key honest. Refused
  by name: a
  computed member whose initializer is not a constant expression, a
  non-finite member value, merged enum declarations, a string member
  followed by an uninitialized one (TS1061), a dynamic key of a const enum
  (TS2476), `declare enum`, and a const enum used as a value (TS2475).
  A non-const enum used as a value (`Object.keys(E)`, `f(E)`, `typeof E`,
  `keyof typeof E`) is its enum object: a generated module constant with
  JavaScript's own keys and order (array-index reverse keys ascending, then
  member names and other reverse keys in creation order), unread ones
  pruned; a string-keyed `E[k]` reads it. An enum with a non-integer member
  value has no object.
- **Namespaces.** `namespace N { … }`, nested and dotted (`namespace
  A.B.C`), exported or not. Every member is hoisted to a module declaration
  under a generated name and every reference to it, unqualified inside the
  namespace or qualified (`N.x`, `N.Inner.f()`, the type `N.T`,
  `implements N.I`, `typeof N.x`), becomes that name; a local binding that
  shadows a member is never rewritten. Members are functions (with
  overloads), classes, `const`/`let` variables (module constants and
  variables with their initializer rules), interfaces, type aliases, enums
  and namespaces. Declaration merging follows TypeScript: namespaces merge
  with namespaces (exported members are visible unqualified in every
  declaration; unexported ones only in their own), and with a function,
  class or enum of the same name (`f.helper`, `C.create()`, `E.parse()`);
  interfaces merge with interfaces. An exported namespace or enum is used
  from other modules through its generated declarations, also under an
  import alias and through re-exports (`export { E } from`, `export *`,
  `export { E }` of an import); generated names carry a hash of their
  module path (`__vartaDecl$m<hash>$…`), so two modules' declarations never
  collide. A namespace without a value of its own used as a value (or in
  `typeof`) is its namespace object, a generated module constant after its
  last declaration whose properties are its exported functions, constants,
  enum objects and nested namespace objects in declaration order, typed
  member by member; a namespace with a class or `let` member, or a constant
  without an annotation or literal initializer, has none (`namespace object
  … used as a value`). Refused by name: statements in a namespace body, ambient
  namespaces and modules, an
  unexported member reached qualified (`namespace N has no exported member
  …`), a type-only import of a namespace, and import aliases
  (`import x = N.y`).
- **Abstract classes.** `abstract class` with abstract methods, getters
  and fields. An abstract class cannot be constructed (TS2511), a concrete
  descendant must implement every inherited abstract member (TS2515),
  `super.m()` of an abstract method is refused (TS2513), and abstract
  members appear only in abstract classes (TS1244). An abstract method's
  slot dispatches to the overriding implementations like any overridden
  method (its own body throws and is unreachable); an abstract field is a
  declared slot that the concrete descendant defines, which the abstract
  class's constructor may not read.
- **Overloads.** Function, method, static method and constructor overload
  signatures (`function f(x: string): string;` before the implementation).
  A call resolves to the first signature in declaration order whose arity
  admits the arguments and whose parameters accept them (a literal
  argument, including an enum member, has its literal type); no match is
  TS2769. The implementation signature is hidden: the arguments are bound
  to it, and its result is checked against the selected signature's result
  type, free for an upcast and otherwise tested like `x as T` (a
  `TypeError` if the implementation returns a value its overload does not
  admit). Signatures need return annotations and must be compatible with the
  implementation (TS2394); they precede it directly with the same export
  state (TS2391, TS2383). Generic overloads and an overloaded function used
  as a value are refused by name.
- **Setters and accessors.** `set x(v)` with or without a `get x()`: an
  assignment `o.x = v` evaluates `o`, then `v`, calls the setter and yields
  `v`; `o.x op= v` and `o.x++` read through the getter first. Accessors are
  inherited and overridden like methods; a class that declares only one
  half of an inherited get/set pair is refused (JavaScript would drop the
  other half), as are logical assignments through accessors and compound
  updates of setter-only accessors. `accessor x = v` (an ECMAScript
  auto-accessor) is a private storage field with a get/set pair; `static
  accessor x` is a static field.
- **Static fields and static blocks.** `static x: T = v` of a class (at
  module level or in a namespace) is the module variable `__vartaDecl$C$x`
  declared right after the class, and `static { … }` is a module variable
  initialized by calling the block as an arrow, so both run in the module
  initializer sequence at the class's position, as ECMAScript evaluates
  them at class definition ([module evaluation](#module-evaluation-module_evaluation)).
  `C.x`, and `this.x` in static code, read and write the field; a subclass
  reads an inherited static field through the same variable, and writing
  it through the subclass (which creates an own property of the subclass in
  JavaScript) is refused. `private`, `protected` (TS2341) and `readonly`
  (TS2540) are checked. Another module writes an exported class's static
  field through a setter function the declaring module exports
  (`C.x = v`, `op=`, `++`/`--`); a field without an annotation or literal
  initializer has none.
- **Static methods, `this` and `super`.** In static methods, static field
  initializers and static blocks `this` is the class. A static method that
  uses `this` or `super` is copied into each module-level subclass that
  inherits it and is named through that subclass (or that is exported),
  with `this` naming the subclass, so `Derived.create()` calls
  `Derived.kind()` as in JavaScript. `super.m()` in static code calls the
  parent's `m` with the calling class as `this` (a copy of `m` in the
  calling class when `m` uses `this`), and `super.x` reads the parent's
  static field. A `this`-using static method inherited from a class of
  another module, and `super.m()` of such a method from a static field
  initializer or block, are refused by name.
- **Class expressions and local classes.** `const X = class [N] { … }` at
  module level or in a function body, and a class declaration in a function
  body, is a module class declaration (named `X`, or the class's own name
  `N`); a class in a function may not reference the function's local
  bindings (`class expression that captures the local binding …`, `local
  class that captures …`), and class expressions in any other position are
  refused.
- **Other class forms.** `override` on methods and accessors, `declare`
  field redeclarations, `implements` of several interfaces, and
  constructor parameter properties with default values (a non-literal
  default needs a type annotation).
- **Class index signatures.** `[key: string]: T` gives a class's instances
  own properties beyond their declared members: they live in a hidden
  dictionary field the constructor creates empty (inherited by
  subclasses), and a read, write, compound assignment or update of a member
  the class does not declare, by name or by a computed string key, is a
  dictionary operation on it (a missing key reads `undefined`). Every
  declared field must be of the index's value type and methods and
  accessors are refused unless it is `unknown` (TS2411). Static, readonly
  and non-string index signatures are refused by name, and `JSON.stringify`
  of such an instance is refused (JavaScript would list the extra
  properties after the fields).
- **Not admitted yet.** Standard decorators (they need classes as values
  and the decorator context objects) and generic overload signatures are
  refused by name (`decorator`, `generic overload signature`). Legacy
  `experimentalDecorators` are not planned.

#### Module evaluation (`module_evaluation`)

V38 (2026-11-06, K9 B, owner decision) evaluates modules as ECMAScript
does: each instance evaluates its module graph once, in dependency order and
in source order within a module, before `main`; an HTTP v2 request's fresh
Store is its own instance, so module code runs again for each request (as
the call-free initializers already did). Tool entries keep refusing stored
module values (`module constants with tool/HTTP entry points`). A module
initializer may call functions and construct objects (`const registry =
load()`, `static instance = new C()`, static blocks); a top-level `await`
is admitted under `expression_forms` (below). A primitive `const` whose initializer runs code is
stored like a module variable that no code may assign. Initializers that
run code are never pruned as unread (`program_limits`).

JavaScript throws `ReferenceError` when code reads a binding before its
initialization. Varta refuses such a read at compile time whenever an
effectful initializer can reach it: the reachable code is the initializer
plus, transitively, every module function, function-valued binding and
class it names (a class with its constructor, instance fields and instance
methods; a static method through `C.m`), and no binding of the module
declared at or after the initializer may be read by it (`binding used
before initialization: X is read by code this initializer runs`). The
analysis over-approximates calls (a program that only names a later
binding on a path it never takes is refused too); other modules cannot
reach this module's bindings early, since imports are acyclic and
initialized first. A module variable whose type is `undefined` or `null`
alone is refused (it has no boxed form).

**Evaluation order and top-level `await`** (2026-11-06, K9 C, owner
decision; `expression_forms`). Modules are evaluated in the order of
Evaluate() (§16.2.1.5.3): a depth-first walk from the entry module over each
module's requested modules in source order (imports and re-exports; `import
type` and `export type` declarations request nothing, as TypeScript's
`verbatimModuleSyntax` and Node's type stripping erase them), each module
after the modules it requests; compiler-owned engine preludes come first.
Imported functions may be called by initializers. A module whose
initializers `await` (outside function values) is evaluated as one async
function, its initializers in source order. Without such a module the
initializers still run in that order before `main`. With one, the
program's entry is a synthesized evaluator (guest code, no host change)
that follows InnerModuleEvaluation and the asynchronous module algorithm
exactly, the graph being acyclic: in the walk, a module that neither awaits
nor waits for an asynchronously evaluating dependency runs at once, an
awaiting one without such dependencies starts, and the others wait. When an
async module's evaluation completes (one job after its promise settles, as
the spec's reaction does), AsyncModuleExecutionFulfilled gathers the
waiting ancestors whose last pending dependency it was (through
synchronous ones) and runs or starts them in the order they became
asynchronous; a synchronous sibling therefore runs while an earlier sibling
is suspended, as in Node. A rejection marks the module and every waiting
ancestor failed (AsyncModuleExecutionRejected): none of them runs, and the
entry module's failure is an unhandled rejection, so the execution fails as
Node's does. The entry module calls `main` at the end of its own
evaluation, as `await main();` appended to it would. Refused with top-level
`await`: tool and HTTP entry points (`top-level await with tool or HTTP
entry points`); a throw of a synchronous module during the initial walk
ends the execution as an uncaught exception.

#### Console notation (`node_console`)

K9 D1 (2026-11-06). V38 prints what Node 24 prints: `console.log`,
`console.info` and `console.debug` take any number of arguments and log one
line of `util.formatWithOptions` text with the default `util.inspect`
options (depth 2, `compact: 3`, `breakLength: 80`, `maxArrayLength: 100`,
`maxStringLength: 10000`, no colors). Earlier profiles keep their notation
and their one-argument rule.

- **Lowering.** One string argument is logged as it is (`log_string16`).
  Every other call boxes each argument into an `unknown` cell, collects the
  cells in an `unknown[]` array and logs the text the linked
  `value_format_v12` returns for the array's cell. Under v38
  `value_format_v12` therefore takes the cell of the *argument list*, not of
  one value; it stays a linked intrinsic with no host import. A spread
  argument contributes its elements in source order (the array literal
  path, so its elements box as `unknown` values do), and a call of a `void`
  function logs `undefined` after the call (`console_methods`). Logging
  admits every value `unknown` holds and, for logging only, `Map` and `Set`
  values, `Date` instances and class instances with `#private` fields;
  values that may reach a URL, a RegExp match array or another builtin
  object without a Node notation stay refused (`unsupported logging of a
  value holding a URL, …`).
- **Formatting.** The linked `varta_intrinsics::inspect` follows Node's
  `lib/internal/util/inspect.js` step for step: `%s %d %i %f %j %o %O %c %%`
  directives of a leading string (`%s` inspects objects at depth 0, `%o` with
  `showHidden` at depth 4, `%j` is `JSON.stringify` with `[Circular]`),
  strings unquoted at the top level and quoted in aggregates by Node's quote
  choice and escapes, `-0`, BigInts with `n`, `true`/`false`, depth elision
  (`[Object]`, `[Array]`, `[ClassName]`), single-line output up to 80
  columns with three nesting levels, column grouping of arrays of more than
  six entries, `... n more items`, `<n empty items>`, long strings split
  after line breaks, `<ref *n>`/`[Circular *n]`, `ClassName { … }`,
  `Map(n) { k => v }`, `Set(n) { v }`, `Uint8Array(n) [ … ]`, the ISO text of
  a `Date` (`Invalid Date`), `Promise { … }` and Error objects. As in Node,
  the text has no length limit of its own: fuel, memory and the output
  budget bound it. The literal-format case uses the same linked path as a
  dynamic format string.
- **Test builds.** A build that hosts `value_format_v12`
  (`host_import_test_hook`) lowers logging as v37 does, through the host's
  `value_log_v12` renderer; the corpus comparisons with v37 and of linked
  JSON serialization use it, and `console_tests` pins the linked notation
  against Node.
- **Errors.** Varta records no stack frames, so an Error prints as Node
  prints it under `--stack-trace-limit=0`: `[Name: message]` (`[Name]` for
  an empty message), the constructor named by `improveStack`
  (`[Plain [Error]: m]`), then its own enumerable fields, `[cause]` and
  `AggregateError`'s `[errors]`. A cause that is `undefined` is not shown
  (an instance does not record whether its options had one).
- **`SuppressedError`** (owner decision 2026-11-06; ECMA-262 2026
  §20.5.8, explicit resource management). The engine prelude
  `<varta>/builtins/suppressed.ts` (`modules::engine::SUPPRESSED`, admitted
  by `node_console()`) declares `class SuppressedError extends Error` with
  the constructor `(error: unknown, suppressed: unknown, message?: string)`:
  `name` is `"SuppressedError"`, `error` and `suppressed` hold the given
  values as `unknown`, an `undefined` message leaves no own message and
  there is no options argument. It is an Error class like `AggregateError`
  (prototype chain to `Error`, `instanceof`, catch narrowing, the exception
  channel); its fields are not own enumerable properties to `JSON.stringify`
  or the console notation, which prints `[SuppressedError: message]` as
  Node 24 does. `typeof SuppressedError` is `"function"`; v37 does not know
  the name. Track K9 C throws it from `using`/`await using` when a disposal
  throws after the body threw.
- **Record display trailers (value layout 18).** Every value18 record
  descriptor ends, after its entries and a wide record's edge bitmap, with
  a display trailer: a kind word (`value::RecordDisplay`: 0 object, 1
  class, 2 Error class, 3 `AggregateError`, 4 `Map` storage, 5 `Set`
  storage, 6 `Date`), a name length word and the UTF-8 name (none for an
  object; at most 256 bytes otherwise; a generic class instance carries its
  template's name). `value::record_display` validates it inside the static
  region. Readers that do not display records read the descriptor prefix
  (`value::descriptor_bytes`) unchanged; earlier layouts have no trailer.
  This is the only layout change of the stream; it adds no value tag.
- **Deviations from Node** (documented, not silent): functions carry no
  name or source text, so every function prints `[Function (anonymous)]`
  and `%s` of a function prints the same; `%s`, `%d`, `%i` and `%f` never
  call program code (a class's own `toString`/`valueOf` is not used; objects
  convert as `[object Object]`, arrays by their elements, a `Date` by its
  time value); `%o` of a function or a typed array shows no hidden
  properties; the column width of non-ASCII entries uses Node's non-ICU
  width tables instead of ICU's; `%j` of a value holding a BigInt ends the
  execution with the serializer's failure where Node throws. Standard error
  and the rest of Node's console: [console methods](#console-methods-console_methods).

#### Console methods (`console_methods`)

K9 D1, owner decision 2026-11-06. V38 has the whole Node 24 console of
`lib/internal/console/constructor.js`, printed as Node prints it; earlier
profiles keep refusing every method but `log`.

- **Standard error (host ABI 34, additive).** `log_stderr16(level, ptr,
  len)` (`HostOperation::LogStderr16`) writes one standard-error line of
  the UTF-16 text at `ptr`/`len`. The level word
  (`console::StderrLevel`: 0 `error`, 1 `warn`) names the console method
  that wrote it; any other word traps before the text is read. It is
  capability-free and bounded like `log_string16`: the module's string limit,
  one host call, fair fuel per byte and the shared output budget. The native
  runtime records the line in the execution's ordered output with the
  level's prefix (`varta error: `, `varta warn: `; standard output keeps
  `varta log: `), so a host routes a line by its prefix alone
  (`console::is_standard_error`); `varta` and `varta-runtime` print those
  lines to standard error. The official browser host's worker implements
  the same import, and its loader only forwards each standard-error line to
  the page's `console.error` or `console.warn` (the registry's `console`
  section names prefixes and methods); the line stays in the ordered output.
  Validation admits the import only under host ABI 34 profiles.
- **Methods.** `console.error` and `console.warn` format as `console.log`
  does and write standard error at their level; `console.dirxml` is
  `console.log`. The other methods live in the engine prelude
  `<varta>/builtins/console.ts` (`modules::engine::CONSOLE`), which a
  program loads by naming one of them: `trace` (the stack of a `Trace`
  error without frames: `Trace: message`, or `Trace`), `assert` (a falsy
  condition writes `Assertion failed[: first string]` and the remaining
  arguments through `warn`), `group`/`groupCollapsed`/`groupEnd` (two
  spaces of indentation before every line, standard error included, as
  `kWriteToConsole` indents), `count`/`countReset`, `time`/`timeEnd`/
  `timeLog` (`formatTime` of `internal/util/debuglog`), `dir` and `table`.
  A program that loads the prelude writes every console call through its
  `consoleWrite`, so the indentation applies to all of them; a program
  that names none of these methods writes directly and keeps its bytes.
- **`dir` and `table`.** The linked intrinsic `console_render(mode, cell)`
  (`HostOperation::ConsoleRender`, `console::RenderMode`, never imported)
  renders the request array the prelude builds:
  `util.inspect(value, options)` for `dir` with `depth` (`null` unbounded),
  `showHidden`, `breakLength`, `compact` (a number, `false` or `true`),
  `maxArrayLength`, `maxStringLength`, `sorted` (`true`) and
  `numericSeparator`, and `Console.prototype.table` with
  `internal/cli_table` for `table` (index, column and `Values` columns,
  `Map` and `Set` iteration tables, `properties` filters, cells inspected
  at depth 0 or `-1` with `maxArrayLength` 3 and no line breaking, column
  widths by `getStringWidth`). A primitive or a function given to `table`
  is logged as `console.log` logs it.
- **Clock.** `time`, `timeEnd` and `timeLog` read the `time.now` clock of
  `Date.now` (its grant decides; a denial reports itself as `Date.now`
  does). Durations therefore have whole milliseconds.
- **Deviations from Node** (documented, not silent): Node writes its process
  warnings (`countReset` of an unknown label, a repeated `time` label, an
  unknown `timeEnd`/`timeLog` label) asynchronously as `(node:PID) Warning:
  …` with a one-time `--trace-warnings` hint; Varta writes them at once as
  one `Warning: …` line on standard error (`warn` level, outside the group
  indentation). Timer durations come from the millisecond `time.now` clock,
  not a monotonic high-resolution one. `dir` ignores `colors`,
  `customInspect`, `getters` and `showProxy` (no ANSI colors, no custom
  inspection or accessor properties exist) and admits only `sorted: true`
  (a comparator function is a type error of its typed options).

#### Bytes held by unknown (`byte_values`)

Wave 3 of v38, selector `LanguageProfile::byte_values()` (owner decision of
2026-11-05, replacing the earlier refusal): a `Uint8Array` carries a value
tag of its own, so `unknown` holds one and every value reader serializes
or refuses it by name. No host import or budget changes; v37 and earlier
keep value layout 17, which has no byte-array tag, and their diagnostics
(`sdk_path_forms_stay_refused_by_v37`). Owner decision (2026-11-05): the
value ABI number stays 18, and `ValueKind::Bytes` (tag 15) is an additive
tag of the in-development value layout 18, not a step to a new value ABI.

- **Tag and layout.** `value::ValueKind::Bytes` is an additive tag of the
  in-development value layout 18 (`value::bytes_layout`): only value18
  readers accept it, every other value18 tag keeps its meaning, and value17
  and earlier readers reject it. The value ABI number stays 18 (v38 is in
  development; an artifact built before the tag never contains it, and a
  reader built before it fails on it as noncanonical). The payload of a
  Bytes kind (in a union or `unknown` cell, a record or class field, an
  array element or a dictionary value) is the handle of the `Uint8Array`'s
  byte storage: a canonical value18 vector of Numbers whose every element is
  present and an integer from 0 to 255 (`value::byte_vector`, which checks
  every element with `value::byte_at`; a hole, a fraction, 256, `-0` or NaN
  is a noncanonical layout). It is a reference kind, so a cell holding it
  has the reference flag. The browser registry lists it among each v38
  profile's `supportedKinds` and the layout's `tags`.
- **Compilation.** The compiler erases a `Uint8Array` type to an array type
  of its own (`ValueTypes::bytes`), physically the byte storage's `number[]`,
  so every tag it writes for one (cell tags, descriptor field kinds, vector
  element kinds, the kind word of `JSON.stringify` and `kv_stage`) is Bytes,
  while the binary prelude keeps operating on the storage. Unions keep the
  wave-2 rule: a `Uint8Array` shares no union with another array type.
- **`unknown` and `object`.** Both hold a `Uint8Array` and every value that
  reaches one without a `Map`, `Set` or opaque builtin, without copying:
  writes through either reference are seen through the other. The identity
  of a `Uint8Array` is its byte storage, which every view of one
  `ArrayBuffer` shares (`new Uint8Array(buffer)` twice), so two such views
  would compare equal where JavaScript tells them apart. Identity
  comparisons of two values that may both hold a `Uint8Array` (a
  `Uint8Array`, `unknown`, `object` or a union with such a member, in a
  program with the binary prelude) are refused at compile time with
  `unsupported <operation> of two values that may both hold a Uint8Array`:
  `===`, `!==` (also as `switch` case tests), `Object.is` and the
  `includes`/`indexOf`/`lastIndexOf` searches of an array whose elements may
  hold one (`lower::byte_values::refuse_view_identity`). A comparison with a
  value that cannot hold one (a primitive, a record) is admitted and
  answers as Node does. `typeof` is `"object"`, the value is truthy and
  `Array.isArray` is false. `x instanceof Uint8Array` and
  `ArrayBuffer.isView(x)` test the tag, and the positive branch narrows
  `x` to `Uint8Array`; a checked `x as Uint8Array`, and `x as` a union with a
  `Uint8Array` member (such as `BlobPart`), tests it too. `String(x)` joins
  the elements with commas, as `Uint8Array.prototype.toString` does.
- **Readers.** `JSON.stringify` (the linked `json_stringify_owned` and the
  runtime's value18 encoder) writes a `Uint8Array` as an object of its index
  keys, `{"0":1,"1":255}`, and `{}` when it is empty, as Node does; an
  `ArrayBuffer` instance is `{}` (its storage is private state). The logged
  text of a cell holding one (`value_format_v12`) uses the same notation.
  Typed `JSON.stringify` of a `Uint8Array`, or of a value reaching one, is
  admitted; logging a typed `Uint8Array` stays `cannot log Uint8Array`, like
  any typed array, while a union that may hold one logs through its cell.
  `kv_stage` refuses a tagged `Uint8Array` (held by `unknown` or nested in
  another value) with the recoverable `TypeError("a Uint8Array held by
  unknown or nested in another value cannot be stored in a KV value")`; a
  top-level `Uint8Array` keeps its raw-byte staging. A thrown `unknown`
  holding one fails the v34 thrown-value check; a thrown Error instance with
  a field holding one is read as before (the exception channel copies only
  its `name` and `message`).
- **Checked JSON decoding.** JSON never produces a `Uint8Array`, and a
  decoder would tag a JSON number array (of any numbers) as one, so a
  checked decode target that reaches a `Uint8Array` (through fields,
  elements, dictionary values, the declared fields of mixed records or
  union members) is refused at compile time with `unsupported checked JSON
  decode target: … reaching a Uint8Array`: `JSON.parse(text) as T` (the
  checked and the direct decoder) and `varta.json.parse<T>`. KV reads keep
  their own rule: keys decode at the prelude's fixed `KvKey`, a top-level
  `Uint8Array` value is stored as raw bytes, and a nested one, including
  one in a mixed record's declared field, is refused by `kv_checked`. `Response.json()` returns
  `Promise<unknown>`, a JSON graph that never holds a `Uint8Array`, so a
  later checked `as T` reaching one throws its `type assertion to T failed`
  `TypeError` unless the bytes field is absent. V37 keeps its targets.
- **JSON-object view.** A closed record held by `unknown`, read as
  `Record<string, unknown>` (`as`, `Object.keys`/`values`/`entries`,
  checked conversions), lists its present fields in its own-key order
  (canonical array indices ascending, then insertion order, as
  `Object.entries` does; the wave-1 view used the canonical field order)
  and a `Uint8Array` field as an `unknown` cell holding it (wave 2 threw a
  `TypeError`). A `Uint8Array`, an array or a class instance (an
  `ArrayBuffer`, `Blob`, `File` or any other) held by `unknown` still has no
  JSON-object view: the conversion throws its `TypeError` (`type assertion to
  … failed`, `object held by unknown is not a Record<string, unknown>
  dictionary`, `a class instance held by unknown cannot be read as a JSON
  object`), because reads through a snapshot dictionary would miss the
  object's prototype members.
- **`in`.** `"key" in (x as Record<string, unknown>)` of an `unknown` or
  `object` value and `"key" in x` of a value narrowed to `object`, with a
  string literal key, answer from the cell as Node 24.20.0 does: for a
  `Uint8Array`, true for a canonical array index below its length and for a
  string member of `Uint8Array.prototype`, `%TypedArray%.prototype` or
  `Object.prototype`, false for any other key; for an exact `ArrayBuffer`,
  `Blob` or `File` instance (a program's subclass is not matched), true for
  a string member of its prototype chain (none has an own enumerable
  property). The member lists (`lower::byte_values`) are Node's
  `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` along each chain, pinned by
  `sdk_path_cases/byte_in.ts`. Any other value, and a key that is no string
  literal, takes the JSON-object view and its `TypeError`.
- **SDK multipart parts.** The SDK's own `encodeBody`/`appendPart`/
  `toBodyInit` (`multipart?: object` read through
  `Object.entries(… as Record<string, unknown>)`, then `'data' in`,
  `instanceof ArrayBuffer`, `ArrayBuffer.isView` and `as BlobPart` on
  `unknown`) produce Node's wire bytes, part order included, for
  `Uint8Array`, `ArrayBuffer`, `string`, `Blob`/`File` and `{ data,
  filename, contentType }` parts (`sdk_path_cases/byte_parts.ts`).
- **Not admitted.** Own-key enumeration of a `Uint8Array`, an array or an
  engine instance held by `unknown`, and `in` with a key that is no string
  literal on one (the JSON-object view's `TypeError`; Node enumerates and
  answers); `'data' in` an array part of `appendPart` (a `TypeError`, where
  Node answers false); a `Uint8Array` with another array type in one union;
  logging a typed `Uint8Array`; a tagged `Uint8Array` in a KV value;
  identity comparisons of two values that may both hold a `Uint8Array`;
  checked JSON decode targets that reach a `Uint8Array`.

#### Virtual file roots (`file_roots`)

Under v38 a guest never sees or names a host path. Every `fs.read`/`fs.print`
path and every `fs.*` grant pattern is a **virtual path** `/<root>/...` whose
first component names a root; the host maps each root to a directory it pins
once, before any guest code runs. The same package then runs unchanged on any
host layout (desktop, a Raspberry Pi, a browser host). No host import, value
layout or ABI changes: the guest calls the same `fs_read16`/`fs_print16`, and
the manifest and host-policy schemas gain one member under host ABI 34
([Filesystem](#filesystem) has the rules). V1–v37 keep absolute host paths
with their exact behaviour; the runtime chooses the mode from the module's
declared profile (`LanguageProfile::file_roots`), never from the manifest.
The values of the `files::MAX_*` bounds are in the embedding contract's
[manifest limits](embedding.md#manifest-limits).

- **Roots and names.** A root name is 1 to `files::MAX_ROOT_NAME_BYTES` bytes of
  lowercase ASCII letters, digits, `-` and `_`, starting with a letter, and
  compares exactly. At most `files::MAX_FILE_ROOTS` roots appear in a
  configuration, manifest or host policy; a duplicate is an error, including
  a repeated JSON object key.
- **Project configuration.** `"fs": {"roots": {"project": "."}}` maps each
  name to a directory inside the configuration directory: a relative
  `/`-separated path of ordinary components (no empty, `.` or `..` component,
  no `\`), or `.` for the directory itself. It requires
  `checked-f64-utf16-v38`. `check`, `dev` and `build` open every root when the
  project loads, from the configuration directory with no-follow at every
  component (a symlinked root is an error); `varta dev` reads under those
  descriptors. Every v38 `fs.*` pattern must start with `/<declared root>`,
  with a literal root component (`/proj*/x` and `/**` are rejected).
- **Package manifest.** The build writes only the names:
  `"fsRoots": ["project"]` (requires `abiVersion` 34; a manifest of an earlier
  host ABI that carries `fsRoots` is rejected). A package never maps a root to
  a directory: an `fsRoots` object in a package manifest is rejected, and so
  is, under host ABI 34, an `fs.*` pattern outside a declared root.
- **Host policy.** The host maps names to absolute host directories:
  `"fsRoots": {"project": "/srv/app/data"}` (requires `abiVersion` 34; each
  directory absolute, at most `files::MAX_PATH_BYTES` bytes, no `..` component
  and no control character). A host policy that lists names instead is
  rejected. For `run`, the companion, a packaged application and `invoke`, the
  host policy is the only mapping: each root the package declares and the host
  maps is opened once at startup (a mapped directory that cannot be opened is
  an error before any guest code runs); a declared root the host does not map
  stays absent and denies every path under it, and a mapping for a root the
  package does not declare is ignored. Without a host policy no root is
  mapped. `varta dev --policy` uses the policy's mapping when it has one and
  the configuration's roots otherwise.
- **Paths.** A guest path is accepted only in canonical form: at most
  `files::MAX_PATH_BYTES` bytes, starting with `/`, a valid root name, then
  ordinary components (no empty, `.` or `..` component, so no doubled or
  trailing `/`), no NUL, control character or `\`. Anything else, including
  every absolute host path that does not happen to start with a declared and
  mapped root name, is a denial.
- **Matching.** A pattern's literal directory prefix must be a whole-component
  prefix of the path (`/project/**` never matches `/project-x/a` or
  `/project` itself) and the rest is matched by the component-aware glob
  (`*` within one component, `**` across components, `?` one non-separator
  character). The operation id is exact. The package request and, when
  supplied, the host ceiling must each have a matching pattern for that id,
  and the root must be mapped; all of this is decided before anything is
  opened. A ceiling never adds a pattern or an operation.
- **Opening.** The path's components below the root are opened from the
  root's pinned descriptor with no-follow at every component; a symlink below
  the root (to a file or directory, inside or outside the root) fails with the
  I/O status, as do directories and other non-regular files. Reads are capped
  as for every profile.
- **Review.** `inspect` reports the manifest's `fsRoots`; the authorization
  review lists each declared root as `mapped` or `denied` under a host policy
  and `declared` without one. The permission broker's `fs.*` descriptors
  ([broker v1](#permission-broker-v1-turn_budgets)) use the same virtual
  matching.
- **Embedding.** A third-party host builds `RunOptions::file_roots` from
  `FileRoots::open` (a trusted absolute host directory) or `FileRoots::insert`
  (a directory handle it opened itself), or from the manifests with
  `FileRoots::from_manifests`; `invoke_tool_with_roots` does the same for tool
  invocation. The older grant-only entry points run a v38 module with no
  roots, so every `fs.*` path is denied.

#### KV storage (`kv`)

Selector `kv()`. V38 opens **Deno KV database files** and reads and writes
them through Deno KV's own SQLite backend (`denokv_sqlite` 0.14.0 with
`denokv_proto` 0.14.0, rusqlite 0.40.1 over libsqlite3-sys 0.38.1 with the
bundled SQLite, exactly the versions Deno 2.9.4 and 2.9.7 lock), so the same
file serves a Deno program and a Varta program without a migration, in both
directions. The guest API is Deno-shaped (`varta.kv.open`, `Kv`,
`AtomicOperation`, `KvListIterator`, `KvU64`); every operation is checked by
the exact `kv.read`/`kv.write` grants before any effect and decodes strictly
into the static type the program names. V37 and earlier profiles reject
`varta.kv.open` as an unknown name and cannot import the `kv_*` operations
(minimum host ABI 34).

- **Grants.** Two path-scoped operation ids over virtual paths
  (`GrantKind::Patterns`, the [virtual file roots](#virtual-file-roots-file_roots)
  rules and roots): `kv.read` opens a database and reads from it, `kv.write`
  writes to it. Project form `"capabilities": {"kv": {"read":
  ["/data/*.kv"], "write": ["/data/app.kv"]}}`; manifest form `{"id":
  "kv.read", "patterns": [...]}`. Both require `abiVersion` 34 (a manifest of
  an earlier host ABI with a `kv.*` grant is rejected) and, in a package,
  patterns under a declared root. Opening needs `kv.read` on the path; the
  database is opened read-write only when `kv.write` also covers it (in the
  request and the ceiling), and read-only otherwise. A missing file is created
  only for a writable open; opened read-only it is a `NotFoundError`. Every read
  checks `kv.read` and every commit `kv.write` again through the
  [permission broker](#permission-broker-v1-turn_budgets), which audits each
  decision. Operations are exact: a `kv.write` grant never opens, and a
  `kv.read` grant never writes. Denials are recoverable: the operation rejects
  with a `NotAllowedError` `DOMException` (`<capability denied: kv.read>
  (/data/app.kv)`), logged like other denials.
- **Pinning.** SQLite opens files by path, never by descriptor, so the file is
  pinned and the path verified in this order before SQLite writes anything:
  every directory below the root is opened from the root's pinned descriptor
  with no-follow, then the file itself no-follow (created exclusively when
  missing and writable); its device and inode are the database's identity and
  the descriptor stays open while the database is. The host path is the root's
  host directory (`FileRoots::open`, `FileRoots::insert_at` or the project
  configuration; a root inserted without a directory cannot hold a database),
  canonicalized and checked to be the pinned root directory, joined with the
  components, and its no-follow metadata must name the pinned file. SQLite then
  opens it with `SQLITE_OPEN_NOFOLLOW` (a symbolic link in any component fails)
  and without `SQLITE_OPEN_CREATE`. After the schema check, the process's open
  descriptors (`/dev/fd`, `/proc/self/fd` on Linux, read with `stat` only, since
  closing any descriptor of a file drops the process's POSIX locks on it) must
  show a new descriptor of the pinned file for each SQLite connection (the
  worker's, and the lock probe of a writable database): a swap of the path between the
  check and SQLite's open makes SQLite open another file, which this rejects
  (`the KV database … changed while it was opened`). KV opens are serialized in
  the process. SQLite opens the `-wal` and `-shm` files beside the verified
  file by name with `O_NOFOLLOW`; a process that can rename directories inside
  the host root already controls the database and is outside the check. KV
  storage needs a Unix host.
- **Schema.** An empty file is a new database (writable opens only):
  `denokv_sqlite` creates its schema exactly as Deno does. Any other file must
  have exactly the tables `data_version`, `kv`, `migration_state`, `queue` and
  `queue_running` (`kv::SCHEMA_TABLES`), `migration_state` version 3
  (`kv::SCHEMA_VERSION`) and the `kv` columns `k, v, v_encoding, version, seq,
  expiration_ms`, checked in a read transaction before anything is written;
  another file (an older or newer schema, another SQLite database, a non-SQLite
  file) fails with a `TypeError` and is left unchanged. A writable open then
  sets WAL mode as Deno does.
- **Locking.** Varta takes SQLite's own locks, as Deno does (WAL mode,
  POSIX advisory locks), so a Deno process and a Varta process may share a
  file. A writable open probes the write lock without waiting (`BEGIN
  IMMEDIATE`); a file another writer holds fails with `TypeError: the KV
  database … is locked by another writer`.
- **Commits fail fast and never outlive their turn.** No guest write commits
  after its turn has ended or after the guest was told it failed:
  - A commit first probes the write lock on a second connection to the
    verified file, waiting at most `kv::LOCK_WAIT_MS` and never past the
    cutoff (the worker's own expiry collection holds it for a moment); a
    lock another connection or process holds fails then with `TypeError: … is locked by another writer;
    nothing was applied`, before anything is submitted.
  - The **commit cutoff** is `kv::COMMIT_RESERVE_MS` before the turn
    deadline. A commit started later fails at once with a `TypeError` and
    applies nothing.
  - The worker connection's SQLite commit hook decides, at SQLite's commit
    point (before anything of the transaction is in the file), whether a
    guest commit may go through: only before the cutoff. A commit it let
    through is waited for until SQLite reports it durable (WAL with
    `synchronous = FULL`) and only then reported `ok`.
  - A commit still undecided at the cutoff (another writer took the lock
    after the probe, or the worker is still busy) fails with `TypeError: the
    commit … did not finish in this turn …; nothing was applied`. Whenever
    the worker later reaches that commit's commit point, the hook refuses it,
    so it is never applied. The database then accepts no further commit,
    `denokv_sqlite`'s own maintenance included, and every later operation on
    it fails with a `TypeError` until it is closed and opened again.
  - So a commit never ends a turn with the deadline error, and nothing
    commits in the background on behalf of the guest. The only commits
    outside a guest commit are `denokv_sqlite`'s schema creation for a new
    file and its expiry collection (deleting entries whose `expireIn` has
    passed, as Deno does), which carry no guest data.
- **Execution.** Each database has one `denokv_sqlite` worker thread (Deno's
  configuration: one worker, no batching). KV operations are synchronous
  within the turn: a read or commit is one host call that waits for the
  worker on a current-thread Tokio runtime (a commit until its cutoff, a read
  until the turn deadline, after which the database is unavailable), and the
  guest API returns promises, like `Deno.Kv`, that settle in the same turn.
  Event-loop completions like `net.request`'s are an
  [open item](development-plan.md#batch-v38-in-development).
- **Imports.** Nine host ABI 34 imports. `kv_open (ptr, len) -> f64` (a
  UTF-16 virtual path; capability `kv.read`), `kv_read (ptr, len) -> f64`
  (capability `kv.read`) and `kv_commit (ptr, len) -> f64` (capability
  `kv.write`) take `kv::DESCRIPTOR_VERSION` text descriptors of decimal
  fields; `kv_stage (mode, kind, lo, hi) -> f64` hands one guest value to the
  host in a `kv::StageMode`; `kv_key` and `kv_value (index: f64, schema_ptr,
  schema_len) -> i64` decode an entry of the last read into a JSON schema 18
  target like `json_parse_v19`; `kv_entry (index, field) -> i32` and `kv_text ()
  -> i32` return text in the host result buffer; `kv_close (id)`. Open, read,
  commit, stage and the two decoders are charged to the host-call budget; the
  entry, text and close bookkeeping observes the deadline only. Every import
  also pays [fair host fuel](#fair-host-fuel-fair_fuel): the call and its
  descriptor and result bytes, `KV_OPERATION` per open, read and commit,
  `KV_BYTE` per key or value byte staged, committed or returned, `KV_ENTRY`
  per entry returned, and the checked JSON schema and value rates for a
  decode. SQLite's own time is bounded by the turn deadline and the
  commit cutoff above, not by fuel. A read descriptor is the version, the database id, the range count and per range
  the `kv::Selector`, one or two stage ids, the limit, the reverse flag and the
  cursor; a commit descriptor is the version, the id, the check count with
  each check's key stage and versionstamp (empty for null), and the mutation
  count with each `kv::MutationCode`, key stage, value stage and `expireIn`. A
  failed operation returns `kv::FAILED` and leaves `<ErrorName>\n<message>` in
  `kv_text`; a commit returns `kv::COMMITTED` (its versionstamp in `kv_text`)
  or `kv::CHECK_FAILED`. A malformed descriptor, an unknown stage, database or
  entry id and more than `kv::MAX_STAGED` staged values are fatal, because
  only a tampered module produces them. Staged values are consumed by the next
  read or commit; at most `kv::MAX_OPEN_DATABASES` databases are open at once.
- **Limits.** Deno 2.9.4's `KvConfig` defaults, with Deno's messages: keys of
  at most `kv::MAX_WRITE_KEY_BYTES` encoded bytes to write
  (`kv::MAX_READ_KEY_BYTES` in a range), values of at most `kv::MAX_VALUE_BYTES`
  encoded bytes, `kv::MAX_READ_RANGES` ranges and `kv::MAX_READ_ENTRIES`
  entries per read, `kv::MAX_CHECKS` checks and `kv::MAX_MUTATIONS` mutations
  per commit, `kv::MAX_TOTAL_MUTATION_BYTES` and `kv::MAX_TOTAL_KEY_BYTES` per
  commit (values in the [KV limits](embedding.md#kv-storage-v38)); empty keys
  cannot be written. Decoding uses the module's data limits
