  (depth, nodes, string and element limits); a stored value beyond them is a
  recoverable `TypeError`. A list reads at most its batch size per read.
- **Keys.** Arrays of strings and numbers (`KvKeyPart = string | number`),
  encoded by `denokv_proto` exactly as Deno encodes them (the FoundationDB
  tuple order: strings before numbers, numbers by value, `-0` and NaN as
  distinct doubles). A stored key with a BigInt, boolean or `Uint8Array` part
  has no checked type yet: reading it is a `TypeError`.
- **Values.** Deno KV's three encodings (`v_encoding`): `1` V8 serializer
  bytes, `2` `KvU64` (8 bytes little-endian), `3` raw bytes. The static type
  chooses: a top-level `KvU64` is stored as `2`, a top-level `Uint8Array` as
  `3`, any other value as `1`. Storable values are the checked JSON types
  (records, including optional fields; dictionaries and index signatures;
  arrays without holes; unions; `unknown`; strings; numbers; booleans; `null`;
  `undefined`) and literal types; a class instance (`Date`, a `KvU64` inside a
  value), `Map`, `Set`, a nested `Uint8Array`, BigInt, functions and promises
  are rejected at compile time (`unsupported KV value type …`), and an
  `unknown` holding an Error, a function, a promise, a BigInt, an array with
  holes or a cyclic graph rejects at run time with a `TypeError` before
  anything is stored.
- **Depth.** A value nests at most `varta_kv_codec::MAX_VALUE_DEPTH` levels
  below its root (the legacy checked-JSON depth `value::MAX_JSON_DEPTH`;
  every element, property or entry is one level below its aggregate). A
  part reached more than once (one object, written once with
  back-references) counts at its deepest reach, so a value stores exactly
  when its expansion, which a read classifies, is within the limit,
  whatever the property order, and the depth limit never refuses on a `get`
  what a `set` stored. The stage walk and the V8 writer refuse a deeper value
  before anything is stored, and the V8 reader and the classifier refuse a
  deeper stored value (one Deno wrote), each with the recoverable
  `TypeError` `a KV value cannot
  nest deeper than <limit> levels` (on a read prefixed by `KV value does not
  match the checked type: `), on every host; the construction of a result is
  iterative. The limit is derived from measured engine stacks (the crate
  documentation records the derivation): each walk recurses once per level,
  and a browser's wasm frames live on the engine's native stack, which
  Chrome and WebKit exhaust at a few hundred levels and a native debug build
  at about 1500.
- **Extent.** A read builds a part shared within a value at every reach, so
  a small stored value can expand exponentially (`x = { a: x, b: x }`
  repeated). A value expands to at most `kv::MAX_VALUE_NODES` values and
  `kv::MAX_VALUE_UNITS` code units of text (its
  `varta_kv_codec::Extent`): every stored value (an element, a property's
  value, a `Map` key or value, a `Set` value; not a hole), every code unit
  of a string and every code unit of a plain object's property key (an
  array-index key as its decimal digits) counts again at every reach of a
  shared part. The bounds stop only sharing-driven blow-up: every value
  Deno stores without shared parts within `kv::MAX_VALUE_BYTES` is within
  them, so no such value is refused here. Their derivation, asserted at
  compile time in `varta_common::kv`:
  - values: each value Deno's serializer writes takes at least
    `kv::MIN_ENCODED_VALUE_BYTES` (a tag alone: `null`, `undefined`,
    `true`, `false`), so `kv::MAX_VALUE_NODES` is `kv::MAX_VALUE_BYTES`
    divided by it;
  - text: a Latin-1 (one-byte) string carries at most one code unit per
    encoded byte, a two-byte string at most half of one (a UTF-8 string,
    which the reader also accepts, at most one); an array-index key of `d`
    digits takes a number tag and a varint (`I` zigzag or `U` plain, the
    shorter counted) and its value at least one byte, densest at nine
    digits: `kv::DENSEST_TEXT_UNITS` code units in `kv::DENSEST_TEXT_BYTES`
    bytes, checked for every digit count of a `u32` index. So
    `kv::MAX_VALUE_UNITS` is `kv::MAX_VALUE_BYTES` at that rate.

  The `undefined` a read builds for an absent optional field is no stored
  value and does not count: what a read builds for absent fields costs the
  same with or without sharing, and it pays its fuel (below). The V8 codec
  keeps the bounds, on every host: on `set` the V8 writer counts the whole
  value (it never expands a shared part, so it need not stop early) after
  Deno's encoded-size check, whose `Value too large` wins for a value both
  refuse; on `get` the V8 reader refuses a stored value (one Deno or an
  earlier build wrote) as soon as it passes the bounds, before the
  classifier builds anything. Each records the extent below every aggregate
  with its height and adds it again at every later reach, in constant time.
  The refusal is the recoverable `TypeError` `a KV value cannot expand to
  more than <values> values or <units> code units of text` (on a read
  prefixed as above). Both walks count alike, so a `get` never refuses by
  extent what a `set` stored.
- **Staged values and keys.** The guest stages keys and values alike, so a
  stage never fails for its value form: a value Deno's size check, the
  depth limit of the V8 writer or the extent bounds refuse is staged with
  that refusal, which a commit reports where Deno checks value sizes (after
  every key check of the commit). A staged key never meets a value's
  bounds: keys and range selectors keep Deno's own `Key too large for
  write` and `Key too large for read` limits exactly, whatever their parts
  (also a key whose V8 form is past `kv::MAX_VALUE_BYTES`).
- **Decoding cost.** A read pays `fuel::JSON_PARSE_VALUE` for every value it
  decodes and every absent optional field it builds, in the turn that reads
  it, as checked JSON does; the classifier pays as it goes, every
  `varta_kv_codec::DEADLINE_STRIDE` values, before it builds anything in the
  guest. A value within the bounds whose decoding costs more than the
  turn's remaining fuel, or whose result needs more than the instance's
  memory, ends the run with the ordinary fatal fuel or memory exhaustion,
  as any other too expensive operation does, on every host; such a value
  is not refused by name. What one turn decodes:
  - `get`: its one entry;
  - `getMany`: every entry found, all in the turn of the call (several
    values that each fit a turn can together exhaust it);
  - `list`: every entry of one batch (`batchSize`, Deno's default when
    omitted), decoded together when the batch is read, before the first of
    them is yielded; the next batch is read when the iteration reaches it,
    in the same turn unless the program awaited a task (a timer) between.

  A program spreads the decoding of large values over turns by reading
  them one per task or with a smaller `batchSize`.

  What a read builds on the host is bounded by the fuel it can pay, not by
  the extent: the `undefined` of an absent optional field stores nothing,
  so the extent does not count it, but the classifier pays for every one it
  builds and stops at the first stride it cannot pay. A read therefore holds
  at most the values its remaining fuel pays for plus one stride
  (`varta_kv_codec::DEADLINE_STRIDE`) on the host, whatever the type it is
  read as (pinned by `host_work_of_a_read_is_bounded_by_its_fuel`). A host
  that raises the turn fuel raises this bound with it: about 43 MB of host
  memory was measured natively for a read of 21000 stored `{}` as a record
  of 128 optional fields under the largest admitted turn fuel.
- **V8 codec** (`varta-runtime` `kv::v8`, owned code, no V8). The writer emits
  the header `0xFF 0x10` (serializer version 16, what V8 15.0 in Deno 2.9.x
  writes) and one value: an integral number in the 32-bit Smi range other than
  `-0` as `I` (zigzag varint), every other number as `N` (binary64, NaN as the
  canonical quiet NaN `0x7FF8000000000000`); a string as `"` (Latin-1 bytes)
  when every UTF-16 code unit is at most 0xFF and otherwise as `c` (UTF-16LE,
  lone surrogates kept) after one padding byte when the code units would start
  at an odd offset; an object as `o` … `{`count with its own properties in
  JavaScript order (array-index keys as numbers, `I` or `N` above the Smi
  range, ascending, then the other keys in insertion order; a present field
  holding `undefined` is a property); an array as dense `A` … `$`; `undefined`,
  `null`, `true`, `false`; an object reached twice as one object and a `^`
  back-reference (object ids in V8's order). The reader accepts serializer
  versions 13 to 16, padding, `U` and `S`, sparse arrays `a` … `@`, BigInt `Z`
  (canonical digits), `Date` `D`, `Map` `;` … `:`, `Set` `'` … `,` and a
  `Uint8Array` over its own `ArrayBuffer` (`B` then `V` with subtag `B`, flags
  zero), resolving back-references to completed objects; it rejects every
  other tag (other typed arrays, standalone or shared buffers, primitive
  wrappers, `RegExp`, errors, host objects, transfers), cycles, a truncated or
  overlong field, a non-canonical BigInt, a duplicate key, an array with named
  properties and trailing bytes with a typed error and no partial value. V8
  chooses `N` for an integral number it holds as a heap number (for example
  the result of `Date.now() - start`) and the two-byte form for a Latin-1
  string sliced from a two-byte one; both read back as the same value, and
  Varta writes the canonical forms above, which equal Deno's bytes for values
  written from literals and integer arithmetic. For an integer-valued double
  V8 holds as a heap number, Varta's bytes (`I`) therefore differ from Deno's
  (`N`) while the stored values are identical, and Deno reads both. Every Deno 2.9.4 fixture value
  and every Deno 2.9.7 probe value re-encodes byte-identically.
- **Strict reads.** `get<T>`, `getMany<T>` and `list<T>` decode each value
  into `T` exactly like `varta.json.parse<T>`: the same targets (literal types
  are rejected as parse targets; read the base type and narrow), unions
  selecting their unique member of the value's kind, records rejecting unknown
  properties and missing required fields, `Record<string, unknown>` and index
  signatures admitting any keys, and mixed records validating their declared
  fields. Unlike JSON a number keeps `-0`, NaN and the infinities, and
  `undefined` fills an optional or `undefined`-admitting position: a property
  holding `undefined` fills a required `x: T | undefined` field and reads as
  absent for an optional `x?: T`. An array that V8 wrote in sparse form
  because of its holey elements kind (`new Array(n)` filled, or a deleted
  element written again) but that misses no index reads as a dense array; a
  missing index is a `TypeError`. A sub-object referenced twice (`^`) reads as
  two equal, independent copies: Varta values keep no aliasing across
  storage. Records take the schema's field order, as checked JSON parsing
  does, so a record read and written back is equal to the stored one but its
  properties may be written in another order. A stored `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, nested
  `Uint8Array`, BigInt or an array with holes has no checked type yet. Any
  mismatch rejects with a catchable `TypeError: KV value does not match the
  checked type: …`; reading a `KvU64` or `Uint8Array` entry needs that type.
- **Expiry.** `set(key, value, { expireIn })` stores `expiration_ms` = the
  commit's instant on the KV clock plus `expireIn`, as Deno stamps it. The KV
  clock (`varta-runtime` `kv::clock`) is the only time Varta's KV code reads,
  once per commit: the system clock in production, a fixed instant in tests.
  Whether an entry has expired is the storage engine's decision on the
  system clock, exactly as in Deno and in every Deno process sharing the
  file: `denokv_sqlite`'s worker deletes the entries whose expiration has
  passed when a database is opened writable, and later on its own schedule
  (by the earliest expiration and at least once a minute, with up to a
  second of jitter), as one version step. Reads, lists and atomic checks see
  what the file holds, so an expired entry may still be read, and still
  match a check, until it is collected (Deno documents the same for
  `expireIn`); a read-only database is never collected. Scripted sessions do
  not move the KV clock: virtual time governs timers only, and an
  expiration is an instant every process opening the file shares.
- **Versionstamps.** 20 lowercase hex digits: the 8-byte big-endian
  `data_version.version` of the commit followed by two zero bytes, as Deno
  formats them. `denokv_sqlite` advances the version by a random step of 1 to
  9 per commit (and by 1 per expiry collection), so a Varta commit never
  reproduces a Deno versionstamp; values and keys are byte-identical, the
  versions only grow. `check({ key, versionstamp })` compares exactly; `null`
  checks absence.
- **Guest API** (engine prelude `<varta>/app/kv.ts`, loaded when a module
  names `varta.kv.open` or one of its types): `varta.kv.open(path):
  Promise<Kv>`; `Kv.get<T>(key)` → `KvEntryMaybe<T>` (`value` and
  `versionstamp` null when missing), `getMany<T>(keys)` (one entry per key, in
  order), `list<T>(selector, options)` with `{ prefix }`, `{ prefix, start }`,
  `{ prefix, end }` or `{ start, end }` and `{ limit, cursor, reverse,
  batchSize }` (Deno's batch defaults and validation) returning a
  `KvListIterator<T>` for `for await` with a `cursor` getter (Deno's base64url
  cursor of the key bytes after the selector's common prefix, empty once
  exhausted), `set<T>(key, value, { expireIn })` → `{ ok: true, versionstamp }`,
  `delete(key)`, `atomic()` and `close()`; `AtomicOperation` with
  `check(...checks)`, `set`, `delete`, `sum`, `min` and `max` (a `bigint`
  operand checked as a `KvU64`) and `commit()` → `KvCommitResult |
  KvCommitError` (narrow with `result.ok === true`); `KvU64` with `value` and
  `toString()` and Deno's `RangeError`s. Keys and values of an atomic operation
  are staged when it commits. Errors are catchable: `NotAllowedError` and
  `NotFoundError` `DOMException`s, `TypeError` (storage, schema, limits,
  strict decoding) and `RangeError` (`KvU64`).
- **Deviations from Deno.** `KvEntryMaybe<T>` is one record type, not a union;
  `getMany` is homogeneous in `T`; `consistency` options, `watch`,
  `enqueue`/`listenQueue`, `commitVersionstamp()` and `Deno.openKv()` without a
  path or with `:memory:` are not available (a program naming them fails to
  compile); `sum` takes no `min`/`max`/`clamp`; operations settle in the turn
  that started them.
- **Shared value layer.** Everything the imports do to values is one safe
  `no_std` crate, `varta-kv-codec`: the value18 staging walk, the V8
  serializer subset, Deno's key codec (byte-identical with `denokv_proto`
  0.14.0, checked by a differential test), the read and commit descriptors
  with Deno's limits, cursors and versionstamp text, the fair fuel of KV work,
  the classification of a stored entry into the module's schema and the
  top-down construction of the result (or the recoverable `TypeError`)
  through the guest's own allocator. The native runtime calls it directly
  (its checked JSON values and recoverable JSON errors build through the same
  `build` and `guest` modules); the browser host runs the same crate compiled
  to wasm32 (`varta-kv-codec-wasm`, a checked-in build with a source
  fingerprint, `scripts/build-kv-codec.py`). Only the storage engine differs.
- **Browser host.** The official browser host stores KV databases in the
  origin private file system (OPFS) and implements the
  [embedding contract](embedding.md#kv-storage-v38) with the
  [mapping](embedding.md#browser-effect-mapping-official-host) there:
  - one Varta KV container file per artifact,
    `varta-kv/sha256-<digest>/kv.varta`, named from the artifact identity, so
    two artifacts on one origin never share databases and a new artifact
    version starts empty, as the native `varta-shell` keys
    `<data-dir>/sha256-<digest>/`; a virtual path names one database inside
    it; the guest never chooses an OPFS name;
  - the dedicated Worker acquires the container's
    `FileSystemSyncAccessHandle` before instantiation, only when the program
    imports KV and a package `kv.read` grant is covered by the ceiling; its
    reads, writes and flushes are synchronous, so the imports stay
    synchronous host calls; a Worker without sync access handles refuses
    such a program by name before instantiation (`browser KV storage needs
    OPFS sync access handles …`), never as a silent denial;
  - `kv.read` and `kv.write` are decided like native virtual file roots
    (declared root, request and ceiling patterns, the broker's state) before
    any storage is touched; as natively, a database opens writable when the
    request and the ceiling cover `kv.write`, whatever the broker's state,
    and the broker decides each commit; `resolvePermissions` validates a KV
    path-pattern ceiling like a native host ceiling's grant;
  - the container (format version 1) is a write-ahead log behind two
    checksummed header slots: a commit appends one record, flushes, then
    writes the other header slot and flushes again, and reports `COMMITTED`
    only after that last flush; a crash or a closed tab leaves the old or the
    new state; the log is compacted into a checkpoint without changing the
    logical state;
  - the observable semantics are native's: per-database data versions
    advance by a random step of 1 to 9 per commit and by one per expiry
    collection (versionstamps keep Deno's format and order, not its values),
    checks, `set`/`delete`/`sum`/`min`/`max` and expiry collection at a
    writable open follow `denokv_sqlite` 0.14.0, including its partial
    application of a commit whose `sum`, `min` or `max` meets a non-`KvU64`
    value;
  - failures are recoverable `kv::FAILED` with a named `TypeError`, never
    `COMMITTED` and never a trap: a second tab or Worker holding the
    container (native's "locked by another writer" text), a corrupt
    container, an exhausted quota (nothing applied), storage the origin
    cannot provide, and a header write whose outcome is unknown (the
    container then refuses every operation until the application reloads).
  Deviations:
  - the lock is per artifact, so a second tab cannot open even a read-only
    database (accepted by the owner, 2026-11-05; coordination between tabs
    may come later); the Worker acquires the container once, at start,
    whenever the package's `kv.read` is covered (a later prompt or decision
    may still grant it) and holds it until the run or application ends, so a
    tab that found it locked stays locked out until it reloads, where native
    probes the lock at every open;
  - a database path with a directory below its root (`/data/sub/app.kv`) is
    refused by name (`cannot open the KV database <path>: the browser host
    keeps KV databases only directly in a file root, with no directories`,
    `registry.kv.noDirectories`), since the container has no directories;
    native opens it only inside a directory the host created, and fails
    otherwise;
  - expired entries are collected at a writable open only, never later in
    the instance; a commit never waits for a lock.

  For the programs `scripts/test-browser-kv.mjs` compares with native
  (commits, checks, sums, lists, a strict decode mismatch, a reload over
  stored data, another artifact, a missing grant, a narrower ceiling and
  values at, below and above the depth limit) a browser run
  equals the native run, logs and exact fair fuel, host calls, microtasks,
  output bytes and turns included.
- **Tests** never use production data: the Deno 2.9.4 fixture
  (`kv_cases/deno-2.9.4`, written in a throwaway container by its generator,
  with every row in hex) and the Deno 2.9.7 serializer probe
  (`kv_cases/deno-2.9.7-probe`) are synthetic. No test depends on the date:
  the fixture's one expiring entry (`["fixture", "expire"]`, written
  2026-10-30T16:53:27.447Z with a day to live, its `expiration_ms` minus its
  `expireIn`) has expired on the system clock, so the tests that read the
  fixture as Deno wrote it open it read-only, the `expireIn` stamp is checked
  against Deno's row on a KV clock pinned to that write time, and collection
  is tested with stamps relative to the system clock.

### V38 closure narrowing (`closure_narrowing()`)

Profile v38 adopts TypeScript 5.4's preserved narrowing in closures created
after the last assignment, for every closure: arrows, function expressions
and the getter holes of TSX templates. A `const` binding's narrowing reaches
every closure since v24. A parameter or `let` binding B of a function F
keeps its narrowing (union members, literal and `unknown` refinements of
the write-aware flow analysis) inside a closure C created at position P
when, by the syntactic scan of F's parameters and body:

1. no function, arrow, function expression or class nested in F assigns the
   name of B (an assignment in another closure, called or not, withholds it);
2. every assignment to the name in F (`=`, compound and logical assignment,
   `++`/`--`, a destructuring target, a `for…in`/`for…of` head) lies before
   P, where an assignment inside a loop of F counts at the end of the
   outermost such loop (a later iteration may run it after C was created);
3. C is not a hoisted function declaration (it can run before P).

Assignments are matched by name, so a shadowing binding of the same name
counts and only ever withholds narrowing; TypeScript also exempts a loop
that contains B's own declaration, which this rule does not. Such a binding
is never written after C is created, so inside C, and in closures created
inside C, the narrowing is a fact: a call inside C does not invalidate it
(the binding is excluded from the mutable cells an unknown call may write).
Reads keep the checks of the current narrowing model; the closure captures
the binding's cell as before, so the emitted capture layout is unchanged,
and v1–v37 keep narrowing only `const` bindings into closures. A binding
that fails the rule keeps the existing diagnostic (`… is not declared by
every member of the union; narrow it first`).

### V38 view protocol and TSX (`view_protocol()`, `tsx()`)

The view-protocol and TSX streams implement increment P7 and the start of P8
of the [platform design](development-plan.md#view-layer-l0l3) under v38. The
wire format, codes and rules are the L0 protocol draft v0 of the
[embedding contract](embedding.md#view-protocol-draft-v0-unstable), whose
table there states which parts are implemented; codes stay unstable until the
freeze criterion. Earlier profiles are unchanged: they neither import
`view_commit`, export the event function, load the view prelude nor parse
JSX, and their Wasm bytes do not change.

**Host operation.** `view_commit(ptr: i32, len: i32) -> i32`
(`HostOperation::ViewCommit`, minimum host ABI 34, no capability, charged to
the host-call budget). The runtime copies `len` bytes of guest memory after
a bounds check and the batch byte limit, decodes the whole batch and applies
it to a copy of the instance's view; only a batch whose every operation and
final invariant (unique `id` values) holds replaces the view. Any violation
ends the instance with `RuntimeError::View` (`ViewError::Invalid` with the
operation index and the violated rule) before any effect of the batch. A
turn commits at most one batch; a second `view_commit` in the same turn is
`ViewError::SecondCommit`. The status result is 0.

**Event delivery.** A module that loads the view prelude exports
`varta.view_abi.event(len: i32) -> ()`, synthesized by the compiler: it
copies the record the host wrote at `abi::RESULT_BASE` into an owned string
(the snapshot helper, before any host operation) and calls the prelude's
dispatcher, which decodes the record, runs the handler of its listener (or a
`copy_text` callback, or the link-result handlers for `command_result`) and
then commits the turn's pending operations. A pending exception stays in the
exception channel and is finished by the host like one escaping `main`. The
export is valid only in a profile that admits `view_protocol()` and only
with the registry signature; validation rejects it elsewhere.

**Records as host tasks.** A [long-lived application
instance](#turn-budgets-and-application-instances-turn_budgets) hosts the
view. Every record the renderer produces, from a committed batch or from a
trusted platform input, leaves it at once and becomes a host task of the
instance's one task queue (`TaskKind::View`), ordered with host events,
timers and network completions by arrival; it is delivered in its binary
form through the event export, never as text. One record is one turn
(`TurnKind::View`) with a fresh per-turn fuel, host-call, microtask and
deadline allowance. The task's gesture flag, true exactly for a trusted
`click`, `keydown` or `submit` record, makes the turn a user-gesture turn of
the permission broker, which gates `copy_text` and permission prompts. A
coalescible record (`input`, `scroll`) replaces the pending record of the
same listener under the queue's coalescing rule; at most
`DRAFT_MAX_PENDING_EVENTS` view records (and the queue's host-task bound) may
be pending, a full queue drops a coalescible record, and any other overflow is
`ViewError::QueueOverflow`. Platform inputs are host work between turns
(`Application::view_input`; `VartaRuntime::run_view` and `varta dev
--view-script` perform a script's inputs on virtual time, below) and run
no guest code. A committed view keeps the instance alive like an open event
source. A bounded execution (`run`, `dev` without `--app` or a script)
renders but has no event delivery: its records are discarded. `Session` in
`varta-runtime/src/view.rs` owns the renderer and the one-commit rule;
`turns::begin` renews the commit allowance.

**Scripted sessions and virtual time.** `VartaRuntime::run_view` (`varta
dev --view-script`) runs the application instance on a virtual clock: loop
time starts at 0 with the instance, a fired timer sets it to its due time,
as in every execution, and only a script step advances it otherwise; no
timer ever waits for the wall clock and a network completion does not move
loop time. A script's `inputs` are steps in order, each an input (the
trusted platform inputs above, and `prompts`) or a wait,
`{"input":"wait","ms":N}` with N a number of milliseconds in
`0..=TIMER_MAX_DELAY_MS`.

- **Settling.** Before an input the session runs every runnable task, each
  as its own turn with its own budgets: host tasks (view records and host
  events) by arrival first, then timers, then network completions that have
  already arrived. A timer is runnable when its due time is at most the loop
  time, and, while any timer armed with Node's minimum delay
  (`TIMER_MIN_DELAY_MS`: a zero, omitted or sub-millisecond delay, including
  an interval's re-arm) is pending, the earliest timer in (due time,
  sequence) order is runnable too. A zero-delay timer and every zero-delay
  timer it arms therefore fire before the input, keeping Node's 1 ms minimum
  and order: a chain interleaves with a 2 ms timer exactly as in Node, and a
  timer due within the minimum delay of a pending zero-delay timer fires
  before it. The input is performed only when nothing is runnable. It takes
  no virtual time.
- **Wait.** A wait of N ms from loop time V runs every runnable task whose
  timers are due at or before V + N (records and completions as above), in
  order, then sets loop time to V + N. A zero-delay timer armed during the
  wait fires within it when due by V + N, otherwise in the next step's
  settling.
- **Explicit network wait.** `{"input":"wait_network","ms":N}` accepts a
  positive finite wall-clock duration up to `Script::MAX_NETWORK_WAIT_MS`.
  It first performs ordinary input settling, then holds virtual loop time fixed
  while armed network operations and their reactions settle. Future virtual
  timers do not become due through wall time. A response with no armed body read
  is quiescent; its body can be read by a later input. The step caps native
  waits, guest turns and idle maintenance, without changing the instance lifetime
  or the original deadlines of surviving transfers. Existing smaller lifetime,
  turn and resource limits still apply. Expiry terminates the instance with
  `ApplicationError::NetworkWait` naming the step and duration, and no later
  script input runs. Request resources close when the failed session is dropped.
  Directly constructed scripts are validated before starting guest execution.
- **End.** After the last step the session settles once more and reports.
  A timer that no wait reaches never fires; requests still in flight are not
  waited for.
- **Bounds.** One step (its settling, or a wait) runs at most
  `Script::MAX_STEP_TURNS` turns; a task that keeps re-arming with the
  minimum delay (`setInterval(f, 0)`) ends the session with
  `ApplicationError::Unsettled` naming the step (the final settling is the
  step after the last). Production budgets are unchanged.
- **Network.** Pending requests are never waited for implicitly: a
  completion that has arrived when the session settles runs in Node's order
  after timers, otherwise it runs at a later settling or not at all. Its
  arrival follows the wall clock, so only a script without network requests
  in flight is deterministic. `wait_network` explicitly permits bounded real I/O;
  it is not replay. A [recorded network log](#recorded-network-replay-v38)
  replaces the transport when completion order, response bytes and errors
  must be reproducible.
- `Date.now()` and `performance.now()` keep reading the clock their
  `time.now` grant authorizes; virtual time governs timers only.

**Determinism guarantee.** For a scripted session without network requests
in flight, the same artifact, script, grants and host policy give the same
sequence of turns (kinds and order, and the fuel, host calls and
microtasks of each), the same output and the same final snapshot on every
run and every host speed. No wall-clock read decides whether a timer is
due, how tasks are ordered or when a step is performed: host tasks keep
their queue order, timers their (due time, sequence) key, and the wall
clock bounds only the per-turn deadline and the optional lifetime, whose
exhaustion fails the session instead of reordering it. The guarantee does
not cover the `wall` and memory fields of the budget report, `Date.now()`
and `performance.now()`, the audit log's timestamps, or the arrival of
network completions. (Before this rule, `run_view` compared each timer's
wall-clock target, `started` + due time, with `Instant::now()` after every
turn, so a `setTimeout(…, 0)` due at 1 ms fired before or after the next
input depending on how long the previous turns took.)

**Live applications.** An embedder that drives `Application::step` itself
(a native or browser shell) keeps the wall clock: timers are due by
`Instant::now()` and real inputs arrive whenever the user acts, so the
order of an input and a timer due at about the same moment, of network
completions and timers, and the number of interval firings before an input
are inherently racy and are not guaranteed. What every host guarantees is
the turn model itself: one task per turn, microtasks drained in the turn,
timers in (due time, sequence) order, host tasks in arrival order.

#### Recorded network replay (v38)

A native application instance can record its real transfers into a
versioned, bounded log, and every host can replay such a log in place of its
transport (`varta_common::net::replay`, runtime `NetworkMode`). Recording and
replay serve `net_request_start_v2` requests of application instances only; a
v37 descriptor fails with `ReplayError::Descriptor`. A module that imports
`varta.net.get` or `varta.net.fetch` (`net_get*`, `net_fetch*`,
`net::replay::unserved`) reads the network outside that transport, so a
recording would miss the read and a replay would make it for real: recording
and replay refuse such a module before its instance is set up (before any
prompt, guest code or socket) with `ReplayError::Unserved`.

- **Log.** One JSON object: `format` (`net::replay::LOG_FORMAT`), `version`
  (`LOG_VERSION`), `requests` and `events`, with no other member. A request is
  `{method, url}`: the descriptor's method and the URL as the host parsed it
  (WHATWG serialization), in the order requests reached the transport. An
  event names its request by index and the scripted-session `step` during
  which the guest received it (1-based, the settling after the last step is
  one more, `UNSCRIPTED_STEP` outside a scripted session). Its `kind` is
  `head` (`status`, `statusText`, `location` resolved against the request
  URL, and `headers`: the canonical names and values the recording grant
  showed), `chunk` (`read`: `text` or `bytes`, the mode of the read that armed
  it, and `text`: the completion text, at most one read's delivery), `end`,
  `failed` (`text`: the failure text) or `abort` (the guest aborted the open
  transfer). A request's events are a head or a failure, then chunks, then
  an end or a failure; an abort may close it at any point; nothing follows.
  Steps never decrease. A reader refuses any other shape (a leading byte
  order mark, a duplicate member, a number that is no unsigned integer
  literal, a `step` or `request` above `MAX_LOG_INDEX`, a string escaping a
  lone surrogate), a head that is no canonical visible set within the
  response head limits (field text counts one byte per code unit, as on the
  wire), a chunk that is empty or beyond one read, a byte chunk with a unit
  above 0xFF, a request that is no `fetch` method or no URL in its own
  serialization, and the [resource limits](#resource-limits)
  (`NetworkLogError`).
- **Recording** (`varta dev --view-script S --network-record LOG`, or
  `varta dev --app --network-record LOG` for an application instance without
  a scripted session, whose events carry `UNSCRIPTED_STEP`) keeps the
  real transfers. It logs a request when it reaches the transport, every
  completion when the guest receives it (`Net::deliver`, so a completion
  discarded after an abort is not logged), and every abort of a transfer
  that is still open. Immediate completions (denials, invalid URLs, methods,
  headers or bodies) are produced by the host and never logged. A recording
  that would exceed the log limits, or a completion the log cannot hold,
  fails the instance (`ReplayError::RecordingLimit`, `Unrecordable`). The CLI
  writes the log to a new file, also when the session failed after it
  started, and never overwrites one; a session refused before it starts
  writes none.
- **Authorization.** Before the instance starts, every logged request must
  be admitted by the package's `net.request` grants and the host ceiling;
  otherwise the session fails with `ReplayError::Ungranted` before any guest
  code runs. Each replayed request is then planned exactly as a real one:
  descriptor checks, the pending-request limit, the permission broker's
  decision and audit entry, the body and header checks. A denied or invalid
  request completes immediately as without replay and claims no logged
  request. A granted request claims the next logged request when it starts,
  in start order, which must have the same method and URL
  (`ReplayError::Request`, `Unlogged`); a request aborted before its
  transfer could deliver anything keeps that claim, so its abort meets the
  log's abort of its own index. A
  replayed head shows only the logged names the replay grant also shows,
  with the replaying request's own URL: a replay never reveals a header its
  grant hides.
- **Release and arrival.** Logged events are released strictly in log order:
  each once its request has the matching operation armed (the head after the
  start; a chunk, end or failure after a body read, whose mode must match a
  logged chunk's, `ReplayError::Read`) and, in a scripted session, once the
  session reached the event's step. A logged abort is released by the
  guest's own abort of that request; any other abort of an open replayed
  transfer fails with `ReplayError::Abort`. A released completion arrives as
  a transfer's does: when the instance next waits for network, after its idle
  period's maintenance, every completion released by then arrives at once,
  in log order, and each is one network turn. Nothing waits for the wall
  clock and no socket opens (a module importing a direct network read is
  refused before it starts, above). An unscripted `--app` replay
  (`varta dev --app --network-replay LOG`) keeps real timers: its timers
  fire on the wall clock as in the recording, so a program whose timers race
  its network completions (a request timeout, a backoff) replays the order
  the log holds only when the guest's own timers produce it.
- **Failures.** A `wait_network` step that ends with a watched request armed,
  or an unscripted application that ends so, fails with
  `ReplayError::Stalled` naming the next log event. A session that ends without
  another failure while logged events are undelivered fails with
  `ReplayError::Unconsumed`. Every replay failure is fatal for the instance.
- **Usage.** The guest uses the same imports and receives the same completion
  texts as from a real transfer, so each turn's fuel, host calls, microtasks
  and memory are those of the corresponding real transfer turn (checked
  against the recording by `replay_tests`).
- **What replay reproduces.** Which requests reach the transport and in which
  order; each completion's kind and text; their delivery order among network
  completions; the script step in which each was received; aborts at their
  place.
- **What it does not reproduce.** Wall-clock latency and arrival times within
  a step (a replayed completion arrives at the first idle period after its
  operation is armed); request headers and bodies (only the method and URL
  are compared); response headers the recording grant hid; transport
  behavior the log does not hold (connections, TLS, DNS, retries the guest
  did not make); `Date.now()`, `Math.random()` and other inputs that are not
  network completions. A replayed session whose guest behaves differently
  from the recording (another order of requests or reads) fails as a
  divergence instead of reaching an unrecorded state.
- **Browser host.** The generated loader accepts the log's JSON text as the
  embedder option `networkReplay` of `run` and `mount`, validates it with the
  same rules before anything loads (a decoder keeping the byte order mark,
  which `JSON.parse` then refuses, plus a scan refusing the duplicate
  members, non-integer numbers and escaped lone surrogates that serde
  refuses), and the Worker refuses an ungranted logged request before
  instantiation. The replay transport replaces Fetch behind the same request
  planning and grant checks; a request claims its logged request in
  `net_request_start_v2`, in start order as natively, although its transfer
  is created later by the network pump. It releases events by the same rules
  and settles each completion as Fetch does, so it reaches the event loop
  after the turn and its idle period. The browser host has no scripted
  session and does not interpret steps. An armed request the log cannot
  complete stays pending, as with a silent server (a bounded run then ends
  at its deadline); an instance that ends, by settling or by an authorized
  exit, with logged events undelivered fails with the `Unconsumed` text,
  while a `mount` closed by its embedder ends without that check. Its
  divergence texts are the native ones (`registry.network.replay.errors`).
  The [embedding contract](embedding.md#recorded-network-replay-v38) states
  the wire rules for third-party hosts.

**Capabilities.** `ui.open_url` (`GrantKind::OpenUrls`: URL patterns under
the network URL rules over `https://` and `http://`, plus the exact
`view::ANY_HTTPS_PATTERN` `https://*`, which no other capability admits) and
`clipboard.write` (boolean). At patch time an external `href` must match a
pattern of the package request, or the batch is invalid. On activation the
decision is permission broker v1's ([permission broker v1](#turn-budgets-and-application-instances-turn_budgets)):
the request within the host ceiling, the grant's broker state (a revoked or
withheld grant denies) and an audit entry with the URL for every outcome. A
URL matched by explicit patterns of the request and the host ceiling is
granted by policy; a URL matched on either side only through `https://*`
prompts with the full URL on every activation and the answer is never
stored; anything else is denied. The prompt goes through the instance's
prompt seam (`PermissionPrompter`, between turns); a scripted headless
session has no seam and its simulated platform answers instead
(`platform.prompt`; unanswered = `not_allowed`), reported to the broker's
audit; any other host never prompts and denies. `copy_text` is attempted
only in a user-gesture turn (`invalid_context` otherwise) and needs
`clipboard.write` in both the request and the ceiling and an open broker
state (`not_allowed` otherwise). Every outcome is one `command_result`
record (`ok`, `not_allowed`, `refused_by_platform`, `invalid_context`); a
denial never traps.

**Headless renderer (`varta-view`).** An engine crate depending only on
`varta-common` (no Wasm, file, network or clock access); the runtime is its
only production dependent. It holds the node tree, stylesheets, focus and
field state; checks every operation against the registry (element, attribute
and command tables, attribute value grammars of `view::attributes`, the CSS
value grammars of `view::css` with at most `css::MAX_VALUE_TOKENS` tokens per
value, the stylesheet grammar and forbidden tokens, listener filters,
content model: void elements and text nodes take no children, `select` only
`option`, `option` only text); simulates trusted platform inputs (click with
activation behaviour, typing, keys with modifiers and IME composition, focus,
select, scroll, Esc in a modal dialog, Tab) with bubbling, `preventDefault`
and `stopPropagation`; and serializes a deterministic JSON snapshot: the
tree (tags, attributes, classes, computed styles, field values and edit
counters, listeners), the accessibility tree (roles, names, states), title,
focus, stylesheets and the simulated clipboard, opened URLs and prompt count.
The cascade orders by cascade layer, specificity, sheet id, then source
order; inline styles win ([view CSS engine](#view-css-engine-k8-t2-and-t3)); custom properties resolve through an iterative dependency graph at
each element before inheritance. The native resolver invalidates active dependency
cycles, evaluates only selected fallbacks, freezes inherited aliases, preserves token
boundaries/quoted text and revalidates selected values for geometry and paint.
Arena indices share resolved fragments without recursively owned dependency
chains; native per-value limits are checked before materialization. Zero-length
fragments are folded away without making their valid empty binding missing, so
empty-reference fan-out cannot produce an exponential traversal with zero output.
A shared 8 MiB potential expanded-component byte allowance now checks every
component, including detached nodes, before style-reading commands and final
publication. Cached candidate programs and iterative inherited bound scopes count
fresh custom literals and per-property maxima without materializing values.
Media, pseudo-state and declaration winners cannot discount candidates. Standard
literals without references retain their full UTF-16 length; custom substitution
bounds retain the per-value cap. Command reads share the final-read allowance and
excess rejects the copied transaction before effects. See the embedding contract
for graph, fallback, alias and reclamation rules. Serialized output, retained
frames, backend overhead, repeated getter work, process RSS and cross-engine
late-value subset parity remain open. Other
properties report their cascaded value.

*Modal dialogs (top layer).* `show_modal` puts a closed `dialog` on top of the
headless top layer (an open one stays where it is) and runs Chrome's dialog
focusing steps: the first displayed, enabled, focusable descendant with
`autofocus`, else the first such descendant in tree order, else the dialog
itself. While a modal dialog is open everything outside the topmost one is
inert: a scripted input naming an inert element fails with
`InputError::Inert` (a platform pointer lands on the dialog's backdrop
instead), `focus`/`select` ignore it, Tab and Shift+Tab cycle over the
topmost dialog's focusable descendants only, and the accessibility tree drops
it except the dialog's ancestors (Chrome ignores inert content). Esc cancels
the topmost dialog only: `cancel`, then, unless prevented, it closes. Closing
(Esc or `close`) removes the dialog from the top layer and focuses again the
element focused before it was shown when that element can still take focus;
otherwise focus inside the closed dialog is dropped; then `close` fires. A
dialog removed from the document or moved leaves the top layer. A closed
dialog renders nothing, so its contents take no focus. These rules follow
Chrome 156 as probed (`modal_dialogs_trap_focus_and_make_the_rest_inert`).
Ordinary snapshots do not include layout
rectangles; the opt-in geometry section below adds them on request. An experimental separate `layout_boxes` API uses pinned Taffy to
compute a bounded subset of div and semantic block/flex/grid geometry and
single-text-child paragraphs with pixel and percentage dimensions,
min/max sizes, automatic and signed pixel/percentage margins, padding, border shorthands and uniform border width/style,
gap, direction, wrapping, alignment, grow/shrink, static/relative/absolute/fixed
positioning and pixel/percentage insets
and pixel or percentage flex basis. Stylesheet shorthands are expanded in cascade order before
inline properties. For these geometry properties the headless tree retains the
last inline writer for each affected longhand, including shorthand updates and
removals. Border width and style are likewise resolved per side through stylesheet
and inline cascade. Unsupported content and computed CSS fail explicitly.
Paint-only color, opacity, outline, border radius, text decoration, cursor and
stacking-order properties do not affect these rectangles; this does not implement
their rendering. Translations move boxes ([native transforms](#native-css-transforms)); scaling transforms and other unsupported geometry effects still fail.
`TextMeasurer` separately shapes bounded text using explicitly supplied fonts
and Parley; its font collection disables system-font discovery. It reports
advance, height and line count. The separate experimental `layout_boxes_with_text`
uses it for isolated Unicode text and collapsed CSS whitespace in flex/grid
containers and blocks with one text child, with caller-supplied fonts and base
size. Symbols, supplementary scalars, combining marks, bidirectional runs and
Unicode line breaking use the same bounded shaper as fields. NUL is rejected
by the view protocol; other control characters except TAB/LF/CR/FF are rejected
by native text layout. The general 64 KiB UTF-8 source allowance still applies.
Supported `white-space` modes are `normal`, `nowrap`, `pre-wrap` and the
user-agent `pre` of `<pre>` (below); preserved tabs and spaces follow
[native preserved white space](#native-preserved-white-space). Pixel/rem/percentage
font sizes, supported weights/styles, and normal, numeric, pixel/rem or percentage line heights inherit along
the element tree. A CSS family list resolves against the supplied fonts; an
unmapped generic family before a match is rejected. The embedding host may
explicitly map aliases, including generic families, to a supplied font and must ensure
the same fonts and glyph coverage on comparison targets. Glyph fallback is limited
to the explicit collection; missing glyphs use its `.notdef`, with no ambient
system-font discovery. A face with an `opsz` variation axis is shaped and drawn at
an optical size equal to the used font size in CSS pixels, clamped by the axis
range: CSS `font-optical-sizing: auto`, the initial value (the property itself is
outside the view subset), as Chrome 156 sets it for web fonts and the macOS system
UI font alike (`text_takes_the_optical_size_of_its_font_size`). A text node's rectangle
is its anonymous layout box, not a glyph-ink bound, on the single-text-child
path. Inline-only formatting contexts instead expose unions of their font-box
fragments for descendants; those unions are not themselves hit regions.

**Opt-in snapshot geometry.** `View::snapshot_with_geometry` adds one top-level
`geometry` key to the snapshot, computed by `layout_geometry_with_text` with a
`GeometryRequest`'s explicit fonts at the environment's viewport width and
reference root font size and the request's viewport height. It lists, in
document order, every displayed element except `br`: its id, used outer display
and border box. The runtime computes it once from the final view of a scripted
session (`VartaRuntime::run_view_with_geometry`, `varta dev --view-script
--view-geometry --view-font PATH FAMILY`) only when the session did not fail;
a refused layout becomes `RuntimeError::ViewLayout` and no partial section is
published. Without a request, snapshots, reports and the printed output are
unchanged. The tree keeps cascaded values: a flex or grid item with a
text-level display keeps it in `style.display`, while its geometry entry reports
the used `block`. The session itself, its turns, budgets and scroll handling do
not change: geometry is an observer of the final state, not a layout-aware
session. Field semantics, number formatting, failure rules and the Chrome oracle
are specified in the [embedding contract](embedding.md#headless-geometry-output).

The text-aware native path admits adjacent text and nested `span`, `strong`,
`em`, `code`, `label`, explicitly styled links and `br` inside supported block containers.
Inline flex/grid items are blockified by their parent, including an element
with an explicit `display: inline` whose only child is text (a `div` or an
author-styled `button` lays out as with `display: block`); ordinary inline nodes
share one shaped paragraph with style ranges. Whitespace collapses across node
boundaries, line breaks preserve source order, and hanging break spaces do not
extend normal-whitespace fragments. Parent and inline-ancestor line struts share
a baseline; each inline element retains its own font-box height. Empty inline
anchors retain their source position and contribute line metrics when a line
exists. Strong/em/code defaults participate before explicit author declarations;
code's monospace family still needs an explicit host font mapping.

Shaping context crosses source-node boundaries for ligatures, combining marks,
Arabic joining and bidi runs. As in the checked Chrome fixtures, the first
source node of a shaped cluster owns its glyph color and full advance; continuation
nodes retain zero-width fragments. This does not supply caret subdivision or
inline text selection. Fragment backgrounds, rectangular clipping, vertical
scroll offsets and descendant hit regions use the final shaped layout; overflow
of bare text targets its container. Rendering reuses that layout for glyphs.

The context shares the existing node/depth, aggregate text/leaf, per-paragraph
UTF-8 and shaping limits. A separate 1000000-operation native request allowance
charges inline collection, copied ancestor paths, span styles, line/cluster/glyph
projection and fragment assignment; geometry and layout-command nesting cannot
refill it. One geometry request admits at most 65536 fragments. These counters
are work bounds, not proof of total CPU time/RSS, and no prior ceiling is raised.
Distinct inline border side colors, non-solid border styles, horizontal
percentages, decoration edges in bidirectional text, mixed block/inline contexts,
mixed whitespace-preservation modes, full inline formatting, platform font
selection and general typography acceptance remain open; unsupported styles
fail explicitly.

Native text admits solid `text-decoration: none | underline`. Decoration
propagates through supported inline/in-flow block descendants; a descendant
`none` cannot cancel an ancestor's line. Color and auto thickness belong to the
decorating box, and nested decorations retain outer-to-inner order. Replaced
fields/selects stop ancestor propagation and admit their own line. Paragraph font
boxes round CSS ascent/descent before dividing leading (smaller half above),
while horizontal advances and containing line heights remain fractional. This
rule is independent of whether text is underlined. Field editing keeps its one
shared shaped-control geometry.

Underlines paint before each line's text, retaining per-line/source ordering with
backgrounds, overhanging glyphs, nested opacity and clips. Ink skipping uses the
selected font's unhinted contours, not a platform-smoothed coverage mask; quadratic
and cubic stripe intersections use bounded analytic splitting/root refinement.
CJK auto skipping is excluded. Temporary strokes and interception work consume
the existing shared text-paint allowance; no glyph-cache, frame, texture or GPU
layer allowance is added. Both pixel and neutral-vector paths receive ordinary
rectangle spans. Additional decoration styles, mixed preserved whitespace and
full real-font/control/platform typography acceptance remain open.

Native inline background radii use the initial `box-decoration-break: slice`
behavior: positive-width fragments are assembled in visual order into a
continuous horizontal strip and each fragment paints its slice. No extra rounded
ends are inserted at a line or bidi break. Radius percentages and side-overlap
normalization for logical hit regions use the current fragment's font border box before those radii are
applied to the whole strip. This matches the sampled Chrome/WebKit fragment
behavior and Blink's explicit flow-box radius reference, rather than resolving
percentages against the strip's total width. `clone` is not added to the admitted
native style surface. See [CSS Fragmentation §5.4](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-break/#break-decoration)
and [Blink's inline background painter](https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/main/third_party/blink/renderer/core/paint/inline_box_fragment_painter.cc).

Shared radius normalization and tangent-arc emission retain f64 coordinates until
the strip contour has been clipped to the local fragment. Converting a wide strip
to f32 before clipping can erase a narrow trailing fragment. Hit geometry retains
the same analytic slice for an inline's own font box; descendant text font boxes
remain independent, including when their visible ink or hits extend through a
background cutout. Painting never turns a background radius into a glyph clip.
These records consume the existing aggregate fragment bound. A conservative
per-fragment contour-work reservation shares the existing text-paint allowance;
it is charged before generating the path, not renewed for each inline element.
Zero-alpha backgrounds and descendants of zero-opacity groups skip pixel contour
work while preserving styles and hit geometry. Inline borders are described
below; inline opacity's implementation
and remaining raster interoperability are described below.

Solid inline outlines surround the union of the element's border-box fragments.
The outer offset rectangles are united before deriving the inset contour, so
small gaps bridged by the stroke have no internal bars. Negative offsets clamp
independently on each fragment axis. Rounded contours use the first fragment as
their radius reference, exchange convex/concave corner radii at inset corners,
and shorten incident radii when an edge cannot accommodate both. Real cubic
subcurves survive intersection and local clipping; there is no flattened or
viewport-sized outline mask. The filled region is outer nonzero winding with
the inner winding of exactly +1 removed; folded inset contours are not equivalent
to subtracting every positive winding. Square contours use disjoint spans in one
path. Thus translucent outlines apply alpha once, including overlaps and folds.

Outline width and offset use signed integral CSS pixels (a nonzero magnitude
below one becomes one), before host DPI scaling. Authored styles remain intact.
Outlines paint after descendants in tree postorder, including inline descendants
and enclosing block outlines, with their original clips and opacity isolation.
Their geometry consumes the existing shared text-paint allowance and captured
commands share the existing frame limit. No texture, retained-cache or GPU-layer
allowance is added. Distinct inline border side colors remain open, as does
real-font/platform interoperability.

Non-replaced inline top/bottom padding expands each own fragment's background,
rounded hit region and outline without moving text or changing line metrics.
Nested descendants retain their independent font boxes. The public content-box
union excludes that padding. Pixel/rem lengths and percentages are admitted;
both percentage sides resolve against the containing block's content width,
including after wrapping. Top/bottom margins have no effect on line layout;
horizontal `auto` margins resolve to zero. Cascade expansion, longhand overrides
and removal use the same geometry declaration store as block layout. Resolved
padding and expanded height retain the existing native length limit;
fragment/work/cache limits are unchanged.
See [CSS2 inline height](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/visudet.html#inline-non-replaced)
and [padding percentages](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/box.html#padding-properties).

Non-replaced inline left/right padding, solid borders and margins (signed px/rem
margins; `auto` is zero) become owned decoration edges in the shaped text: an
opening edge carries margin+border+padding of the left side at the box's first
source position, a closing edge those of the right side after its last. Source text and byte offsets are
unchanged. A side whose margin, border and padding are all zero adds no edge, so
shaping, ligatures and joining continue across it; a nonzero side separates
shaping as [CSS Text boundary shaping](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-text-3/#boundary-shaping)
requires. Edges introduce no break opportunity: an opening edge moves to the
preceding text break and wraps with the following word, a closing edge stays
with the preceding word and is fitted together with its last cluster, and
intrinsic min/max widths use the same rule. A collapsible space pending at a
boundary keeps its source owner: an edge recorded after it follows the space
only if the space is emitted, and a forced break or the end of the flow drops
the space without moving the edge past it. Trailing spaces removed at a line end
do not separate a closing edge from its word.

Slice decoration applies: the opening edge belongs to the box's first fragment
and the closing edge to its last; fragments at line breaks receive none. The
box's own fragment covers its border and padding, while margins extend only
enclosing fragments. A negative margin moves later content and shortens enclosing
fragments; no fragment width becomes negative. Backgrounds, slice radii,
outlines and pointer targets use these fragments; underlines remain under text.
An empty box with nonzero edges keeps its padding box and line contribution.
The content box of an unbroken box excludes its horizontal border and padding; a
broken box's union has no single content edge and keeps only the vertical inset.
Edges count against the existing fragment/inline-work, glyph-slot and shaping
operation ceilings and are part of the shape-cache key; no ceiling is raised.
Nonzero horizontal percentages are refused because intrinsic sizing has no
definite containing width; `<br>` with nonzero horizontal spacing and edges in
a flow containing right-to-left runs are refused rather than reordered.

Top/bottom inline borders paint outside the line like vertical padding and add
to the fragment's vertical extent without changing line metrics; `<br>` with a
border is refused. Each fragment paints its border right after its own
background, before content. With `slice` decoration the border ring belongs to
the continuous visual-order strip, like a rounded background: the first fragment
shows the left side, the last the right side, every fragment its top and bottom,
and corner curves appear only at the strip's ends. Outer and inner (padding-edge)
contours stay f64 until clipped to the local fragment, then fill even-odd. Only
solid styles are admitted, and all visible sides must share one color; a second
visible color is refused at paint time rather than approximated. Each ring
reserves twice the slice contour work from the shared text-paint allowance.
Border widths follow block boxes: logical CSS pixels, not snapped to device
pixels (CSS Values 4 border-width snapping remains open for every box).

A broken inline box's fragment resolves its radii with the corners of its absent
edges zeroed before side-overlap normalization: the first fragment keeps only
left corners, the last only right corners, middle fragments none. Absent corners
therefore no longer shrink present ones on a narrow fragment, matching Blink's
per-fragment rounded border. Middle fragments paint plain rectangles.

Inline pointer hits follow browser line-box order. For each line after the
first, the horizontal gaps between that line's visible fragments, over the line
box's vertical extent, become block hit regions placed after every earlier
line's targets and before the line's own. A point in a later line's margin gap
therefore hits the block even where an earlier line's decorated fragment
overlaps it, while a point inside a later fragment's rectangle (even outside its
curve) or beyond the line's contents still reaches earlier fragments.

#### Native preserved white space

Each text node keeps its own inherited `white-space` mode inside one inline
flow, so collapsing (`normal`, `nowrap`) and preserving (`pre-wrap`, `pre`)
nodes mix. Collapsible spaces collapse across node boundaries as before; one
following a preserved space is kept, as in CSS Text 3. Min-content honours each
node's own mode, so a wrapping node inside a `pre` or `nowrap` root wraps at
every opportunity it owns. A flow whose preserved
text holds a tab, or a preserved space next to other white space or before a
newline or the end of the text, is shaped and broken by `text::whitespace`;
every other flow keeps Parley's own line breaking. Field display is unchanged.

- A preserved tab shapes as a space in its own run and advances to the next tab
  stop at `tab-size: 8`: eight space advances of the flow root's (block
  container's) font, measured from the start of its line, whatever the tab's
  own font or size, as in Chrome. A stop closer than half of that space is
  skipped (Blink's `Font::TabWidth`). Because stops depend on where lines
  break, the flow is reshaped until every tab's advance agrees with the stop
  computed from its final line; a flow that does not agree within the bounded
  number of passes is refused.
- At a soft wrap a whole run of preserved spaces and tabs hangs past the line
  end, and the next line starts after it; a forced break that follows the run
  stays on its line. Parley alone hangs only the first overflowing space, so
  such a line is broken again with an advance that admits the whole run, and
  Parley's own break opportunities end it.
- A line's width excludes the white space that hangs at a soft wrap and
  collapsible spaces at its end. Before a forced break or the end of the text,
  `pre-wrap` spaces conditionally hang: they count while they fit, fully in
  max-content and not in min-content; `pre` spaces always count. Center and
  right alignment use these widths; a soft-wrapped line's hanging run is
  excluded, as in Chrome.
- Inline fragments, hits and underlines keep preserved spaces, including
  hanging ones and the trailing spaces of a plain `pre` or `pre-wrap` text
  node, and drop collapsible spaces at a line end. As in Chrome, where a
  preserved tab is a control item without a text fragment, underlines skip
  each tab's whole advance, inside a line or at its end, on plain and rich
  flows.

The model is logical-order only: a flow on this path with a right-to-left run
or base direction is refused, as is a `text-overflow: ellipsis` root on it.
Preserved tabs per shaping request are bounded (`MAX_PRESERVED_TABS`), because
each is its own styled run. The line breaker is driven through Parley's public
API (per-line advances and reverts) plus one hidden hook:
`BreakLines::set_prior_line_width`, `#[doc(hidden)]` in the vendored Parley,
sets the width center/right alignment uses for each re-broken line. Every
realized line is checked against the line the model located; any disagreement
refuses the layout, with the flow's node (a rich flow's root, a plain text
node's parent element) as an unsupported-content error,
instead of painting a different one. The extra breaking work is charged to the view
request's shaping-operation allowance and repaid by cached results. Min-content
reuses the final lines' tab advances, so a tab that cannot end a min-content
line (before a character that admits no break) is not re-stopped. Chrome breaks
before a closing bracket that follows spaces, which Parley's Unicode line
breaking does not; that difference predates this model and applies to every
`white-space` mode.

#### Native structure and user-agent defaults

Native layout admits `h1`–`h3`,
`ul`, `ol`, `li` and `pre` as block boxes and `label` as an inline box (blockified
in flex/grid like `span`). Their defaults come from one versioned native
user-agent table in `varta-view` (`style::NATIVE_UA_DEFAULTS`, published as
`varta_view::NATIVE_UA_VERSION`); any change of a row's value is a new version.
The official browser host adds no normalization for these tags, so each row
mirrors Chrome's user-agent stylesheet: headings scale the inherited size
(2/1.5/1.17em), are bold and have 0.67/0.83/1em block margins of their own size;
`p` keeps 1em margins; `ul`/`ol` have 1em block margins (zero for a list nested
in a list) and 40px inline-start padding; `pre` is `font-family: monospace` and
`white-space: pre` with 1em margins; `strong`, `em` and `code` keep their bolder,
italic and monospace defaults; `button` is `text-align: center` and the other
form controls `start`, which stops inherited alignment at the control. Author
declarations always replace a row's value. Font sizes follow Blink's
generic-family switch. Along the path each size is either the initial `medium`
keyword, absolute (set by a `px` or `rem` length) or relative (a user-agent
heading scale or a percentage of a non-absolute size, which keep the parent's
state). At an element whose family switches between exactly `monospace` and
anything else (a list such as `monospace, monospace` is not monospace), a
non-absolute size is re-derived after the element's own `font-size` applies:
`medium` becomes the host medium size times 13/16 (Chrome's 13px fixed
default over its 16px proportional default) for monospace and the host medium
size otherwise; a relative size is multiplied by 13/16 into monospace and
divided by it out of monospace. So `pre` is 13px, `h1 > code` 26px, `h3 > pre`
15.21px, `p { font-size: 150% } > code` 19.5px and `pre > span { font-size:
200% }` 26px, while `pre { font-size: 16px }` stays 16px and a fixture-font
child of a 26px `code` returns to 32px. A percentage `line-height` resolves
against the element's size after that step (`pre { line-height: 150% }` is
19.5px). The user-agent family must resolve through the host's explicit
aliases; an unmapped `monospace` is refused, and bold without a bold face stays
a refused synthesized face (see the weight rule below). Em margins need the host text size, so the
geometry-only path refuses them. A size that is not fixed by an absolute
length (the initial `medium` keyword, user-agent scales and percentages of
them) computes to at least Chrome's minimum logical font size,
`layout::MINIMUM_LOGICAL_FONT_SIZE` (observed in headless Chrome 156 with a
fresh profile), for shaping, normal and numeric line heights and percentage
`line-height`. Absolute lengths keep their value, and em margins and
descendant percentages keep deriving from the unclamped specified size: with
16px `medium`, `div { font-size: 50% } > span` draws at the minimum,
`> span { font-size: 200% }` at 16px and `p { font-size: 50% }` keeps 8px
margins, while `div { font-size: 8px } > span` stays 8px.

`white-space: pre` preserves spaces, tabs and forced breaks and never wraps
softly; tabs advance to tab stops and trailing spaces count in the line's width
([native preserved white space](#native-preserved-white-space)). A `li` whose display is the
user-agent `list-item` paints an outside marker: `ul` items a disc, a `ul`
inside one list a circle and inside two or more a square, `ol` items `N. ` with
the `list-item` counter over rendered sibling items. Symbols follow Blink's
integer arithmetic on the item font's rounded ascent `a` in CSS pixels, with
`o = ⌊2a/3⌋`: a marker box starting `o+8` pixels before the content edge and
`⌊(o+1)/2⌋+2` pixels wide holds, one pixel inside its left edge, a square of
side `⌊(o+1)/2⌋` whose top is `⌊3(a−o)/2⌋` below `baseline − a` (the top of
the font's rounded content area on the marker baseline), with its edges rounded
to whole CSS pixels; a disc fills, a circle strokes a one-pixel ring centered
on the inscribed ellipse. Decimal text ends at the content edge in the item's
font and color. The marker aligns with the first line baseline found in the
item's leading content (through nested blocks) and its box, the line box united
with the font's content area, is the item's pointer target and part of its
frame bounds. Markers never change layout. Marker resolution walks the tree
once, counts each `ol`'s items in one pass over its children and debits the
frame's existing native inline work allowance per visited node, counted child,
item path element and examined baseline child; exhausting it refuses the frame
with the layout limit error. An item without
a line, an item with a non-visible overflow, an `ol` item that is not a direct
child and a missing font are refused. Ordinal attributes, `list-style`, marker
`font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` feature shaping and `::marker` styling are
not admitted.

`text-align: left | center | right` is inherited along the element path and
applied with Parley alignment to lines broken at the box's definite width, after
inline edges, so wrapped, decorated and bidirectional lines move as whole lines;
overflowing lines stay at the start edge. CSS `direction` is always `ltr`, while
the shaper derives a paragraph's base direction from its first strong character;
center/right alignment of a right-to-left-based paragraph is refused. Field text,
caret and selection geometry ignore alignment; an authored `text-align` on a
field is refused.

`text-overflow: ellipsis` with `overflow: hidden` truncates a single unbroken
line (`nowrap` or `pre`) of an inline formatting root without inline paint
decorations or edges; `clip` and a visible overflow are no-ops, and a scroll
container, wrapping text, forced breaks, decorated inline content and
right-to-left runs are refused. The ellipsis is U+2026 (three full stops if the
resolved families do not map it) in the root's font and color, placed after the
last whole cluster or ligature that fits before the content edge minus its width;
an overflowing line is start-aligned first. As in Chrome, truncation only hides
glyphs: element geometry and pointer fragments stay untruncated, so hidden text
positions still hit their element, and the accessible name keeps the full text.
The truncated projection shares the existing fragment and inline-work allowances.

Native `rem` resolution uses `Environment::root_font_size`, a host-supplied
document-root reference in CSS pixels, initially the subset's initial font size.
It is independent of the shaper's default text size and the view root's own
`font-size`: the official browser root lives inside a shadow tree, where `rem`
still refers to the containing document root. An embedding comparison sets the
native reference to that document's computed root size. Native standalone hosts
retain the initial default unless explicitly configured. No OS font lookup or
new guest operation is involved. `ViewLayout::with_root_font_size` applies the
reference before the initial guest turn; later environment and viewport updates
retain the configured reference unless the host supplies a different one.

The reference must be finite and within 0..=1000000 CSS pixels. Invalid setters
and native layout reject with `LayoutError::RootFont`; zero is valid for geometry,
while existing text-size minima still apply. Rust environment literals can retain
the default with `..Environment::default()`. This is an embedding API extension,
not a wire/host-ABI change; scripted viewport JSON still defaults to the initial
reference. Existing media-query parsing continues to use its separate initial-
font reference, unaffected by author document/view font changes.

One native converter handles pixel/rem lengths, signed offsets/margins,
percentages and auto margins. It checks both the numeric coefficient and the
resolved length against the existing 1000000 magnitude ceiling, preserving each
property's signed/nonnegative rule. Grid dimensions are converted as complete
tokens before the bounded track parser, including nested minmax/repeat tracks.
Geometry, font sizes, absolute line heights, border widths, outline widths and
signed outline offsets use the same host reference; DPI scaling follows logical
CSS conversion. Zero radii use the existing rectangular paint path. The open
native painting batch adds rounded backgrounds and common-color borders/outline
contours for static boxes with
visible descendant overflow (or no descendants), while existing rectangular
ancestor clips still apply. One-to-four px/rem/percentage radii share the CSS
side-overlap normalization; large finite values normalize before multiplication.
Only the element's own border-box hit region uses its rounded contour: visible
text/descendant fragments keep their independent hits. The same neutral cubic
path is used by ordinary, retained and vector software consumers. Padding-edge
radii subtract adjacent border widths without a second normalization. If an
inner arc extends past the opposite padding edge, four axis half-plane
passes clip its contour to that rectangle, preserving cubic segments. The shared
line/cubic clipper also supports diagonal planes: it splits a projected cubic at
its derivative roots before a fixed48-step crossing search, including two
crossings when the arc endpoints lie on the same side. Monotone control values
skip that root analysis. Plane normalization rejects nonfinite coefficients;
closed outer/hole components stay separate under the caller's fill rule. This
geometry is shared with mixed side colors, whose native CPU painter is described
below. The
border uses an even-odd outer/inner path, retaining transparent holes. Outline
radii follow the border curve; very negative offsets retain an outer width and
height of at least twice the outline width, independently per axis. Large-radius
quarter ellipses use up to eight tangent cubics, with an error target and a source
f32 precision floor. These are host geometry choices, not new guest limits.
Rounded overflow padding edges now form closed physical clip chains for static
box descendants. CPU reference, retained replay and the neutral drawing data
carry the same paths; `DrawClip` exposes immutable segments/parents to the GPU
consumer. Per-region hit records retain their proper inherited/content chain,
while outlines and top-layer select popups restore the intended scope. Empty
clips paint and hit nothing. Reusable software masking reserves three viewport
buffers, independent of depth; existing rectangle-only paths stay separate.
Strictly interior primitives/damage omit complex masks with an AA/coordinate
rounding safety margin. A cache-capacity overflow preserves the same clips when
flushing and continuing ordinary rasterization. Repeating an identical immediate
clip reuses its scope rather than multiplying the same AA fringe again. Native
fields, checkables and collapsed selects clip their content to the inset content
curve; their backgrounds/borders/outlines retain their own scope. Buttons keep
visible descendant overflow unless their overflow style clips it. Native field,
assistive character and IME visibility now use these same closed physical shapes,
separately from full logical advances. Inline backgrounds now have sliced rounded
contours as above; inline borders/outlines and direct GPU
group composition remain open (direct GPU color fields are described with the
side-color painter below). The Debug Metal fixture
probe covers boxes and native controls against shared input geometry and the
existing RGB mean-error threshold; it does not establish application/window/
VoiceOver or other-target acceptance. Raw view styles/custom values and snapshots
retain their authored units.

Native static box opacity is an isolated subtree operation: paint the box's own
background, border, contents, descendants and outline, then apply its opacity
once. Overlapping children must not receive that opacity separately. Nested groups
compose atomically in their containing context. Zero opacity suppresses pixel work while preserving
ordinary input/text geometry; root opacity includes the root background. Select
popups retain their established top-layer scope.
Each static box with opacity below1 creates a zero-level context. An iterative
source traversal postpones that whole subtree until ordinary content in its
nearest root/opacity context has painted; sibling contexts then paint in source
order. Descendant contexts lift through nonisolating block/flex/grid ancestors,
retaining those ancestors' original rectangular/curved clips, and never escape
an opacity context. The same traversal orders hit regions, including invisible
zero-opacity contexts. Creating/removing a context can conservatively invalidate
`same_input_geometry` even when its boxes do not overlap. This follows the
[CSS Color4 context placement rule](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-color-4/#transparency).
An explicit bounded paint-phase scheduler draws ordinary descendant block
backgrounds before inline content, then zero-level contexts and outlines. Flex/grid
items and replaced controls paint atomically in the content phase; these pseudo
contexts let descendant opacity contexts join the nearest real context. Original
ancestor clips survive deferral. Text pointer regions use occupied line fragments,
including their font-box height, rather than the anonymous block's available width.
Positioned boxes and z-index layers follow
[native positioned painting](#native-positioned-painting-and-stacking).
Paragraph text paints with its containing vertical origin rounded in CSS paint
pixels before DPI scaling. Horizontal positions and intrinsic per-line/font/glyph
offsets remain fractional. This is a paint-only adjustment: logical bounds,
fragment hits and selection geometry retain their authored fractional positions.
The position-independent unhinted outline cache is unchanged. Native field ink
keeps its existing direct shaped-control path.
