Native inline opacity now uses the same isolated-subtree compositor. Rich text is
shaped once across opacity boundaries; a cross-source ligature retains its first
source owner. Flows with nonunit inline opacity or painted inline backgrounds
capture a temporary source program; undecorated text keeps its direct glyph path.
Ordinary hit fragments are sorted by line and source even on that direct path. Capture retains logical rectangle clips and original physical clip
chains; scope removal happens when its context paints, so inherited clips apply
to the completed group once. Each glyph outline is prepared once, and source work
is charged during preparation, never renewed for a context. The source-derived
frame-command ceiling also bounds capture; the retained cache is unchanged.

Fragment line identities and source-node ordinals order backgrounds, glyphs and
hits within each context. This preserves later-line backgrounds covering earlier
ink when line boxes overlap. Inline contexts join their nearest root/opacity
context's deferred queue, including through nonisolating block ancestors; nested
inline contexts remain atomic. Opacity0 retains targets while skipping contour/
glyph pixel work. A large captured program takes temporary CPU replay, then a
smaller frame recovers ordinary cache reuse and vector output when isolation is
removed. Direct GPU group composition remains open.

Native decoration now rounds paint edges separately from layout. Box backgrounds,
borders, outlines and curved overflow share the snapped box; percentage radii
still resolve against the logical box before normalization against paint extents.
Broken inline decorations take paint radii from the floored fragment dimensions
and install them on the snapped continuous strip, matching Blink's
[contoured border construction](https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/main/third_party/blink/renderer/core/paint/contoured_border_geometry.cc)
and inline fragment override. Wide strip coordinates remain f64 through local
clipping. Paint rounding occurs in CSS paint pixels **before DPI scaling**;
Chrome diagnostics at1×/1.25×/2× confirm identical background pixels at3px,3.25px
and3.49px offsets, then changed pixels at3.51px. The tiny positive paint-size
floor affects rasterization, never source admission or layout dimensions.

Clip chains retain independent logical bounds/curves and physical paint paths.
Pointer, text-range, IME and assistive queries use logical geometry even when a
tiny positive source clip has no painted pixel. Pixel consumers and neutral GPU
commands use the snapped paths; mask-elision safety margins remain conservative.
Glyph coordinates keep their subpixel offsets. The implicit canvas retains its
physical far edges at nonintegral DPI, so rounding a CSS viewport dimension does
not leave an unpainted last row or column. Raw authored styles remain unchanged.

The original33-scene Chrome comparison at1× now passes its unchanged2/255 mean
bound, including the earlier fractional curves. Broader DPI/text raster parity
remains separate acceptance work; neither glyph coordinates nor thresholds are
changed to hide remaining font/clip differences at fractional DPI.

The private software program has balanced enter/exit markers checked before any
destination effect. An explicit stack and reusable 128×128 RGBA tiles bound pixel
layers by the existing native box depth plus the root (less than9MiB of layer
payload), independently of viewport dimensions. This is not a total renderer/RSS
bound: source commands, retained images, a reusable path-coverage mask and the
existing clip masks remain separate. Paths crossing tiles use global physical AA
coverage to avoid tile-local curve seams. Ancestor rectangular/curved scopes apply
when the completed layer is composited; child draws carry only scopes introduced
inside it. Raw source clips still define hit/text/IME metadata. Pointer-keyed
relative-scope memo entries retain their source chains, including the validated
base, until the frame cache is dropped; freed addresses must never identify a
different scope. Separate additive groups can accumulate complementary AA pieces
before ordinary source-over composition, without an opaque under-paint; this is
foundation retained separately from the single-field side-color painter below.

The retained scene limits remain65536 commands/16MiB. If an isolated frame exceeds
them, a fallibly allocated temporary program is bounded by the unchanged native
text-work, box and inline-fragment ceilings, rendered once and dropped. It is not
a larger retained cache. Ordinary earlier pixels survive if recording starts
after a streamed prefix; following draws and masks stay ordered. Source execution,
layout and shaping are not repeated to build layers. A subsequent small frame
recovers normal retention. Group preparation returns explicit software pixels
under the existing vector/GPU contract; repeated preparation retains those CPU
pixels and local mutations replay their damage. Switching back to vector commands
invalidates old CPU pixels. The desktop's existing raster fallback disables GPU
presentation; no layer textures, larger GPU allowance or direct GPU group support
is inferred. Actual window, platform accessibility and release acceptance remain
separate requirements.

Distinct native border-side colors use one premultiplied color field over the
same closed even-odd ring; the outer edge and hole coverage are applied once.
There is no opaque under-paint or repeated source-over at internal color seams.
The existing one-color path remains the fast vector path. Color ownership follows
the first inward-moving padding edge/arc to reach a point, using the admitted
inset radii without re-normalization. Within a corner the angle split is monotone
in the adjacent width ratio, with exact zero-width donation. This is the native
choice within CSS Backgrounds3§4.4's underdefined transition mapping, not a claim
of pixel identity with a particular browser. Large asymmetric corners compare
actual curved fronts with opposite edges; whole-ring weighted nearest-edge and
midpoint-only partitions are insufficient. Ordinary one-corner ownership uses an
analytic sign test. Opposing corner fronts use a search bounded by48 steps.
If exactly one front has arrived at a tested depth, it is already proven first
and its analytic angle test decides ownership immediately. Close or tied fronts
retain the bounded search. Uniform-block interval checks likewise stop as soon
as separation is proved or overlapping arrival intervals disprove that shortcut;
they do not approximate roots to a smaller fixed iteration count.

The existing contour mask skips empty color blocks and restricts partial blocks
to the bounding rectangle of whole nonzero-mask pixels before testing ownership.
This adds no mask or retained storage and includes the full sampling area of
every contributing pixel. Color blocks are filled uniformly only after interval
bounds prove their owner;
remaining pixels use center/corner color probes, with differing probes triggering
a fixed rotated16-sample pattern near color seams. This is a fixed native AA policy,
not exact analytic color integration or a particular browser's raster. Samples are
averaged in premultiplied space and normalized over the ring; curve coverage
still comes from the shared raster path, not sampled replacement geometry. Global
physical coordinates preserve tile phase. The software painter's private
color-field command uses one reusable extra128×128 RGBA tile, independent of
depth, and the existing global coverage/clip masks; software rendering shares
retained damage and source-derived overflow/prefix handling with groups.
Fractional pixel bounds enclose each edge independently: flooring the origin and
ceiling only the width/height can omit the last partial row/column.

Vector preparation (`Renderer::prepare`) lowers each field instead of returning
CPU fallback: `DrawPrimitive::ColorField` carries the closed even-odd contour,
transformed like a path, and disjoint `ColorCell` rectangles with integral
physical-pixel edges and unpremultiplied sRGB colors. Every pixel inside the
contour or crossed by one of its edges takes exactly the software painter's color
(the same partition, block proofs and sampling); other pixels are unconstrained,
so a run of one color may bridge the hole. Lowering scans bands of eight rows
with one band-sized coverage mask, marking the filled contour plus a stroked
outline two physical pixels wide, because band-local antialiasing is not
invariant under the band offset and can read zero on a thin taper that the global
mask covers. Equal runs merge, and rows repeating a run extend its rectangle.
Cells start at nonnegative coordinates and stop at the validated 4096-pixel
viewport edge. Contour segments are charged to the unchanged 16MiB scene budget
before allocation, like any path. Lowering itself must fit the remaining budget at
its peak: the band mask and color row, the transformed contour and its stroked
outline (charged once stroked; both are proportional to the already charged
contour), the cell lists counted by allocated capacity, including a growing
list's old buffer, and the converted cells, which are collected into the shared
slice in one exact allocation. Afterwards only the retained cells stay charged. A
field that does not fit makes the whole frame take the existing explicit software
fallback (unit-tested at the display-list level). An equal border at the
same physical placement reuses its lowered field from the existing 8MiB
neutral-path cache. The GPU consumer pushes the contour as an even-odd clip and
fills each cell inside it: contour coverage applies once and cells never overlap,
so no color seam is composited twice and no layer or intermediate texture is
needed. The software `DisplayList::rasterize` consumer builds one viewport
coverage mask from the contour and the command's clips, then fills each cell
through it, so a field costs one mask plus its cells' area rather than a mask per
cell; it matches the CPU painter within one channel unit in the border-color
tests. CPU `Renderer::render` keeps retained damage for mixed borders. This adds
one host-side `varta-view` drawing primitive; the guest ABI and view protocol
acquire no operation. Isolated opacity groups still use explicit CPU fallback.

`overflow-wrap: normal` and `anywhere` inherit and participate in line breaking
and flex/grid minimum-content sizing; `nowrap` still suppresses soft breaks.
For a supported `p`, default vertical margins are one supplied-font em unless
overridden by the cascade; text-aware paragraphs also admit the inline-only contexts above.
`display: none` subtrees produce zero rectangles without measuring or validating
their hidden layout contents; visible unsupported content still fails closed.
Vertical scroll offsets for `overflow: auto` and `hidden` affect descendant
rectangles and are bounded by the computed scrollable content; fixed and
absolute positioning use their respective viewport and containing block.
The separate `layout_geometry` and `layout_geometry_with_text` APIs also expose
the viewport and rectangular ancestor clipping bounds for each box. Nested
overflow clips use padding boxes; fixed and absolute descendants follow their
viewport and containing-block clip chains. These bounds are for a host renderer:
they do not paint, model rounded clips, or implement hit testing. Geometry uses
overlay scrollbars and does not implement horizontal scrolling; it does not
change the stored scroll state or snapshots.
Native layout construction uses an explicit enter/exit work list, resolving one
node's styles before visiting the next and attaching ordered native children on
exit. It keeps the existing 128-depth/4096-box limits and prunes hidden/rich-text/
select contents as before; it does not retain large recursive style frames or
increase host thread stacks. Scheduling is bounded before extending the list.

The experimental `rasterize_boxes` API uses a bounded, transparent CPU image
with premultiplied RGBA8 pixels. It paints solid CSS background colors for the
supported box tree in the stacking order of
[native positioned painting](#native-positioned-painting-and-stacking),
respecting rectangular ancestor clips. Solid rectangular borders with a common color across visible
sides use the CSS border cascade, including inherited `currentcolor` and
shorthand resets. `rasterize_with_text` also paints the supported shaped text
using the host's explicit fonts and bounded unhinted glyph outlines; it shares
the text layout restrictions and rejects synthetic font styling and decoration.
The box-only variant rejects text. Buttons, text/search/password/number inputs and
textareas are paintable with the user-agent defaults of
[native control defaults](#native-control-defaults), themed or author-styled;
a select still needs explicit box, font, foreground and background styles, an
admitted radius and an explicit outline style. Text inputs paint
their value, keyboard selection and a non-blinking caret; missing glyphs use the supplied font's
`.notdef` outline. Each nonempty field reuses one shaped layout for glyph painting,
caret/selection geometry and source-position hit testing, rather than retaining a
second layout for painting. Ordinary values and placeholders are borrowed;
composition overlays and password masks own only their required display buffer.
The public shaper and general text path keep their 64 KiB UTF-8 allowance.
Private field display requests instead validate the existing 32768-UTF-16-unit
value bound and its derived 98304-byte UTF-8 reservation, including placeholders
and the combined IME replacement. This permits fewer scalar inputs than the
public path's ASCII maximum; aggregate layout/paint and glyph limits still apply.
The pinned Parley 0.11.1 dependency is locally patched to use wide cluster text
byte offsets and glyph/coverage counts, preserving whole-run contextual shaping,
bidi and source indices without count wrapping or inline-sentinel collisions.
Font coverage scans the complete grapheme without a fixed scratch prefix; only
a better candidate updates nominal glyph IDs in a second allocation-free pass.
See `vendor/parley/VARTA-PATCH.md` and its diff for provenance and exact changes. The text host additionally requests at most 65536 completed glyphs across a
layout, 262144 intermediate slots in each HarfRust glyph-info/position array and
an initial allowance of one million upstream-charged operations across its runs. Successful reusable
arrays retain at most 65536 slots each; refusal discards them. Source reservation
uses scalars, not encoded bytes. Incomplete shaping is detected before copying
glyphs into layout or calculating text metrics. The pinned HarfRust 0.12.0 local
patch supplies limits/status/accounting; context cloning preserves the limits.
The Varta adapter also shares 16777216 charged operations across an outer native
view request: intrinsic measurement, Taffy remeasurement and painting for one
raster; one geometry/box query; or all layout commands in one `commit_with_layout`
batch. Nested calls reuse the active scope and cannot reset it. A temporary
Parley operation ceiling uses the lesser of that remaining allowance and the
per-layout limit. Both successful and refused charged work is accounted before
returning; a guard releases the scope on normal/error/unwind exit. Standalone
measurements retain their independent per-layout profile. The diagnostic
`TextMeasurer::last_view_shaping_operations()` reports the most recent outer view
request using that measurer, including failed work; it is not a CPU/RSS metric.
The scope uses pointer-sized atomics without changing the measurer's thread
traits. Budget-state unwind cleanup does not prove arbitrary dependency-cache
unwind safety.

Taffy's measurement callback cannot propagate failure directly. After its first
text error (including aggregate measurement-work refusal), that geometry pass
uses only the intrinsic fallback metrics for further callbacks; it does not
construct more text builders, re-run font analysis or overwrite the first text
diagnostic. The complete geometry is then rejected before publication or paint.
A failed layout command also rejects its transaction before deferred effects.
This stops text preparation for an already rejected pass; it does not interrupt
Taffy's remaining traversal or permanently poison later independent requests.

These are draft native-host request bounds. Array capacity totals are at most
10 MiB (2.5 MiB retained), excluding allocator/reallocation overlap and other
buffers. All upstream debit sites now reserve their full amount before the corresponding
mutation/allocation/transition; unaffordable work refuses without overspending.
An exactly consumed budget remains successful when no more charged work is
needed. The charged meter still excludes some parser/Unicode-analysis/plan work;
no complete RSS or wall-clock deadline guarantee follows. Fonts with excessive
glyph/outline expansion can still hit the resource budgets; complete backend
memory/platform acceptance remains open.
Other controls and differently colored border sides still fail explicitly;
positioned elements and stacking follow
[native positioned painting](#native-positioned-painting-and-stacking). Static rounded boxes and the explicit controls
above use the shared corner/clip pipeline described earlier.
Password painting shapes one `•` per extended grapheme, including transient
preedit, with source-byte positions retained for hit testing and selection.
Guest values and input events retain the original text. Selection, caret,
horizontal clipping and Undo use the same editing model as text fields;
placeholders remain unmasked. The supplied font provides the mask glyph or its
`.notdef` outline, under the unchanged shaping bounds. This matches the sampled
Chrome password caret behavior; sampled WebKit uses UTF-16-unit masks instead,
so full cross-browser password editing parity remains open. Native search fields
use plain text editing; a platform search-clear affordance is not supplied.
Native Tab builds one document/form/name partition for all radio groups and
reuses it through the navigation step, including checked/disabled/hidden members.
It does not scan the complete tree for each distinct name. The partition is
transient, so a later name/form mutation is reflected on the next key. Membership
checks use node sets; activation reuses its captured peer states for unchecking
and cancellation. CSS/display work and all-target input performance remain
separate acceptance work.

Explicitly styled checkbox/radio inputs use the same rectangular box subset and
paint a scalable check mark or circular checked dot in `currentcolor`, clipped
to the content box and ancestor scrollports. They require explicit foreground,
background, outline and geometry, with zero border radius, and need no font.
Unchecked controls paint their specified box without a mark. Checkbox/radio
inputs without author box styles paint Chrome's theme instead
([native control defaults](#native-control-defaults)); indeterminate checkbox
state is not supplied.
Radio groups follow the [shared ownership rules](embedding.md#view-protocol-draft-v0-unstable)
in both native and browser models. Unmodified arrow keys move and activate within
the visible, enabled group in document order, wrapping at either end; Left/Up
move backward and Right/Down forward. Tab visits its checked eligible member,
or the first eligible member in the traversal direction when none is checked.
Leaving a radio skips its remaining group peers. Space activates either control.
Keydown prevention stops the default action; click prevention restores the group
after preactivation, without a field edit or counter increment. Checking a peer
does not emit a second edit for the automatically unchecked radio.
Explicitly styled single-select controls paint the selected label and an arrow.
Their transient popup paints above the ordinary scene, stays inside the window
and scrolls a bounded row viewport independently of ancestor scrollports. Option
subtrees have no ordinary layout boxes. Pointer choice, wheel scrolling, keyboard
preview/accept/cancel and character cycling use concrete option identities;
disabled or hidden options are skipped. Focus loss dismisses the popup. Relevant
guest mutations close it, and stale-frame input is discarded. Option styling is
limited to display and foreground color; platform themes and
timed multi-character search remain open. Native and browser transactions share
the [single-select work admission rules](embedding.md#view-protocol-draft-v0-unstable):
ownership walks, option source bytes and final inventory consume one allowance.
Accounting precedes selection mutations/derived-value validation, includes detached options and
rejects atomically. Admission is independent of locally edited value/sequence state
that may still await Worker delivery. Consecutive identical select writes share a
lookup; stale/equal patches retain their selection/value no-op semantics. DOM replay
skips those duplicates while preserving original indices for prepared fonts,
resources and stylesheets.
For select typeahead, a character key with no committed text uses its logical key
as the prefix after keydown prevention and modifier checks. Text-field insertion
continues to require committed text. The preview's macOS keyboard, pointer,
scrolling, cancellation and character-input observations are recorded in
[history](history.md#native-form-controls--2026-11-02); other-platform and complete
input-method acceptance remain open.
TSX initializes a select's value after inserting its options. Dynamic value getters
still execute once in attribute source order under the reactive runner, retain
their subscriptions and precede refs; the final assignment reuses the cached value.
Solid rectangular outlines support explicit pixel widths, colors and offsets,
including focus-visible styles and shorthand/longhand cascade. They paint after
the element's contents, clip to ancestor bounds, do not affect layout and do not
extend hit regions. Rounded outlines remain open; the platform-default focus ring
of controls is part of [native control defaults](#native-control-defaults).
Empty text inputs display Chrome's light-scheme placeholder gray without changing
the field value or selection; IME preedit hides it. Placeholder pseudo-element
styling remains open.
Disabled buttons and text inputs do not activate or accept edits; their default
disabled colors are part of [native control defaults](#native-control-defaults).
Setting `disabled` or `readonly` clears transient IME preedit.
For a focused input that subsequently becomes disabled, Varta can still deliver
keydown but Enter does not submit its form. In a focused test Chrome did not
submit, whereas WebKit submitted; complete cross-browser parity remains open.
The experimental desktop preview uses these CPU images. Its retained-renderer/
pointer implementation and the TSX Showcase are committed in `be85c981` with
scoped local verification; later consolidated gates cover their code inputs.
See the [current UI checkpoint](development-plan.md#current-ui-checkpoint-and-proposed-continuation)
for evidence and remaining acceptance. The browser/native Showcase comparison
also records root/control sizing and OS accessibility gaps; a shared patch stream
does not yet establish complete visual or platform parity.
Explicitly styled textareas preserve newlines, wrap long text to the content
width, paint multiline selection/caret and keep the caret vertically visible.
Physical two-dimensional text hit testing places and selects text across rows.
Wheel/trackpad input scrolls the text with bounded offsets and ancestor chaining.
Editing or changing the selection restores caret-following; unchanged guest echoes
preserve a manual scroll. Frame geometry clamps the requested offset, as for
other scrollports. Unmodified Up/Down and Home/End use shaped visual lines;
Shift extends the selection, and a preferred horizontal position survives short
intermediate lines. Frame-derived moves validate UTF-8 boundaries and honor
keydown prevention before applying selection changes. Undo preserves soft-wrap
caret affinity. Explicit-width textareas also support `field-sizing: content`
with absent or automatic height, wrapping within the content width and respecting
explicit minimum/maximum heights. Empty fields reserve one text line; a placeholder
or IME preedit contributes to measurement. Host-supplied fonts and the text shaping
limits apply. `resize: none` is accepted; interactive resize handles, modifier
shortcuts and full bidi navigation remain open.
An experimental scaled raster API keeps geometry and font sizes in CSS pixels
while drawing paths directly into a physical-resolution image. Hit regions,
text hit positions and IME cursor areas use physical coordinates; scroll offsets
remain in CSS pixels. Pixel allocations retain the existing image bounds. The
desktop preview uses the window scale factor at startup and after DPI changes,
updates logical viewport conditions and rejects frames/inputs for obsolete
scales. Pixel-based wheel deltas are converted to CSS pixels.
Native wheel records carry the frame's CSS-pixel `scrollHeight` and `clientHeight`
as well as its new offset. Textarea metrics include padding and exclude borders.
Measured host inputs reject non-finite, negative or inconsistent geometry before
mutating the view; basic unmeasured script scroll inputs retain their old behavior.
An application host may request the current CPU frame between guest turns via
`Application::view_rasterize`, with the same bounds and fail-closed subset.
Hosts can instead keep a `varta_view::Renderer` and call
`Application::view_render` between turns. The desktop preview uses this path.
It owns explicit fonts, memoizes computed style reads, expanded geometry
declarations, border widths and shaped text, retains
portable unhinted glyph outlines, optional host glyph coverage and a bounded
display list, and replays changed pixel
bounds. Hit, focus, selection and IME metadata are rebuilt for each frame even
when its pixels do not change. Media conditions, style sources, element
identity/parentage, inline side precedence, focus, pointer, checked and disabled states invalidate style reads;
text, editor and scroll state remain fresh inputs to layout and painting.
The live view never holds render-only memoized state. Stateless raster APIs
remain available as reference paths. Both paths route narrow rectangles through
the path converter to handle fractional one-pixel carets without a debug assertion.

Renderer cache bounds are 128 shaped requests with 2 MiB of key payload and
65,536 glyphs, 4,096 shared glyph entries with 8 MiB of estimated payload
(including outlines, coverage rectangles and host-retained font bytes),
4,096 pure CSS validation/variable-detection entries with 2 MiB of string
payload, and 65,536 display-list commands with 16 MiB of estimated payload.
Eviction or a display-list overflow changes reuse, not admission; an overflow
falls back to full painting with the original clips. Cached shaping and glyph
outlines still debit the original native work charges. Existing image, text,
depth and work ceilings remain in force. Geometry-read memos have at most one
property map and border-width tuple per prepared visible node, within the
admitted tree inventory. Retained pixels and a scratch image stay within the
existing image dimensions; these cache accounting limits are
not total allocator or RSS quotas. A failed frame publishes neither pixels nor
new input metadata. `Renderer::damage` reports physical pixel bounds;
`Renderer::stats` reports avoided-work counts, not CPU timings. The preview
also keeps packed RGB pixels, converts only damaged regions and copies those
packed pixels on the window thread. Debug builds retain Varta debug assertions
and unoptimized engine code while optimizing the tiny-skia graphics dependencies
and enabling their portable SIMD paths. The small desktop host uses dev opt-level
3 for its RGB packing loop, with debug assertions and debug information retained;
the compiler, runtime and view engine remain at dev opt-level 0.
Hosts may install a `GlyphRasterizer` with `Renderer::set_glyph_rasterizer`;
replacement clears retained pixels and glyph data. The stateless reference APIs
and a new renderer without a provider keep the portable outline path. Shaping,
font selection, glyph identifiers, advances, bidi and logical hit/selection data
remain in Varta. Requests carry the selected immutable font bytes, collection
index, normalized coordinates, physical size, horizontal quarter-pixel phase
and existing resource allowances. The baseline for coverage is integer-aligned
in physical pixels; paragraph-origin rounding remains a separate earlier step.
A provider may decline; it must not substitute a font or glyph.

A host returns checked integer ink bounds, followed by one-byte grayscale
coverage. Varta validates dimensions, length, offset arithmetic and the existing
one-million-cell text preparation bound before producing commands. Disjoint
coverage runs merge vertically only when their x extent and alpha agree. They
use existing physical rectangle commands, clips and isolated composition: no
new image/GPU texture resource or display-list allowance is introduced. Visible
coverage cells debit the shared text work identically on cache hits and misses;
nonintersecting glyph bounds skip pixel preparation without erasing logical hits.
An unaffordable optional coverage request selects the original outline path
without renewing that allowance. Hidden groups request no host ink. Provider
font bytes share the existing glyph-cache ceiling, and an oversized provider is
dropped. These remain logical cache estimates, not OS font-cache/RSS quotas.
`RenderStats::raster_glyphs` and `outline_glyphs` distinguish preparation paths;
neither counts actual GPU presentation.

The macOS preview installs the host-only CoreText adapter. It creates faces from
the supplied bytes without system discovery or process-wide registration, keeps
bounded face data, renders monochrome glyph coverage with platform smoothing,
and preserves the existing outline fallback for color fonts, resource refusal
or unsupported platform instances. It instantiates the exact selected face: a
collection member is rebuilt as a standalone face from that member's own
tables (CoreText's `head` table and glyph count must then match the member),
and a variation instance is a CoreGraphics copy of the face with every `fvar`
axis set to the user value whose default normalization followed by the `avar`
(version 1) map yields the shaper's normalized coordinate. No font is looked up
by name. CoreGraphics keys variation values by axis names of its own choosing
(its Mac name record wins over the Windows one; the names are never localised)
and silently ignores an unknown key, so the adapter keys each `fvar` axis by the
name of CoreGraphics's axis record at the same index. CoreText's axis record at
that index must carry the axis's `fvar` tag, both records'
minimum/default/maximum must match `fvar`, and the record counts must be equal.
CoreText's axis names follow the process's preferred languages and are never
compared, so instances do not depend on the user's language. A mismatched tag,
range or count, two axes with one name, or an instance whose read-back values
differ from the requested ones are declined (`declined_variation`), never drawn
at the default instance. `sbix` faces draw in their own colours: the glyph is
drawn into a premultiplied RGBA context, as Chrome's CoreText scaler draws
colour glyphs, and the host returns it as a colour image
(`GlyphRasterMask::color`, premultiplied RGBA validated against its alpha and
kept unpremultiplied per pixel); the renderer keeps those colours, applies the
text colour's alpha, and places the image at the whole pixel nearest the
quarter-pixel position (`GlyphRasterizer::subpixel` is false), which Chrome
does too (a position past three eighths of a pixel takes the next one). An
`sbix` table without strikes is declined unless its exact bytes belong to a
registered platform face ([native fallback faces](#native-fallback-faces)).
Faces with other bitmap or color glyph tables (`COLR`, `CBDT`, `EBDT`,
`SVG `), an `opsz` axis (CoreText would size it from the point size while the
shaper keeps its default) or `avar` version 2 are declined, and their glyphs
keep the portable path. That path paints outlines in the text colour, so it
refuses a glyph a face draws in colour (every glyph of a face with `sbix`,
`CBDT` or `SVG ` tables, and a glyph its `COLR` table paints) rather than draw
it without its colours; it also takes over under a non-uniform scale. A face is charged its
standalone bytes (a collection member's own tables, not the whole file), twice
for a variable face whose copy CoreGraphics retains. At most 16 variation
instances are kept per face; each is charged a fixed 32 KiB native estimate
(a measured 6 to 20 KiB process footprint per instance on macOS 27), since
CoreGraphics's per-instance memory is not observable. Declined glyph requests
are counted by reason (`CoreTextRasterizer::statistics`).
The safe pinned `core-text=21.0.0` wrapper reuses the locked CoreGraphics0.24 and
CoreFoundation0.10 stack; only the desktop host depends on it, and it names that
stack's CoreFoundation types through the same locked `core-foundation=0.10.1`
to read CoreGraphics's and CoreText's axis records. This implements
the platform raster distinction visible in
[Skia's CoreText scaler](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google/skia/main/src/ports/SkScalerContext_mac_ct.cpp).
The same optional interface can serve other platform adapters; they are not
implemented by the macOS adapter. No Wasm ABI or capability grant changes.

Characters typed immediately after pointer activation wait in the bounded input
FIFO for its resulting focus frame, just as they wait for a preceding key turn.
Trusted embedders can call `View::set_pointer_state` or
`Application::view_set_pointer_state` between turns. The pointed element and its
attached ancestors match `:hover`; the indicated primary-down element and its
ancestors match `:active`, as in [CSS Selectors](https://www.w3.org/TR/selectors-4/#useraction-pseudos).
The targets carry opaque element identities: removal and numeric ID reuse cannot
transfer a pointer state to a replacement. With no host pointer input those
states stay inactive. Updating them does not create a guest event, activation,
commit, edit or user-gesture grant. The desktop host coalesces pointer position
and button state outside its bounded activation/key FIFO, resolves them only
against current presented geometry, and clears them on leave or focus loss.
Cosmetic repaints retain the model revision so they cannot swallow a pending
click or key; changed input geometry advances it and preserves stale-frame
rejection. Worker and window share the current immutable image with `Arc`,
without copying its pixel buffer for hit testing. Native cursor hints honor the
four checked CSS cursor values and inherit through inline fragments. An enabled
select row has separate pointer shading without changing keyboard preview or
committed selection.
The frame carries bounded rectangular hit regions in paint order. The desktop
preview uses those regions for left-button activation and discards events when
the view state or viewport has changed since the displayed frame. For vertical
wheel input it chooses the nearest `overflow: auto` ancestor with available
scroll range, propagates remaining movement outward and sends `scroll` events;
`overflow: hidden` remains programmatically scrollable but ignores the wheel.
The experimental geometry API can plan nearest-edge vertical scrolling through
nested auto and hidden scrollports without applying changes. Absolute and fixed
paths follow their containing block chain
([native positioned painting](#native-positioned-painting-and-stacking)). A separate experimental view API applies the plan atomically and
emits scroll records without a user-gesture grant. An application-host API
queues those records as later guest turns.
An opt-in layout-aware batch API executes `scroll_into_view` and `scroll_to`
in batch order, computing geometry at each command and atomically rejecting the
batch when layout is unsupported. Layout-dependent commands per batch are bounded
by the pending-command limit. Application hosts opt into this mode by supplying
an initial viewport and explicit font; the native preview does so before the
first turn and updates its geometry after resize. Other hosts retain their
existing behavior when they do not supply layout resources.
Scroll records produced within a batch retain the originating element's identity;
removing and recreating its numeric ID in that batch cannot redirect the record.
The experimental view API can capture an opaque identity for an attached
element and apply a deferred scroll only while that same element remains
attached. Removal and reuse of its numeric ID, including in another view or
divergent cloned tree, cannot redirect the action.
The preview forwards admitted keydown keys and modifiers to the focused element;
Tab uses the view's focus order and skips `display: none` subtrees. The host
updates viewport conditions before processing inputs and rendering after resize.
The native preview reads the window's system color scheme at startup and follows
theme changes through `prefers-color-scheme`. Frame and input checks include the
color scheme so events from a stale themed frame are discarded.
Guest `set_title` updates the native window title when its current frame is
presented. An empty guest title uses the preview's default title.
The preview supports direct keyboard insertion, grapheme-aware deletion,
arrow/Home/End navigation and Shift selection in focused text inputs. Space and
Backspace follow the view's keydown rules. Host edits that would
exceed the 64 KiB UTF-16 value limit are ignored without mutating the value.
Character keys dispatch `keydown` before insertion so `preventDefault` can stop
the edit. Ctrl/Command+A selects the input's text using the physical shortcut key;
printable Ctrl+Alt input remains available for AltGr layouts. IME composition
continues through the separate preedit/commit path.
Native text editing supports per-edit undo and redo, restoring the selection and
emitting an input record with a fresh edit sequence. History shares a one MiB
UTF-8 text budget and a 64-edit cap across the view. A changed guest `set_value`
starts a new history epoch; equal echoes and stale patches preserve history.
Successful commits immediately release history for removed fields and replaced
values; rejected batches leave history intact.
Ctrl/Command+Z undoes; Shift+Ctrl/Command+Z or Ctrl/Command+Y redoes. The host maps
physical shortcut keys for non-Latin layouts. Typing-run grouping and full browser
undo parity remain open.
The shared view's `select` command selects the complete text of a text, search or
password input or textarea without changing its value or edit sequence; a
later edit replaces that selection. It focuses an attached, enabled control and
dispatches focus records; number and checkable inputs receive focus but no text
selection. Detached and disabled controls do not receive focus. Chrome and WebKit
were checked for these cases; controls under `display: none` also retain the
previous focus. Firefox remains unverified.
Pointer clicks and same-window drags resolve shaped cluster positions from the
displayed frame; a drag applies its selection on release. The resulting offsets
are validated against the current UTF-8 value. Experimental IME preedit is
displayed without changing the field value; commit replaces the selection and
dispatches an input event. The preview positions the system candidate window at
the caret, bounds and validates incoming composition data, and cancels preedit
on focus changes or a guest view commit. Composition events are not exposed to
the guest and platform IME acceptance remains unverified. Host-owned native
clipboard defaults are implemented as described below; system/platform acceptance
is separate. Live drag highlighting and bidirectional visual navigation are not
yet provided by this preview. Native accessibility has the bounded foundation
described below. Firefox can delete
part of a ZWJ emoji sequence where this editor removes its whole grapheme;
cross-renderer equivalence for those cases remains open.
The native GUI backlog has separate host limits: 64 pending key/IME records and
1 MiB of retained owned text buffers; the GUI-to-worker channel remains eight
messages. `varta-desktop/src/input_queue.rs` owns those limits and accounting.
Ordinary key/character/IME-commit records remain FIFO. Only a consecutive preedit
for the same node and guest-commit binding replaces its predecessor. Check the
prospective count/bytes with the old record refunded before changing the queue or
compacting incoming text. Admitted strings release spare platform capacity, so a
short valid value is not refused solely because its incoming buffer was large;
retained `String` capacity equals its UTF-8 length. Rejection leaves the prior
queue/preedit intact and follows the preview's existing queue-full error/exit
policy, without truncating committed text. Pop, binding-filter retention and
focus-loss clear all release accounted capacity. Focus-loss cleanup uses the same
checked enqueue path. Existing per-key and IME value/cursor guards remain in force.
This is distinct from runtime event queues and whole-backend/RSS accounting.

**Host-owned native clipboard defaults.** The public host APIs
`View::clipboard_target`, `begin_clipboard` and `complete_clipboard`, and their
Application wrappers, describe a two-stage copy/cut/paste operation without
performing I/O in the headless engine. The native worker validates the presented
model/viewport/theme/scale before capturing the current field; there is no extra
selection/style projection on every frame. An opaque target binds source
identity, content revision and directional UTF-8 selection. A private nonce
admits one outstanding operation and one completion; foreign/replayed results
cannot consume another operation.

The original logical key and modifiers bubble as a trusted keydown. Static
`preventDefault` runs before a platform task exists. On a non-field target the
keydown still bubbles, without clipboard I/O or select typeahead. Disabled,
closed/hidden and composing fields cannot start I/O. Readonly fields allow copy;
password fields never offer default copy/cut. Cut deletes only after a successful
write and a fresh source/selection/focus check. Paste uses the same checks and
ordinary editor/Undo/maxlength path. Completion input events retain coalescing
and carry no new user-gesture authority; later guest changes and termination
invalidate pending edits. Guest `copy_text` retains its existing capability and
gesture rules. No clipboard-read import or frozen script/guest ABI change is added.

The desktop pins text-only `arboard` 3.7.0 (MIT OR Apache-2.0), with optional
Wayland data-control support and no image codecs. It is a desktop-only dependency;
the engine and runtime have no OS clipboard dependency. A lazy dedicated worker
owns the SDK object and executes one operation at a time through bounded channels.
The UI/application loops keep running; following keys wait in their existing
bounded FIFO until the completion frame. OS failures/refused reads preserve the
field and permit a later attempt. Retained read responses release spare capacity
and fit the existing field byte/UTF-16 allowance; oversized data is refused whole.
The SDK/OS transient read allocation is outside this retained-buffer accounting,
as are whole-backend/RSS guarantees.

Single-line paste trims trailing CR/LF and maps remaining line breaks to spaces;
textarea paste normalizes CRLF/CR to LF. UTF-16 maxlength truncation preserves
scalar boundaries. The single-line rule follows Chromium's
[`TextFieldInputType::FilterBeforeTextInserted`](https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/main/third_party/blink/renderer/core/html/forms/text_field_input_type.cc);
this does not establish browser/platform equivalence. Source copies keep original
bytes. Physical Command+C/X/V on macOS and Control+C/X/V elsewhere preserve
shortcuts under non-Latin layouts; Control+Insert and Shift+Insert/Delete are also
recognized outside macOS. Actual system clipboard and target acceptance require
separate native observations.

**Native accessibility foundation.** The desktop host pins AccessKit 0.25.2 and
accesskit_winit 0.34.2 (Apache-2.0), installs the adapter before showing the winit
window and forwards its window events. These dependencies remain outside the
engine/runtime dependency graph. The host-only `View::accessibility_tree` and
`Application::view_accessibility_tree` return `Result<AccessibilityTree,
AccessibilityError>` with flat owned semantic data using the
same admitted roles and accessible-name algorithm as the headless snapshot.
Actionable roleless containers additionally appear as generic native nodes;
the established headless JSON output is unchanged. Password values are masked.
Caller-owned semantic copies, like ordinary snapshots, belong to the embedder.
No Wasm import, profile or ABI changes are introduced.

**Native text alternatives and observer limits.** `aria-describedby` contributes
a separate `description` to the typed native snapshot and AccessKit node. It
does not replace the accessible name or add fields to the established headless
JSON. Attached references are visited in attribute order, including repetitions;
missing references are skipped. Each referenced text alternative uses the
admitted name algorithm, including author labels, image alternatives, live
embedded control values and password masks. A relation starting at a hidden node
includes that hidden subtree; a visible referenced node excludes hidden descendants.
Whitespace is flattened by the existing ASCII rule. `describedby` is not followed
recursively; nested `labelledby` retains its existing finite traversal rule.
Empty/unresolved descriptions have no fallback because `aria-description` and
tooltip/title attributes are outside this subset. This follows the applicable
[AccName 1.2 description steps](https://www.w3.org/TR/2026/WD-accname-1.2-20261012/).

Before allocating native text alternatives, indexed numeric summaries preflight
all visible semantic names, actionable generic-container names and descriptions.
The observer has a fixed `ACCESSIBILITY_TEXT_WORK_LIMIT` of 8 MiB potential work,
using the existing name-cost node units and conservative future field-value
reservations. Description id-list bytes, per-reference lookup/separator work and
the referenced subtree summaries share that one allowance. Exceeding it returns
`AccessibilityError::WorkLimit`, with no partial tree or guest-state mutation.
Guest commit admission, its name-work recurrence, wire budgets and the existing
browser contract remain unchanged. Trusted action validation reads interaction
flags and visibility without evaluating a name or description.

The native snapshot carries the remaining preflight allowance into desktop
projection as `AccessibilityWork`; fields do not each receive a fresh allowance.
Curved visibility queries charge shape visits and reserve their maximum bounded
search work before searching. The solver intersects convex rounded rectangles
analytically: fixed-position cross sections define a convex feasibility gap,
followed by fixed ternary/binary searches for both projected extrema. Interior
queries use four-vertex containment. It allocates no viewport mask or shaped
layout. Zero-width carets and empty intersections are explicit. These potential
work units are not an instruction count or CPU-time guarantee. The focused
editable IME caret uses one independently bounded host query per frame, rather
than searching the carets of all unfocused fields.

The desktop host continues ordinary rendering/input after observer refusal.
At matching frame presentation it replaces the old native guest tree with a
host-owned static-text explanation, clears queued assistive actions and bindings,
and logs at most one observer warning per activation. Later successful projection
restores the guest tree with fresh monotonically allocated native IDs. Root and
refusal-message IDs are reserved outside guest-node allocation. This is an
observer resource limit, not a guest trap or a whole-backend memory guarantee.

Semantic snapshots are built only while the platform adapter is active. The GUI
publishes them after matching frame presentation, using visible element-fragment
unions in physical pixels. A source node keeps its native ID while its opaque
identity matches; replacement nodes receive monotonically allocated IDs, never
recycled within the bridge's lifetime. Deactivation clears cached trees,
bindings and queued actions, preserving the ID counter. Allocation exhaustion
clears action bindings before any further effect.

**Native logical field text.** Text fields expose owned logical text metadata
and auxiliary AccessKit TextRun children. Plain-field selection units follow the editor's
Unicode scalar boundaries, with CRLF grouped into one unit. Each run contains
at most 255 units so both word indices and end positions fit the adapter's u8
word-navigation representation. Long logical lines link adjacent chunks with
previous/next-on-line; LF and CRLF retain their original bytes, and a trailing
newline has an empty final line. Unicode word starts are independent of chunks.
The logical model retains hard lines. When a matching rendered frame is present,
the desktop projection uses its visual wrapping and directional spans instead.

The observer preflights a separate 4096 auxiliary-run ceiling and charges source
text and metadata work against its existing shared work allowance before
allocating. Exceeding the run ceiling returns `AccessibilityError::TextRunLimit`
through the same recoverable observer-refusal path. Guest live-node limits and
headless JSON do not change. Source UTF-8 offsets stay host-owned; native runs
carry displayed UTF-8 lengths for the platform adapter's UTF-16 conversion.
Password runs contain one mask per rendered grapheme and no original word/line
structure. This matches the renderer even for combining marks and joined emoji;
the established headless JSON mask count remains unchanged. Native password
selection endpoints follow those rendered grapheme boundaries.

`FrameMetadata::field_text_geometry` borrows the actual painted field clusters,
visual lines and content clip in physical pixels. Cluster ranges still address
original UTF-8, including for password masks. This data also drives ordinary
pointer navigation; the observer does not reshape text. The getter requires
matching opaque source and content identities and refuses transient IME display.
Bounds retain full advances while the content clip describes visibility.
`FieldTextGeometry::visible_bounds` intersects a physical query with the field
content rectangle and its curved ancestor/content chain under one caller-supplied
observer allowance. The getter retains source identity/revision/composition
checks. Text reveal continues to use full logical bounds rather than losing
unseen source ranges. CRLF
textareas retain the source pair and place keyboard End before the whole pair.
The desktop adapter splits source-ordered native runs by visual line, direction
the character-index bound and differing clipped vertical extents, with
previous/next-on-line links. Run bounds,
character positions and widths come from these clusters, clipped to the same
content rectangle/curved shapes as painting. Fully clipped units keep zero-area
geometry and their complete source mapping; this describes visible fragments rather than unbounded offscreen
glyph boxes. Combining-scalar interiors share the cluster's leading caret and
its final scalar advances to the trailing caret, matching painted byte-index
cursor snapping. Password spans additionally split whenever clipped widths or
steps cease to be uniform, as required by the adapter's password metric rules.

Native selection endpoints choose the visual position nearest the frame's actual
anchor/focus carets, preserving soft-wrap and bidi affinity. Collapsed selection
always uses the same native position for both endpoints. A native run ID can be
reused only for the same content revision and exact source-unit range; an equal
number of differently wrapped runs is insufficient. Previously decoded absolute
selections can survive layout-only acknowledgement frames, while removed run IDs
can no longer decode new callbacks. Missing/mismatched/composing geometry keeps
logical text without publishing invented character rectangles.

The shared auxiliary-run ceiling also bounds actual visual/directional spans,
which can exceed the logical model's count. Overflow uses the same explicit
observer refusal and fresh-ID recovery path, with no partial native update or
guest-state rejection. These host-side checks do not prove OS/VoiceOver acceptance.

Directional selection endpoints map exactly to source bytes. Disabled/composing
fields do not advertise selection; readonly fields permit selection while
rejecting edits. A pre-existing editor selection inside CRLF is unavailable to
the native observer without rounding or mutating it. Every range carries an
opaque content revision, separate from the wrapping field sequence. Actual
value changes, Undo/Redo and input-type changes rotate that revision; equal
value echoes and selection-only updates preserve it. Native run IDs are reused
only for the same content revision and are never recycled. Old, foreign-owner,
out-of-range and mismatched-generation endpoints are discarded before effects.

**Frame-dependent assistive scrolling (UI-2.4, in progress).** The host-only
`View::accessibility_input_from_frame` and matching Application API accept
vertical page/item movements, finite absolute offsets, edge-aligned element
reveal and revision-guarded text-range reveal. The acknowledged frame retains CSS layout boxes, original
source identities/topology, field content revisions and scroll state. The
desktop worker retains its model revision, viewport, theme and scale checks;
the core adds source/path/content/scroll guards before effects. Layout-free
assistive input ignores these frame-dependent actions.

Page metrics include the textarea's actual painted scroll range. Item movement
uses its shaped line height, or the root font size as the admitted approximation
for other containers. Absolute offsets are finite nonnegative typed values and
clamp to the measured maximum. Native scroll properties and incoming offsets
use physical node coordinates; the adapter converts offsets to CSS coordinates
using that frame's scale. Horizontal SetScrollOffset payloads are ignored while vertical
scroll controls are the admitted surface.

Nearest-edge reveal uses unclipped target boxes and the existing inner-to-outer
ancestor plan. It preserves focus, selection and values. Scroll notifications
use the established measured fields, later guest turns and coalescible queue
policy, without gesture authority. A full queue may omit coalescible notifications
while preserving its fixed capacity. Readonly text can still scroll. Roleless
overflow/live-region containers remain in native semantics; headless JSON keeps
its previous shape. Native scroll controls advertise only available vertical
ranges and ancestor reveal paths. Rebinding discards newly unsupported actions.
Text-range reveal derives original UTF-8 bounds from painted clusters, with
CRLF/scalar boundaries for plain text and mask grapheme boundaries for passwords.
Platform text-run IDs decode to source identity, revision and byte range before
enqueue; the semantic FIFO retains that decoded meaning across presentation ACKs
and rejects changed content or unsupported bindings. Edge hints align each
specified axis; other axes use nearest-edge behavior. No-hint oversized targets
already spanning both viewport edges need not move.

Single-line fields retain a host-only horizontal display offset. Range reveal can
pan away from the caret without changing the value, selection, content revision
or focus. Offscreen carets are clipped instead of being painted at a false edge.
Ordinary selection, navigation, IME and real content/type changes restore caret
following; equal guest value echoes preserve panning. Horizontal display changes
create no guest event or new frozen wire field. Textarea reveal uses its content
viewport, then scrolls ancestors from inside out; vertical notifications retain
the established scroll metrics and coalescing rules. Geometry stays physical for
text, CSS for scroll arithmetic, with one explicit scale conversion.

Native text runs and their field owners advertise reveal only with matching
painted geometry and an available own/ancestor scroll range. The pinned macOS
adapter validates NSRange end addition and exact UTF-16 round trips before
effects; surrogate/CRLF interior boundaries are refused. Its standard visible-range
setter sends ScrollIntoView with the existing SetTextSelection payload as a
typed range address. The action selects scrolling, not selection mutation. Both
endpoints must decode through the same current field and source revision before
entering the semantic FIFO. Ordinary owner reveal uses its logical selection,
or the full source when no representable selection is available.

The macOS visible-character getter uses acknowledged clipped run bounds and
returns whole vertically visible lines, including horizontally clipped text,
per [Apple's contract](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appkit/nsaccessibilitystatictext/accessibilityvisiblecharacterrange%28%29).
Empty/nonprinting lines retain their range; missing geometry does not fabricate
a full-document range. ScrollView maps to the public AppKit scroll-area role.
These are implementation contracts, not proof of native/VoiceOver acceptance.
Page/item/absolute actions still need separately proven native platform routes;
no private page-action name is invented. Live-update implementation follows.

**Native live updates.** The native projection preserves roleless busy containers
and root live/busy settings; the frozen headless projection retains its prior
shape. Explicit `aria-live` in the ancestor chain determines priority; otherwise
admitted `status` and `alert` roles supply polite/assertive defaults, with atomic
content. Explicit local settings override inherited settings. Unadmitted ARIA
attributes are not added to v38 to implement this host behavior. The semantics
follow [ARIA 1.2 live regions](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/#aria-live),
[status](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/#status) and
[busy](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/#aria-busy).

A local pinned macOS adapter patch plans live updates after a complete tree
publication. Trigger channels are separate from message content: a changed live
channel triggers its nearest atomic owner, whose entire visible subtree (including
nested live/off text and the author label) is then presented. Off changes alone
do not trigger delivery. Nested atomic owners retain their own triggers. Several
changed channels for one owner coalesce at the highest changed priority; an
unchanged assertive child does not escalate a polite change. Messages preserve
owner tree order. Busy ancestors or atomic descendants defer the affected message.
Fixed-size SHA-256 baselines track individual source parts as well as channel
and owner content. Source-part changes classify additions/text changes; removal
alone does not announce the remaining text. Relative order changes use only the
participating parts' priority. Same-content child replacement within one atomic
owner/presentation coalesces to a no-op. Busy baselines keep no historical strings;
removed source identities are pruned and retained order consists only of IDs. Only current complete ready content is delivered. Unchanged
repaints, cancellations back to delivered content, empty messages and removals
are silent. Newly appearing content and changed priority can announce once.
Activation primes a baseline; initially busy regions can announce on release.
Native text folding follows the effective name-from-content role, rather than
just the physical tag. The name traversal records whether the actual fallback
used content, distinguishing author/host labels, relations and placeholders.
Mixed semantic children retain the resolved name plus `labelled_by` links to
those children; the message planner omits this derived-name copy while keeping
actual author labels. Frozen JSON preserves its earlier folding. Field values
already contain password grapheme masks, and native name/description references
use the same mask units. Legacy naming keeps scalar masks. Auxiliary run children
are not a second announcement copy. Geometry/selection-only updates skip planning.
The observer's existing work allowance preflights possible full atomic-message
traversal/output as well, including external label relations and field/mask
capacity. Excess work takes the recoverable refusal path without changing guest
admission. A flat fragment buffer and subtree ranges avoid copying full messages
before delivery. These and the run ceiling bound Varta's projected inputs; they
are not a complete RSS/CPU guarantee for the toolkit. Existing AppKit notification
raising and medium/high priorities are reused without new unsafe host code.
[Patch provenance and exact diff](../vendor/accesskit_macos/VARTA-PATCH.md).
VoiceOver delivery and non-macOS behavior require their own acceptance evidence.

Native Focus, Click, string SetValue, ReplaceSelectedText, SetTextSelection and scroll callbacks only enqueue
host requests. Admission requires a current binding, an advertised action,
at most eight pending requests and at most 1 MiB of retained owned text. String
payloads also obey the existing per-field reservation/UTF-16 limits. Unsupported,
oversized, disabled and unknown requests are ignored; readonly targets reject
editing actions. A coalesced
data-free wake prevents an unbounded queue of platform payloads. The GUI sends
one request per acknowledged frame through the existing bounded worker channel.
Pending semantic requests rebind to the latest presented frame only while their
native ID, opaque source identity and advertised action still match; absolute
text selections additionally require the current content revision. This keeps
FIFO focus-then-edit bursts across their own acknowledgement frames; removed,
hidden, replaced or newly unsupported targets are discarded. The worker then
rechecks the refreshed revision, viewport, scale and theme before effects.
Coordinate input retains its original frame guards. Current no-op requests still
receive an acknowledgement frame. The ordinary input path owns edits, sequence
numbers, history, select-option identity, event budgets and permission checks;
guest listeners run on later application turns. Input records retain their
ordinary gesture classification.

Native bounds and clipping come from the presented frame alone
(`FrameMetadata::accessibility_geometry`, physical pixels): the union of a
node's visible element fragments when it has any; for a presented row of the
open select list, that row; for another laid-out node that is partly presented
(such as a text node, whose box is its anonymous block or inline fragment box),
the presented part of its layout box. A node that is not presented at all
(scrolled out, clipped away, or a row scrolled out of the open list) gets its
unclipped layout box at the presented scroll offsets only where a hit test
cannot reach it: outside the frame or outside one of its clipping ancestors.
An `overflow` hidden or scroll container clips (AccessKit `clips_children`) when
it has bounds and every presented descendant lies inside them; a descendant
that escapes it (an absolute box whose containing block is outside, or an open
list drawn over it) keeps it from clipping. Other hidden nodes, such as a box
under a scroll container's border or a row scrolled out of the open list over
the page, and options of a closed select stay unbounded. Every AccessKit
platform adapter (macOS, AT-SPI on Linux, UIA on Windows) hit-tests through
`accesskit_consumer`'s `node_at_point`, which upstream ignores clipping; the
vendored consumer searches a clipping node's descendants only inside its bounds
([patch record](../vendor/accesskit_consumer/VARTA-PATCH.md)), so a point
returns only a node presented there. Only the macOS build and the consumer's
own search are verified; the AT-SPI and UIA builds were not compiled for this
change. AccessKit's unchanged
filter omits a clipping scroll area's children beyond the nearest one past each
edge from the platform tree until scrolling brings them next to the area;
scrolling the nearest included one into view brings the next one in.

A node with a vertical scroll range also publishes a geometry-free vertical
`ScrollBar` child at its 0..1 scroll position in the platform-independent
projection (built and observed on macOS only; the Linux and Windows adapters
are not yet compiled or run); its native ID is kept while the owner keeps its identity and a
scroll range (a changed range keeps it). The pinned macOS adapter maps
AppKit's scroll-area `AXScrollUpByPage`/`AXScrollDownByPage` to page scrolls,
exposes that child as `AXVerticalScrollBar`, and maps the bar's
increment/decrement to item scrolls and its settable value (finite, clamped to
0..1) to an absolute offset. These are the existing typed actions, so the host
queue, frame guards and core validation above apply unchanged; no new action or
unsafe host code is added.

This is not complete platform accessibility: platform acceptance of visual text
ranges, assistive scrolling through a real assistive client, announcements and
screen-reader/target acceptance remain open. Native API exposure and
performance require direct platform evidence; headless projection tests alone
do not establish it.

Explicitly sized text inputs and buttons with explicit display, minimum sizes,
padding and border can participate in this experimental geometry. A button with
text requires one text child, flex display and explicit font and alignment
properties. The admitted inputs include text/search/password and checkbox/radio;
explicit textareas also follow the rules above. Remaining control types and
intrinsic or platform-default control sizing are rejected. The geometry path
itself only calculates boxes. Full text editing,
full IME support, CSS and general geometry remain open.
Grid supports a subset of the validated track grammar, numeric line/span placement, and
bounded explicit and implicit grid work; unsupported values and oversized
track lists fail closed. General grid, typography and target parity remain open.

For layout comparison, `View::snapshot_flex_blockified()` provides a separate
projection of the existing snapshot. It changes an explicit cascaded `inline`
display to `block` on direct children of an explicit `flex` parent. It leaves
the ordinary snapshot and accessibility output unchanged, does not infer missing
user-agent defaults, and is not a complete computed-style or geometry model.
The same projection is available as `project_flex_blockification` for an already
captured snapshot; its iterative walk does not alter non-tree fields.

**Accessible names.** The accessibility tree names a node by the steps of
[accname 1.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/accname-1.2/) that the L0 v1 subset
admits (`varta-view/src/name.rs`). An element is *hidden* when it has
`aria-hidden="true"`, a computed `display: none`, or is a `dialog` that is not
open; a hidden element and its subtree are absent from the accessibility tree.
In the headless role mapping, a `section` with an `aria-label` or
`aria-labelledby` attribute has the implicit `region` role; an explicit role
overrides it. An empty or unresolved name is omitted from the snapshot.
The name of an element E with role R is computed by visiting nodes, starting
at E (the root step):

1. **2A, hidden.** A hidden element contributes the empty string, unless the
   relation (`aria-labelledby` or `label`) that reached it started at a hidden
   node (the referenced node or an ancestor is hidden): then its hidden
   descendants take part.
2. **2B, `aria-labelledby`.** Outside an `aria-labelledby` traversal, the
   attribute's ASCII-whitespace-separated ids that name attached elements are
   visited in order, each as a referenced node of a traversal that does not
   apply 2B again, and the results are joined with one space. A blank result,
   or no id that resolves, falls through to 2C.
3. **2C, embedded control.** Below the root step, a text field gives its
   live value (a `password` field its masked value) and a `select` the text of
   the `option` whose `value` equals its value.
4. **2D, `aria-label`.** A value that is not blank after trimming ASCII
   whitespace.
5. **2E, host language label.** An `img` gives its `alt` when present. At the
   root step only, an `input`, `textarea`, `select` or `progress` with an `id`
   gives the names of the attached `label` elements whose `for` equals that
   id, in document order, each visited as a referenced node and joined with
   one space, when not blank. Below the root step the `label` relation is not
   followed (a field already gave its value at 2C), so every traversal is
   finite.
6. **2F and 2H, name from content.** At the root step when R is one of
   `button`, `link`, `heading`, `option`, `cell`, `columnheader`, `row`,
   `tab`, `checkbox` or `radio` (ARIA 1.2 "name from contents"), and at every
   step below the root, the results of visiting the children in order are
   concatenated without separators; at the root step a blank result falls
   through. A text node (2G) gives its text. E met again below the root step
   (a field inside its own label, for example) gives the empty string.
7. **HTML-AAM last resort.** A text field gives its `placeholder`.

Before publication, native and browser admission check a shared potential
accessible-name inventory across all components. Indexed numeric descendant and
relation summaries include repeated ids, native-label alternatives and future
live-field capacity without evaluating names. Hidden state and author precedence
do not discount them; relation-disabled references keep cyclic ids finite. See
[the embedding contract](embedding.md) for the work recurrence and final-only
rollback semantics. Raw text leaves and stored source retain their separate
limits; browser accessibility-engine CPU, complete JSON/frame/backend memory and
RSS guarantees remain separate requirements.

Each native snapshot builds attached id/label and visibility indices once. Label
order follows document order. Descendant text remains an ordered fragment range
until the traversal ends, avoiding a fresh concatenation at each ancestor. These
indices belong to one snapshot, so edits, reparenting, environment changes and
removal cannot reuse stale names or visibility.

The name is the result as a flat string: every run of ASCII whitespace
becomes one space and the ends are trimmed. A node whose name is empty has
no `name` member. Every other role (`list`, `listitem`, `dialog`,
`navigation` and the other landmarks, `alert`, `status`, `table`, `tablist`,
`tabpanel`, `paragraph`, `progressbar`, `image`, the fields) is named only by
its author through 2B–2E. The subset has no `title` attribute (2I), no
`presentation`/`none` role, no generated content (`::before`/`::after`) and
no layout, so a block-level child adds no separating space; these parts of
accname do not apply. Example: `<button><span aria-hidden="true">◇</span>
<span>Reasoning</span><span aria-hidden="true">▸</span></button>` is
`button "Reasoning"`.

**Diagnostic export.** Native view/application JSON export uses a separate
encoded-byte allowance. A bounded writer counts compact/pretty keys, escaping and
indentation before allocating/copying each fragment. Export refusal returns a
typed observer error without terminating the application or exposing partial JSON.
The CLI's scripted-view path uses this encoder and retains budget diagnostics on
refusal. Structured inspection remains available to trusted embedders; their own
copies/formatting and complete allocator/RSS accounting are separate. The
simulated platform retains a bounded tail of successful
opened URLs in chronological order, with complete strings, entry/UTF-8
byte ceilings and an explicit `openedDropped` counter after eviction. Actual
permission decisions and action results do not depend on diagnostic retention.

**View prelude.** `<varta>/view/view.ts`, loaded when a module names a
`View.*` member or `ViewEvent` (TSX compiles to `View.*` calls). It encodes
operations into a string whose UTF-16 code units are the batch bytes, packing
each operation's fixed operands with the prelude-only intrinsic
`varta.view.units(…)` (`ir::Intrinsic::Units`, one allocation, no host call)
and appending string operands as themselves; `varta.view.commit(batch)` is the
only path to the host import. Node and handler ids are allocated in
increasing order and never reused.

**TSX.** Under `tsx()`, modules whose path ends in `.tsx` parse with SWC's
TSX syntax (other modules, and every module of earlier profiles, parse as
before). Before scanning, each outermost intrinsic JSX element becomes a
generated module function `__vartaJsxN` (a static template of L0 operations:
create, attributes, classes, styles, listeners, children, insert) whose
parameters are the template's dynamic holes, and the JSX expression becomes
its call with the holes as arguments in source order. Holes are getters
`() => T` bound through `View.bindText`/`bindAttribute`/`bindFlag`/
`bindClass`/`bindStyle`/`bindValue`/`bindChecked`, which run the getter
through the effect runner installed by `View.setEffect` (the hook of a
reactive L1 package; without one a getter runs once). Event attributes
`on<Event>[:filter]` register listeners with a static key filter
(`Enter-noShift-notComposing-preventDefault`); `ref` receives the node id; a
component `<Name a={x} />` is the call `Name({ a: x })` returning a node id.
Element names, attributes per element, static attribute values, static CSS
declarations and filters are checked against the registry at compile time
with `TypeError` diagnostics at the JSX attribute; hole types are checked by
the ordinary checker against the generated parameter types. Fragments,
spread attributes and children, and component children are rejected; names
starting with `__vartaJsx` are reserved. `varta.d.ts` carries the typed
`JSX` namespace generated from the same tables.

**`className` (K8).** `className` is an alias of `class` with the same
operations, static check and hole: `<p className="a">` compiles to the same
bytes as `<p class="a">`. An element carrying both (or either twice) is a
`TypeError` at the element; `htmlFor` stays rejected in favour of `for`. The
static class value is checked against the L0 class-token grammar, so
Tailwind tokens such as `hover:bg-red-500` or `w-1/2` are refused there until
the T2 class-token stage (S1) widens that grammar.

**Limits.** The `view::DRAFT_*` placeholders bound batch bytes and
operations, live nodes and listeners, value and stylesheet bytes, pending
events and pending `copy_text` requests; `view::css::MAX_VALUE_TOKENS` bounds
one CSS value; a headless script is at most `Script::MAX_BYTES` bytes and
`Script::MAX_INPUTS` steps (inputs and waits), and one step settles within
`Script::MAX_STEP_TURNS` turns.

#### Native control defaults

Native rendering gives form controls Chrome's user-agent defaults under the
official browser host's normalization (`box-sizing: border-box; margin: 0`
and, with packaged faces, an inherited family), instead of refusing controls
without explicit styles. The defaults are part of the versioned native
user-agent table (`style::NATIVE_UA_DEFAULTS` and
`style::NATIVE_CONTROL_DEFAULTS`, published as `varta_view::NATIVE_UA_VERSION`;
the control rows started a new version). The reference is headless Chrome 156
on macOS in the light scheme (the host never sets `color-scheme`).

*Placement.* An absent `display` is Chrome's `inline-block`, an atomic inline
in a line box, which native layout does not model: such a control is refused
unless it is a flex or grid item (blockified). With `display: block` (or as a
block-level item) an automatic width fits the content
(`LayoutBox::AutoWidthShouldFitContent`). A `button` that is not a flex or grid
container centers its content vertically, with `text-align: center` lines; a
flex or grid button is an ordinary container with the initial alignment, as in
Chrome.

*Control font.* Each control row resets what the author does not set to
Chrome's `font: -webkit-small-control`: a 13.333px (10pt) absolute size,
`normal` weight and style and `line-height: normal`; the family stays
inherited. `line-height: normal` of control text (field values, placeholders
and button labels, including every text node and inline element of a rich
label) is the primary font's ascent, descent and line gap of that text's own
font each rounded to whole pixels, as Chrome's line spacing; other text keeps
the shaper's `normal`. A rich flow measures each text run with the line height
of the span that owns it (the shaper's run metrics would take the following
span's). Label and field glyphs put their first baseline on a whole device
pixel.

*Themed and author-styled controls.* A control without an author
`background-color`, border or `border-radius` declaration keeps Chrome's
native theme (`LayoutTheme::IsControlStyled`). Otherwise it needs the
`border` shorthand: any other partial author box style would need Chrome's
inset/outset user-agent borders and is refused. An author-styled control
takes the user-agent padding, font, `buttonface`/`field` background and
`buttontext`/`fieldtext` color where the author sets none. Checkbox and radio
inputs with author box styles keep the explicit-style path above (Chrome would
keep its theme), and a select keeps its explicit-style requirement.

| Kind | Padding (px) | Border (px) | Unsized content box |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `button` | 1 6 | 2 | its children |
| `input` text, search, password, number | 1 2 | 2 | ⌈(20 − 1)·round(a) + max(a, ascent)⌉ wide, one line high |
| `textarea` | 2 | 1 | 20·round(a) + 16 wide, `rows` (default 2) lines high |
| `input` checkbox, radio | 0 | 0 | a 13px square, intrinsic |

`a` is the advance of the primary font's `x` (Chrome on macOS); a field whose
primary font has no `x` is refused, since Chrome would use a platform x-height.
The 16px textarea term is Chrome's scrollbar gutter; an author-styled textarea
needs an explicit width. The text-field size needs the host text measurer, so
the geometry-only path refuses an unsized field. A checkable square is an
intrinsic size, not a specified one: stretch alignment grows an automatic axis
(beside a 4-row textarea in a flex row with the default `align-items` a
checkbox is 13×62, and in a 150×34 stretch grid area 150×34, as in Chrome),
and the theme paints the largest centered square. The square is also the
automatic minimum, while a textarea flex item can shrink to its padding and
borders. A themed checkable drops author padding (Blink's
`AdjustCheckboxStyle`/`AdjustRadioStyle` reset padding and borders), so its
square stays the border box: with `padding: 6px` it is 13×13 at `flex-start`,
13×40 stretched in a 40px row and fills a stretch grid area, as in Chrome; any
