author border makes the checkable author-styled instead. Themed controls paint a fill and a one-pixel frame with a 2px radius
(the fill inset by half the frame): buttons `#efefef`, fields and unchecked
checkables `#ffffff`, frames `#767676`. Field themes snap to device pixels with
a whole-pixel frame; a button frame scales with the device. A checked checkbox
fills with `#0075ff` and strokes a white check mark (`NativeThemeBase`
proportions); a radio has an accent frame and a dot inset by 20%, and its
`border-radius: 50%` shapes its pointer target. Disabled controls use
translucent frames (`rgba(118, 118, 118, 0.3)`) and the single layers
equivalent to Chrome's disabled fills, measured over black and white; disabled
text is `rgba(16, 16, 16, 0.3)` in buttons and `rgb(84, 84, 84)` in fields. A
control's user-agent color stops `color` inheritance at the control.
Placeholders are `#757575`. Hover and active theme colors are not applied.

*Focus ring.* A focused control whose `outline-style` stays the user agent's
`auto` (no author `outline` shorthand and no `outline-style`) draws Chrome's
`:focus-visible { outline: auto }` ring: two pixels centered on the border box
outset by the `outline-offset`, less one pixel when every border is at least
one pixel wide. An author `outline-color` replaces the ring color `#005fcc`
(`currentcolor` is the control's color) and an author `outline-offset`
replaces the user-agent offset (2px for checkboxes and radios, otherwise 0);
an author `outline-width` does not change the ring, which stays two pixels as
in Chrome. A themed control keeps its theme part radius at the ring's center
(a radio's is half its longer side, limited to the ring, so a stretched radio's
ring is a stadium); an author radius is outset by half the ring. Native
`:focus-visible` matches any focus, so the ring follows the same rule. An
author `outline` shorthand or `outline-style` ends `auto`: `solid` draws the
author outline, while `none`, or a shorthand without `solid`, draws nothing.
Under the colored ring Chrome's light scheme paints a white ring of the same
width one pixel further out, with radii grown by that pixel (Blink's
`PaintFocusRing` outer ring): it shows as a white pixel outside the colored
ring on a non-white background, and through a translucent or transparent
author `outline-color`. Dark-scheme rings are not modelled (the official host
sets no `color-scheme`).
The ring paints after the contents and does not change layout or hit regions.

*Number fields.* `input type=number` edits its value with the shared field
editor and Undo, and its value stays the string L0 decides; there is no
sanitization and no spin button (Chrome shows one on hover or focus). Up and
Down step the value as Chrome does (owner decision of 2026-11-05). L0 admits
no `step`, `min` or `max` on inputs, so the step is Chrome's default 1 with
step base 0 and no bounds; the attributes are an open L0 item. The value is
read with Chrome's number sanitization (an optional `-`, digits with an
optional fraction or a fraction alone, an optional exponent, no trailing `.`;
a value that rounds beyond `f64::MAX` is invalid), and an invalid or empty
value counts as 0; `varta_view::number_value_is_valid` exposes this grammar.
A value within 2⁻²⁴ of an integer (Blink's acceptable step error) becomes that
integer ± 1; any other value rounds to the next integer above (Up) or below
(Down). The result is written as a plain integer string (`0`, never `-0`)
with the caret at its end, as one Undo entry, and fires `input` and then
`change`. Up steps with any modifier, Down unless Alt is held; a disabled or
read-only field does not step, and `Input::TextNavigate` refuses Up/Down on a
number field. Chrome computes the step in Blink's 18-digit decimal, which
truncates long values and prints large results in exponent form; native
stepping is exact and admits only values whose first 18 typed digits hold all
their nonzero digits: integers below 10¹⁸ in magnitude, other values below
10¹⁵ with at most 18 fraction digits, and results below 10¹⁸ (Chrome prints
10¹⁸ as `1e+18`). Any other valid value is refused
(`number_step::StepRefusal::OutsideExactRange`): the key changes nothing, and
the view's platform effects count the refusal as `stepsRefused` (present in the
snapshot only after a refusal, saturating), so the host can see it.
Two differences from Chrome remain: Chrome converts typed text through the
platform locale before sanitizing it (so typed `5.`, `+5` or `1,000` step from
5 or 1000 there), whereas L0 keeps the typed string and native reads it as
invalid; and Chrome 156's Undo does not revert a step, whereas the owner's
decision makes each step an Undo entry. The browser host keeps Chrome's own
stepping.

*Font families.* A `font-family` value naming a CSS-wide keyword (`inherit`,
`initial`, `unset`, `revert`, `revert-layer`; the shared
`css::CSS_WIDE_KEYWORDS`) unquoted is outside the L0 grammar note and refused
by the shared validator. The refusal names the keyword: native `set_style`
fails with `Violation::FontFamilyKeyword`, the stylesheet checker with
`stylesheet::Violation::FontFamilyKeyword` and the TSX compiler with a
diagnostic naming it (`css::font_family_css_wide_keyword`). The browser host's
font namespace (`view-fonts.mjs`) refuses it while preparing a batch, before
the batch commits, instead of letting Chrome roll back to its own font; the
DOM boundary reports it as an indexed `ViewProtocolError` (`font-family
keyword` for `set_style`, `stylesheet value` for a stylesheet). Custom
property values keep such keywords. A quoted name is an ordinary family.

#### Native scrollbars

`Environment::scrollbars` selects the platform's scrollbar style, as Chrome on
macOS follows the system's "Show scroll bars" setting. `Scrollbars::Overlay`
(the default, and headless Chrome's style on a Mac with a trackpad) reserves
no space and shows a container's bar only while it scrolls
([overlay scrollbars](#native-overlay-scrollbars)).
`Scrollbars::Classic` (always shown) gives every scroll container
(`overflow: auto`, and the top-layer dialog) whose content overflows on an
axis that axis's bar: a gutter of `CLASSIC_SCROLLBAR_THICKNESS` inside the
borders (the vertical bar at the right, the horizontal one at the bottom),
which the content box, the scrollport and the content clip leave out. Layout
runs again after adding gutters; a gutter can make content overflow on the
other axis, so gutters are only added, for at most `MAX_GUTTER_PASSES` more
passes, and gutters still growing after them are refused
(`LayoutError::Unsupported`). `BoxGeometry::scrollbars` gives each bar's
track and its axis's range (`ScrollbarGeometry::overlay` false). Paint
follows Chrome 156's `NativeThemeMac` in
the light scheme (the subset has no `color-scheme`, and the official host
never sets one, so Chrome paints light scrollbars in either OS scheme), in
device pixels: the track filled `#FAFAFA` with a one-pixel (floored when
scaled) inner border `#E8E8E8` on the content side and outer border `#EDEDED`
on the outer edge; the corner where both bars meet filled likewise with its
inner square and both outer borders; and the thumb, a pill of black at alpha
`0x3A`, whose length and position are Blink's (`round(visible / total ·
track)`, at least 20 pixels scaled, at `trunc(offset · (track − thumb) /
max)`, one pixel for an offset under one), inset by 3 pixels (rounded when
scaled) on every side plus the border on the content side, the insets
shrinking (`ConstrainInsets`) to keep a 6 by 18 pixel minimum. A bar paints
after its container's border and before its content, clipped to the
container's clip; a classic scroll container with rounded corners is refused
at paint. Pointers over a bar hit the container. Native layout scrolls only
vertically, so a horizontal thumb stays at the start. Geometry, hits and
pixels match Chrome 156 run with `-AppleShowScrollBars Always` (its argument
domain only) at 1x, 1.25x and 2x within the 2/255 mean bound
(`native_scrollbar_probe` with `scripts/test-native-positioned.mjs`); at 2x
Chrome's scrollbar layer filters the track borders over two more pixels,
which native does not. Not implemented: the hover color of the classic
thumb (`#000` at alpha `0x80`), dragging a thumb and clicking a track (with
either style), and Chrome's Linux (Aura) scrollbars.

`varta-shell` reads AppKit's preferred scroller style
(`NSScroller.preferredScrollerStyle`, where "Automatically" resolves by the
attached pointing devices) on the main thread when its window opens and hands
it to the instance (`ViewLayout::with_scrollbars`); a later change of the
setting applies after a restart. Other platforms keep overlay scrollbars.

#### Native overlay scrollbars

With `Scrollbars::Overlay` a scroll container (`overflow: auto`, and the
top-layer dialog) whose content overflows on an axis has that axis's bar
frame, `OVERLAY_SCROLLBAR_THICKNESS` thick, over the edge of its padding box:
the vertical one at the right, above the corner a horizontal frame leaves as
in Blink's `ScrollCornerRect`, and the horizontal one at the bottom.
`BoxGeometry::scrollbars` gives them with `ScrollbarGeometry::overlay` true
and the axis ranges; they take no layout space, and a hidden bar paints
nothing and takes no pointer.

When a bar shows follows Chrome 156's `ui::OverlayScrollbarAnimatorMac` as
Blink's `MacScrollbarImplV2` drives it, on the view's animation clock
([transitions](#native-css-transitions)), so a headless render at a given
clock is deterministic. A scroll that changes a container's offset (wheel
and `Scroll`/`ScrollMeasured` input, a commit's `ScrollTo` and
`ScrollIntoView`, `View::scroll_into_view` and assistive scrolls; Chrome's
explicit scroll types, not a clamp) shows its thumb at full opacity at once
or keeps it, cancelling a running fade-out. The fade-out starts 500 ms
(`kFadeOutDelay`) after the last such scroll and lasts 250 ms
(`kAnimationDuration`), ease-in-out; the bar is then hidden. A host reports
which container's bar frame the pointer is over (`FrameMetadata::scrollbar_at`
of the presented frame: the last painted frame there whose container is the
hit element or its ancestor; then `View::set_scrollbar_hover`, which
dispatches no guest event). A
shown bar under the pointer does not fade: its track fades in and its thumb
box widens from 12 to 16 pixels (truncated to whole pixels), each over
250 ms ease-in-out, and it stays wide until it has faded out; leaving the
frame restarts the 500 ms delay, and the track fades out with the thumb. A
hidden bar ignores the pointer, but a scroll under a resting pointer shows
the bar and then takes the pointer at once, as Blink's hover update after
the scroll does. `View::animating` is true while a bar waits for its fade-out
or animates, and `View::set_animation_time` reports a change only when a bar
paints differently, so the delay itself needs no frame.

Paint follows `NativeThemeMac` with `is_overlay`. The colors are light, or
dark when the scroller's own background color is not transparent and its HSL
lightness is at most one half (`RecalculateOverlayScrollbarColorScheme`); a
transparent background keeps the page's light scheme, as the subset has no
`color-scheme`. The thumb is a pill of black (dark: white) at alpha `0x80`
times its opacity, in the thumb box at the bar's outer edge, inset 2 pixels
plus the 1-pixel border on the content side and kept at least 6 by 18
(`ConstrainInsets`). Its length and offset are the compositor's: `round(visible
/ total · track)`, at least 26 pixels, at `trunc(offset · (track − thumb) /
max)` (an offset under one pixel leaves the thumb at the start, unlike the
classic thumb), computed in CSS pixels and drawn scaled and anti-aliased, as
Chrome draws them at 1.25x and 2x. The track, once shown, fills the frame in
device pixels with one layer at the track's opacity: the gradient along the
track (`0.973` at alpha `0.776` easing to `0.761` over the first third; dark
`0.847` at `0.157` to `0.8` at `0.149`), the inner border `#DFDFDF` at
`0xF9` (dark `#E5E5E5` at `0x33`) on the content side and the outer border
`#E8E8E8` at `0xC6` (dark `#D8D8D8` at `0x28`) on the outer edge, each one
pixel wide (floored when scaled). A bar paints in its container's outline
phase, after the container's content and outline, clipped by its ancestors'
clips but not by its container's rounded corners (as Chrome); while it shows,
its frame takes the pointer for the container, so a wheel over it scrolls the
container. Only vertical bars paint: native layout scrolls only vertically,
and a horizontal overlay bar shows only while its axis scrolls. A textarea's
own text scrolling shows no bar.

Geometry, hits and pixels match Chrome 156 headless on macOS (overlay
scrollbars) running the same steps in real time at 1x, 1.25x and 2x within
the 2/255 mean bound (`native_overlay_scrollbar_probe` with
`scripts/test-native-overlay-scrollbars.mjs`): just after a wheel or
programmatic scroll, after the pointer rested on the bar and after the
fade-out, on light, dark, bordered, rounded and two-axis scrollers and with
the minimum thumb. Chrome advances its animations on a 60 Hz timer, so its
frames can lag native's by up to one tick. `varta-shell` passes
the frame's `scrollbar_at` for each pointer sample of the presented frame
(`Application::view_set_scrollbar_hover`) and none when the pointer leaves the
window, and presents frames while a bar animates.

#### Native fallback faces

A host that lays text out with the platform's own fonts may give a
`TextMeasurer` a `FontFallback` (`TextMeasurer::set_fallback`); `varta-shell
--system-fonts` does, and no other host or font set looks anything up (a
cluster none of the families covers keeps `.notdef`). The shaper first shapes
with the CSS families. Then, as Blink's shaper falls back over a segment, the
`.notdef` ranges of one style (adjacent clusters form one range; line breaks
and control characters are not missing) all try the face the host names for
the first range's first character (`FallbackRequest { character, family,
weight, italic }`, `family` being the element's primary family), appended
after the families each range had, and the text is shaped again; ranges that
still miss repeat this, at most `MAX_FALLBACK_PASSES` times, and every pass is
charged to the view's shaping budget. A covered character never changes face.
The measurer registers each face once (by its `FallbackFace::key`); a face of
a family the set already loads adds nothing and that family's faces are used.
At most `MAX_FALLBACK_FACES` faces of at most `MAX_FALLBACK_FACE_BYTES` each
and `MAX_FALLBACK_BYTES` in all are registered per measurer. A face past
these limits, one that cannot be read, or one whose colour glyphs the host
does not draw (every colour face on Linux; on macOS faces with `COLR`, `CBDT`,
`EBDT` or `SVG ` tables) refuses the text (`TextMeasureError::Fallback {
character, refusal }`, a layout or paint failure) rather than drawing another
face.

As Blink's emoji segmentation does, a grapheme with emoji presentation
(Unicode TR51: an `Emoji_Presentation` character, an emoji followed by VS16, a
keycap, regional-indicator pair, modifier or ZWJ sequence; VS15 asks for text)
that a face without colour glyphs draws, covered or not, is a range of its
own: it asks the host with `FallbackRequest::emoji` set, and the face comes
before the element's families for it, so `©\u{FE0F}` draws with the emoji
face even where the CSS font has `©`. On macOS the host answers with Apple
Color Emoji (Chrome's `kColorEmojiFontMac`). That face's `sbix` strikes are
about 183 MiB, so the measurer is given its own tables with an empty `sbix`
(about 1 MiB) and the rasterizer of the same font set draws its glyphs with
the platform face registered for exactly those bytes
(`FontSet::glyph_rasterizer`). CoreText enlarges small emoji (by a quarter up
to 16px, by nothing from 24px) and Chrome lays them out at that size: the
face's `FallbackFace::metrics` (`PlatformMetrics`) give each glyph its `hmtx`
advance scaled by CoreText's ascent over the face's own and rounded to whole
pixels, and CoreText's ascent and descent, which the measurer rounds as
Chrome rounds font metrics (a 16px emoji is 20px wide; a Helvetica line with
one is 26px tall under `line-height: normal`). The advances replace the
shaped ones before line breaking through a recorded Parley hook
(`Layout::adjust_glyph_advances`, [patch
record](../vendor/parley/VARTA-PATCH.md)). Chrome draws colour glyph images
unemboldened, so synthetic bold on such a face paints them as they are;
synthetic italic stays refused. As in Blink, a
fallback face's run under a `line-height` other than `normal` takes its
element's primary font ascent and descent, so it does not change the line box;
under `normal` its own metrics take part (in an inline formatting context;
plain text with `normal` keeps Parley's largest line height, a remaining
difference). Weight and style select among the family's registered faces, and
synthesis follows the paint rules of packaged faces (only the bold Chrome
would synthesize stays refused).

The shell names the face as Chrome does: on macOS CoreText's
`CTFontCreateForStringWithLanguage` for the primary font (the UI font for the
family `system-ui` maps, otherwise the named family) with the bold
(weight 600 or more) and italic traits, then that family's face with those
traits; the face is the platform font's own tables assembled as a standalone
face, so no file is read. On Linux fontconfig's sorted match (`FcFontSort`)
for a pattern of the character and the process locale (`LC_ALL`,
`LC_MESSAGES`, then `LANG`), the first scalable face whose character map has
it, extracted from its file or collection; like Chrome on Linux it does not
ask for the weight or style. Answers and faces are cached per font set and
shared by its measurers. Blink also splits fallback segments at script runs,
which native grouping by style does not; they differ only when one segment's
fallback face covers another script's missing characters. On macOS 27 with
Chrome 156, `native_fallback_probe` with `scripts/test-native-inline.mjs`
matches Chrome's boxes at 1x and 2x and its pixels within the 2/255 mean bound
for lines whose primary font is Helvetica, Times or Menlo; lines in the UI
font compare geometry only, because its `opsz` axis makes the CoreText
rasterizer decline its glyphs (portable outlines, about 2.7/255 mean). Its
emoji lines (single emoji, skin-tone, ZWJ family and flag sequences, emoji and
text presentation selectors, a keycap, bold and half-transparent emoji) match
Chrome's boxes and pixels at 1x, 1.5x, 2x and 3x (at most 0.13/255 mean).

#### Native modal dialogs (top layer)

A closed `dialog` renders nothing. A modal one (`show_modal`) lays out as
Chrome's `dialog:modal` with the L0 base sheet's `border: none; padding: 0`:
fixed in the viewport whatever its author `position`, centred by auto
margins over zero insets, sized to fit its content, at most the viewport
minus `2em + 6px` of its computed font size in each axis, its overflow
scrolling; author styles then apply to its own box. It paints in the top
layer: after the root stacking context has painted everything else (every
z-index layer included), each modal dialog in the order it was shown paints
its backdrop over the viewport in the
[defaults table](embedding.md#view-draft-v0-round-4-subset-fixes)
colour of the scheme, then itself as a stacking context with the default
background and text colours unless the author sets them. A backdrop's hit
region takes every pointer for its dialog (as Chrome's `::backdrop` does),
so the inert page below never receives one; it is not part of the dialog's
accessibility bounds, which are the dialog's own box. A dialog that is open
but no longer modal (moved after `show_modal`) is refused with
`LayoutError::Unsupported`. Geometry, hits and pixels match Chrome 156 at
1x, 1.25x and 2x within the 2/255 mean bound (`native_dialog_probe` with
`scripts/test-native-dialog.mjs`); AccessKit publishes a modal `Dialog` with
those bounds and drops the inert page.

#### Native CSS transitions

The native view runs CSS Transitions 1 as Chrome 156 does for the subset's
animatable properties: the paint-only `color`, `background-color` and
`opacity`, and `transform` ([native transforms](#native-css-transforms)), whose
lists interpolate function by function when they pair (CSS Transforms 1 §9:
the same length and the same primitive in each position, `translate()` and
its one-axis forms being one primitive; `none` stands for the identity
functions of the other list), each argument linearly (a translation's pixel
and box-fraction parts separately). Lists that do not pair, which Chrome
interpolates as matrices, start no transition: the value changes at once. `transition-property` (initially `all`; `none` matches
nothing), `-duration`, `-timing-function` (`linear`, `ease`, `ease-in`,
`ease-out`, `ease-in-out` as their cubic Béziers) and `-delay` are
paint-only: layout admits them and they change no box. A property's
transition takes the last `transition-property` entry naming it (or `all`),
and the other lists at that entry's index, each list repeating.

Time is the view's animation clock in milliseconds, which the host sets
(`View::set_animation_time`, never moving back). Every style change (a
commit, an input, a pointer state or environment change) is evaluated at
that clock: for each displayed element and property, the value before the
change is the running transition's current value, otherwise the static value
after the previous change. A transition starts when that value differs from
the new static value and the combined duration (`max(duration, 0) + delay`)
is positive; a running one is kept while its end value stays, reversed to
its start value with the reversing shortening factor, restarted from its
current value toward a third value, and cancelled when no declaration
matches or the current value already equals the new one. Removing
`transition-property` leaves its initial `all`, so the transition runs on.
No transition starts for an element's first style or across `display: none`.
Colours interpolate in sRGB with premultiplied alpha, `opacity` linearly; an
undeclared `background-color` is transparent, `opacity` 1 and `transform`
`none`, and `color` inherits. Layout and paint read the current values; snapshots keep the
static cascade. Pixels match Chrome with every transition paused at the same
time since its style change, and box positions with Chrome's
`getBoundingClientRect` during a translation (`native_transition_probe` with
`scripts/test-native-transitions.mjs`).

#### Native CSS transforms

`transform` takes a list of `translate()`, `translateX()`, `translateY()` and
`scale()` with the initial `transform-origin` (the border box's centre). A
translation, a percentage of the element's own border box on its axis,
moves the element's box and everything in it for paint, hits, geometry,
accessibility bounds and scroll-into-view; no other box moves, as in
layout. Any transform makes the element a stacking context painted at level
zero (CSS2 Appendix E with CSS Transforms 1 §3), so it paints over later
in-flow siblings it overlaps. A list that scales (positive factors, at most
`MAX_TRANSFORM_FUNCTIONS` functions, applied in list order around the
origin) keeps every box where layout put it: its stacking context paints
untransformed into the recorded scene and its draws and hit regions (and
rounded hit regions) are then mapped through the transform in device
pixels, nested scales composing. Under a uniform scale a host glyph
rasterizer draws the text at the scaled size (the font size times the device
and transform scales) where the transforms put each glyph, and the glyph is
recorded through their inverse, which mapping undoes; Chrome rasterizes such
text at the scaled size too, colour emoji included. Under a non-uniform scale
text draws its portable outlines (which refuse colour glyphs). The
context's ancestors' clip is taken back through the inverse transform, so
the same pixels clip. `BoxGeometry::transform` carries the element's own
scaling transform; the public geometry (`layout_boxes`, `layout_geometry`,
scroll-into-view and accessibility bounds) maps every box of the subtree as
`getBoundingClientRect` does. Refused with `LayoutError::Unsupported`: a
factor that is not positive, a scroll container or clip (`overflow` other
than `visible`), text field or select in a scaled subtree or on the scaled
box, a scaled stacking context inside an inline capture or under a curved
clip (`PaintError::Unsupported`), and a fixed descendant of a transformed box
or an absolute one whose containing block would be a transformed box that is
not positioned (the transformed box contains them, which native layout does
not model yet); a transform on an inline box has no effect, as in CSS.
Geometry, hits and pixels match Chrome at 1x, 1.25x and 2x for whole-pixel
and percentage translations and for scales (the `transform-*` and `scale-*`
cases of `native_positioned_probe`: a scaled button with radii, outline and
text, list order with anisotropic factors, nested scales with a stacked
child). Blink paints an element's outline before its stacking-context
children at level zero, native after them (CSS2 Appendix E), a difference
that is not specific to transforms. A translation that is not a whole CSS pixel
moves the box exactly but its edges are snapped with it, while Chrome draws
the snapped box at the fraction; its edges then differ by under one pixel.
Native scrollable overflow does not include translated boxes.

#### View CSS engine (K8 T2 and T3)

One Rust implementation decides stylesheets, `set_style` values, class
names, the cascade and computed values for every host: the grammars in
`varta-common` (`view::syntax`, `view::css`, `view::stylesheet`, behind the
`view` feature, `no_std` with `alloc` and `libm` so every target computes
the same bits) and the cascade, custom-property substitution and computed
values in `varta-style`. The native renderer and the compiler's static
checks link it directly; the official browser host runs the same code as
`view-engine.wasm` (below). It follows the published specifications; an
admitted construct behaves as its specification says, and anything outside
the subset is a violation with a typed diagnostic (the subset fails closed
rather than ignoring what it does not admit). Chrome is the verification
oracle, not the definition.

- **Tokens (CSS Syntax 3).** Stylesheets and values are tokenized by §4:
  input preprocessing (§3.3: CR, CR LF and FF are newlines, NUL is U+FFFD),
  comments dropped (§4.3.2), escapes decoded (§4.3.7, at most six hex
  digits, NUL, surrogates and values above U+10FFFF become U+FFFD), numbers
  with exponents (§4.3.12), dimensions, percentages and `url(` (§4.3.6). The
  rule list is parsed by §5.4, and `!` followed by `important` (whitespace
  and comments between them allowed) ends a declaration as important
  (§5.4.6). A stored value that had comments or escapes is its §9
  serialization (an empty comment keeps two tokens apart), so a later
  `var()` scan sees neither; other values keep their source text.
- **Forbidden constructs** are found on decoded tokens, so no escape or
  comment hides them: a url token, the functions of `css::FORBIDDEN_FUNCTIONS`
  (`url`, `image-set`, `-webkit-image-set`, `expression`, `attr`, `element`,
  `-moz-element`), the at-rule `@import` and the HTML comment tokens
  `<!--`/`-->`. Inline `set_style` values cannot be important.
- **Class names (HTML class model).** `set_class`, TSX `class` literals and
  selectors take any token without ASCII whitespace or control characters,
  at most `css::MAX_CLASS_NAME_BYTES` UTF-8 bytes. A class selector is
  `.` and an ident token (Selectors 4 §6.6), so Tailwind's escaped classes
  (`.sm\:flex`, `.w-1\/2`, `.p-0\.5`, `.\[…\]`, `.\!p-1`, `.\32 xl\:…`)
  match the decoded names; class names are case-sensitive.
- **Selectors (Selectors 4).** Compound selectors (§3.1) of class
  selectors and the pseudo-classes `:hover` (§9.1), `:active` (§9.2),
  `:focus-visible` (§9.4), `:disabled` (§12.1.1) and `:checked` (§12.2.1), in
  any order, with at least one class, or `:root` alone (§13.1); pseudo-class
  names are ASCII case-insensitive. Specificity is §15 (every admitted
  simple selector is in the B component). Combinators, type, id,
  attribute, functional pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements are K8 S5.
- **Cascade (Cascade 5 §6).** Declarations are sorted by importance
  (§6.1): normal author declarations by layer, then specificity, then sheet
  id and source order, with inline `set_style` values (element-attached,
  §6.3) above them; important author declarations above inline ones, with
  their layers in reverse order, so an earlier layer's important
  declaration wins (§6.4.4). Unlayered declarations win over every layer
  when normal and lose to every layer when important.
- **Cascade layers (Cascade 5 §6.4).** `@layer` statements and blocks at
  the top level and nested in `@layer`, `@media` and `@supports` blocks,
  with dotted names (§6.4.2; CSS-wide keywords are invalid names) and
  anonymous blocks (§6.4.2.1, each distinct). The layer order is the order
  of first declaration across the document's sheets in ascending sheet id
  (§6.4.3); a layer's own rules form an implicit final sublayer after its
  sublayers. A declaration inside a conditional group rule counts only
  while its condition holds (§6.4.3), so the order is decided per media
  environment; a false `@supports` block declares nothing.
- **CSS-wide keywords (Cascade 5 §7.3).** Every property takes `initial`
  (the property's initial value, §7.3.1), `inherit` (the parent's computed
  value, also for non-inherited properties, §7.3.2), `unset` (§7.3.3),
  `revert` (§7.3.4: author declarations roll back to the user agent's own
  style) and `revert-layer` (§7.3.5: the value of earlier layers, then of
  the user-agent origin) as its whole value. `font-family: initial` is
  refused: its initial value is the user agent's own font (Fonts 4 §2.1),
  which no native host can name; `inherit`, `unset` and `revert` on it are
  admitted.
- **Registered custom properties (Properties and Values API 1 §3).**
  `@property --name { syntax; inherits; initial-value }` at the top level:
  `syntax` (§3.1, §5) is `"*"` or `|`-separated components of `<length>`,
  `<number>`, `<percentage>`, `<length-percentage>`, `<color>`, `<integer>`,
  `<angle>`, `<time>`, `<custom-ident>`, `<string>` or an identifier, each
  with an optional `+` or `#`; `inherits` (§3.2) is required; `initial-value`
  (§3.3) is required unless the syntax is universal and must be
  computationally independent (§4.1: no `var()`, font- or viewport-relative
  unit or `currentcolor`). Registrations are document-wide, the last one in
  sheet order winning (§2.1, §2.8), and at most
  `stylesheet::MAX_REGISTERED_PROPERTIES` across all sheets. A registered
  property starts at its initial value, a non-inheriting one is reset to it
  at every element, and a value that does not match the syntax after
  substitution is invalid at computed-value time and computes as `unset`
  (§2.7): the parent's value for an inheriting registration, the initial
  value otherwise. A registered value whose syntax has lengths computes at
  the declaring element (§2.4): every length becomes `px` against that
  element's font and the viewport, and a math function over lengths alone
  is evaluated, so a child inherits `20px`, not `2em` of its own font; a sum
  with a percentage stays as written. Other registered values keep the
  substituted text.
- **Conditional rules.** `@supports` (Conditional 3 §6.1) with declaration
  conditions, `not`, `and`, `or`, parentheses and `selector()`
  (Conditional 4 §6.1) is decided statically by this engine's own
  grammars: a declaration is supported when the engine admits it, a
  selector when it is in the selector subset, and `<general-enclosed>` is
  false. Conditions nest at most `stylesheet::media::MAX_CONDITION_DEPTH`
  deep; `@media`, `@supports` and `@layer` blocks nest up to
  `stylesheet::MAX_NESTING`.
- **Media queries (Media Queries 4/5).** Query lists (§2.1), `not`/`only`
  with the media types `all`, `screen` and `print` (§2.3; the renderer is
  `screen`), conditions with `not`, `and`, `or` and parentheses (§2.5, no
  mixing of `and` and `or` at one level), boolean context (§2.4.2) and the
  range syntax with `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `=` (§2.4.3), and the features
  `width`, `height` (§4.1, §4.2, also `min-`/`max-`), `orientation` (§4.4),
  `pointer`, `hover`, `any-pointer`, `any-hover` (§7.1–§7.3),
  `prefers-reduced-motion`, `prefers-contrast`, `forced-colors` and
  `prefers-color-scheme` (§12.1, §12.3–§12.5). Lengths are `0`, absolute
  units, `em` and `rem`, relative units being based on the initial font size
  (§1.3, 16px). The environment features are recorded host inputs, so
  rendering stays deterministic: the native `Environment` (`height`, `dark`
  and `preferences`, by default a desktop with a mouse and no stated
  preference, which is what headless Chrome reports) is filled by the
  desktop shell from the system's accessibility display options on macOS
  ("Reduce motion" and "Increase contrast", read again when the window
  regains focus or the theme changes) and by an embedder through
  `ViewLayout::with_preferences`; the browser host records the same
  features from `matchMedia` and its change events. An unknown feature,
  value or `<general-enclosed>` is a violation, not the `unknown` of §3.2.
- **Values (CSS Values 4).** Wherever a property grammar has a numeric type,
  the engine admits every length unit of §6 (`px`, `cm`, `mm`, `Q`, `in`,
  `pt`, `pc`, `em`, `rem`, `ex`, `ch`, `lh`, …, the viewport units with
  their `s`/`l`/`d` forms of §6.1.2), angles and times, and the math
  functions `calc()`, `min()`, `max()` and `clamp()` (§10) with `+`, `-`,
  `*`, `/`, nested parentheses and the constants `e`, `pi`, `infinity`,
  `-infinity` and `NaN`. `+` and `-` need whitespace on both sides, which the
  tokenizer enforces (`1px +2px` is two operands). Types follow §10.7, with
  percentages typed by the property's percentage basis. A top-level NaN is
  0 and infinities are clamped (§10.12) to `css::MAX_LOWERED_MAGNITUDE`, the
  native length range; a math result is clamped to the property's allowed
  range (§10.12: 0 in nonnegative properties, [1, 1000] in `font-weight`),
  and in integer properties (`z-index`, grid lines) rounded to the nearest
  integer, halves towards +∞ (§5.2). Other math functions are outside the
  subset.
- **Colours (CSS Color 4 and 5).** Hexadecimal colours with 3, 4, 6 or 8
  digits (§5.2), the 148 named colours (§6.1, ASCII case-insensitive),
  `transparent`, `currentcolor`, `rgb()`/`rgba()` (§5.1) and
  `hsl()`/`hsla()` (§7) in the legacy comma and the modern space syntax with
  `/ alpha`, `hwb()` (§8), `lab()`/`lch()` (§9.3), `oklab()`/`oklch()` (§9.4),
  `none` components (§4.4) and `color-mix()` (Color 5 §3) of one to
  `css::color::MAX_MIX_COLORS` colours with an optional interpolation method
  (Oklab by default) in `srgb`, `srgb-linear`, `lab`, `oklab`, `xyz`,
  `xyz-d50`, `xyz-d65`, `hsl`, `hwb`, `lch` or `oklch` and any hue method
  (Color 4 §13.4), premultiplied interpolation (§13.3) and missing
  components carried forward. Percentages are normalized by Values 5 §6.1
  with forced normalization: omitted percentages share what the specified
  ones leave, a total above 100% scales down, and a total below 100%
  multiplies the result's alpha by the total (Color 5 §3.3), so a zero total
  is transparent. Conversions use the sample code's matrices (§18); a
  colour outside sRGB is mapped by the CSS gamut mapping algorithm (§14.2,
  binary search, JND 0.02 ΔEOK, ε 0.0001). System colours, `color()`,
  relative colours and `currentcolor` inside `color-mix()` are outside the
  subset.
- **Other values.** `opacity` takes any number or percentage
  (`<opacity-value>`, Color 4 §15.1), clamped to [0, 1] at computed-value
  time; `font-weight` literal numbers must be in [1, 1000] (Fonts 4 §2.2);
  `white-space: pre`, `text-align: start | end` (Text 3 §7.1; the renderer is
  left-to-right), `transition-property` any property names (Transitions 1
  §2.1; unknown ones are ignored), and `transition-timing-function`
  `cubic-bezier()` (x in [0, 1]), `steps()` with every jump position,
  `step-start` and `step-end` (Easing 1 §2.2, §2.3).
- **Computed font sizes (Fonts 4 §2.5, Inline 3 §4.2).** The engine
  computes every element's font size and line height (`varta_style::font`),
  the references of the font-relative units: the host's `medium` size, the
  user-agent rows (`h1`–`h3` scale the inherited size by 2, 1.5 and 1.17,
  `pre` and `code` take `monospace`, form controls the 13.333px
  `-webkit-small-control` size and `line-height: normal`), author values
  (`medium`, percentages and `em` of the parent's size, absolute lengths),
  Blink's re-derivation where the generic family switches to or from the
  sole `monospace` (13/16 of the size unless an absolute length fixed it, and
  not once a packaged face names `monospace`) and Blink's minimum logical
  font size of 9px for sizes no absolute length fixed (em lengths keep the
  specified size, as in Blink). A computed `line-height` is `normal`, a
  number (a multiple of each element's size), or a length (a percentage of
  the element's computed size). It computes `font-weight` (`normal`, `bold`,
  numbers; the user-agent rows: `h1`–`h3` bold, `strong` `bolder` by the
  Fonts 4 §2.2.1 table, form controls `normal`) and `font-style` (`em`
  italic, form controls `normal`) the same way. The native renderer shapes
  text with these fonts; the browser host's Chrome derives the same ones
  from its user-agent sheet.
- **First available font and its metrics (Values 4 §6.1.1, Fonts 4 §5).**
  `ex`, `cap`, `ch`, `ic`, their root forms `rex`, `rcap`, `rch`, `ric`,
  `lh` where `line-height` is `normal` and `rlh` take the metrics of the
  element's (the root's) first available font (`varta_style::fonts`): the
  first family of its computed `font-family` list that the view's font set
  has a face for, else the set's default family, else the host's default
  font. A named family matches a packaged face's family or a named alias
  (ASCII case-insensitively), a generic family a face it aliases or else
  the host's own font for it; a family with neither is skipped. Within a
  family the face is matched by Fonts 4 §5.2 step 4 (stretch, then style:
  italic, oblique, normal or the reverse, then weight with the 400–500
  rule), weight ranges of variable faces included. A **packaged face** is
  read from its own tables (`read-fonts`, the same code in both hosts): the
  `OS/2` x-height, else the top of the `x` glyph's `glyf` outline, else
  0.5em; the `OS/2` cap-height, else the ascent; the `0` and `水` (U+6C34)
  advances (`hmtx` with `HVAR` deltas), else 0.5em and 1em; and for
  `normal` the ascent, descent and line gap of the shaper's selection
  (`OS/2` typographic metrics under `USE_TYPO_METRICS`, else `hhea`, else
  typographic, else Windows), each rounded to whole pixels at the used size
  and summed, as Blink's line spacing. A variable face is read at its
  location for the element (`wght` the matched weight, `opsz` the used size,
  `ital` for italic; `fvar`/`avar` normalization and `MVAR` deltas). A
  **host font** (a generic family no packaged face names, the default font,
  a native system-font set's families, a packaged face the engine cannot
  read) is measured by the host (`HostFonts`): natively through CoreText as
  Chrome on macOS measures it (CoreText's ascent, descent and leading
  rounded, with Blink's enlarged ascent of Times, Helvetica and Courier;
  CoreText's cap-height; the top of the `x` glyph's CoreText bounds; the
  `0` and `水` advances from the platform face's own tables at its location),
  and in the browser host by the bridge through the browser's own units (a
  hidden probe element in the view's shadow tree reports `1ex`, `1cap`,
  `1ch`, `1ic` and `1lh` through `computedStyleMap`); the engine decides
  which font is asked for. The root element's font is the initial family
  at the root font size. In `font-size`, `ex`, `cap`, `ch` and `ic` take the
  parent's font, and the result is an absolute size. Only when no font has
  metrics (a native host without faces or platform measurements) do the
  Values 4 fallbacks apply: `ex` and `ch` 0.5em, `ic` 1em; `cap` and a
  `normal` `lh` then stay unresolved. Recorded deviations of Chrome on
  macOS for packaged faces: it measures the `x` outline instead of the
  `OS/2` x-height (equal in well-formed faces), takes CoreText's estimates
  for a face without `OS/2` x- and cap-heights (without `x` and `H` glyphs,
  2/3 and 8/9 of the ascent) instead of the `x` outline, the ascent and the
  Values 4 fallbacks, applies no `MVAR` cap-height delta, and ignores
  `USE_TYPO_METRICS` for `normal`.
- **Lowering.** After `var()` substitution (Variables 1 §3), a valid value
  is lowered to the host grammar the renderer's consumers read
  (`css::lower`): math functions are evaluated, absolute and viewport units
  become `px`, the font-relative units become `px` against the element's
  font (Values 4 §6.1.1; in `font-size`, `em` alone stays a percentage of the
  parent's size and a sum with other lengths is the parent's absolute size;
  in `font-size` and `line-height`, `lh` is the parent's), named colours and
  colour functions `rgba()` with 8-bit channels after gamut mapping, and
  `opacity` clamped numbers. A math function that sums lengths with
  percentages (Values 4 §10.10) keeps its form with every length in `px`
  (`calc(50% - 16px)`, in nonnegative properties wrapped as
  `max(0px, …)` for the clamp of §10.12) and resolves at layout against the
  percentage basis of its context, for the properties of
  `css::layout_math_property` (box sizes, margins, padding, gaps, the flex
  basis, insets and `vertical-align`): native layout interns it in a
  per-thread table of at most `calc::MAX_CALC_EXPRESSIONS` expressions and
  hands Taffy the index as its opaque calc handle (Taffy 0.15.1 with the
  recorded patch `vendor/taffy/VARTA-PATCH.md`, which lets the high-level
  tree resolve calc handles), and the browser host sets it inline. A value
  the native renderer cannot render yet is refused at parse time with
  `Unrenderable` and, when it only appears after substitution, is invalid at
  computed-value time natively: `cap` and a `normal` `lh` without any font
  metrics, a sum of lengths and percentages in other
  properties (`border-radius`, `transform`, `object-position`, grid tracks),
  and values of the specifications that native layout lacks
  (`display: inline-block` and the other inner/outer display types,
  `position: sticky`, intrinsic sizes, `overflow: scroll | clip`,
  `white-space: pre-line | break-spaces`, `text-align: justify`, border
  styles other than `solid`).
- **Layout and text properties (S4).** Mapped properties are expanded
  when a stylesheet is parsed (`view::mapped`): the flow-relative box
  properties of CSS Logical 1 §4 (`padding-`, `margin-` and `inset-`
  `inline`/`block` with their `-start`/`-end` forms) in the subset's only
  writing mode (`horizontal-tb`, `ltr`: inline start left, block start
  top), `inset` (Positioned Layout 3 §3.1, the box rule) and `flex`
  (Flexbox 1 §7.1: `none`, `auto`, factors with omitted factors 1 and an
  omitted basis `0%`, Chrome's computed form of the specification's 0).
  Each mapped declaration declares its physical longhands at its own place
  in the cascade, so a mapped property and its physical longhand win over
  each other by the ordinary order (Logical 1 §4). A value with `var()`
  gives every longhand the whole value and its part, split after
  substitution (Variables 1 §3.1, pending-substitution values); a split
  that fails is invalid at computed-value time. Mapped properties are
  stylesheet-only: the engine's computed values, the native renderer and
  the browser bridge see only physical longhands. New properties:
  `translate` and `scale` (Transforms 2 §4, two-dimensional; `scale`
  percentages compute to numbers; the renderer takes positive factors
  only), `transform-origin` (Transforms 1 §5, keywords and two
  length-percentages, lowered to `<x> <y>` lengths or percentages; a sum of
  a length and a percentage is refused as unrenderable) and
  `letter-spacing` (Text 3 §8.2, `normal | <length>`, inherited, absolute
  at computed-value time). Natively the effective transform is the
  `translate`, then `scale`, then `transform` list (Transforms 2 §6.1)
  around the `transform-origin`; letter spacing is added after every
  typographic character unit by the shaper.
- **Selectors (S5, first part; Selectors 4).** Selector lists of complex
  selectors (`stylesheet::selector`): type and universal selectors (the view
  tags), classes, the descendant, child, next-sibling and
  subsequent-sibling combinators, `:is()` and `:where()` (forgiving lists)
  and `:not()`, nested at most `selector::MAX_SELECTOR_NESTING` deep with at
  most `selector::MAX_COMPOUNDS` compounds per complex selector; `:root`;
  `:host`, which in the view's sheets matches nothing (Scoping 1 §3.2.1);
  `:first-child`, `:last-child`, `:only-child`, their `-of-type` forms and
  `:nth-child()`, `:nth-last-child()`, `:nth-of-type()`,
  `:nth-last-of-type()` with `An+B` (no `of S`), counting element siblings;
  `:hover`, `:active`, `:focus`, `:focus-within`, `:focus-visible`,
  `:enabled`, `:disabled` and `:checked`. Specificity is the
  `(ids, classes, types)` triple of §17 (`:where()` adds nothing, `:is()`
  and `:not()` their most specific argument). The engine matches right to
  left with the restart rules of Servo's matcher, so a failed descendant
  search never retries above its closest failing ancestor; selectors that
  search ancestors, siblings or arguments charge
  `compounds × (ancestors + siblings + 1)` to the cascade work estimate per
  candidate element. The browser bridge records the focused element
  (`view_engine_focus`) apart from the focus-visible one; natively every
  focus is visible, as before. A shorthand that wins over its longhand
  (`margin`, `padding`, `gap`) gives the longhand its component in the
  computed values, so the bridge's inline order cannot reverse the
  cascade. Native style reads are recomputed when an element's children
  change order. Refused: pseudo-elements, attribute and id selectors,
  `:has()`, `:nth-child(… of S)` and the form-validity pseudo-classes.
- **Not yet admitted:** `@keyframes`, `@container`, nesting, the rest of
  S4 (per-side border longhands, `overflow-x`/`-y`, `visibility`,
  `text-transform`, `rotate`, and the display types and sizes native
  layout lacks: `inline-block`, `inline-flex`, `fit-content`, `sticky`),
  the rest of S5 (above), and the paint stages S6–S8.

**Browser bridge (K8 T3).** The official browser host runs the engine as
`view-engine.wasm`: `varta-style-wasm`, a `wasm32` shim of `varta-style`
built by `scripts/build-view-engine.py` with the locked toolchain and the
`intrinsics` profile and checked in under `crates/varta-project/src/browser/`
with `view-engine.json` (source fingerprint, target, compiler and size; a
test fails when the sources change without a rebuild), as
`varta-kv-codec-wasm` is. Its only `unsafe` code reads and writes its
arguments in linear memory and calls its one import,
`varta_view.font_metrics(kind, family, family_len, weight, italic, size,
out) -> u32`, through which the DOM bridge measures a host font (`kind` 0 a
named family, 1 a generic family, 2 the default font; five `f64` written at
`out`: `ex`, `cap`, `ch`, `ic` and the `normal` line height; 1 when
measured, 0 when the browser renders no such font); the module keeps at
most 1024 answers. The packaged faces reach it through `view_engine_face`
(family name and font file in the input buffer, a bit per generic family it
stands for) and the default family through `view_engine_default_family`;
the Worker's view model, which has no DOM, measures nothing. The view model mirrors every batch into an
engine `Session` inside a transaction (`begin`, then `commit` or `abort`,
so a refused batch changes nothing), and the engine checks each class,
style value and stylesheet with the native verdicts. The DOM bridge keeps
only DOM calls: it asks the engine for each element's computed values
(cascade with layers and importance, `@property` registrations, `var()`
substitution and lowering) and sets them as inline styles, and it records
the media features, the viewport and the `:hover`, `:active` and
`:focus-visible` states as host inputs for the engine. No stylesheet text
reaches the DOM, so Chrome's own handling of `@property` in shadow trees
and its colour clipping do not apply. The L0 grammar tables of
[embedding.md](embedding.md#view-protocol-draft-v0-unstable) remain the
contract for third-party hosts that do not run the engine. Cross-host
equality is a test: `browser::view_engine_tests` runs the corpus
`view-engine-corpus.json` through the Wasm module (under Wasmtime), the
native `Session` and the native renderer, requires the same acceptance,
refusal and computed values and records them in
`view-engine-expected.json`, which the Node test of the browser view model
must reproduce.

Chrome comparisons (`native_css_engine_probe` with
`scripts/test-native-css-engine.mjs` at 1x, 1.25x and 2x) run in two modes:
`bridge`, the official browser host applying the scenes through its engine,
and `platform`, Chrome's own cascade over the stylesheet text as the
specification oracle. Each scene must match within a mean of 2/255 and
each box's centre pixel within 1/255. Deviations of Chrome recorded by the platform mode:
Chrome clips out-of-gamut colours per channel instead of gamut mapping (all
286 Tailwind 4 palette colours lie in sRGB within rounding and match to
1/255; the bridge, which applies the engine's mapped colours, matches
exactly); Chrome ignores `@property` rules in shadow trees, although
registrations are not scoped to a tree scope (§2.8), so the platform mode
registers them in the document; Chrome accepts `color-mix()` with exactly
two colours and drops a declaration with one or more than two, which
Color 5 §3 admits; and Chrome snaps lengths to its 1/64 px
layout unit, which native layout does not (pre-existing, not specific to
these values).

`varta-runtime` sets the clock before each view commit, input, pointer and
environment change: a scripted headless session uses its virtual loop time
(a `wait` step moves transitions deterministically), an application
instance the wall clock since it started. `Application::view_animating`
tells a host that a transition runs (or an overlay scrollbar waits for its
fade-out or animates) and `view_advance_animations` moves the clock to now
before a frame, reporting whether anything paints differently; `varta-shell`
then presents a new frame each time the previous one was presented and that
report is true, and the last shows the end value.

#### Native positioned painting and stacking

Native paint, hit testing and scrolling admit `position: static | relative |
absolute | fixed`, their insets and `z-index: auto | <integer>` with the paint
order of [CSS2 Appendix E](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS2/zindex.html) for the
admitted subset. Real stacking contexts are the view root, a box with opacity
below 1, every `position: fixed` box, and a positioned box or an in-flow
flex/grid item with an integer `z-index`; `z-index` on any other box has no
effect, including a static block that opacity makes a context. A context
paints its own background and border, then its negative layers, the
backgrounds of its in-flow blocks, its content phase (inline content, atomic
flex/grid items and controls), then its layers at level zero and above, then
outlines. Layers are ordered by z-index and then tree order; opacity contexts
that are neither positioned nor flex/grid items, including inline opacity
contexts, are at level zero. A positioned box with `z-index: auto` paints
atomically at level zero as a pseudo context: its positioned and
context-creating descendants join the nearest real context at their own
tree-order place, including those found while it paints.
A pre-pass over the painted element tree assigns every layer to its context
before painting, so a negative layer paints before the in-flow ancestors that
contain it; the same pre-pass builds each element's curved clip scope in tree
order. The view root is the root stacking context: a root-level negative layer
paints above the root's own background and below unpositioned blocks. The
Chrome oracle therefore gives its stand-in root `div` `isolation: isolate`.

Clips and scroll offsets follow the containing block chain. An in-flow box
takes its parent's clip scope and scroll offset; an absolute box takes its
containing block's (the nearest positioned ancestor, or none for the initial
containing block, which does not scroll with the view root); a fixed box takes
none and stays anchored to the viewport. The same chain drives wheel scroll
chaining (`scroll_target`), `scroll_into_view_supported`, `scroll_into_view`
planning and assistive reveal: absolute and fixed paths are admitted, and a
scroller outside an absolute box's containing block neither moves nor clips it.
Hit regions are recorded in paint order, so the topmost painted box is the
target.

An opacity group composites under its own rectangular and curved clip. An
absolute or fixed descendant whose rectangular clip is not inside the innermost
enclosing opacity group's clip, or whose curved scope does not descend from the
group's scope, fails with `PaintError::Unsupported` instead of being clipped
incorrectly. Positioned layers use only the existing rectangle, path, border,
glyph and group commands: retained damage remains the existing command diff,
vector preparation of positioned frames without opacity groups is
pixel-identical to the CPU reference, and frames with opacity groups keep the
existing explicit CPU fallback. Budgets, command limits and the guest ABI are
unchanged. A positioned or z-indexed box inside an inline formatting context is
refused by inline layout; `position: sticky` and other containing-block
creating properties are not admitted. Chrome snaps scrolled content to whole
device pixels while native paint keeps fractional scroll offsets, so the
oracle's scroll offsets are whole device pixels at its scales.

#### Native images (`img`)

The native renderer lays out and draws `img` elements to the HTML Standard
and the CSS image, sizing and inline specifications; Chrome is the
verification oracle, never the definition. An image is a file of the
artifact's [resource section](#packaged-images-section-version-2)
(version 2), decoded once by the host into a `varta_view::ImageSet` and
given to the view with `View::set_images` (`varta-runtime`:
`ViewLayout::with_images`; `varta-shell` does both for every packaged
artifact, with an empty set for an artifact without images). With a set, a
batch whose `img` `src` or `srcset` names an image outside it is refused as
a whole (`Violation::UnpackagedImage`), as the browser host refuses an
unpackaged asset before any effect; a view without a set (headless
snapshots, `varta-preview`) keeps the grammar-only check and shows no image,
so its `img` elements represent nothing (below). The browser bundle carries the same files
under the same names and leaves every rule below to the browser: web stays
web, native stays native.

- **Formats.** A file is told apart by its signature, as the WHATWG MIME
  Sniffing Standard's image type pattern table (§6.1) defines
  (`varta_common::view::images::sniff`), never by its name: PNG (with APNG,
  PNG 3rd edition), JPEG, GIF87a/89a, WebP (lossy, lossless, animated; RFC
  9649), BMP and ICO (its largest entry). Decoding uses the image-rs decoders
  in safe Rust (`png`; `image` with `zune-jpeg`, `gif`, `image-webp`), every
  one with dimension and allocation limits. AVIF is refused
  (`ImageRefusal::Avif`): its only image-rs decoder is the C `dav1d` library.
  SVG as an image is refused (`ImageRefusal::Svg`): drawing it needs an SVG
  renderer (SVG 2 with CSS, fonts and the HTML §4.8.4.3 secure-static
  mode), a separate engine decision. Any other file is
  `ImageRefusal::Unknown`; a file that does not decode refuses the set
  (`ImageError::Malformed`).
- **Limits.** `ImageSet::decode` checks every image before any is decoded:
  the count (`MAX_IMAGES`), names (the view resource grammar, at most
  `MAX_IMAGE_NAME_BYTES`), unique names and the encoded total
  (`MAX_IMAGE_TOTAL_BYTES`); each file within `MAX_IMAGE_BYTES` and
  `MAX_IMAGE_DIMENSION` per axis, at most `MAX_IMAGE_FRAMES` frames, the
  pixels of every frame charged to `MAX_IMAGE_DECODED_BYTES` before they are
  decoded, and the retained frames with their downscaling levels within
  `MAX_IMAGE_CACHE_BYTES` (each level at most halves the previous one).
  These are conservative initial values pending an owner decision.
- **Colour** (CSS Color 4 §10, PNG 3rd edition §4.3, §11.3.2). Images are
  converted to sRGB, the colour space Chrome draws them in on an sRGB
  output, with `moxcms`: a PNG's space comes from `cICP`, then `iCCP`, then
  `sRGB`, then `cHRM`/`gAMA` (a `gAMA` of 1/2.2 without `cHRM` is sRGB, as
  Chrome treats it); JPEG and WebP from an embedded ICC profile; an untagged
  image is sRGB and an ICC profile that does not parse is ignored. PNG,
  WebP and the other formats convert their straight-alpha pixels at decode,
  as Skia's decoders apply `skcms`; JPEG converts what is sampled, as Skia
  draws a JPEG in its own space and transforms at draw (measured: converting
  JPEG at decode differs from Chrome by about 5/255 when upscaled). `cICP`
  with an HDR transfer (PQ, HLG), narrow range or a non-RGB matrix is
  refused (`ImageError::Color`): Chrome tone-maps HDR for its output, which
  is not modelled. 16-bit channels round to 8 bits; pixels are premultiplied
  as Skia premultiplies.
- **Orientation** (CSS Images 3 §5.1). The EXIF orientation (PNG `eXIf`,
  JPEG and WebP `Exif`) is kept with the pixels and applied when sampling:
  `image-orientation: from-image`, the initial value, shows the oriented
  image with its natural size swapped for quarter turns, and `none` the
  stored pixels. The property is inherited.
- **Animation** (HTML §4.8.4.3 "update the image data"; PNG 3rd edition
  §4.9 APNG, GIF89a, RFC 9649). Animated PNG, GIF and WebP frames are
  composited by their decoders and advance on the view's animation clock
  (`View::set_animation_time`) from the time the element's `src` or
  `srcset` was set, so frames are deterministic like transitions and
  `View::animating` keeps a playing image's frames requested. A frame of 10
  ms or less lasts 100 ms (Chrome's and Firefox's rule); a GIF plays its
  NETSCAPE loop count plus one time (0 forever, none once), APNG `num_plays`
  and WebP `loop_count` times (0 forever); a finished animation stays on its
  last frame.
- **Selection** (HTML §4.8.4.3, the source set, `srcset` and `sizes`
  parsing and "select an image source"). `srcset` and `sizes` are
  parsed as the source set and source size grammars define (density and
  width descriptors; source sizes with `max-width`/`min-width` media
  conditions in `px`, `rem` at the initial 16px, `vw`), `src` joins as the
  `1x` candidate when no candidate has density 1 and none has a width, and
  a width descriptor becomes a density through the first matching source
  size (`100vw` by default). The user agent chooses the candidate; this is
  Chromium's choice (`HTMLSrcsetParser` selection): candidates by density,
  the first whose density reaches the device pixel ratio unless the ratio
  is below the geometric mean of it and the one before. The chosen
  candidate's density divides the natural size (the density-corrected
  natural size). Chromium's preference for an already cached candidate is a
  cache heuristic, not a rule, and is not modelled.
- **Missing image** (HTML §15.4.2). An `img` that names no image represents
  nothing: a replaced box with zero natural size. One that would render its
  `alt` text (a non-empty `alt`) or a sized broken-image box (`width`/
  `height` attributes or sizes) is refused: its look is the user agent's
  choice (Chrome draws an icon and a grey border) and is not a standard
  rendering. `decoding` and `loading` are admitted and change nothing
  natively: every image is local and decoded before guest code runs, so
  `async`/`lazy` show the same pixels as `sync`/`eager` (HTML §4.8.4:
  `decoding` is a hint and `loading` defers only fetching); the browser
  bundle passes them to the browser.
- **Sizing** (CSS 2.1 §10.3.2, §10.6.2, §10.4; CSS Sizing 4 §4.1; HTML
  §15.4.3). The image is a replaced box with its natural size and ratio:
  `width` and `height` (lengths and percentages), `min-*`/`max-*`, padding,
  border and margins apply; with one size `auto` the other follows the
  ratio, with both `auto` the §10.4 constraint table applies (so
  `max-width: 100%` scales both axes). The `width`/`height` attributes are
  presentational hints for `width`/`height` and map to `aspect-ratio: auto
  w / h` (HTML §15.2, §15.4.3): the image's own ratio wins once it is known,
  as for an image without a ratio the hint gives one. `aspect-ratio` takes
  `auto`, a ratio or both (CSS Sizing 4 §4.1). A size a parent imposes (a
  stretched or flexed flex item, a grid area) is final on its axis; flex
  items do not shrink below their natural size (the automatic minimum).
- **Placement** (CSS 2.1 §9.2.2, §10.8; CSS Inline 3 §2.2, §4.2). A
  block-level image is `display: block`, a flex or grid item or an absolutely
  or fixed positioned image. An inline image alone on its line (its parent a
  block container, no inline-level neighbour, baseline-aligned) has its line
  box: the parent's strut and the image's margin box standing on the
  baseline, placed by `text-align` and start-aligned when it overflows (CSS
  Text 3 §6.1). Any other inline image is an atomic inline of its parent's
  inline formatting context ([lines of text](#images-in-lines-of-text)).
- **Object** (CSS Images 3 §4.5, §4.6). `object-fit` (`fill`, `contain`,
  `cover`, `none`, `scale-down`) sizes the image in its content box and
  `object-position` (keywords, lengths, percentages) places it; the content
  box clips it.
- **Sampling** (CSS Images 3 §5.2). Measured against Chrome (Skia): each
  device pixel is sampled at its centre with bilinear filtering between
  texels, edges clamped. Drawn smaller than half its size, an image is
  sampled from a level chain built as `SkMipmap` builds it (every axis longer
  than one pixel halves, rounding down; a two-tap box on an even axis, a
  1-2-1 kernel on an odd one, integer channels truncated) with linear
  filtering between the two levels around the level of detail
  `max(0, log2(1 / s) - 0.5)`, where `s` is the larger of the two axis
  scales in device pixels per image pixel. `image-rendering` (inherited):
  `auto`, `smooth` and `high-quality` sample so; `pixelated` scales each axis
  by nearest neighbour to the integer multiple of the natural size closest
  to the target (at least one) and the rest of the way smoothly, as §5.2
  defines; `crisp-edges` samples the nearest texel, which §5.2 admits.
- **Painting** (CSS2 Appendix E). An image paints in its element's content
  phase as an atomic replaced element, after its background and border, in
  its object rectangle, whose edges are its layout box in Blink's 1/64 px
  layout units snapped to whole paint pixels before DPI. A rounded image is
  clipped by its content-box curve whatever its `overflow` (CSS Backgrounds
  3 §5.3), whose coverage is then its only edge coverage; otherwise
  fractional device edges are covered by area, and a clip that cuts the
  image masks only where it cuts. Opacity, the ancestors' clips and
  `transform` (translations and `scale()`) apply as to any box.
- **Hits and accessibility** (HTML-AAM `img`). The image box is its own
  pointer target (rounded by its radii). An image is named by its `alt`; an
  `img` with an empty `alt` and no `aria-label`/`aria-labelledby` is
  presentational and has no role, as Chrome exposes it.
- **Display list.** An image is the software-only scene primitive
  `Primitive::Image`; a frame with images is retained and damaged like any
  software frame, and `Renderer::prepare` returns it as the explicit
  `PreparedFrame::Raster`, so the optional GPU backend presents its pixels.
  The public `DisplayList` has no image command.

##### Images in lines of text

An inline image that shares its line box with text or other inline content
is an atomic inline of the parent block's inline formatting context
(`inline::atoms`, CSS 2.1 §9.2.2). Its margin box is one unbreakable advance
of the line, a Parley `InFlow` box (the [Parley
patch](../vendor/parley/VARTA-PATCH.md) records the line breaking):

- **Breaking** (CSS Text 3 §5.1). There is a soft wrap opportunity before
  and after an atomic inline, even next to a letter. The opening edges of
  inline boxes right before it and the closing edges right after it move
  and wrap with it; an image wider than an otherwise empty line overflows
  it. The image and those edges are one word of the min-content width. A
  collapsible space before or after an image is content (CSS Text 3 §4.1.1
  collapses only adjacent spaces).
- **Vertical alignment** (CSS 2.1 §10.8.1; CSS Inline 3 §4.2). The image's
  baseline is its bottom margin edge. `vertical-align` places that edge
  against the parent's baseline and first available font, with Chrome's
  shifts in Blink's 1/64 px layout units: `baseline` on it; `sub` a fifth of
  the parent's font size plus one pixel below; `super` a third plus one
  above; `middle` with its margin box's centre half the parent's x-height
  above the baseline (a font without an x-height, OS/2 `sxHeight`, is
  refused: Chrome then measures glyphs); `text-top`/`text-bottom` with its
  top/bottom on the parent's rounded ascent/descent; a length raises it by
  that length and a percentage by that part of the image's own line height.
  `top` and `bottom` align the margin box with the line box's top or bottom
  once the rest of the line is placed, and grow the line downwards or
  upwards when the image is taller (the aligned subtree, CSS Inline 3
  §4.2.3). The line box spans the strut, the text and every image's margin
  box (CSS 2.1 §10.8).
- **Boxes.** An enclosing inline box's fragment spans the image's advance at
  that box's own font box (its background and border do not grow with the
  image), and the image's geometry is its border box. The image paints, is
  hit and is named as any image, right after its line's text in tree order
  (or in its stacking layer when it has opacity).
- **Refused.** Percentages in the image's sizes, margins or padding (the
  line is measured before its containing block is fixed), a positioned or
  transformed image, an image inside an inline box with opacity, and images
  in a `text-overflow: ellipsis` flow or a flow whose preserved white space
  takes the native white-space model.

##### Conformance

| Feature | Specification | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src`, `alt` | HTML §4.8.4 | Native; `alt` names the image |
| Image that represents nothing | HTML §15.4.2 | Native: zero-size replaced box |
| Alternative text, broken-image box | HTML §15.4.2 | Refused (user agent rendering) |
| `width`/`height` attributes, ratio hint | HTML §15.2, §15.4.3; CSS Sizing 4 §4.1 | Native |
| `srcset`, `sizes`, density selection | HTML §4.8.4.3 | Native (Chromium selection) |
| `decoding`, `loading` | HTML §4.8.4 | Admitted; no effect on local images |
| PNG, APNG | PNG 3rd edition | Native |
| JPEG | ITU T.81, JFIF | Native |
| GIF, animated | GIF89a | Native |
| WebP, animated | RFC 9649 | Native |
| BMP, ICO | Microsoft formats | Native (largest ICO entry) |
| AVIF | AV1 Image File Format | Refused (no safe-Rust decoder) |
| SVG as an image | SVG 2, HTML §4.8.4.3 | Refused (no SVG renderer) |
| Format by signature | MIME Sniffing §6.1 | Native |
| ICC, `cICP`, `iCCP`, `sRGB`, `cHRM`/`gAMA` | CSS Color 4 §10; PNG 3rd edition §11.3.2 | Native (SDR); HDR, narrow range refused |
| EXIF orientation, `image-orientation` | CSS Images 3 §5.1; PNG §11.3.4.5 | Native |
| Animation timing and loops | HTML §4.8.4.3; GIF89a; PNG §4.9; RFC 9649 | Native, on the view clock |
| `object-fit` | CSS Images 3 §4.5 | Native |
| `object-position` | CSS Images 3 §4.6 | Native |
| `image-rendering` | CSS Images 3 §5.2 | Native |
| `aspect-ratio` | CSS Sizing 4 §4.1 | Native (images) |
| Replaced sizing and constraints | CSS 2.1 §10.3.2, §10.4, §10.6.2 | Native |
| Inline image alone on a line | CSS 2.1 §10.8 | Native |
| Inline image in a line of text | CSS 2.1 §9.2.2, §10.8; CSS Text 3 §5.1 | Native |
| `vertical-align` | CSS 2.1 §10.8.1; CSS Inline 3 §4.2 | Native (`middle` needs an x-height) |
| Painting order | CSS2 Appendix E | Native |

Geometry, hits, image roles and names, animation timing and pixels match
Chrome at 1x, 1.5x, 2x and 3x (`native_image_probe` with
`scripts/test-native-images.mjs`; the viewport and each image's box are
compared separately within the mean bound of the other probes, and frame
durations and loop counts with Chrome's `ImageDecoder`). The cases cover
every format, colour source and orientation, `object-fit` and
`object-position`, `image-rendering`, `aspect-ratio` and the attribute
hints, `srcset` and `sizes`, animation frames on the clock, natural,
explicit, ratio-derived and constrained sizes, inline lines alone and in
text with every `vertical-align`, flex and grid items, downscaling levels,
rounded clips, opacity, `transform`, fractional and positioned boxes.
Chrome draws a downscaled `pixelated` image by nearest neighbour where §5.2
asks for the smooth rest, and drops `crisp-edges`; the oracle compares those
cases with the values Chrome implements. Curved clip edges differ by up to
about a quarter of full intensity on a few pixels (path antialiasing),
within the bound.

## Local modules

The compiler accepts named function imports (`import { f as g } from "./lib.ts"`),
direct function exports (`export function f(...)`) and local export lists
(`export { f as g }`). Local export lists may forward an imported function.
Each module has a separate function scope; private helpers with the same name in
different files do not collide. Imports must name exported functions, and their
parameter/result types are checked at each call. Duplicate or reserved bindings,
duplicate exports and unresolved exports fail before emission. Before v31, type
aliases and interfaces retain their existing erased behavior and are not
importable.
Profile v31 adds [named types](#checked-f64-utf16-v31--named-types), including
type-only imports/exports and `./x.js` specifiers for `.ts` sources. Profile v32
adds [re-exports](#module-re-exports-module_reexports): `export { … } from` and
`export * from` forward functions, module constants, named types and classes
without binding them locally; their sources are ordinary graph dependencies.

The entry module must declare its own `main(): void` with no parameters. An
imported binding or an export alias cannot supply the entry point. A dependency
may declare an ordinary function named `main`, with its own signature. Recursion
within a file is supported; calls to the entry function remain rejected.

The dependency graph is a DAG: cycles, including self-imports, fail with an import
site diagnostic. There are no top-level execution or initialization semantics,
except that v32 initializes [module constants](#module-constants-module_constants)
in dependency order before `main`.
Dependencies are visited in sorted path order, once per resolved identity, and
linked before their dependents. Function slots are then allocated in module order
and declaration order, independent of import declaration order. Modules are
linked at compile time: running a built artifact never loads source files.
All linked host calls use the application's manifest and optional host ceiling;
an imported module cannot introduce permissions of its own. Source imports read
build inputs and do not grant guest filesystem access.

The project loader requires explicit relative `.ts` paths starting with `./` or
`../`. It normalizes dot segments lexically and rejects paths outside the
canonical directory containing the configuration file. Absolute/bare paths,
URLs, backslashes, controls, query strings and fragments are rejected; there is
no extension probing, directory/index lookup or network loading, and before v38
no package resolution (v38 package specifiers are described below).
Parent segments are allowed when the normalized path stays inside the root.
The root directory is pinned once; every dependency is opened relative to that
descriptor with no-follow at every component. Both external and internal
symlinks are rejected. Inputs must be bounded regular UTF-8 files. The explicitly
configured entry retains support for legacy layouts outside the config directory;
this does not expand the boundary for discovered dependencies.

Profile v38 (`tsx()`) extends the specifier mapping, following TypeScript's
extension substitution under `node16`/`nodenext` and `bundler` resolution
(`./x.js` tries `x.ts`, then `x.tsx`; `./x.jsx` tries `x.tsx`; TypeScript
then falls back to declaration and JavaScript files, which Varta never
loads). An explicit `./x.tsx` specifier names that file. A `./x.js`
specifier probes `x.ts` and then `x.tsx` in that order: exactly one must
exist, and it is the module identity. Where TypeScript silently prefers
`x.ts`, Varta rejects the import when both exist ("ambiguous import"; rename
one or import it with its explicit `.ts`/`.tsx` extension) and reports both
candidates when neither exists, as module errors at the import site. A
`./x.jsx` specifier names `x.tsx` only, never `x.ts`, without probing. The
probe is a no-follow metadata lookup through the same pinned root
descriptor, with no-follow directory opens at every component: a symlinked
directory on the way fails the import, and a symlinked candidate counts as
existing, so loading it is then rejected. Probing never reads a file; only
the resolved source is loaded, within the same path, size and graph
budgets. Profiles v31–v37 keep `./x.js` → `x.ts` without probing and reject
`.jsx` (and `.tsx`) specifiers.

Profile v38 (`package_specifiers()`) adds **package specifiers**: a bare
specifier imports a typed npm package by name and compiles the TypeScript
source the package ships.

```ts
import { UarpClient } from "uarp-sdk";
import { extra } from "@scope/name/extra";
```

- **Specifier.** `name`, `@scope/name`, optionally followed by `/subpath`.
  Names follow npm's rules for new packages: at most 214 bytes with the
  scope, lowercase `a-z`, `0-9`, `-`, `.`, `_`, `~`, not starting with `.` or
  `_`, not `node_modules` or `favicon.ico`. A subpath is `/`-separated
  segments without empty, `.` or `..` segments, controls, `\`, `?`, `#`, `%`,
  `:` or `*`. An invalid name or subpath is a module error. A specifier with
  a scheme (`node:fs`, `https:`) or a leading `.` or `/` is not a package
  specifier and keeps the relative-path rules above.
- **Location.** The package directory is exactly
  `<config dir>/node_modules/<name>` (or `node_modules/@scope/<name>`). No
  parent directory and no nested `node_modules` is searched, so bare
  imports inside a package resolve from the same directory (npm's flat
  layout). Every read walks the pinned configuration-directory descriptor
  with no-follow at every component: a symlinked `node_modules`, scope,
  package directory, manifest, source map or source is refused (npm/pnpm
  links included).
- **Manifest.** `package.json` is read once per package as a bounded
  regular UTF-8 JSON object (1 MiB). Manifests and source maps count against
  one loader budget of 4 MiB across the graph, each source map once per path
  however many exports share it; each specifier resolves once.
- **Export selection.** With `exports` (not `null`), the export key is `.`
  or `./subpath`. A string, array or conditions object exports only `.`; an
  empty object exports nothing, so the top-level `types` never applies; a
  subpath map is matched by exact key only. When no exact key matches and
  the map has a `*` or trailing-`/` key, the import is refused as an
  unsupported export pattern; otherwise the subpath is not exported. A
  `null` entry is not exported; a fallback array, a nested condition under
  `types` and an object mixing subpath and condition keys are refused. Only
  the `types` condition directly under the entry is read, wherever it
  appears among the conditions; `import`, `require`, `default` and every
  other condition are ignored, so JavaScript targets never matter. When the
  `.` entry has no `types` condition, or there is no `exports`, the root
  uses the top-level `types` string. A subpath has no fallback, and without
  `exports` a subpath (a deep import) is refused.
- **Declaration.** The target must be a `.d.ts` path inside the package
  (export targets start with `./`; the top-level `types` may omit it),
  without `.`/`..` segments, empty segments, controls, `\`, `?`, `#`, `%`,
  `:` or `*`, and the file must exist. `.d.mts`/`.d.cts` and a types target
  naming a `.ts` source are refused. The declaration is never read.
- **Source.** The adjacent `<declaration>.map` (Source Map revision 3, no
  `sections`, empty or absent `sourceRoot`) must name exactly one source.
  That path, relative to the map's directory without a scheme, an absolute
  path, `\`, `?` or `#`, is normalized lexically and must stay inside the
  package directory; it must name an existing `.ts` or `.tsx` source, not a
  declaration. Extensions are classified ASCII-case-insensitively and must
  be lowercase: `index.D.ts` is a declaration and `index.TS` is refused, so a
  case-insensitive file system cannot open a file under another identity. The source is then the module identity, loaded like any
  module: a package imported by name and by a relative path is one module.
- **Typed packages only.** A package whose `types` export or top-level
  `types` is missing ("unsupported untyped package"), whose declarations
  have no source map or whose mapped source is not shipped ("unsupported
  declarations-only package"), or whose declarations map to JavaScript is
  refused. There is no fallback to declarations or JavaScript.
- **Graph.** Relative imports inside the package follow the module rules
  above, within the same module, import, depth and source budgets and the
  same sorted dependency order. All failures are module errors at the
  import that named the package.

Profiles v1–v37 reject a valid package specifier with "package specifier
`name` requires profile checked-f64-utf16-v38". Package resolution adds no
capability and no runtime input: packages are linked at build time like any
module.

Profile v38 (`text_imports()`) adds **text resources**, in the TC39 import
attributes syntax that Deno, Bun and the Import Text proposal use:

```ts
import css from "./console.css" with { type: "text" };
View.stylesheet(1, css);
```

- **Attributes.** Exactly one attribute, `type: "text"` (an identifier or
  string key, a string value). No attribute list (`with {}`), another key, a
  duplicate key or another type (`"json"`) is a module error at the import;
  every earlier profile keeps rejecting attributed imports as unsupported
  syntax. Re-exports with attributes stay unsupported. The host declarations
