  (`varta.d.ts`) declare ambient `*.css`, `*.txt` and `*.md` modules with a
  `string` default export for editor typing only; they admit nothing, and
  the attribute rule here is authoritative for every extension.
- **Binding.** Only a default import, of type `string`; named, namespace and
  type-only imports of a text resource are module errors. The text is
  verbatim: nothing is transformed, decoded or normalized.
- **Resolution and loading.** `ModuleLoader::resolve_text` resolves the
  specifier with the module rules except the extension rule (relative only,
  no URL/query/fragment syntax or backslashes, no trailing `/`, normalized
  lexically inside the configuration directory), and `load` reads it
  through the same pinned root descriptor with no-follow at every component
  as a bounded regular UTF-8 file; a symlinked file or directory, invalid
  UTF-8 or a file over 1 MiB fails. A leading byte order mark (U+FEFF) is
  rejected rather than stripped. The trait's default `resolve_text` refuses,
  so an embedder's loader admits text resources only by implementing it.
- **Graph.** A resource is a unit of the module graph: read once per
  resolved identity, it counts against the module, import and aggregate
  source budgets, is visited in the sorted dependency order and appears in
  the dependency metadata (`check --json` `modules`) with no imports of its
  own. One path cannot be both a module and a text resource. Its unit holds
  the text as the module constant `default: string`, so it is stored once
  in the static data like any string literal (the v38 multi-page static
  region admits more than 64 KiB) and linked into the artifact, which never
  reads it at run time: `build --single` is reproducible from the same
  inputs.
- **Stylesheet check.** When the default binding is passed directly as the
  text argument of `View.stylesheet(id, text)` and the module declares no
  other binding of that name, the compiler checks the text against the L0
  stylesheet grammar (`varta_common::view::stylesheet`, the parser the
  headless renderer applies) and reports the first violation as a
  `type_error` inside the resource file, with one-based Unicode-scalar
  columns and zero-based UTF-8 byte offsets like every diagnostic. Any other
  use is validated by the host when the batch is applied.

Profile v32 also adds [default exports](#default-exports-default_exports):
`export default` declarations and bindings, `import x from` and `default` in
export and re-export lists, linked as the name `default`.

Limits: 256 unique modules including the entry, 2048 import declarations, 32 modules
on the active dependency path, 1 MiB per source, 4 MiB aggregate source and 256
user functions across the graph. Re-export declarations (v32) count as import
declarations. Existing per-file lexical/semantic complexity
limits still apply. Namespace, side-effect and attributed imports, type-only
imports before v31, default imports/exports and export-from/export-star before
v32, namespace re-exports and dynamic imports fail explicitly. Unused imports and re-exports still
resolve and validate their dependency.

Embeddings use `compile_modules(ModuleSource, &dyn ModuleLoader)`. The loader
separates stable identity resolution from bounded text loading and owns its
source-access policy; the compiler performs no filesystem or network I/O.
`resolve_text` (v38 text resources) has a refusing default implementation.
Single-source `compile_typescript[_with_path]` remains available and requires an
explicit loader when source imports dependencies. Parse-only helpers do not link.
The result returns Wasm plus dependency metadata. `CheckedProject.modules` and
successful `check --json` expose `modules` as dependency-first `{path, imports}`
records, with sorted, deduplicated import paths. This metadata is for build-time
inspection and is not persisted into Wasm or manifests. ABI and artifact format
are unchanged.

## Build-time Tailwind stylesheets (K8 T1)

`varta-tailwind` (tooling layer: `varta-project` depends on it; no engine
crate, the runtime or the launcher does) is a Rust port of the CSS-first
compiler of Tailwind CSS v4.3.5 (MIT, Tailwind Labs; `LICENSE-TAILWIND` in
the crate). A project names its entry stylesheet in the configuration:

```json
{ "languageProfile": "checked-f64-utf16-v38", "tailwind": { "entry": "src/app.css" } }
```

```css
/* src/app.css */
@import "tailwindcss";
@theme { --color-brand-500: oklch(0.6 0.2 250); }
```

```tsx
import css from "./app.css" with { type: "text" };
View.stylesheet(1, css);
View.mount(<button className="rounded-lg bg-brand-500 px-4 py-2">Save</button>);
```

**Configuration.** `tailwind.entry` is a relative path inside the
configuration directory (no absolute path, backslash, query or fragment) and
requires profile v38 (`text_imports()`); otherwise the manifest is invalid.
The program must import the entry as a [text resource](#local-modules):
an entry the graph does not import is an error (`TailwindUnused`), so a
configured stylesheet is never silently dropped.

**Pipeline** (`check`, `dev`, `build` alike; `CheckedProject::load`):

1. The entry file is read through the project loader (pinned root,
   no-follow, 1 MiB).
2. The module graph is loaded with the entry's text served as the empty
   sheet and scanned for class tokens (`varta_compiler::
   scan_classes_with_profile`, below). When a class position composes a
   name, the program is type-checked to resolve it (with TypeScript's
   literal inference, [type level](#type-level-type_level): `const size =
   "sm"` has the type `"sm"`); a composition that cannot be enumerated is a
   located `type_error` and stops the build.
3. The entry is compiled (`varta_tailwind::compile_with_loader`, its
   relative `@import`s read through the same loader, below) and built with
   the tokens plus its `@source inline(…)` safelist (`Compiler::build`).
4. The generated stylesheet is served as the text of the entry's text
   resource and the program is compiled as usual: it is a string constant in
   the static data, checked against the L0 stylesheet grammar where it is
   passed directly to `View.stylesheet` (the first violation is reported
   inside the entry file with the position in the generated text), and
   applied by the host exactly like any `View.stylesheet` text. The artifact
   never reads the entry, a theme or the oracle at run time.

**Determinism.** The tokens are a sorted set; Tailwind's sort (variant order
bitmask, property order, declaration count, then the natural compare of the
class) is total over them; the theme keeps JavaScript `Map` insertion order
through a sequence index; every map in the port is ordered. The same entry
and sources give the same stylesheet bytes, and therefore the same Wasm and
`build --single` bytes (tested by rebuilding).

**Class tokens.** Read from the parsed program, never from a filesystem
walk: every string literal value and template literal text (the cooked
value, ECMA-262 Static Semantics: TV), every string literal *type* (TypeScript
literal types, so a `class` whose static type is a finite union of string
literals, `type Tone = "bg-red-500" | "bg-blue-500"`, contributes exactly
its members), and the static values of TSX attributes and text, of every
program module; engine preludes and text resources are skipped. Each text is
split on ASCII whitespace (Infra Standard "split a string on ASCII
whitespace"), the HTML model of the `class` attribute (HTML Standard,
global attribute `class`: a set of space-separated tokens). At most
`varta_compiler::MAX_CLASS_TOKENS` distinct tokens of at most
`MAX_CLASS_TOKEN_BYTES` bytes are kept (longer tokens are skipped; more
tokens is an error). Tokens that are not Tailwind candidates produce no CSS,
as in Tailwind.

**Compositions (Varta extension beyond Tailwind's scanner).** In a class
position (a TSX `class`/`className` expression, the class argument of
`View.setClass`/`View.bindClass`), a template literal or a `+`
concatenation chain whose hole touches non-whitespace literal text or
another hole (`` `btn-${size}` ``, `"bg-" + tone + "-500"`, `` `${a}${b}` ``)
builds a class name at run time, which Tailwind's own scanner cannot see.
Varta resolves it through the checker's types: the program is lowered once
with the touching holes watched, and each hole's type is recorded where the
expression is checked (through aliases, parameters, fields, annotated
bindings, conditional and union types; generic instantiations are merged).
When every touching hole has a finite union of string-literal types, every
combination (the hole values spliced into the literal text, ECMAScript
template and `+` string concatenation) is a token; holes separated by
whitespace are independent tokens. More than
`varta_compiler::MAX_CLASS_COMBINATIONS` combinations in one composition
is a located `type_error`, as is a touching hole of any other type
(`string`, a number, a union with non-literal members), naming the
remedies (a literal union type, complete literals such as
`cond ? "btn-lg" : "btn-sm"`, or `@source inline(…)`). The types are the
v38 checker's, which follow TypeScript's literal inference ([type
level](#type-level-type_level)): an unannotated `const x = "a"` has the
type `"a"` and the elements of an `as const` tuple their literal types, so
both are enumerated; a number or boolean literal type contributes its
ECMAScript string (`const weight = 600` gives `font-600`), while a widened
`let` (`string`) stays an error.

**Supported Tailwind surface.** Candidates (variants, static and functional
utilities, named, fractional, bare and arbitrary values, `(--var)`
shorthands, type hints, modifiers, `!` prefix and suffix, negative values,
arbitrary properties and variants), every built-in utility and variant of
v4.3.5 including the legacy utilities its compatibility layer registers,
compound variants (`group-*`, `peer-*`, `not-*`, `has-*`, `in-*`, named
groups), theme resolution (`theme.css` defaults, `@theme` with `default`,
`inline`, `reference`, `static` and `prefix(…)`, namespace resets
`--color-*: initial`, `@keyframes`), Preflight, `@apply` (including inside
`@utility`, in dependency order), `@utility` (static and functional with
`--value()`/`--modifier()`), `@custom-variant` (selector list or `@slot`
body), `@variant`, `@source inline(…)`/`@source not inline(…)` with brace
expansion, `--theme()`, `--spacing()`, `--alpha()` and `theme(--var)`,
`@reference`, and `@import` with `layer()`, `supports()`, media,
`important`, `prefix()`, `theme(…)` and `source(none)` parameters.

**`@import`.** Resolved only at build time, never at run time or over a
network. A package name (`tailwindcss`, `tailwindcss/theme`,
`tailwindcss/preflight`, `tailwindcss/utilities`) names the embedded pinned
copy of the published package (`index.css`, `theme.css`, `preflight.css`,
`utilities.css` of npm `tailwindcss@4.3.5`). A relative `./` or `../` path
names a project stylesheet, resolved from the importing stylesheet and
loaded through the host's `StylesheetLoader` (in `varta-project`, the
project loader: the text-resource rules — inside the configuration
directory, no URL, query or fragment syntax, backslashes or trailing `/` —
and a read through the pinned root descriptor with no-follow at every
component, as a bounded (1 MiB) UTF-8 regular file). Following CSS
Cascade 5 (§2 "Importing Style Sheets"), an `@import` is valid only at the
top level before every rule except `@charset`, `@layer` statements and
other imports (a misplaced or nested one is an error rather than silently
ignored), and its conditions apply to the imported sheet: `layer()` as an
`@layer` block, media queries as `@media`, `supports()` as `@supports`
(Tailwind's `buildImportNodes`), resolved like any written condition. An
import cycle, a chain deeper than `MAX_IMPORT_DEPTH` (32, the module
graph's depth), more than `MAX_IMPORTED_FILES` (256) project stylesheets or
more than `MAX_INPUT_BYTES` (1 MiB) of entry and imported text together is
an error; a stylesheet imported twice is inlined twice, as CSS does.
`url()`, `data:`, `http(s):` and bare names other than the package are
refused.

**Rejected, with typed errors (`TailwindError`).** `@plugin` and `@config`
(they load JavaScript; Varta compiles Tailwind without a JavaScript
runtime); `@source "path"` and `source("path")` (filesystem scanning; classes
come from the module graph); `@import` of a URL, an absolute path or an
unknown package, a cycle or a misplaced import (above); legacy dot-path
`theme()`
(Tailwind resolves it only through the JavaScript configuration layer);
Tailwind's own directive errors (nested or empty `@utility`, invalid names,
`@apply` of unknown classes, circular `@apply` or `@custom-variant`). Bounds:
`MAX_INPUT_BYTES` (1 MiB of entry and imported text), `MAX_IMPORT_DEPTH`,
`MAX_IMPORTED_FILES`,
`MAX_CANDIDATES`, `MAX_CANDIDATE_BYTES`, `MAX_OUTPUT_BYTES` (1 MiB, the
text-resource bound), parser, selector, nesting, condition, variant and
brace-expansion depth constants in the crate.

**Canonical output.** The build runs Tailwind's `optimizeAst` without
polyfills (unused theme variables and theme keyframes removed, `@property`
deduplicated, at-root nodes hoisted, nesting resolved as Tailwind resolves
it), then puts the sheet in canonical form, defined by the specifications:

- no comments (Tailwind's `/*!` licence header included);
- no nesting: remaining nested style rules are flattened by CSS Nesting 1
  ("Nesting Style Rules" and the nesting selector `&`, with `:is()` where
  the parent is a list), nested conditional group rules become the group
  rule around a copy of the parent rule ("Nesting Other At-Rules"), and
  declarations after a nested rule keep their order as a following rule
  with the same selector (the nested declarations rule);
- `@supports` resolved statically (CSS Conditional 3 "Feature Queries: the
  `@supports` rule", Conditional 4 `selector()`): the condition grammar (`not`, `and`, `or`, `(declaration)`,
  `selector()`; `<general-enclosed>` is false) is evaluated against Varta's
  own engine, the L0 stylesheet grammar of `varta_common::view::stylesheet`
  (a UA "supports" a declaration it would accept); a true block is replaced
  by its contents in place, a false one is dropped. The answer therefore
  follows the engine: as T2 widens the grammar, more blocks resolve true;
- Media Queries 4 range syntax ("range context" of media features)
  normalized to the
  `min-`/`max-` forms (`(width >= X)` is `(min-width: X)`, `(width < X)` is
  `not (min-width: X)`, `(width <= X)` is `(max-width: X)`, `(width > X)` is
  `not (max-width: X)`, reversed and double ranges likewise, a `not` operand
  of `and`/`or` parenthesized), for media and container size queries
  (Containment 3), with directly nested single `@media` rules merged by
  `and` (Conditional 3: nested conditional rules apply when all their
  conditions hold);
- printed in Tailwind's format (two-space indentation).

The emitted CSS uses Cascade 5 `@layer`, Properties and Values API 1
`@property`, Color 4/5 (`oklch()`, `color-mix(in oklab, …)`), Values 4
`calc()`, Selectors 4 (`:where()`, `:is()`, `:not()`, `:has()`) and Media
Queries 4 / Containment 3 queries. Tailwind's output also relies on browser
behaviour beyond those specifications, which the compiler passes through
unchanged and the engine's grammar decides: vendor-prefixed properties and
pseudo-elements in Preflight and utilities (`-webkit-text-size-adjust`,
`-webkit-tap-highlight-color`, `-webkit-font-smoothing`,
`-moz-osx-font-smoothing`, `-webkit-box-decoration-break`,
`::-webkit-*` and `::-moz-*`), draft features (`:open`, `:popover-open`,
`field-sizing`, `::details-content`, `text-wrap`), and the `@supports`
fallbacks it writes for older browsers (resolved as above).

**Conformance.** The official compiler is only an oracle. Committed fixtures
(`crates/varta-tailwind/tests/fixtures`, with the MIT notice): 2,986
candidates of `candidatesToCss` (one utility per family, every variant and
arbitrary form, a sample application's 312 class uses) and eight whole
entry-stylesheet builds (`compile(css, { polyfills: 0 }).build(…)`:
defaults, a customized theme with `@utility`, `@custom-variant`, `@apply`,
`@variant`, `@source inline`, functions; `important`, `prefix()`, layered
imports, `theme(static)`, `@reference`, utilities only). Both sides are put
in canonical form before comparison; every case must match. The full corpus
of 39,152 candidates runs as a manual test (`oracle_full`, ignored).

**Application status.** Track T2 widens the engine grammar
([view CSS engine](#view-css-engine-k8-t2-and-t3)). Static Tailwind class
tokens (`w-1/2`) and utilities built from them apply since T2 S1–S3; a full
`@import "tailwindcss"` build is still refused, and the CLI tests assert its
precise first violation (the theme layer's `:root, :host` selector list,
stage S5). The end-to-end application test is ignored until S5.

## Source diagnostics

The project service resolves the configured entry to its canonical file path and
passes that identity into the compiler. Public `compile_typescript_with_path`
and `parse_typescript_with_path` accept source text and a diagnostic path without
reading that path; the original in-memory helpers retain `input.ts` as their
compatibility name. Naming a source does not change emitted Wasm bytes.

Parsing, lexical resolution, subset checking and type checking share one source
context per file. Nested failures keep the innermost available span rather than being
relabeled as the containing call or function. Function and expression spans also
survive typed IR lowering, so static-data emission errors identify the source
literal that exceeds the budget. This is compile-time source metadata; Wasm
runtime source maps and stack-trace symbolication are not implemented yet.

Diagnostics have stable category codes: `syntax_error`, `type_error`,
`module_error`, `unsupported_syntax`, `invalid_program` and `internal_error`. Missing
modules, cycles and path-policy failures point to the import site; dependency
syntax, type and static-data failures retain the dependency's filename and range.
Type mismatches
include expected/actual scalar types where available. The shared diagnostic
record contains the filename, message, a half-open source range, and an optional
bounded source excerpt. Lines and columns are **one-based Unicode scalar**
positions, not UTF-16 editor offsets; `byte_offset` is zero-based UTF-8 in the
original supplied text. A leading BOM is excluded from character columns but
included in byte offsets. CRLF, non-ASCII identifiers and end-of-file positions
preserve these conventions. Excerpts are windowed to 160 source characters around
the error, expand tabs for display and replace control characters; full ranges
remain available even when the displayed excerpt is truncated. Source-wide size
limits report the file start without copying an oversized source into the parser.

`check --json` preserves `status` and the human-readable `error` string and adds a
`diagnostics` array. Successful checks return an empty array; non-source failures,
such as an unreadable configuration file, also return an empty array rather than
inventing an entry-file location. The compiler currently stops at the first
failure. One diagnostic object for `let x: string = 7` is:

```json
{
  "code": "type_error",
  "message": "type mismatch for x: expected string, found number",
  "file": "/work/app/src/main.ts",
  "range": {
    "start": { "line": 2, "column": 19, "byte_offset": 49 },
    "end": { "line": 2, "column": 20, "byte_offset": 50 }
  },
  "snippet": {
    "text": "  let x: string = 7;",
    "highlight_start": 18,
    "highlight_width": 1
  }
}
```

Human-facing failures use `file:line:column: message` followed by the excerpt and
a caret. JSON stdout remains valid JSON; human diagnostics go to stderr. All
project commands use the same source validation path and return nonzero on these
failures before producing artifacts.

## Capabilities and trust

All host access is denied unless the **exact operation** is granted. A grant for
`env.has` cannot authorize `env.get`; `fs.read` cannot authorize `fs.print`.
Logging has no system-access capability but is output-budgeted.

The [permission model](development-plan.md#permission-model) makes every denial
in new profiles recoverable (`NotAllowedError` or a failed `VartaResult`, never a
trap) and adds permission states, a host permission broker and user consent as a
grant source bounded by the host ceiling. V38 adopts its first part
([permission broker v1](#permission-broker-v1-turn_budgets)): a manifest with
`abiVersion` 34 may mark a grant `"required": false` and give it a `"purpose"`,
and may request `"budgets"` ([turn budgets](#turn-budgets-and-application-instances-turn_budgets))
and name its file roots (`"fsRoots"`, [virtual file roots](#virtual-file-roots-file_roots));
a host policy may cap budgets but never carries `required` or `purpose`; and
`--decisions PATH` supplies stored decisions keyed by the artifact's identity
for `run`, `dev` and packaged applications. Everything below holds for every
profile; earlier profiles never read the new members.

Configuration shorthand:

```json
{
  "entry": "src/main.ts",
  "target": "native",
  "policy": "strict",
  "out": "dist/app",
  "capabilities": {
    "time": { "now": true },
    "env": { "get": ["APP_NAME"] },
    "fs": { "read": ["/data/**"] },
    "net": { "fetch": ["http://example.com/public/**"] }
  }
}
```

`time.timer` (v36) is a separate boolean operation: it authorizes arming
timers (`setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `AbortSignal.timeout`) and neither implies
nor is implied by `time.now`; see [Timers](#timers-timers).

Only `strict` is implemented. `compat` is rejected until it has an actual
behavioral contract. Unknown operations, unknown fields, duplicate manifest
grants, wrong value types and unsafe patterns are errors. Empty lists and false
are valid explicit denials; omitted grants also deny. Policy complexity is capped
by `MAX_POLICY_GRANTS` grants and `MAX_POLICY_PATTERNS` patterns, with at most
`MAX_GRANT_PATTERNS` patterns per grant and `MAX_PATTERN_BYTES` bytes per
pattern. A wildcard comparison also fails closed when the product of
pattern/input byte lengths exceeds `MAX_PATTERN_MATCH_WORK`, bounding work
outside Wasm fuel. The values are in the embedding contract's
[manifest limits](embedding.md#manifest-limits).

Canonical manifest:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "abiVersion": 1,
  "policy": "strict",
  "capabilities": [
    { "id": "env.get", "patterns": ["APP_NAME"] },
    { "id": "time.now", "enabled": true }
  ]
}
```

`entry` and `target` metadata are optional. Legacy unversioned JSON manifests use
schema/ABI version 1 defaults but must pass the same strict grant validation.
Legacy string grants and implicit `enabled: true` are no longer accepted.

The embedding application can supply trusted grants directly, or use
`run_wasm_bytes_with_policy(bytes, requested, ceiling)` to constrain package
requests with a separate trusted host ceiling. The two policies are independently
validated and checked for every concrete operation/resource. Wildcard patterns
are never flattened into an approximate intersection. A ceiling can only restrict
requested permissions, never introduce an operation or resource the package did
not request.

The CLI preserves declared-manifest behavior when `--policy` is absent. Supply
`--policy host-policy.json` to constrain `run`, `dev`, `inspect`, `validate` or the
packaged application's own invocation. The host file uses the same strict
manifest schema; with `abiVersion` 34 it may map v38 file roots (`fsRoots`, an
object of root names to absolute host directories, see [Filesystem](#filesystem)),
which a package manifest only names. An explicit `{"capabilities":[]}` denies all privileged access;
a missing, unreadable or malformed policy is an error, never a fallback to the
package's permissions. Policy paths are resolved relative to the invocation's
working directory. Host policy is local execution input and is never embedded or
written into the artifact; `init`, `check` and `build` reject this flag.

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "abiVersion": 1,
  "capabilities": [
    { "id": "env.get", "patterns": ["APP_NAME"] },
    { "id": "time.now", "enabled": false }
  ]
}
```

```sh
varta run dist/app.wasm --policy host-policy.json
varta dev --policy host-policy.json
varta inspect dist/app.wasm --policy host-policy.json --json
./dist/app --policy host-policy.json
```

Inspection and JSON validation include an `authorization` object with the mode,
`combination: "allOf"`, complete requested and host-ceiling scopes, and one review
decision per requested operation. `denied` means an omitted/false/empty filter;
`granted` applies to enabled boolean operations; `runtime_check` means that the
scoped filters must both accept the actual resource. It does not promise that
arbitrary wildcard scopes overlap or that every call will succeed. A null
`hostCeiling` means no ceiling was supplied; an empty array is an explicit denial.
Validation still checks artifact/ABI/schema/declarations, not application behavior:
a valid deny-all policy can validate successfully while its operations are denied
at execution. `inspect` without a host policy continues to describe the declared
permissions and labels its authorization mode `declared`.

A native launcher itself has the authority of the OS user launching that
executable. Rebuild existing launchers to make their own CLI accept `--policy`;
the portable artifact format and ABI are unchanged.

### Planned GPU rendering and application graphics

**Direction recorded 2026-11-03; optional UI prototype committed in `be85c981`.**
GPU rendering of Varta UI, a guest graphics API for games, and compatibility with Three.js are
three separate deliverables. This direction extends the native renderer design
without expanding the current L0 subset or admitting new host imports. Delivery
and acceptance are tracked as [P13a–P13c](development-plan.md#gpu-and-game-graphics-future-direction).

**UI renderer (P13a).** Keep application logic in Wasm and CSS, layout, shaping,
hit testing and accessibility semantics on the CPU. Extract a bounded,
backend-independent scene from the current tiny-skia-specific retained display
list; CPU and GPU renderers consume the same scene and preserve model revisions
and stale-input rejection. The host owns GPU submission and window presentation.
Retain the CPU implementation for fallback and reference checks. Render on changes
and during active animations rather than continuously repainting an idle UI.
Cache reusable geometry, glyphs and images; avoid per-frame GPU-to-CPU readback.

The optional desktop `gpu` feature pins wgpu 30.0.0, vello_gpu 0.3.0 and
pollster 0.4.0. It uses host-owned vector commands and shared frame/input metadata;
no guest import, capability or language ABI changes. The software reference can
replay the same neutral commands exactly (lowered border color fields within one
channel unit of the CPU painter). Native presentation has no per-frame
readback. Recording overflow or device/surface failure switches to CPU without
restarting Wasm; stale vector frames are acknowledged before CPU regeneration.
One GPU submission can remain outstanding; nonblocking completion polling ends
in a two-second recovery timeout. macOS output explicitly tags Display P3 and
converts sRGB paint primaries per draw and per color-field cell. Distinct
border-side colors draw directly as contour-clipped whole-pixel cells, with no
layer or intermediate texture (the layer texture allowance stays zero);
isolated opacity groups still switch the frame to CPU. Neutral paths and lowered
color fields share an 8 MiB estimated cache and retain full scene admission
charges on hits. Existing 4096-per-axis limits and
64 MiB individual GPU buffer limits do not establish total GPU-memory accounting.
The default build/backend remains CPU pending broader acceptance.
The [Vello renderer families](https://github.com/linebender/vello#choose-a-renderer)
have distinct maturity and device requirements. Pin and review the chosen
dependencies at adoption. Metal, Vulkan and DX12 paths are candidates through
[wgpu](https://github.com/gfx-rs/wgpu#supported-platforms); actual Pi and desktop
device acceptance remains necessary. GPU acceleration does not itself implement
missing CSS, controls, IME, clipboard or accessibility.

**Application graphics (P13b).** Plan a separately versioned, typed Wasm-to-host
graphics API for buffers, textures, shaders, render pipelines and batched command
submission. A graphics surface can be composed with TSX UI using host-owned GPU
resources and coordinated frame presentation. It needs explicit surface sizing,
DPI, clipping, layering and input ownership, a bounded frame callback with timing,
and game input beyond the current L0 event subset. A frame callback remains a
budgeted application turn, not an unmetered callback into the guest.

Define capability admission, opaque resource ownership, validation before effects,
resource destruction, cancellation and shutdown, bounded upload/queue sizes,
GPU-memory accounting, and device/surface-loss recovery before exposing the API.
Shader admission and GPU execution need their own limits and failure policy:
Wasm fuel does not meter GPU execution. Retain the existing guest isolation and
host ceilings; do not promise exact GPU instruction accounting or deterministic
pixels across devices. Audio, gamepads, pointer lock and other game services
need separately specified contracts; a 3D rendering demo does not establish a
complete game platform.

**Three.js compatibility (P13c).** Unmodified Three.js is not supported today.
Its [WebGLRenderer](https://threejs.org/docs/pages/WebGLRenderer.html) requires
WebGL 2; its [WebGPURenderer](https://threejs.org/manual/pages/webgpurenderer)
uses WebGPU with a WebGL 2 fallback. An internal wgpu device supplies neither
those JavaScript APIs nor a compatible canvas/environment. JavaScript sources
with `.d.ts` declarations also do not satisfy Varta's typed-source admission.

The preferred native direction is a typed graphics library or a port over P13b.
An adapter alone is insufficient unless the library sources also compile and
their language, binary-value, loader and host dependencies are supported. Pin a
candidate library version and publish a dependency/admission inventory before
claiming compatibility. Running original Three.js in a browser/WebView is a
separate compatibility option requiring a future architecture decision; it is
not an accepted fallback and does not inherit Varta's Wasm metering guarantees.
The existing no-WebView native direction remains in force.

**Acceptance.** First compare the same Showcase UI under CPU and GPU in Debug
and Release: startup, input-to-present latency, median/p95 frame costs, CPU/GPU
memory and artifact size. Check geometry, clipping, text, hover, editing,
scrolling, resize/DPI and failure recovery; compare geometry and visual output
with stated tolerances rather than requiring CPU/GPU pixel identity. Then prove
a bounded animated 3D scene alongside interactive TSX UI, resource cleanup,
limit rejection and device-loss behavior on declared targets. Three.js acceptance
requires a separately pinned port or compatibility mode and its own conformance
matrix. These future increments do not close P10, M7 or release acceptance.

### Filesystem

Through v37 guest paths and `fs.*` patterns are absolute **host** paths. Under
v38 they are **virtual** paths `/<root>/...` under roots that the host maps
(below, and [virtual file roots](#virtual-file-roots-file_roots)); an absolute
host path that is not under a declared and mapped root is denied. The
pattern language and the descriptor rules are the same in both modes.

Patterns must be absolute and cannot contain traversal. `*` matches within a
single path component, `**` can span separators, and `?` matches one non-separator
character. Root/component boundaries remain intact: `/data/**` cannot match
`/data-secret/file`.

A v38 project names its roots and requests virtual paths; the directories are
relative to the configuration directory and stay inside it:

```json
{
  "languageProfile": "checked-f64-utf16-v38",
  "entry": "src/main.ts",
  "target": "native",
  "out": "dist/app",
  "fs": { "roots": { "project": "." } },
  "capabilities": { "fs": { "read": ["/project/fixtures/**"] } }
}
```

The built manifest carries `"fsRoots": ["project"]` and the virtual patterns,
never a directory. `varta dev` reads under the configuration's roots; every
other run maps them through the host policy, whose `fsRoots` object names an
absolute host directory per root (a root the host does not map denies):

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "abiVersion": 34,
  "fsRoots": { "project": "/srv/app" },
  "capabilities": [{ "id": "fs.read", "patterns": ["/project/fixtures/**"] }]
}
```

Under v38 the pinned descriptor is the root's (from the configuration or the
host mapping), not the static prefix of a pattern: the request and the
ceiling are matched lexically against the whole virtual path, and the file is
opened below the root descriptor with no-follow at every component.

The rest of this section describes the host-path mode of v1–v37; its
descriptor and read rules hold for v38 roots as well.

At execution setup, explicitly granted directory roots are opened and pinned as
capability descriptors. With a host ceiling, these descriptors come from the
host's scopes. Requested paths must also pass the package's lexical scopes before
any file is opened; a package-supplied root alias cannot acquire authority outside
the pinned host root. Each guest path is matched relative to the corresponding
root and opened through those descriptors, with **no-follow at every component**.
Symlinks below the granted root are rejected, including links to other files
inside that root. Directory and file opens do not reuse a checked ambient path.
This closes the canonicalize/open race. Root authority is acquired once at setup;
a declared root alias is resolved at that time.

Only regular files are read. Reads are nonblocking at open, capped before the
result is allocated unboundedly, and checked for UTF-8 where the ABI returns text.
OS filesystem operations remain synchronous; a stalled remote filesystem is not
made cancellable by the guest's fuel budget.

### KV databases

V38 `kv.read` and `kv.write` are path grants over the same virtual paths and
roots as `fs.*`; a database file is pinned through the root's descriptor and
SQLite's path open is verified against it ([KV storage](#kv-storage-kv)).
`kv.read` opens and reads, `kv.write` writes (and makes an open writable);
neither authorizes the other or any `fs.*` operation.

### Network

`net.get` and `net.fetch` implement HTTP only: HTTPS grants and unsupported
schemes are rejected for them. V37's `net.request` admits `http` and `https`
under the same URL rules ([network requests](#network-requests-net_request)).
URLs are parsed before authorization; scheme, normalized hostname and effective
port must match exactly. Wildcards are permitted only after the authority; `*`
can match path/query characters and `?` retains its URL query-separator meaning.
Control characters, whitespace, credentials and fragments are rejected. Encoded
paths are conservatively rejected to avoid server-specific decoding aliases.

The same parsed URL is passed to the transport. Automatic redirects and ambient
proxies are disabled, so a permitted response cannot silently grant another
request target. The HTTP client bounds headers and body and applies an end-to-end
remaining deadline including name resolution, connect and body reading. There is
no handwritten request-line/header construction.

## Tool Contract v1 and offline discovery

The entry module may explicitly publish an exported named function:

```ts
export function echo(value: string): string { return value; }
export function main(): void {}
varta.tool({ name: "text.echo", description: "Return supplied text" }, echo);
```

`varta.tool` is a compile-time form, accepted only as a direct top-level call in
the entry module. It emits no guest initialization or object allocation. Its two
arguments must be a literal object with exactly `name` and `description` string
fields and a named function binding explicitly exported by that module. A local
function or an imported/re-exported function may be the handler; exporting a
function alone never publishes it. Dependencies cannot publish tools implicitly.
`main` cannot be a tool. Spreads, computed fields, dynamic metadata, extra fields,
duplicate fields/names and inline callbacks fail with source diagnostics.

The compiler derives ordered named parameters and the result from the checked
function signature. Supported input types are `number` (signed i32), `boolean`
and `string`; `void` is additionally supported as a result. Optional/default/rest
parameters, objects, arrays, `VartaResult` and generic tool signatures are not
supported. Parameter names use ASCII JS identifier characters, at most
`MAX_TOOL_NAME_BYTES` bytes. Tool names start with an ASCII letter and contain
ASCII letters/digits, `_`, `-` or `.`, at most `MAX_TOOL_NAME_BYTES` bytes.
Descriptions are nonblank UTF-8, at most `MAX_TOOL_DESCRIPTION_BYTES` bytes,
without NUL. There are at most `MAX_TOOLS` tools and `MAX_TOOL_PARAMETERS`
parameters per tool (values in the
[entry-point limits](embedding.md#entry-point-limits)).

One `varta.tools` custom section contains strict JSON `ToolCatalog` metadata,
bounded to `MAX_TOOL_CATALOG_BYTES`, with independent `contractVersion: 1` and
`invocationAbiVersion: 1`. Unknown/duplicate JSON fields, unsupported versions,
noncanonical ordering and invalid limits/types fail closed. The catalog is sorted
by tool name; parameters retain signature order. Applications with no tools omit
the section. Host ABI v1, manifest schema v1 and container format v1 are unchanged.

`inspect` adds `toolCatalog` (null for no-tool artifacts). It projects canonical
types into closed JSON input schemas with every named field required, and output
schemas wrapping the result as `{ "value": ... }`; void maps to null. i32 bounds
are explicit. String schemas describe a character ceiling, while a separate UTF-8
byte ceiling remains authoritative. Schemas are generated, not separately stored
or accepted as a second source of type authority. Version 1 exposes no declared
domain errors (`domainErrors: []`); typed application errors belong to C2.

Each tool exports `varta.tool.<name>` with the checked physical Wasm signature.
Artifact validation requires the listed exports and matching signatures, rejects
unlisted reserved exports and recomputes each handler's transitive privileged
host operations from its direct call graph, including recursive calls. The exact
sorted set must match `requiredEffects`. Unprivileged logging is excluded.
Handlers must be guest-defined functions; string-transfer helpers cannot call
any host imports. Indirect/ref calls are outside tool ABI v1. Tool modules require exactly one
valid `varta.abi` section and cannot have a Wasm start function. Code validation
does not instantiate the module, call `_start`/handlers or run a native launcher.
All artifact commands validate contracts; `validate` additionally reviews grants.

Catalog limits currently equal the shared runtime ceilings: 64 KiB serialized
input, 1 MiB serialized output, 1 MiB per UTF-8 string, 8 MiB guest memory,
1,000,000 fuel, 1024 host calls and a five-second deadline. They are fixed in
contract v1, not configurable grants. The JSON invocation boundary below enforces
input/output envelopes. Metadata is public and untrusted:
it is neither an authenticity proof nor an authorization decision. Type/ABI checks
cannot prove semantic equivalence between same-signature implementations. Runtime
capability enforcement remains necessary for every actual operation.

### Tool invocation ABI v1 ownership

The low-level ABI uses a **fresh instance per invocation**. The shared dispatcher
validates inputs, enforces budgets, instantiates without calling `_start`, and uses:

| Value/operation | Physical representation |
| --- | --- |
| number | i32, signed integer bounds |
| boolean | i32, host must accept/produce only 0 or 1 |
| string | i64 immutable handle: high 32 bits UTF-8 byte length, low 32 bits pointer |
| void result | no Wasm result; JSON projection is null |
| `varta.tool_abi.copy_string` | `(i32 ptr, i32 len) -> i64`, copies into the owned string heap |
| `varta.tool_abi.retain_string` | `(i64 handle) -> i64`, retains a copied input in the root stack |

Modules with any string tool parameters/results export both helpers and bounded
32-bit ABI memory. For each string argument, the host writes validated UTF-8 into
the reusable host buffer, copies it, and immediately retains the returned handle
**before another allocation**. This prevents the next input or a host call from
overwriting it and prevents collection during later argument transfer. These
helpers are trusted-host primitives, not tools for untrusted callers. The host
must never accept raw pointers/handles from external JSON.

The host calls the selected tool once, validates the result type/boolean/range,
bounds-checks and UTF-8-validates any string, and copies it into host-owned memory
before another guest allocation or dropping the instance. Result handles are not
retained after return; reading them immediately is required. Every invocation,
including traps, ends by dropping the instance; helpers do not support persistent
instances or releasing host roots between repeated calls. Input roots, allocator
metadata and helper work consume the existing memory/root/fuel budgets. The shared
dispatcher implements these obligations, including validation of copy/retain
results before passing transferred inputs to the handler.

### Checked JSON invocation

`VartaRuntime::invoke_tool` and `invoke_tool_with_policy` accept portable code, a
published tool name, raw JSON parameter bytes and trusted package/host grants.
The project APIs `invoke_tool` and `invoke_tool_with_policy` use an artifact's
validated manifest and, optionally, a `HostPolicy`. The CLI exposes these through
`varta invoke <artifact> <name> --params '<object>' [--policy <file>] [--json]`.
The default parameter object is `{}`. Native containers are read as portable
artifacts; their launchers are not executed. Source files are unnecessary.

Dispatch order is bounded request/name and grant checks, full portable-code and
catalog validation, exact name lookup in the catalog, complete parameter parsing,
fresh store creation, argument transfer, handler call and result validation. No
lookup falls back to an arbitrary export. All arguments are validated before
instantiation; a bad later argument cannot allow an earlier guest effect. Tool
modules cannot contain a Wasm start function, and invocation never calls `_start`.

Parameters must form exactly one JSON object, with every declared field present,
no extras and no duplicate decoded keys (including escaped spellings of a key).
Object field order is independent of physical argument order. The parser rejects
trailing data, arrays/objects/null in primitive fields, invalid UTF-8, lone escaped
surrogates, numeric strings, integer booleans and out-of-range numbers. Integer
input uses exact plain signed i32 JSON tokens; decimal, exponent and negative-zero
forms are rejected instead of rounding external values through floating point.
This is a deliberately narrower wire profile than JSON Schema's mathematical
integer interpretation. Input bytes include JSON whitespace/escapes. JSON recursion
limits remain enabled and strings also retain their independent UTF-8 byte cap.

Argument copying, retaining and the handler share one store and fuel/deadline
budget. Two string arguments cannot alias the reusable input buffer. Copy-helper
results are bounds/length/UTF-8 checked and compared with the supplied input;
retention must preserve the handle. Returned strings are bounds/byte-limit/UTF-8
checked and copied before any further guest allocation. Returned booleans must be
exactly 0 or 1. Integer and void results preserve their specified representations.

`ToolInvocationOutput` contains `result: { value: <primitive-or-null> }` and
separately captured `logs`. Serialized result size is checked with a bounded
counting writer, so escaped output cannot cause an oversized temporary JSON
allocation. Logs remain subject to the existing separate output budget. There
is no store, borrowed guest pointer or handle in a successful host result.

`ToolInvocationError` has stable codes: `invalid_arguments`, `unknown_tool`,
`invalid_artifact`, `invalid_policy`, `invalid_result`, `execution_failed` and
`guest_exit`. Traps and resource exhaustion are invocation failures, not host
status values. An authorized guest exit, including exit code 0, does not fabricate
a successful tool result. The ordinary run/start path retains its exit-code and
captured-log behavior. Domain/revision errors remain future application work.

Concrete host operations still use the package/host conjunction and descriptor
scopes. Denials and I/O failures keep their recoverable host statuses; a handler
may deliberately return a fallback after checking `VartaResult`. Successful tool
execution is not proof that every attempted host operation succeeded. No rights
are accepted in the JSON arguments. The API is a trusted local embedding surface;
caller identities, per-caller tool subsets and remote authentication are not yet
implemented.

With `--json`, CLI success is one `{status:"ok",result,logs}` record; invocation
failure is `{status:"failed",code,error,diagnostics:[]}` and exit code 1. Errors
reading an artifact/policy before dispatch retain ordinary project error handling
and may have no invocation code. Without `--json`, stdout is the result envelope
and logs go to stderr. Failures expose no partial result and are never retried.
Already-performed authorized host effects are not rolled back. Each call has its
own budgets; shared state, atomic application commits and aggregate queue/accounting
are not part of this dispatcher milestone.

## HTTP service v1

The compiler recognizes exactly one entry-module top-level
`varta.http.serve({hostname:"127.0.0.1",port:8080}, handler)` declaration. Options
must be literal IP and u16 port values, with no unknown/duplicate fields; DNS
hostnames and dynamic registration are not part of this profile. The named handler
may be local or imported and has signature
`(VartaHttpRequest) => VartaHttpResponse`. It need not be an exported source
function or AI tool. Entry `main():void` still performs bounded bootstrap; a
controlled exit from main skips service startup. Registration does not execute at
source top level and adds no application routes/models to the engine.

The built-in structural transport types are:

```ts
interface VartaHttpHeader { name: string; value: string }
interface VartaHttpRequest {
  method: string; target: string; body: string; headers: VartaHttpHeader[];
}
interface VartaHttpResponse {
  status: number; body: string; headers: VartaHttpHeader[];
}
```

The request target retains path/query syntax; no route normalization, decoding or
authentication is supplied. Header names are normalized by the HTTP library and
repeated values remain entries. Bodies are UTF-8 text; handlers can use checked
JSON parsing. Response body bytes are sent directly, with no tool/MCP envelope.
The application chooses content type and performs identity/domain validation.
The initial profile supports synchronous stateless requests, not shared guest
state, closures/promises or standard web Request/Response classes.

`net.listen` requires `ListenEndpoints`, serialized as manifest `patterns` and
configured as `"net":{"listen":["127.0.0.1:8080"]}`. Entries must be canonical
SocketAddr strings, including `[::1]:8080` for IPv6. There are no globs, DNS names,
bare numeric port lists or boolean fallback. Empty lists deny. Exact requested
endpoint and exact host ceiling must both permit the bind **before any socket is
opened**. An outbound URL grant never permits listening; all-interface binds
such as `0.0.0.0:8080` need that explicit endpoint. Port 0 authorizes an OS-selected
port for that IP only; it does not match an explicit nonzero-port grant. The actual
address is reported through a readiness event.

A bounded `varta.http` custom section holds strict `HttpContract` v1: canonical
`bind`, the reserved handler `export`, sorted `requiredEffects` (handler effects
plus net.listen), and immutable `limits`. Duplicate/malformed sections, unknown
members, unsupported versions, changed limits, misbound exports or effect mismatch
fail offline validation. The metadata must occur with the internal
`varta.http_service() -> ()` feature import; this no-op marker gives old runtimes
an explicit unknown-import failure. It grants no authority. Host ABI v1 and
structured value ABI v2 are required, with no Wasm start function.

The compiler creates one internal string adapter with signature `(i64)->i64`:
checked parse of the request record, one call to the typed source handler, then
bounded JSON serialization of the response record. It exports
`varta.http_abi.handle`, `varta.http_abi.copy_string(i32,i32)->i64` and
`varta.http_abi.retain_string(i64)->i64`. Copy/retain must be host-free transitively,
including without a tool catalog; indirect calls are rejected. Ordinary source
exports do not become network handlers. HTTP metadata never turns a function into
an AI tool. Named tool invocation does not start the service or execute main.

After bootstrap drops its store/deadline, the host owns one listener and reactor.
Every HTTP request gets a fresh store with existing fuel, five-second execution,
8 MiB memory and host-call/output limits. Input copying, retention, checked parsing
and the handler share that budget; main is not rerun. The response is copied and
validated before the store is released. There is no instance reuse after a trap.
A malformed handler response, guest exit, fuel exhaustion or checked JSON failure
produces a generic 500, with details only in trusted diagnostic events. Already
performed authorized effects are not rolled back; later requests can proceed.

Hyper owns HTTP1 parsing/framing. The initial reactor accepts one connection at a
time and closes it after one response. There is at most one guest worker, guarded
by a permit that survives connection cancellation, and no unbounded worker queue.
Bounds are 32 headers / 4 KiB header data, 1 KiB target, 8 KiB raw body, 64 KiB
encoded request record, and 1 MiB encoded response record/body. Header reads have
a two-second timeout, body reads two seconds and a connection ten seconds. Body
and header overflow, malformed framing, unsupported upgrades/CONNECT/trailers and
invalid UTF-8 fail before guest dispatch. Status must be 200–599; 204/205/304 require
an empty body. Response header names/values use the HTTP library's validation;
connection/framing/hop-by-hop headers are forbidden. The runtime controls length
and connection closure. HEAD suppresses content and reports representation length
where permitted. TLS, HTTP2, streaming and keep-alive remain pending.

`varta.http.stop()` / `varta.http_stop() -> ()` closes only the owning service.
The request context carries its unforgeable shutdown handle and requested endpoint;
the operation checks net.listen again. An outside-service call returns invalid-input
status and cannot stop another instance. Shutdown stops acceptance first and lets
the current response finish within connection bounds. The synchronous embedding
API can use `run_observed` with `RuntimeEvent::Listening {address,shutdown}`;
`HttpShutdown::shutdown` is idempotent and also wakes an idle listener. Observer
callbacks are trusted synchronous sinks and must return promptly; slow sinks apply
backpressure. CLI/project layers report readiness and stream request output, with
no library printing. Without an observer, captured lifetime output is capped at
1 MiB and overflow stops the service with an error. Each request retains its own
output ceiling regardless of observer. The independent runtime companion and
packaged executable serve source-free HTTP through this same runtime event path.

## ABI v1 and errors

Imports live under `varta`. `HostOperation` in `varta-common` owns their names,
capability identifiers and scalar Wasm signatures; the
[embedding contract](embedding.md#host-operation-table) lists every operation
with its signature, minimum host ABI, capability and admitting profiles. Pointer-taking imports require
an exported non-shared 32-bit `memory`. String-returning imports also require
exported mutable i32 globals `env_result_len` and `result_status`. Invalid import
signatures, result globals and advertised ABI versions fail before instantiation.

- Input strings are borrowed for the call and checked for bounds, length and UTF-8.
- Static strings occupy `[0, 65536)`.
- Host string results use a host-owned reusable buffer starting at 65536.
- Result pointers/bytes remain valid until the next host operation; there is no
  unbounded host bump allocation and no guest-controlled host heap pointer.
- Compiled string values snapshot those borrowed bytes into immutable execution
  storage. The layout is static data `[0, 65536)`, reusable host results
  `[65536, 1114112)`, exact reference roots `[1114112, 1179648)`, then the managed
  string/record/array heap `[1179648, 8388608)`, including block headers. Unreachable blocks are
  reused during execution; the entire instance is released when execution ends.
  V38 may insert a static extension before the heap; see
  [multi-page static region](#multi-page-static-region-program_limits).
- Every privileged system operation first clears result length/status. Failed string calls
  return pointer 0 and length 0. No previous result length can be reused.
- Logging and pure JSON serialization/parsing preserve the last system status. Serialization
  replaces result bytes/length; compiled code snapshots retained results immediately.
- `varta.result.status()` reads the structured status without clearing it.

Status codes:

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Success |
| 1 | Capability denied |
| 2 | Invalid input or UTF-8 |
| 3 | I/O failure |
| 4 | Result too large |

`net.fetch` returns the HTTP status or -1 on failure. String failures return an
empty result plus the status above. Human-readable diagnostics remain available.
Guest exit is a controlled runtime outcome, never `std::process::exit` inside the
library. The CLI alone translates the result into a process exit code. Runtime,
compilation and artifact errors return nonzero CLI status; JSON errors stay
machine-readable on stdout, with diagnostics on stderr.

## Programmatic host results

`varta.result.capture` is a compiler intrinsic that executes one direct privileged
host call and immediately pairs its value with that call's status:

```ts
function read(path: string): VartaResult<string> {
  return varta.result.capture(varta.fs.read(path));
}

export function main(): void {
  const result = read("/data/config.txt");
  if (result.ok) {
    console.log(result.value);
  } else {
    console.log(result.status);
  }
}
```

The immutable fields are `ok: boolean` (status equals zero), `status: number`
(the ABI codes 0–4 above) and `value: T`. `T` is exactly `string`, `number`,
`boolean` or `void`. Locals can infer their result type; function parameters and
returns use the built-in global `VartaResult<T>` annotation. Copies, aliases,
whole-value reassignment, nested/recursive calls and cross-module parameters and
returns preserve both components. Later host calls, logging and reads of the
legacy `varta.result.status()` cannot change a previously captured result.

The argument is evaluated once. It must lower directly to one privileged host
operation, optionally in parentheses; its own arguments may contain expressions
and calls. For nested host arguments, the result describes the outer call.
Capturing a variable, arbitrary expression, user-function call, status inspection
or logging call is rejected: these would not reliably identify one fresh host
status. Put capture inside a user wrapper and return its `VartaResult<T>` instead.
All existing time, environment, filesystem, network and process operations are
supported. Logging and pure JSON serialization/parsing are excluded because they preserve system status.

A successful empty string, false or zero has `ok == true`; a failed call keeps its
original fallback value with `ok == false`. Fallbacks are empty string, false and
zero, except `net.fetch`, whose failure value remains -1. A void result has no
consumable `.value`; it can expose `.ok` and `.status`, and discarding `.value` has
no effect. Check `.ok` before using a value as a successful result. HTTP response
codes, including 4xx/5xx, are successful `net.fetch` return values when the request
itself completes; transport failures are host errors. Existing human diagnostics
still accompany host failures.

Result values are represented as two Wasm values: payload then i32 status. String
payloads retain the existing immutable i64 slice representation and snapshot
ownership. Number/boolean payloads use i32; void uses an unused zero i32 payload.
Each logical result local/parameter maps to two physical slots, and a result
return uses two Wasm results. Field selection evaluates its base once and keeps
the selected component; `.ok` compares the saved status with zero. Captured results require
no heap allocation or extra host call. The existing 32 physical Wasm-parameter
limit remains, so a result consumes two of those slots. Raw host imports, global
exports, ABI v1, capabilities and artifact formats remain unchanged.

The built-in type cannot be redeclared or fabricated through object literals.
Nested result types, arbitrary generics, destructuring of a result pair, computed fields, field
writes and implicit conversion/comparison of a whole result are unsupported.
The shared editor declarations expose readonly fields and the same capture API.
This provides explicit branching on recoverable host failures, without introducing
general exceptions. Closed objects are provided separately. Fuel/deadline/call/output exhaustion, Wasm traps
and retained-string allocation failure still stop execution. An authorized
`process.exit` still exits with its requested code and produces no result;
a denied exit returns a failed `VartaResult<void>`.

## Resource limits

<!-- generated:limits:begin (checked by crates/varta-common/tests/documentation.rs) -->
| Resource | Limit | Source constant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Guest linear memory, v1–v37 | 8 MiB | `abi::MAX_MEMORY_BYTES` |
| Guest linear memory, v38 (module maximum and default budget) | 256 MiB | `limits::V38_MAX_MEMORY_BYTES` |
| Guest linear memory, one HTTP request instance (cap) | 8 MiB | `http::REQUEST_MEMORY_BYTES` |
| Linked intrinsic stack in memory 0 (v38 `linked_intrinsics`) | 16 KiB | `abi::INTRINSIC_STACK_BYTES` |
| Guest instructions (fuel), v1–v37 per execution | 1000000 | `abi::FUEL` |
| Guest instructions (fuel), v38 per turn (`turn_budgets`) | 1000000000 | `budget::TURN_FUEL` |
| Execution/HTTP deadline | 5 s | `abi::DEADLINE_SECONDS` |
| Host calls per execution | 1024 | `abi::MAX_HOST_CALLS` |
| Captured output | 1 MiB | `abi::MAX_OUTPUT_BYTES` |
| Host input string | 64 KiB | `abi::MAX_INPUT_BYTES` |
| One host result / one string value | 1 MiB | `abi::MAX_RESULT_BYTES` |
| Wasm file | 4 MiB | `abi::MAX_WASM_BYTES` |
| Wasm function body | 65536 bytes | `abi::MAX_WASM_FUNCTION_BODY_BYTES` |
| Distinct Wasm signatures | 256 | `abi::MAX_WASM_SIGNATURES` |
| Physical function parameters | 32 | `abi::MAX_WASM_PARAMETERS` |
| User functions | 256 | `abi::MAX_USER_FUNCTIONS` |
| HTTP adapters | 1 | `abi::MAX_HTTP_HANDLERS` |
| Compiler helpers (legacy / sparse / maximum) | 10 / 12 / 13 | `abi::*_INTERNAL_FUNCTIONS` |
| Record fields | 32 | `value::MAX_RECORD_FIELDS` |
| Record shapes per graph | 128 | `value::MAX_RECORD_SHAPES` |
| Record key bytes | 256 | `value::MAX_RECORD_KEY_BYTES` |
| Array elements / spread arguments | 1024 | `value::MAX_ARRAY_ELEMENTS` |
| Array element types per graph | 128 | `value::MAX_ARRAY_TYPES` |
| Union types | 128 | `value::MAX_UNION_TYPES` |
| JSON depth / visited values | 64 / 4096 | `value::MAX_JSON_*` |
| JSON schema types (legacy / current) | 260 / 389 | `json::*MAX_SCHEMA_TYPES` |
| Language metadata | 1024 bytes | `language::MAX_METADATA_BYTES` |
| Live continuation frames | 64 | `frame::MAX_LIVE_FRAMES` |
| Pending microtask continuations (v34) | 64 | `scheduler::MAX_PENDING_CONTINUATIONS` |
| Microtasks per execution (v34) | 65536 | `scheduler::MAX_EXECUTION_JOBS` |
| Promise serials / rejection ids per execution (v34–v37) | 1048576 | `scheduler::MAX_PROMISE_SERIALS` |
| Promise serials / rejection ids / timer ids per instance, never reused (v38) | 9007199254740991 | `limits::V38_MAX_PROMISE_SERIALS` |
| Unhandled rejections outstanding at once (v38) | 1048576 | `limits::V38_MAX_OUTSTANDING_REJECTIONS` |
| Unhandled-rejection reasons kept / units per field / bytes each | 16 / 256 / 2048 | `scheduler::MAX_*REJECTION_REASON*` |
| Pending timers (v36) | 32 | `scheduler::MAX_PENDING_TIMERS` |

The structural rows above (Wasm file, function body, signatures, user

registry, `LanguageProfile::limits` in `varta_common::limits`: the compiler,
the runtime's module, catalog and schema readers, the value readers'
function-index bounds and the artifact and launcher payload readers all use
it. V38 (`program_limits()`) admits the WebAssembly implementation limits
([program limits](#program-limits-program_limits)); production runtime
budgets are the same for every profile except the v38 per-turn fuel
(`budget::TURN_FUEL`).

(the policy, module, scheduler, network, permission and event limits a host

The per-value rows above (array elements and spread arguments, string
values, JSON depth, visited values, input and output, live frames, pending
continuations and timers) are the frozen limits of every profile before v38.
Profile v38 takes them from `limits::DataLimits::V38`
([data limits](#data-limits-data_limits)); its memory, deadline, host-call
and output budgets are the production budgets above, and its fuel is
`budget::TURN_FUEL` per turn.

In v38 the fuel, host-call and microtask rows apply per event turn, and the
deadline per turn in a long-lived application instance; a manifest may lower
them and a host ceiling may raise them within `budget::MAX_*` ([turn
budgets](#turn-budgets-and-application-instances-turn_budgets)). Memory and
output stay per instance. The values above are the defaults and the caps
without a ceiling.

Preflight limits also bound signatures, function count/body size, memories,
tables and globals before native compilation. Store budgets apply before Wasm
start functions execute. Fuel/epoch interruption bound guest execution; HTTP uses
the remaining deadline. Output is captured with a budget and returned to the
caller. Errors and guest exit do not terminate an embedding process.

### Fuel determinism

Fuel is a function of the module bytes and the guest-visible inputs only:
the same module with the same inputs consumes exactly the same fuel on every
host and platform, so a budget means the same everywhere. The compiler's
output does not depend on the host (no hash-ordered iteration, pointer width
or paths in emission). Fair host fuel charges depend only on the bytes and
values the guest passes or receives.

**Instantiation is not charged to the guest, in every profile (owner
decision, 2026-10-30).** Wasmtime meters instantiation's data-segment copy,
and with copy-on-write memory images it skips that copy where the platform
can map an image (memfd on Linux) and copies host-page-rounded images
elsewhere (16 KiB pages on macOS arm64), so charging it made v1–v37 fuel
host-dependent (a one-byte segment cost 16,385 fuel on macOS and 0 on
Linux). The runtime therefore instantiates on an unmetered tank and restores
the guest's fuel exactly before any guest code runs (`Execution`'s
instantiation); the work is bounded by the validated module size, the memory
budget and the deadline, and an instantiation never fails for fuel. This is
an approved exception to keeping earlier profiles' behaviour: every artifact
that fit its budget before still fits on every platform (Linux fuel is
unchanged, macOS fuel only goes down). A module with a Wasm start function,
which only the profiles before the exception profiles admit and the compiler
never emits, runs guest code during instantiation and pays its whole
instantiation, start function and copy included. For that charge to be the
same everywhere the runtime configures Wasmtime explicitly with fuel, epoch
interruption and no copy-on-write images (`memory_init_cow(false)` in
`VartaRuntime::new`): every host copies exactly the module's segments, one
fuel per byte. Images save no measurable time for one fresh store per
execution (measured within noise on Linux aarch64; macOS never maps them).

`fuel_determinism_tests` pins exact fuel of representative programs, that
instantiation leaves even one unit of guest fuel untouched, and the start
function charge, on every CI host, and compiles the case corpus twice to
compare bytes; a host-dependent engine setting or compiler output fails it.

<a id="browser-fuel-transform-foundation-in-development"></a>

### Browser fuel transform and official browser host

`varta_compiler::browser_meter::instrument` derives a private execution image
from validated portable Wasm. It leaves the original artifact unchanged. The
trusted host must first validate the original artifact, metadata, effects and
permissions; the derivative is never a portable artifact or evidence of trust.
The image imports the private mutable i64 global `varta_browser_meter.fuel` and
carries `varta.browser.meter` version 1. Original global references are remapped;
function indices are preserved. The host owns initialization to negative remaining
fuel and fair host-work deductions. Reporting clamps exhausted fuel to zero.

The implementation follows locked Wasmtime 48's default Cranelift model: entry
cost, buffered operator costs, call save/reload, loop checks and variable memory
work. A sealed-block SSA view preserves integer constant identities through locals
and branches; checks for small constant bulk operations differ from dynamic sizes.
Ordinary traps and statically impossible memory offsets preserve native fuel
publication boundaries. Instrumentation instructions consume no modeled guest fuel.

Supported operation families currently include core numeric/control, bulk memory,
fixed-width SIMD (`simd128`, one unit per operator, its loads checked at their
16-byte width; the v38 JSON decoders' scanner), sign extension, saturating
conversion, multi-value and tail calls. Relaxed SIMD (disabled in the reference
engine: its results differ between hosts), unmodeled
proposals, variable table operations, shared/memory64/custom-page, non-function imports, Wasm
start functions and already instrumented input are rejected. Input/output module,
type and function-body sizes are checked against Wasm implementation limits.
Because Wasm start functions are rejected, their instantiation charge is never
modelled: such a module gets no browser bundle. The official browser host built
on this image (the library loader, `varta build --target browser` and
`varta dev --target browser`) is described below; its multi-browser and pilot
acceptance remain open.
`varta_common::browser` generates the frozen ES registry in
`crates/varta-common/browser/registry.mjs` directly from Rust (profiles, exact
operation signatures/admission, entry points, value/frame acceptance, fair-work
rates and private meter identifiers). A drift test checks regeneration; the
operation enum supplies its own complete iterable inventory. This predicate/data
alone never replaces whole-module validation or permission enforcement.

`varta_project::browser::BrowserArtifact::prepare` now supplies the trusted
preparation boundary. It validates the original artifact manifest/code ABI, then
uses the native runtime's complete module/catalog/helper-effect admission before
instrumenting. The result owns an immutable pairing of original bytes/manifest,
validated inspection, effective budgets, optional host ceiling and private image.
It performs no guest invocation or filesystem-root binding. An explicit empty
ceiling remains distinct from package-only mode; these retained policies are not
permission decisions or grants for browser effects.

For v38, preparation resolves requested budgets against the validated host ceiling
(or production caps); older profiles retain frozen budgets. The private image
clamps memory maxima to whole pages within that effective byte ceiling and table
maxima to the native element ceiling, preserving any smaller declared maximum.
An initial allocation above the ceiling fails preparation. This supplies the JS
equivalent of native Store growth limits without changing portable bytes. Shared,
64-bit and custom-page memories and shared/64-bit tables remain unsupported.
`instrument` uses the production memory cap; `instrument_with_memory_limit` accepts
the already resolved trusted cap. Unsupported input never falls back to an
unmetered image. The bundle supplies integrity binding to this prepared pair.
The browser host loads only such prepared bundles, never arbitrary unprepared
artifacts; its permission enforcement and the effects it implements are described
below, and a module importing any other effect gets no bundle.

`BrowserArtifact::bundle` builds a checked console/view bundle:
`app.wasm`, `app.private.wasm`, `app.manifest.json`, `varta-worker.js`,
`varta-host.js` and `index.html`. It currently accepts only the implemented
logging, Promise scheduler, timer, v38 asynchronous network, view, environment,
clock (`date_now`), entropy (`number_random`), environment snapshot
(`env_snapshot`) and exit (`process_exit_f64`) imports. Other missing effects
fail before output files are produced; jobs are never silently
skipped. `varta build --target browser` exposes this library path,
writing `web` beside the configured output prefix (normally `dist/web`). It uses
the same checked source compilation, then full original admission and bundle
preparation before creating output directories. Unlike native execution loading,
it does not pin configured native filesystem roots. Existing output directories
are refused. The distribution flag does not reinterpret the original manifest
`target` or Wasm bytes. `--target wasm` selects the existing portable build;
`--target native` selects the existing verified companion packaging path, like
`--single`. `--launcher` requires either native selector; `--single` and `--target`
conflict. Host policies remain runtime inputs and cannot be passed to build.
Browser dev (`varta dev --target browser`) and checked view sessions are described
below; an effect outside the accepted import list is not implemented, and its module
gets no bundle.

The browser checkpoint owns a bounded FIFO of resume tokens and pending reaction
serials. It dispatches only through `varta_resume` with the normal/undefined
completion contract, checking the dispatcher outcome and canonical empty
exception channel after every job. Root execution and all jobs share fuel,
host-call allowance and the parent watchdog; awaiting never renews budgets.
Scheduler imports pay fair call fuel but do not increment the ordinary host-call
counter, matching native. Profile continuation limits, serial/job limits,
dispatch codes, errors and diagnostic layouts are generated from Rust.

Rejections are rendered immediately into bounded owned diagnostics. The host
keeps outstanding bits by tracking id and a bounded set of reason strings, never
guest references. Adding a handler during the checkpoint withdraws the report;
after the queue drains, the earliest outstanding report ends execution, including
the native not-retained marker when its text was not kept. The diagnostic reader
validates cells/heap envelopes, Error/BigInt/instance records and descriptor
slots/presence/order before bounded copies. V38 Error and Error-instance messages
use their profile's string limit, including messages above the frozen legacy
limit; older profiles retain their limits. Only bounded field prefixes are copied
for rejection diagnostics. Timer callbacks run after the checkpoint in stable
(logical due time, arm sequence) order. Delays normalize like native; intervals
rearm before callbacks and clearing releases pending cleanup frames. Unreferenced
timers do not keep execution alive. A due time at or beyond the execution deadline
fails immediately. The parent watchdog remains shared across all timer turns.
V38 timer turns renew fuel, host-call and job allowances; output and memory remain
instance-wide. Older profiles retain execution-wide allowances. Usage reports
include total fuel/turns plus the final turn's remaining fuel.

Arming requires the exact enabled package request `time.timer` and, when supplied,
`run({permissionCeiling})`'s own `time.timer: true`. An empty ceiling denies;
`time.now` cannot authorize it. The loader snapshots and validates this separate
boolean-only ceiling before loading. It never grants authority absent from the
package. V38 optional requests without a stored decision/prompt deny, matching
native headless operation. The v38 broker and interactive prompt path are described
below; legacy modes retain their policy behavior.
V2 denial arms nothing, schedules frame cleanup and reports the recoverable
permission error; legacy denial remains fatal. Timer bookkeeping pays fuel but
never ordinary host-call counts. External host-event turns (`app.deliver`) are
described below.

The v38 network adapter consumes only descriptor version 2, with generated ABI,
completion, buffer and limit facts. Starts pay the ordinary host-call budget;
watch/take/text/read/abort pay call fuel without that counter. The broker holds
bounded slots, deferred starts and arrival completions, with one armed operation
and watcher per request. Denials finish without calling Fetch. Transport events
never invoke guest code: explicit delivery wakes the registered reaction, then
v38 renews the turn allowances before the checkpoint. Due timers precede polling;
network completions advance logical timer time to elapsed wall time. Abort replaces
an armed completion, releases idle slots and discards late results.

`run({permissionCeiling})` also accepts an exact `net.request` member shaped as
`{patterns: [...], methods?: [...], responseHeaders?: [...]}`. Both package and
ceiling URL/method scopes must match. Validation bounds and snapshots every list;
empty/missing scopes deny and no other namespace grants requests. Matching uses
exact normalized scheme/host/port and bounded path/query globs (`?` is literal),
with native URL restrictions. Visible response headers are the two declared sets'
intersection, defaulting independently to the native safelist. V38 optional
requests without a decision remain denied. Generated CSP permits only package
request origins in addition to bundle fetching. URL-valid origins that cannot
be represented safely as CSP host tokens (punctuation, underscore or IPv6 literal)
fail before output, preventing attribute/directive injection; runtime URL/method checks remain
narrower and host ceilings are never embedded.

**Pilot effects and idle collection.** The official browser host implements the
clock, entropy, environment snapshot and exit with native results, statuses,
output and fair fuel; the mapping is in
[Browser effect mapping](embedding.md#browser-effect-mapping-official-host).
`date_now` is an audited `time.now` broker operation decided before `Date.now`
is read: the exact enabled package request and, when the embedder supplies a
`permissionCeiling`, its own `"time.now": true` (an empty ceiling denies, and
`time.timer` never authorizes it). A denial logs the native text and returns
NaN. `number_random` is ungated (accepted decision 9) and converts one fresh
`crypto.getRandomValues` 64-bit word exactly as native (top 53 bits times
2^-53); `crypto.getRandomValues`/`randomUUID` reach it through the guest
prelude. `env_snapshot` reads only the embedder's `environmentInputs` snapshot:
the empty name lists the set variables whose exact names both the package and
the ceiling `env.get` scopes list (wildcards name nothing), serialized in native
member order; a named lookup is one `env.get` scope check. Like native, neither
the snapshot nor `process_exit_f64` is an audited broker operation; both observe
the broker's current state. An authorized exit ends the run or `mount` session
with status `ok` and its `exitCode`; a denied or invalid code is a recoverable
status. The effect registry (`browser::registry().effects`) carries the
operation names, capability ids, the entropy conversion widths, the failure
texts and the collector constants; a `varta-project` test compares the
maintenance-exhaustion templates with the runtime's `BudgetExhausted`.

In `mount` sessions of v38 modules with `varta.collector.idle`, the Worker runs
idle collection once per idle period exactly like the native application
instance: after a closed turn, when the instance is alive and no task is
runnable, steps of `collector::IDLE_STEP_UNITS` run under a fresh
`maintenanceFuel` allowance while `budget::MAINTENANCE_STEP_FUEL` remains,
until `IDLE_NONE` or `IDLE_DONE`; any other status is fatal. The turn's
remaining fuel is restored afterwards. A metered trap with an empty tank is the
native maintenance-fuel exhaustion; the maintenance deadline is checked after
every step and is a hard bound through the parent watchdog, which terminates
the Worker (a step is never interrupted inside guest code). Results report the
listed periods (`maintenance`: after-turn, fuel, steps, completion, memory),
`maintenancePeriods` and `maintenanceFuel` with native listing rules. Bounded
`run` executions run no maintenance, like native bounded runs.

The browser transport uses Fetch with omitted credentials, no referrer, no cache,
CORS and manual redirects. Browser-owned request headers fail before Fetch instead
of disappearing silently. Opaque redirects fail without following another hop;
the prelude exposes its normal `TypeError: fetch failed` with the transport reason
as the error cause. Fetch cannot reconstruct v37's arrival/repeated header form,
so its network-start import remains an explicit bundle gap. CORS-hidden headers
and raw header counts are unavailable; limits cover the exposed head. Exposed
non-identity content encoding is rejected because Fetch already decoded its body;
servers used for unchanged-body parity must return identity bytes and expose any
relevant encoding/header metadata. This is a concrete browser transport boundary,
not proof of native parity for arbitrary HTTP servers. Followed redirects, hidden
wire metadata and compressed wire-byte parity require a separately designed
trusted transport bridge. Native request behavior is unchanged.

Response reads retain bounded input/chunks and enforce the shared body limit.
UTF-8 carry follows native decoding, preserving BOMs and carrying raw bytes when
a reader switches modes. Guest result publication uses the reserved UTF-16 result
buffer, checks both UTF-8/UTF-16 limits, charges result bytes and writes the length
only after checked memory growth/copy. Closing a run cancels all transfers.
