Browser view execution is engine-owned and admitted for v38 by the checked bundle path. `browser::registry().view` emits structured opcodes, operand
kinds, tags/content models, attribute rules, CSS grammars/composites, event fields,
flags, commands, defaults and limits directly from `varta_common::view`. Native
and browser validation share `Tag::admits_child`; CSS composite grammars have one
Rust owner. No engine code loads an example, scraped Markdown or the prototype's
contract JSON.

The shared view codec decodes the whole batch before semantics, validating every
code, reserved byte, UTF-16 string and trailing byte. The pure model copies all
mutable state, applies operations in order, checks final unique identifiers and
swaps only after success. It includes field counters, radio groups, listener
filters, child rules, command context/arguments, pending copy ids and stylesheet
limits. Transactions also meter radio owner/group scans, compared UTF-8 name
bytes and insertion-subtree visits through the shared registry. The scan charges
ignore local checked state and stale edit counters so an undelivered edit cannot
change Worker/DOM admission. Failure discards the copied tree and any effects.
Every insertion checks the shared component depth ceiling for the complete moved
subtree, including detached nodes and text leaves, before external effects. A
later repair in the same batch does not admit a transient excessive depth. Native
snapshot/accessibility construction, subtree text and accessible-name descendants
use iterative work lists instead of depth-proportional native calls.
Before explicit style-reading commands and at final admission, a shared potential
cascade allowance charges every live node's class/inline sources and anchored
candidate rule construction costs, ignoring media/pseudo/local-edit state. Raw
var() candidates additionally charge their inherited ancestor scope when custom
properties exist. A transaction-owned incremental JS anchor index and cached
native rule costs avoid reparsing or rebuilding all sheets for each read. Rejected
changes discard these indices with the tree. This is a matching/inheritance
work envelope. A separate potential UTF-16 component-content allowance checks
cached candidate programs and inherited numeric bounds across the same reads.
Final publication also checks a potential accessible-name inventory: descendant
summaries, repeated id relations, native labels and reserved live-field capacity.
The common role tables determine which root roles can read content. Detached
nodes, hidden state and author precedence cannot hide potential naming work;
referenced traversals disable further labelledby relations. These envelopes do
not establish complete serialization, retained-frame, backend or RSS quotas.
Snapshots cannot mutate the authority. Final retained-text accounting covers
UTF-8 source slots plus sticky worst-case UTF-8 reservations for live field values.
Capacity follows surviving nodes across type changes, so deferred edits and stale
patches cannot produce different parent/Worker admission. Deletion reclaims it.
Browser source-size maps are transaction-owned and omitted from snapshots; local
and synchronized values are checked before advancing sequence/state. The Worker
and parent DOM adapter use this model. Invalid batches trap in
`view_commit` before any later guest effect, and the parent checks again before
DOM application. One turn can commit once; it must receive the parent acknowledgement
before taking another task. At most one bounded batch is in flight.

The browser custom-property renderer ports the native iterative scope algorithm,
including active cycles, selected fallbacks, valid empty values and the shared
UTF-16 per-value ceiling. CSSOM custom declarations are compiled from private
prepared sheets and removed before adoption. A separate cached candidate index
follows specificity, sheet id and source order. Component walks use scoped
checkpoints instead of copying inherited maps at every node. Non-ASCII private
literal names are outside the guest grammar; alias bindings reference inherited
literals and the private font namespace uses parallel resolved values. Missing
references cannot inherit ambient page variables. Pending shorthands are inspected
through their authored CSSOM serialization, whose longhands otherwise serialize
as empty before substitution. Root rewriting skips quoted component text.
Class selectors additionally receive a private zero-specificity guard excluding
the implicit root, matching the native root/class split and work inventory even
when the root has guest classes.

Bindings refresh on commits, after focus effects, on coalesced pseudo-state events
and on owned media-query changes. Rejected prepared sheets install no listeners;
replacement/removal and close/freeze release query/state listeners and pending
animation frames. The frozen view retains its last computed bindings. Renderer
indices and bindings stay outside the pure model's transaction authority and
snapshots. The browser still uses platform ordinary-property layout; complete
late-value subset parity, aggregate expansion/output and broader renderer/lifetime
budgets remain open.

The DOM adapter uses a closed shadow root and checked CSSOM/DOM methods,
never HTML parsing. It preserves live node identities, drops stale field patches
and encodes events from the generated layout. After replay it reconciles select
indices against the model, including explicit no-selection and duplicate identity;
equal indices avoid a setter write, and reconciliation emits no field edits.
It blocks ambient asset URLs:
resource paths require an already verified blob map. Browser events only emit
records, never run guest code. Basic DOM/CSP/field/rollback behavior is verified in
Chrome. A bounded `run({container})` renders and discards event records like native
R1; omitting the container keeps its checked rendering headless.

`mount({container, signal, budgetCeiling, permissionCeiling})` returns
`{ready, finished, close, revoke, deliver}` for a long-lived application. A view
application requires an attached container; non-view applications can omit it.
`ready` resolves after
main and its checkpoint/commit acknowledgement. Every event, timer and network
completion starts a fresh v38 turn; memory/output remain instance-wide. The parent
watchdog covers loading and active turns, clears while idle and rearms at the next
turn. Network transfers also keep their own operation deadline. `close` terminates
the Worker, cancels I/O, drops pending records and freezes the last safe DOM.
The same container can then host a new instance; simultaneous ownership fails.
The last reported usage of a forced close is a checkpoint, not a complete active-
turn budget report. Exceptions and invalid transport acknowledgements terminate
the instance. No callback calls guest code reentrantly.

Parent-side pending events use the shared view limit, stable per-listener
coalescing and overflow rules; one additional event is in transport at a time.
The Worker accepts/validates that record and calls only the closed event export
with owned binary bytes. Timers, network completions and view tasks are selected
by due/arrival time. A committed view keeps unreferenced timers alive like native.
Pending copy ids are released at delivery, and gestures come only from trusted
click/keydown/submit records. Other event kinds cannot promote a gesture.

The runtime ceiling accepts `clipboard.write: boolean` and
`"ui.open_url": {patterns: [...]}` as exact view permissions. Both package requests
and supplied ceilings must admit an operation. Optional requests and any-HTTPS
prompt-only links deny without a prompt implementation. Clipboard calls require
a gesture turn; links open only during trusted activation. Platform rejections
remain recoverable command-result records. Actual anchor hrefs are inert, so
hover/speculation cannot contact a denied origin. Persistent navigation guards
survive freezing, and forms never submit ambient requests. The v38 broker, decisions,
audit and owned consent UI are described below; broader control/accessibility/layout
acceptance remains open. Unpackaged image
paths fail in the Worker before a parent effect.

A v38 configuration may specify browser distribution inputs as
`"browser": {"resources": {"icons/red.png": "images/red.png"}}`. Names and paths
use the common view resource grammar. These are build inputs under the config
root, read through pinned no-follow descriptors, never execution filesystem roots
or host grants. This section affects browser distribution only; portable/native
Wasm and manifests retain their existing bytes. `bundle_with_resources` also accepts
owned checked `BrowserResource` values without ambient file loading. Images every
renderer draws are declared in the top-level `images` map instead, which packages
them into the artifact's resource section ([packaged
images](#packaged-images-section-version-2)); the two cannot both be declared.

Images of the top-level `images` map follow the [native image
admission](#native-images-img) instead. `browser.resources` images currently use static PNG. Inventory count, per-file/total bytes,
aggregate decoded RGBA/font bytes, name length and image dimensions are bounded by the packaging constants in
`crates/varta-project/src/browser/resources.rs`. Admission checks the signature,
first/unique IHDR, bounded chunk lengths and final IEND; animated PNG is rejected.
Complete decoding is the browser's job and occurs before any renderer or Worker is
created. A bad CRC or compressed stream therefore cannot reach guest execution.
Every resource receives a generated flat file name and a pinned length/SHA-256
entry in the trusted loader. Logical `src` names never become fetch URLs. The
Worker admits only inventory names and the DOM receives only owned Blob URLs;
CSP permits Blob images, without ambient image origins. Decode bitmaps close
immediately; resource URLs revoke on failure, abort or session completion.
Browser config also accepts `"fonts": {"Brand": "fonts/brand.woff2"}` inside the
`browser` section. `BrowserResource::font` is the corresponding owned-byte API.
Family names are bounded ASCII names, with case-insensitive uniqueness; generic
and CSS-wide names cannot be package family names. TrueType/OpenType, WOFF and
WOFF2 containers have bounded counts/offsets and decoded-size estimates. Duplicate
or overlapping table spans and font collections are rejected. FontFace performs
complete table/decompression sanitization before registration, renderer creation
or guest execution. Fonts and images share the inventory/byte/decoded-size caps.

FontFace receives verified binary bytes, never a URL or `local()` source. Each
session registers a private family namespace; package names, including quoted and
case-folded values, map to it. Only the common generic families pass through;
unpackaged names become a private missing family and use normal fallback rather
than ambient named-font lookup. The checked DOM rewrites inline `font-family`,
stylesheet declarations and media rules. Each custom property also gets a parallel
font-context value with renamed `var()` references/fallbacks; the original variable
retains its meaning in color/layout declarations. Namespace state is bounded by
package families; unknown names and per-turn custom-property names are not cached.

Close, error, abort and deadline remove registered faces. A face whose asynchronous
load completes after termination is never registered. Retained inert DOM may use
fallback fonts after termination releases its faces. Current registration provides
one normal face per logical family; additional weight/style face collections and
other image formats remain open.

The browser host now admits v38 permission query/request and the one-shot
`event_watch`/`event_take`/`event_text` answer path. `run` and `mount` accept a
runtime `decisions` object in the native `DecisionFile` schema; it is validated and
snapshotted before any artifact fetch. Every record is checked, even for another
identity, but only the portable Wasm identity's decisions are applied. Required
stored denials inside the package/ceiling fail before Worker creation; optional
grants without a decision remain denied in this headless broker mode. A stored
allow never widens a resource or host ceiling.

`query` never prompts. In headless mode `request` answers the same state through a bounded
one-shot source and the guest's existing Promise prelude. These calls consume fair
call/input/result fuel but no ordinary host-call allowance. Descriptor decoding is
strict UTF-16, rejects NUL and bounds both UTF-16 and UTF-8 bytes, like native.
Sources use exact, monotonic f64 ids and cannot borrow a continuation already owned
by a timer; network watchers use that same scheduler guard. Resource queries over
boolean grants, v38 request URLs and view links are supported. A package using
these APIs with path/legacy-URL/listener grants fails bundle admission with an
explicit scope gap. Named event-source delivery is described below.

Where the browser exposes `clipboard-write` through `navigator.permissions`, its
state can only narrow Varta's query answer. Unsupported permission names retain
broker-only state. Reads occur only inside requested/host-allowed clipboard scope;
live changes update the parent and Worker, including a coalesced latest state
received during Worker compilation. Denial prevents clipboard calls. Status
listeners are removed on every terminal path. Browser state never grants an
unrequested, host-denied or internally withheld permission.

Results, close reports and execution errors expose an owned `permissions` report
with artifact identity, bounded audit entries/dropped count and stored decisions.
`onAudit` is a synchronous observer of received entries, not an approval hook;
querying itself does not append a decision, matching native. Initial decisions,
operations and platform-state changes are audited. Timestamps are local monotonic
milliseconds; comparisons across hosts exclude wall-clock values. Hard termination
reports only the audit received so far, like its checkpoint-limited usage report.
Worker operation records retain their decision at authorization time; a delayed
record after a page revocation/platform change is not recomputed using newer
state. Audit receipt order is not a cross-thread execution clock, and replaying
an observation never grants authority for a page effect.
Each completed turn, including bounded runs, waits for a parent acknowledgement
before the next task. Together with the per-turn host-call quota and bounded view
queue this bounds pending audit/turn messages. R1 retains its whole-execution
watchdog; application idle time remains uncharged. Protocol faults fail before
subsequent guest effects, and transfers are driven before selecting overdue timers.

The loader also exports `createDecisionStore({name?})`. Pass its result as runtime
`decisionStore` to `run`/`mount` instead of `decisions`; both together are rejected.
The store reads and validates the entire native-schema file before artifact fetch.
It exposes `read`, `set(artifact,id,decision)` and `clear(artifact?)`, with an optional
`{signal}` on each operation. One IndexedDB read/write transaction owns each update,
preserving other capabilities/artifacts under concurrent connections. All native
file bounds still apply: exhausted identity capacity fails instead of evicting
decisions. Results are immutable owned snapshots; abort, corrupt data, quota or
unavailable storage fails closed. Connections close on all terminal paths, including
late opens after abort. Explicit `clear()` can recover a corrupt store; clearing one
identity still requires a valid file. These decisions are local to the page origin
and browser profile, not publisher trust or an authorization ceiling. Importing the
loader never opens storage or starts execution. The generated view bootstrap opts
into the default store only for v38 packages with requested permissions.

`mount` sessions expose `await app.revoke(capability)`: unknown/unrequested grants
return false; v38 requested grants, including required ones, become stored denials
in the current broker and audit. The page withholds effects immediately and a
monotonic, checked control/acknowledgement updates the Worker without reentering
Wasm. Concurrent revocations of one capability share the pending operation. The
promise resolves after the Worker acknowledges and the configured store saves;
storage/observer/protocol failure terminates the session. In-flight operations
already authorized continue, while subsequent operations fail recoverably. A
required denial prevents a later instance from starting. Revocation affects this
live session and future reads of that store; other already-running sessions are
not automatically synchronized. Closing a session rejects pending controls.

Interactive hosts opt into `mount({onPrompt})`. The callback receives an immutable
`{artifact,capability,scope,purpose,required}` and `{signal}`, and returns (or resolves
to) `allow`, `deny` or `dismiss`. Required missing decisions are asked sequentially
in capability order before Worker creation. Refusal prevents guest entry; denial
is stored, dismissal is not. Optional unresolved grants start `prompt` and withhold
every concrete effect. An explicit `request()` opens at most one prompt in a
trusted user-gesture turn, after that turn reaches its parent checkpoint. Background
requests and requests outside package/host coverage return the current state.
Three dismissals become a stored denial. First-use implicit prompting and session-
only choices are not part of broker v1.

The Worker waits at its checked checkpoint while the callback runs; the parent
pauses the startup watchdog or leaves the completed turn uncharged. Returning the
answer never calls guest code directly. A checked acknowledgement queues one-shot
source completion as a host task, ordered by arrival with view/network events and
due timers; only selection of that task renews the turn and wakes its continuation.
The page withholds privileged effects/input delivery while consent is pending.
Callback/answer/storage/observer/protocol failures terminate the instance. Abort
wins over late answers, and revocation while waiting cannot be undone by a stale
Allow. Per-instance writes serialize prompt choices and revocations, so delayed
storage cannot overwrite a later denial. Prompt audit observation occurs before
the asynchronous save; guest resumption waits for the save.

`createPermissionPrompt({document?})` supplies the built-in callback: an owned modal
in a closed shadow outside the guest view, with the capability, original artifact
identity and exact requested scope. Package purpose is quoted text, never HTML or
the operation description. Allow/Deny/Dismiss require trusted input; synthetic
clicks cannot approve. Escape dismisses, abort removes the dialog, and initial focus
is Deny without scrolling away the heading. Generated v38 view pages with requested
permissions use this callback and the default store; capability-free views avoid
storage, and console `run` executions never prompt. API imports remain passive;
explicit `mount` without the callback retains headless permission behavior.
Any-HTTPS activation consent is described below.
No build embeds host decisions.

For a URL covered only by the any-HTTPS form on either side of request ∩ ceiling,
each trusted activation obtains fresh consent with that full captured URL as its
scope, with `activation: true` identifying the ephemeral callback. The dialog labels
the action “Open once” and states that the choice is not saved. Explicit patterns
on both sides continue to open by policy; optional or
revoked grants still deny until granted through the ordinary broker. Without a
prompt callback the broad form denies. The per-address choice is never stored,
does not alter the grant state and does not count toward optional-grant dismissal
limits. Repeated refusals therefore do not authorize or permanently deny a later
address activation.

The parent reserves one navigation request and sends a monotonic pause control.
The Worker finishes the active turn/checkpoint and acknowledges only before
selecting its next task. Inputs and new page effects remain withheld while this
request is pending; an overlapping activation denies rather than opening another
prompt. Human waiting consumes no turn deadline or fuel. Approval is rechecked
against current broker state before any platform call, so revocation defeats a
stale Allow. The original captured URL is opened with `noopener,noreferrer`;
no guest-controlled href is reread after awaiting. Every answer has a prompt audit
row with the full resource (subject to audit truncation) and returns its status
as a nongesture command-result task. The Worker resumes through a checked matching
control, without creating an extra guest turn merely for pausing.

Abort/observer/protocol failures terminate the session and suppress late opens or
results. A platform exception becomes `refused_by_platform`; a denied/dismissed
choice becomes `not_allowed`. Synthetic link clicks do not activate navigation.
The built-in dialog displays the full URL as text outside the guest view. Chrome
acceptance uses platform spies; it does not prove actual OS browser opening or
distinguish every popup-blocker result (a null handle can also be normal with
`noopener`).

The host now admits v38 `event_source_open`/`event_source_close` and exposes
`app.deliver({source,record,gesture=false,coalesce=false})`. The returned promise
reports admission as `queued`, `coalesced` or `dropped`, not callback completion.
Inputs are owned snapshots at invocation, including calls awaiting initial
readiness. Records must be well-formed UTF-8 text within the generated record
bound; NUL/BOM/supplementary characters survive. Missing listeners and oversized
or malformed records reject delivery without ending the instance. A listener
exception or non-coalescible queue overflow ends the instance.

The parent accepts a bounded named-source catalog at each completed checkpoint,
validates unique names/ids and monotonic generations, and pins each delivery to
that opening. A stale message cannot attach to a new listener with the same name.
Incoming batches enqueue records only; one selected host task wakes a continuation
in a fresh turn. Marked pending records coalesce per source while preserving their
first arrival and combining the gesture flag. Other records remain FIFO. Closed
source generations are discarded before guest delivery, and consumed one-shot
sources are never reused. Host tasks and permission answers share the generated
task bound in the Worker. Names/continuations/source capacity follow native rules.

The browser transport separately bounds deliveries awaiting acknowledgement to
the generated task count. Excess coalescible transport input drops; other transport
overflow fails the instance. Await admission or use bounded bursts; this transport
backpressure is additional to the native-equivalent Worker queue, not proof that
arbitrary concurrent host calls have native synchronous admission timing. Delivery
errors/termination release all pending acknowledgements. A host gesture flag is a
trusted embedder assertion, never inferred from guest text. Without a view, named
waiting frames keep an instance alive (and unreferenced timers eligible); the
instance finishes when no listener, timer or active operation holds it. Bounded
`run` never receives external deliveries and retains its existing root policy.

The self-contained loader pins lengths and SHA-256 identities of the original,
private image, manifest, Worker and packaged resources. Responses are streamed within those exact
lengths and verified before Worker creation. The Worker runs from an owned Blob
of verified bytes and follows no unverified module imports. The generated page
pins the loader with SRI and a hash-only script CSP (plus Wasm compilation),
permits same-origin bundle fetches, Blob images and Blob Workers, and requires a narrow
Trusted Types policy that accepts only owned verified Worker URLs. This relies
on the trusted page/loader delivery boundary; integrity is not publisher signing
or admission for arbitrary unprepared browser artifacts. The generated script
explicitly opts into bootstrap with `data-varta-bootstrap`; importing the loader
as an API never starts a package or bypasses a caller's runtime ceiling.

Host policies remain local runtime inputs: `bundle` rejects a preparation with
any supplied host ceiling, including an empty one, rather than embedding it.
`run({budgetCeiling, signal})` accepts a separately trusted runtime budget ceiling;
values are validated and v38 requests resolve against it (or production caps).
Legacy budgets remain frozen. A changed memory ceiling currently fails before
loading, since the private image's maximum cannot be changed by a JS Store
limiter. No capability permission is approved by this budget option. The timer and v38 `net.request`
capabilities currently have browser effect adapters. The generator uses the existing locked
SHA-256 and base64 primitives for SRI, without introducing new crate versions.

The local `varta dev --target browser` host compiles, loads resources and performs
the same admission before binding a loopback listener. Project tooling owns this
server; CLI only selects options, prints the URL and waits for Ctrl-C. It never
executes the guest natively, binds execution roots or writes a distribution.
Requests select from immutable in-memory bundle files, never filesystem paths.
The mutable `/` and `/index.html` pages pin the loader to a content-derived
`/__varta/<revision>/` directory. Every loader fetch resolves relative to that
directory, including the original/image/manifest/Worker and packaged resources.
Bare asset names at the root are rejected. The revision digest uses a domain
separator and length-framed sorted file names/contents before rewriting the page's
single dev script URL. Rewriting preserves loader bytes and CSP/SRI hashes and
fails closed on missing/duplicate opt-ins. The digest identifies prepared bytes,
including local runtime inputs; it is not publisher authentication.

The delivery catalog can retain the newest and preceding distinct revisions.
Publishing an identical current revision is a no-op; reverting to the preceding
one does not duplicate it. Expired/unknown revision paths return missing, never a
file from the newest revision. Owned response bytes survive eviction. Root page
selection switches with the catalog publication, so a previously obtained page
keeps its asset identity. Rebuild completion publishes into this catalog under a
short delivery lock, after compilation/admission has finished off-thread.
Both distribution and dev reject HTTP service contracts before output/listening;
HTTP service execution requires the native target.
Foreign Host/Origin/fetch-site, absolute/non-origin targets, request bodies and
methods outside GET/HEAD are rejected. Responses set no-store, nosniff, same-origin
resource policy and frame-ancestor restrictions. HTTP parsing uses the existing
locked Hyper stack; Tokio's signal feature provides shutdown without new crate
versions. The transport caps active connections at 16, headers at 32, header
buffer at 8192 bytes and connection lifetime at five seconds; these are dev-host
limits, not changes to production guest budgets. Shutdown cancels/drains active
connections and releases the listener.

Development preparation opts into a bounded input journal on the same source
loader used by ordinary compilation. It records SHA-256 of the bytes actually
read, read failures and existence probes, including absent `.ts`/`.tsx` resolution
candidates. Configuration, explicit external entries, imported text and packaged
resource reads participate. The journal retains at most 4096 distinct input/probe
keys and fails preparation on overflow. Rechecks use the original per-read size
limit and pinned no-follow dependency root, rather than directory scans or mtimes.
Unrelated files do not invalidate the attempt. Conflicting repeated observations
invalidate it permanently, even if the first contents are later restored. A
changed journal at the end of preparation rejects startup before listening; this
is a drift check, not an atomic filesystem snapshot. Ordinary compilation does
not enable the journal. Failed attempts retain their observations, including
missing dependency reads and resolution probes, so creating the missing input can
trigger recovery. Input changes are acknowledged before the next attempt; this
prevents repeated compilation of unchanged errors without swallowing a fix made
during an unsuccessful build. Parse-invalid configuration keeps the preceding
watch set, including the configuration read.

Host policy/decisions remain runtime inputs. A dev-only internal preparation can
derive the private memory ceiling from that host; its original Wasm and manifest
remain identical to portable output. The host constructs an ephemeral trusted
bootstrap with supported capability ceilings, budgets and only this artifact's
validated decision records. Native root mappings and other identities never reach
that page. Loader bytes get a new SRI/CSP hash and a separate `data-varta-dev`
opt-in. Format drift fails before listening; rewriting the opt-in cannot alter
requested origins. API imports stay passive. Public distribution builders still
reject every supplied host ceiling and have no dev-policy output path.

`--app` selects a v38 non-view application instance; views already use application
mode. `--budget-report` displays usage in the page. Native fuel profiling/view
scripts are rejected in browser mode, and native dev remains the default. The
initial program must compile/admit before listening. Thereafter a 500ms timer
dispatches at most one off-thread input-check/rebuild job; ticks skip overlap.
Successful admission publishes a new revision. Errors retain the preceding
working revision and a UTF-8-boundary-truncated diagnostic of at most 16KiB.
The same origin/authority/method/body checks protect `/__varta/status`; it returns
the current revision and optional error with no-store and never a 304 response.
Runtime policy and decisions are captured copies, not watched files.

A dev-only SRI-covered bootstrap polls status serially every 750ms, with a 3s
request deadline, 128KiB response ceiling and strict status validation. Diagnostics
are text in an owned host element outside the guest view. Successful unchanged
bytes clear errors without reload. A new revision aborts the owned run/application
signal before navigating to the trusted origin root. Pagehide cancels polling and
the owned session. An unavailable/invalid status stops the session and shows an
owned error; detection is subject to browser timer throttling. API-only imports
do not start this lifecycle. Distribution bootstrap behavior is unchanged.

Shutdown closes/drains HTTP work and cancels future checks/publication. An already
running synchronous compiler call may finish in its single background job; it
cannot publish after shutdown. The CLI runtime does not wait for that blocking
call on exit. This does not claim interruptible compiler execution. Broader
cross-browser/reconnect/initial-error-page acceptance remains open.

A parent-thread watchdog covers loading, verification, compilation and execution;
its deadline or an AbortSignal terminates the entire Worker, aborts fetches and
revokes the Blob URL. Already published log lines survive termination. Logging
charges the shared fuel and enforces host-call/output limits; UTF-16 diagnostics
are decoded in bounded chunks, preserving BOMs and replacing lone units like
native, including surrogate pairs across chunks. The byte count includes the
whole attempted UTF-8 line without allocating a guest-sized failed output.
Initial/final exception-channel checks fail the run on pending guest exceptions.
Full exception diagnostics and CPU-fuel trap classification remain acceptance
work; this console path is not the complete official browser host.

`browser/fuel.mjs` supplies the private mutable global and deducts shared host
work from it. Insufficient work empties the tank before throwing `FuelExhausted`;
exact payment succeeds, matching native. Counts/budgets are checked integers and
bounded by the host ceiling. Resetting a turn and retaining the global are trusted
host operations. Callers must respect each profile's generated `fairFuel` flag;
legacy profiles retain their existing host-charge semantics.

The explicit `browser_meter_probe`/`browser/probe.mjs` and `probe.html` verification
tools compare one trusted v38 fixture with native under Node and Chrome, including
host call/byte-charge boundaries. These are not general artifact loaders. The
full cross-host corpus, other fair host charges, overhead and delivery acceptance
remain open; long-lived application turns and the Firefox/WebKit/Chrome effect
matrix are compared with native by the browser effect acceptance
([verification](verification.md#browser-registry-and-fuel-probe-development)), not
by these probes. The value layouts and view protocol facts the official host reads are
generated from Rust by `varta_common::browser::registry()` and checked by its drift
test; that registry is not a copy of every generated table of the
[embedding contract](embedding.md).

## Artifact format and validation

Standalone Wasm has a strict sidecar `*.manifest.json`. A missing sidecar means
zero capabilities and the payload's declared host ABI (v1 when absent); an
unreadable or malformed sidecar is an error. Manifest/code ABI mismatch is an
error. Embedded
manifests are authoritative even when empty and never fall back to a sidecar.

`build --single` emits:

```text
native launcher | portable Wasm | manifest JSON | fixed 32-byte footer
```

The little-endian footer contains Wasm length (u64), manifest length (u64), format
version 1 (u32), reserved zero flags (u32), and `VARTA3\0\0` (8 bytes). It is read
at a fixed EOF position with checked arithmetic and capped lengths. Payload bytes
are never scanned for markers. Outputs are written through temporary files and
renamed into place.

### Resource section (artifact fonts)

A v38 configuration may declare the font faces the application ships as a
top-level `fonts` list: `{"family", "path", "weight"?, "style"?, "generic"?}` per
face, `weight` 100–900 in steps of 100 (default 400), `style` `normal` (default)
or `italic`, `generic` a list of `sans-serif`, `serif`, `monospace` and
`system-ui`. Paths use the common view resource grammar and are read under the
configuration directory through the project's pinned no-follow loader; they are
package files, never host grants. Packaging (`CheckedProject::load`, the
`varta-project` artifact module) bounds every face and the total by
`varta_artifact::MAX_FONT_FACE_BYTES`, `MAX_FONT_BYTES` and `MAX_FONT_FACES`
(the native text shaper's collection ceilings) and builds a
`varta_artifact::Resources`, which admits a face only when it is an
OpenType/TrueType file (collections and WOFF/WOFF2 are refused) with a bounded,
aligned, non-overlapping, duplicate-free table directory, the `cmap`, `head`,
`name` and `OS/2` tables, an `OS/2` `usWeightClass` equal to the declared weight,
`fsSelection` italic or oblique exactly when the declared style is italic, and a
`name` family (typographic family when present, otherwise the legacy family)
equal, ASCII case-insensitively, to the declared family. Family names follow
the browser package-font rule (bounded ASCII, not generic or CSS-wide). Faces
of one family must agree on its spelling and generic families, a generic family
belongs to at most one family, and duplicate family/weight/style faces are
refused. Faces are stored in canonical order: families in first-declaration
order (the first family is the default), each family's faces by weight, then
style; one declaration therefore has one encoding.

The section (version `RESOURCE_VERSION`, little-endian) is the magic
`VARTARS\0`, the version and face count (`u32`), the SHA-256 of the portable
Wasm it was packaged with, one fixed descriptor per face (family length `u16`,
weight `u16`, style `u8`, generic-family bits `u8`, a reserved zero `u16`, font
length `u32` and font SHA-256), then each face's family bytes and font bytes. A
reader refuses another magic or version, a nonzero reserved field, a count
outside 1..=`MAX_FONT_FACES`, any length past the bounds or trailing bytes, a
font that does not match its digest, a section whose payload digest is not the
artifact's Wasm, a non-canonical order and every face rule above. The section
is therefore bound to its payload: it cannot travel to another build. This is
integrity, not authenticity; package signatures remain separate work.

- **Bare form.** `varta build` writes `<out>.resources` beside `<out>.wasm` and
  `<out>.manifest.json` when fonts are declared, and removes a stale
  `<out>.resources` otherwise. A missing sidecar means no resources; an
  unreadable or invalid one is an error.
- **Container form.** Without resources `build --single` writes the unchanged
  format 1 bytes. With resources it writes format 2:

  ```text
  native launcher | portable Wasm | manifest JSON | resource section | resource length (u64) | fixed 32-byte footer
  ```

  The footer keeps its layout with format version 2; the resource length
  (nonzero, at most `MAX_RESOURCE_SECTION_BYTES`) sits immediately before it.
  Formats 1 and 2 are read; any other version fails before anything runs.

`Artifact::read_packaged` returns the artifact with its validated
`Resources`; `Artifact::read` and `Artifact::embedded` validate the section the
same way and drop it, so the `varta-runtime` companion refuses a tampered
section too, before any guest code runs. Every artifact older than the section
reads as one without resources.

`varta build --target browser` (and the browser development server) carries
the same validated faces: the project builds the section once and turns each
face into a browser font resource with its family, weight, style and generic
families, in canonical order. The loader verifies every face's bytes and
registers each as a `FontFace` with its declared `weight` and `style` before
the view renderer is created, so before the first view commit. The applier's
private font namespace maps a face's declared generic families (an unquoted
`monospace`, say) to that family's private name, and the applier's base sheet
(`createFontNamespace(...).rules`) gives the view root the first family and
`font-synthesis: none`, gives the user-agent monospace elements
(`varta_common::view::fonts::UA_MONOSPACE_TAGS`, `pre` and `code`) the family
that declares `monospace`, and makes form controls
(`CONTROL_FONT_TAGS`) inherit their family instead of Chrome's control font.
These rules have zero specificity (or are the root's own) and come first, so
every guest rule and inline style wins as over the user-agent sheet. Text
without a `font-family` therefore uses the default family as in the native
shell. Once the browser sees the private family instead of the generic
`monospace`, Chrome no longer applies its fixed-font size (13/16 of a
non-absolute size); the shell loads a resource section through
`TextMeasurer::new_with_packaged_fonts`, which sizes a mapped `monospace` as
that named family too, so `pre`, `code` and a guest-set `monospace` have the
same geometry with absolute, medium and inherited relative sizes.
`new_with_fonts` keeps the ratio for a host that maps `monospace` as a
stand-in for the browser's own generic font. A configuration may not declare
both `fonts` and `browser.fonts` (refused when the configuration is
validated); `browser.fonts` keeps its meaning (one normal face per family,
generic families passed to the browser, no default family, no base rules).
Remaining differences: a generic family that no face declares (including the
user-agent `monospace` without a `monospace` face) still resolves to the
browser's own fonts in the browser and is refused by the native shaper, a
divergence that predates the section; a run whose weight or style has no
face and would need synthesis (a run of weight 600 or more whose nearest face
is lighter than 600, or an italic run without an italic face) is refused at
native paint, while the browser, with synthesis off, draws the nearest face
unemboldened and upright; and a control's font size stays Chrome's control size in the
browser and the inherited size natively unless the guest sets one.

#### Packaged images (section version 2)

A v38 configuration may also declare the images the application draws as a
top-level `images` map from the view resource name an `img` `src` or
`srcset` uses to a no-follow path under the configuration directory, in the
same grammar: `"images": {"icons/logo.png": "assets/logo.png"}`. Packaging
reads every file through the pinned loader within `MAX_IMAGE_BYTES` each and
`MAX_IMAGE_TOTAL_BYTES` in all (`varta_artifact`, owned by
`varta_common::view::images`), refuses a file whose signature is not an
admitted format (`sniff`; AVIF and SVG with their own reasons), decodes every
image with the native renderer's decoder (`ImageSet::decode`, the [native
image](#native-images-img) limits and colour rules), so a packaged artifact
always loads natively, and builds the section with `Resources::with_images`:
at most `MAX_IMAGES` images, unique names in canonical (bytewise ascending)
order. These limits equal the browser bundle's per-resource limits, and the
browser bundle carries the section's images under the same names with their
formats' media types (with the faces in its inventory, so its shared
inventory caps still apply), so both distributions admit and draw the same
images. A configuration may not declare both `images` and
`browser.resources` (refused when the configuration is validated): a
browser-only image would be refused natively. `browser.resources` keeps its
meaning.

A section with images is version `IMAGE_RESOURCE_VERSION` (2):

```text
magic | version u32 (2) | face count u32 | image count u32 | payload SHA-256 [32]
face count x face descriptor | image count x image descriptor |
face count x (family | font) | image count x (name | file)
image descriptor: name length u16 | format u16 | file length u32 | file SHA-256 [32]
```

The format is the `ImageFormat` code: 1 PNG (and APNG), 2 JPEG, 3 GIF, 4
WebP, 5 BMP, 6 ICO. The section has 1..=`MAX_IMAGES` images and
0..=`MAX_FONT_FACES` faces; a section without images keeps its version 1
bytes, so one declaration still has one encoding and every existing section
reads unchanged. A reader refuses a version 2 section without images, an
unknown format code, a file whose signature is not its descriptor's format,
a file that does not match its digest, names out of canonical order or
duplicated, every bound above and every face rule;
`MAX_RESOURCE_SECTION_BYTES` includes the image bounds. The container format
is unchanged (format 2 carries any section). A runtime companion that reads
only version 1 refuses a version 2 section in `--validate`, before any
output is written. The native host decodes the images again (`varta-shell`:
before storage is created and before any guest code runs), and the browser
decodes them before guest execution, as for `browser.resources`. The limits
are initial conservative values pending an owner decision.

Native AOT payloads, `VARTA1`/`VARTA2` containers and public native deserialization
are removed. Rebuild existing native artifacts. Native launchers currently compile
embedded portable Wasm at startup. Reintroducing cached/AOT machine code requires
a separate, authenticated provenance design; checksums alone are insufficient.

### Independent runtime companion and packaging

`varta-artifact::Artifact` owns portable/container I/O. The tooling re-export
`varta_project::Artifact` remains available; its I/O methods now return the shared
`VartaError`. The format 1 container layout is unchanged; format 2 adds only the
[resource section](#resource-section-artifact-fonts). Existing VARTA3 containers
with a development-CLI native prefix remain readable by both loaders; their own
native argument interface remains whatever was built into that prefix. Embedded
manifests always win over sidecars. This does not restore VARTA1/VARTA2 or AOT.

`varta build --single` resolves only the sibling `varta-runtime` executable, or
explicit `--launcher PATH`; it never searches cwd/PATH or copies the development
CLI as a fallback. Install/build both binaries. Plain Wasm builds need no companion.
The new executable is the independent runtime plus portable payload, not compiler
or source tooling. `CheckedProject::build(true, path)` follows the same validation.

The native companion is a trusted build input. Packaging first opens a bounded
regular file (512 MiB maximum) and copies it into private staging (0700 on Unix).
It closes/syncs the snapshot before executing it and rejects a recognized capsule,
including malformed capsules, so an already packaged application's main cannot
be used as a probe. `--runtime-info` must return strict launcher protocol v3
metadata matching package version, OS, architecture, pointer width, host ABI,
value ABI, HTTP contract, supported language-profile list and the container
formats it reads (`containerFormats`, `varta_common::launcher::CONTAINER_FORMATS`).
A package with a resource section additionally requires container format 2
first: an older companion, whose identity has no `containerFormats`, is refused
with a diagnostic naming the format before any output is written. Protocol v1
and v2 companions must be rebuilt/updated for new builds; their existing VARTA3
payloads remain readable. `--validate` then validates the staged portable Wasm
and manifest, with its sidecar resource section when the package has one,
without instantiation, main, tool handlers or binding a listener.
Each subprocess has a five-second deadline and 4 KiB stdout/stderr limits. Only
after both probes pass are the public output files written. Probe failures leave
existing outputs untouched; staging is removed on success and error.

The protocol checks compatibility; it is not authentication or a sandbox for
arbitrary native inputs. Dependency guards independently enforce the repository
launcher's production graph. Native code executes with the builder/launcher's OS
authority; package authenticity remains separate planned work. Packaging currently
requires a runnable same-OS/CPU companion, not a cross-target executable. Linux
and macOS are the CI matrix; Windows and cross-target distribution are unverified.

The small runtime argument parser provides:

| Context | Interface |
| --- | --- |
| Packaged self | `[--policy PATH]`, `--invoke NAME [--params JSON] [--json] [--policy PATH]`, `--inspect [--json] [--policy PATH]` |
| Explicit portable/native artifact | `run PATH [--policy PATH]`, `invoke PATH NAME [--params JSON] [--json] [--policy PATH]`, `inspect PATH [--json] [--policy PATH]` |
| Build negotiation | `--runtime-info`, `--validate PATH` (bytecode/manifest validation only) |
| Help/version | `--help`, `--version` |

No source/project commands are included. Bare runtime execution without an artifact
fails. Unknown, repeated and misplaced flags fail. Invocation retains the checked
JSON envelope and typed error codes, never runs main, and applies the exact same
host/package conjunction. Inspection validates without executing and emits
`{artifact, manifest, module, toolCatalog, hostCeiling, combination:"allOf"}`.
`module` is the shared `WasmInspection`; top-level `toolCatalog` supplies generated
JSON input/output schemas for discovery. Development CLI inspection retains its existing format.
Internal `--validate` performs code/ABI validation, while the development CLI's
`validate` additionally reviews privileged-import declarations as described below.

`check`, `dev` and `build` share semantic/type/bytecode/ABI checks. Artifact `run`
and `inspect` fully validate bytecode and ABI too. `validate` additionally performs
policy review, requiring a declaration for every privileged import; this does not
mean that false or empty declarations grant access. Missing declarations are safe
to execute because the runtime denies those calls. Inspection includes full grant
scopes, enablement, versions, imports and exports.

### Native shell (`varta-shell`)

`varta-shell` (crate `varta-desktop`) runs a packaged application with a view
in a native window, with the same capability-checked runtime host as the
companion. It is distribution code: neither its production dependencies nor its
dev-dependencies reach the compiler, SWC, project tooling, the CLI or `clap`,
directly or transitively (`crates/varta-project/tests/boundaries.rs`). Its tests
obtain a compiled guest by building and running the workspace's `varta` binary as
an external process, not by linking it. The experimental
`varta-preview` shares its window, input and render core but runs a bare module
unprivileged: no manifest, grants, host ceiling, file roots or storage.

- **Artifact.** `varta-shell ARTIFACT` reads the artifact with
  `varta_artifact::Artifact::read_packaged`, the validation of
  `varta-runtime run ARTIFACT` that keeps the resource section: a portable Wasm
  with its sidecar manifest (a missing sidecar is zero capabilities) and
  optional sidecar resource section, or a VARTA3 container of format 1 or 2
  read at its fixed EOF footer behind any native prefix. Payload bounds,
  matching manifest/code host ABI, the package manifest rules, the resource
  section and the frame surface are checked before grants are resolved or
  a window opens. The runtime then validates code, language profile (the shell
  starts an application instance, so the profile must admit `turn_budgets`),
  contracts, budgets and required grants when the instance starts, before
  instantiation. Native payloads are never deserialized and payload bytes are
  never scanned for markers. A refused artifact has no guest effect: no guest
  output, socket, file or database. The only host effect that can precede the
  runtime's validation is the creation of empty storage directories (below).
- **Grants.** The manifest is the package request. `--policy PATH` names an
  optional host ceiling in the companion's host policy format, read bounded and
  checked by `Manifest::validate_ceiling` (no consent metadata; `fsRoots` only as
  a mapping); an unreadable or invalid ceiling is a typed error before the
  window opens. Options come from `RunOptions::from_manifests`, so budgets, file
  roots and the conjunction follow the companion: every concrete resource must
  match a grant of its exact `namespace.operation` id in the request and, when a
  ceiling is given, in the ceiling. An empty ceiling denies everything and never
  falls back to the request. Stored decisions, first-run approval and prompts
  of the grants within both follow [native permissions](#native-permissions-p10b)
  below.
- **Guest platform effects.** `copy_text` and external link activations follow
  the [command results](embedding.md#view-draft-v0-round-5-command-results) and
  [gesture rules](embedding.md#view-draft-v0-round-6-gestures-and-platform-refusals)
  of the headless and browser hosts. The view performs a granted effect through
  the host's `varta_view::PlatformEffects` sink, which the runtime takes as
  `ApplicationOptions::platform_effects` (a view without a sink keeps simulating
  the platform, as headless sessions do). The sink is reached only after the
  gesture rule (`copy_text` in the batch of a trusted `click`, `keydown` or
  `submit` turn; a link only inside the trusted activation itself) and the
  permission broker's exact grant (`clipboard.write` enabled, or a `ui.open_url`
  pattern of the request and the ceiling): a denial reports `not_allowed` and
  a non-gesture copy `invalid_context` without any effect. `Launch::start`
  takes the sink; the window passes `shell::NativeEffects`, which writes the
  system clipboard (`arboard`) and hands the URL to the system browser through
  an absolute launcher path, never a `PATH` lookup (`/usr/bin/open -u URL` on
  macOS, `/usr/bin/xdg-open URL` on other Unix hosts; elsewhere every opening is
  refused). Only an absolute `https:`/`http:` URL without whitespace or control
  characters reaches the launcher. The launcher is started detached (its own
  process group, with null standard streams) and the opening succeeds once it
  is spawned: view input handling never waits for it, because some launchers
  (`xdg-open` on some Linux desktops) stay in the foreground until the browser
  exits. No thread waits for a launcher: the shell keeps at most
  `MAX_RUNNING_LAUNCHERS` started launchers, collects the exit of finished ones
  (not observed) before each opening, and refuses an opening while that many
  still run. A clipboard error, a launcher that cannot be started or that
  bound reports `refused_by_platform`. With a sink the snapshot records no clipboard text or
  opened URL. The Linux launcher and clipboard paths are not exercised by the
  tests or acceptance runs.
- **Storage.** A root is pinned (`FileRoots::open`) to the host-owned directory
  `<base>/sha256-<digest>/<root>`, where the digest is the lowercase hex SHA-256
  of the portable Wasm, the application identity
  (`varta_runtime::artifact_identity`), when all of these hold: a package
  `kv.read` pattern names the root; without a ceiling, or with a ceiling that
  has a `kv.read` pattern whose first component is that root or contains a glob
  (`*`, `?`; conservatively counted for every root); and the ceiling does not
  map the root itself. Opening a database needs `kv.read` on its path in the
  request and the ceiling, so no other root could hold one: a root reached only
  by `kv.write`, or a ceiling `kv.read` for other roots, creates nothing. A
  ceiling's own `fsRoots` mapping of the root wins, and then no per-artifact
  directory is created for it. The shell creates the directory private to the
  user (mode 0700 on Unix). The same per-artifact directory holds the shell's
  permission decision file and audit log
  ([native permissions](#native-permissions-p10b)); their names contain a `.`,
  which no root name may, so no root can reach them. `--data-dir DIR` selects
  the base (made absolute by the binary; `Launch::packaged` refuses a relative
  base with `ShellError::StorageNotAbsolute`); by default it is
  the per-user data directory (`~/Library/Application Support/Varta/storage` on
  macOS, `$XDG_DATA_HOME/varta/storage` or `~/.local/share/varta/storage` on
  other Unix hosts). The directories are created by `Launch::packaged`, after
  the artifact checks above and the ceiling's validation and, in the binary,
  after the renderer, `--font` and the artifact's fonts are checked, but before the runtime validates
  code and language profile in `Launch::start` (which compiles the module once,
  with the roots already pinned): an artifact the runtime then refuses leaves
  its directories behind, empty. The mapping grants nothing: KV opens, reads
  and commits still need the exact `kv.read` and `kv.write` grants in the
  request and the ceiling, through the permission broker
  ([KV storage](#kv-storage-kv)). An artifact whose Wasm differs in any byte
  has another directory. Other declared roots stay unmapped, and so denied,
  unless the ceiling maps them.
- **Fonts and presentation.** The shell lays out and renders with the faces of
  the artifact's [resource section](#resource-section-artifact-fonts), read with
  the artifact: `shell::FontSet::from_resources` keeps its canonical order (the
  first family is the default) and maps each family's declared generic
  families as CSS aliases, and `TextMeasurer::new_with_fonts` registers every
  face. `Launch::packaged` parses the faces with the text shaper before storage
  directories are created; a refused face is `ShellError::Fonts`, a refused
  section `ShellError::Artifact`, both before any guest code. Weight and style
  select the face whose own tables state them, so bold and italic text uses
  the packaged faces. Chrome 156 emboldens only a requested weight of 600 or
  more on a face lighter than 600, and draws a lighter request (500 on a
  regular face) or a face of 600 or more as it is; native paint follows it,
  so only the synthesis Chrome would apply (and any synthetic italic) stays
  refused at paint (`only_a_bold_request_on_a_lighter_face_needs_synthesized_bold`).
  `--font PATH FAMILY` (nonempty, at most
  `shell::MAX_FONT_BYTES`) supplies one explicit face for an artifact without
  fonts and is refused (`ShellError::FontConflict`) for one that ships fonts.
- **Images.** `Launch::packaged` decodes the section's images once
  (`varta_view::ImageSet::decode`, the [native image](#native-images-img)
  formats, colour conversion and limits) after the faces and before storage directories are created; a
  refused image is `ShellError::Images`, before any guest code. The start
  gives the view the decoded set (`ViewLayout::with_images`), empty for an
  artifact without images, so an `img` naming another image is refused as in
  the browser. `varta-preview` has no images.
- **System fonts.** `--system-fonts`, also only for an artifact without fonts
  (`ShellError::FontConflict` otherwise) and exclusive with `--font`, maps the
  CSS generic families to this computer's fonts as the platform's browser
  does, the standard font first (the family of text without `font-family`):
  - on macOS, as probed with Chrome 156, Times for `serif`, the system UI font
    (its regular and italic files, named by CoreText's UI font) for
    `system-ui`, Helvetica for `sans-serif` and Menlo for `monospace`; a named
    family must be installed under that exact family;
  - on Linux, through fontconfig as Chrome on Linux resolves its defaults
    (Times New Roman for the standard and `serif` font, Arial for
    `sans-serif`, Monospace for `monospace`): the face fontconfig sorts first
    for the name in the regular style counts only when Skia's fontconfig
    interface would accept it (the family the configuration put first, the
    requested family, a metric-compatible one such as Liberation Serif for
    Times New Roman, or any face for `sans`, `serif` and `monospace`),
    otherwise Blink's last resort for the generic (`Serif`, `Sans`,
    `Monospace`) is used; `system-ui` is the family fontconfig matches for
    `sans` (Chrome's UI font without a desktop toolkit). Each family loads the
    faces fontconfig matches for regular and bold, roman and italic.
    libfontconfig is opened at run time (`ShellError::SystemFontsUnavailable`
    when it does not load).

  A family already mapped takes a later generic as an alias, and no file is
  read twice. The host reads each file bounded by `MAX_SYSTEM_FONT_FILE_BYTES`
  (a variable UI font exceeds the packaged-face limit; the collection keeps
  `MAX_FONT_FACES` and `MAX_FONT_BYTES`), checks that the file registers the
  family (`TextMeasurer::system_font_families`; `ShellError::SystemFontFamily`)
  and loads the set with `TextMeasurer::new_with_system_fonts`, before storage
  directories are created; `ShellError::SystemFontMissing` names a generic
  with no face. The application never names a file. A character none of an
  element's families covers takes the platform's fallback face as the
  platform's browser draws it ([native fallback faces](#native-fallback-faces));
  nothing else of the system's fonts is reachable. On macOS the set's faces of
  Times, Helvetica and Courier have their ascent enlarged by
  `varta_view::ENLARGED_ASCENT_FRACTION` of their rounded height, rounded, as
  Chrome's `FontMetrics::AscentDescentWithHacks` does
  (`TextMeasurer::set_enlarged_ascent_families`). Text then depends on the
  machine and its OS version, so pixel and geometry oracles compare a run with
  system fonts only with the platform's browser on the same machine; packaged
  fonts remain the deterministic path. Other platforms refuse the option
  (`ShellError::SystemFontsUnsupported`).
  `--renderer cpu|gpu|auto` selects
  presentation (default `cpu`). An explicit `gpu` is refused before anything
  else in a build without the `gpu` feature, and is an error
  (`ShellError::GpuUnavailable`) when the GPU does not initialize; `auto` then
  presents with the CPU. A GPU lost after initialization falls back to the CPU
  in both modes. Guest output goes to stdout and host diagnostics, prefixed with
  the binary's name, to stderr.
- **Embedding.** `varta_desktop::shell::Launch::packaged(&Package { artifact,
  policy, storage, font })` prepares an application without a window (`font`
  is the optional explicit `FontSet` of `--font`, refused for an artifact that
  ships fonts) and reads its stored decisions,
  `Launch::unprivileged(wasm, font: Option<FontSet>) -> Result<Launch,
  ShellError>` prepares a manifest-less module and parses its optional font
  (no consent state: it is never prompted), `Launch::start(ViewLayout,
  Arc<dyn PlatformEffects>)` starts it with the host's platform-effects sink
  and no prompt, and `Launch::start_with(ViewLayout, Arc<dyn PlatformEffects>,
  Option<shell::consent::HostPrompt>) -> Result<Started, ShellError>` adds
  the host's prompt seam (`HostPrompt { prompter: Box<dyn
  PermissionPrompter>, unpresentable: Box<dyn FnMut(&PromptTooLong) + Send> }`)
  and returns the instance with its `shell::consent::Consent`, which the
  embedder calls `sync` on between turns and `end` on once when the session
  ends. `shell::revoke(artifact, storage, capability)` stores a denial;
  `shell::consent::ConsentStore` reads and writes one identity's decision
  file. Failures are the typed `ShellError` (`Decisions` for an invalid
  decision file, `UnknownCapability` for a revocation of an unregistered id).
- **Not yet.** Manifest `app` metadata, OS bundles and prebuilt per-target
  shells
  ([desktop packaging](development-plan.md#desktop-packaging)), and the open
  permission points below.

#### Native permissions (P10b)

`varta-shell` is a host with a prompt seam for the
[permission broker v1](#permission-broker-v1-turn_budgets). The broker
decides; the shell stores, asks and audits.

- **Stored decisions.** Per application identity, in the host-owned
  `<base>/sha256-<digest>/permissions.json` (`consent::DECISIONS_FILE`): a
  [decision file](#permission-broker-v1-turn_budgets) holding that identity
  only, read bounded like a manifest by `Launch::packaged` before any storage
  directory is created; a malformed or oversized file, or one naming another
  identity, is `ShellError::Decisions`, never an empty set. The decisions
  apply on every start, with or without a prompt (`Launch::start` too).
  Writes validate the file, go to a private (0600 on Unix) temporary file in
  the same directory and are renamed over the old one. Every
  read-modify-write (an instance's sync, a refused start's answers,
  `--revoke`) holds an exclusive advisory lock on `consent::LOCK_FILE` in the
  same directory (`ConsentStore::locked`), so writers of one identity never
  interleave, and an instance writes none of its decisions over an entry
  that changed from outside since it last read the file (a refused start
  compares with the file it read when it was prepared). `consent::CONSENT_FILES` lists every file the store creates;
  each name contains a `.`, so none can be a guest file root.
- **First-run approval.** `Launch::start_with` with a prompter asks for each
  required grant within the request and the ceiling that has no stored
  decision, once, before instantiation; no guest code runs while the user
  decides and no turn deadline is spent. A refusal fails the start with
  `PermissionError::RequiredDenied`; the binary reports it on stderr
  (`varta-shell: application failed: required permission ... cannot run`)
  and exits with failure. Allow and Deny answers are stored (and audited)
  even when the start is refused, as in the browser host; a dismissal stores
  nothing, so the next start asks again. A stored denial of a required grant
  keeps the application from starting until the decision file changes.
- **Optional grants.** Without a decision they are in `prompt` state; the
  runtime asks only for `varta.permissions.request` in a user-gesture turn (a
  trusted click, key or submit), between turns; any other turn resolves to
  the current state without a prompt, and an operation in `prompt` state is
  denied recoverably. A `ui.open_url` matched only by `https://*` prompts on
  each activation through the same window and is never stored.
- **Prompt window.** The worker thread blocks in the seam (`NativePrompter`)
  while the event loop shows the question in a separate top-level window
  titled `Varta permission request`, always on top and not resizable; it is
  never an L0 node. Its content is `consent::PromptLayer`: the capability id,
  the application identity and every exact requested pattern in full (the
  broker's own description), then the package `purpose` as a quote marked by
  a bar, all drawn with the layer's own 5x9 bitmap font, never with artifact
  fonts; every character outside printable ASCII is shown as its `\u{...}`
  escape and a backslash is shown doubled (`\\`), so text that spells
  `\u{430}` never passes for an escaped character. A pattern is never cut
  or left out: patterns are wrapped between whole characters, escapes and
  doubled backslashes (never inside an escape), the first line of each is
  marked by a host square in the margin, and the resource lines are paged,
  `consent::RESOURCE_PAGE_LINES` per page, with a host page line ("Page N of
  M") and a "Next page" button (also Page Down and Page Up). A page counts as
  shown only once the window has presented its frame on a surface that holds
  the whole prompt (`PromptLayer::presented`); selecting it with page keys
  is not enough, so pages skipped in one burst of key presses stay unseen.
  A surface smaller than the prompt (a display shorter than the prompt) is
  reported once as a host diagnostic and its pages never count. Allow is
  drawn disabled, cannot take focus and ignores presses and keys until every
  page has been presented, and it answers only `consent::PROMPT_INPUT_DELAY`
  after the last unseen page was; going back from the first page to the
  last does not count the pages between. Deny and Dismiss work on any page.
  A request whose resources need more than `consent::MAX_RESOURCE_LINES`
  lines (`consent::MAX_RESOURCE_PAGES` pages) is never shown
  (`consent::PromptTooLong`): the consent seam answers it Deny without
  asking (stored like any Deny of a required or optional grant, whose
  package request never changes; never stored for a `ui.open_url` link),
  reports it to `HostPrompt::unpresentable`, which `varta-shell` prints on
  stderr (`varta-shell: denied the ... permission request without asking:
  ... no prompt was shown and no user decided`), and appends an audit row
  with `refused` = `consent::UNPRESENTABLE_PROMPT`, `operation`, `outcome`
  `denied`, `resource_lines` and `max_resource_lines`; the window repeats
  the check, denies and reports too. The broker's own row for that answer
  still has `source` `prompt`; a refused start then also reports the
  broker's `RequiredDenied`, and later starts report the stored decision.
  One pattern of `MAX_PATTERN_BYTES` always fits, whatever its characters;
  as many longest patterns as one grant holds, or a link URL whose shown
  text needs more lines than that (an ASCII URL near `net::MAX_URL_BYTES`),
  do not. **Cross-host difference:** the browser
  host's prompt lists every pattern however long and lets Allow answer at
  once, so such a request is shown and can be allowed in the browser but is
  denied without a prompt natively. No build or validation step warns about
  a request the native prompt cannot show. Only the advisory purpose quote is bounded:
  at most `consent::MAX_QUOTE_LINES` lines, a longer quote is cut with a
  visible `...`. The answer buttons keep their place below the text on every
  page. Deny has the initial focus; Tab and the arrow keys move it among the
  usable buttons, Enter and Space activate, Escape and the close button
  dismiss. Apart from the close button, an answer or a page turn needs a
  press and release on the same button or a non-repeated, non-synthetic key,
  and such input during the first `consent::PROMPT_INPUT_DELAY` after the
  window appears is ignored, so a click or key meant for the application
  cannot answer it. `PROMPT_INPUT_DELAY` is 500 ms (owner decision,
  2026-11-05).
- **Isolation from the guest.** The guest's frame, nodes, styles, fonts and
  title are not inputs of the prompt layer, and the prompt window is a
  separate surface, so guest content cannot paint over it. A guest title
  containing `Varta permission request` (in any ASCII case) is not applied:
  the application's window keeps the host's default title. A lookalike title
  made of other characters remains possible; the prompt is identified as the
  shell's only always-on-top window, not by its title alone. While a prompt is
  open the application's window drops user input (keys, IME, pointer buttons
  and motion, wheel, touch) instead of sending it to the guest, a press begun
  there never completes as a click, the guest's pointer leaves, and focusing
  the application's window hands focus back to the prompt. Window state
  (resize, scale, theme, redraw, close) still applies; closing the
  application's window ends the session and the pending prompt is dismissed.
- **Rate limits.** The broker's, as in the browser host:
  `permission::MAX_OPEN_PROMPTS` open prompts (the window also dismisses a
  request beyond them at once) and `permission::MAX_DISMISSALS` dismissals of a
  grant before they become a stored denial. No cool-down period is applied.
- **Revocation.** `varta-shell ARTIFACT --revoke CAPABILITY [--data-dir DIR]`
  (`shell::revoke`) reads and validates the artifact, stores a denial for its
  identity and exits without a window; an unregistered id is refused. A
  running instance applies it when `Consent::sync` next rereads the file,
  before the turns that follow: the worker calls `sync` before running turns
  whenever turns ran since the last call or `consent::STORE_POLL_INTERVAL`
  elapsed since the last check, and `sync` rereads the file when the
  instance's own decisions changed or, at most once per interval, when its
  size, modification time or (on Unix) inode changed. While a prompt is open
  the worker waits on it, so a revocation made meanwhile applies after the
  answer, and wins over it. A denial stored
  from outside revokes the grant for new operations (operations already
  authorized keep running) and wins over a concurrent answer in the
  instance: the instance's reread and write hold the store lock, so it sees
  a revocation stored before its write and never writes over it, and a
  revocation stored after its write is seen at the next sync. An allow stored from outside applies only to later starts. A
  revocation inside the instance (`Application::revoke`) is stored at the
  next sync.
- **Audit log.** `Consent::sync` appends every new entry of the broker's
  bounded audit log to `<base>/sha256-<digest>/permission-audit.jsonl`
  (`consent::AUDIT_FILE`, mode 0600 on Unix): one JSON object per line with
  the entry's `sequence`, `at_ms`, `source`, `operation`, `resource` and
  `outcome`, plus `artifact` and `run` (the session's start in milliseconds
  since the Unix epoch). Entries the broker dropped before a sync are counted
  in a `dropped` row; the first-run answers of a refused start are written as
  `prompt` rows. Once the log holds `consent::MAX_AUDIT_LOG_BYTES` it is
  moved to `consent::PREVIOUS_AUDIT_FILE` (replacing an older one) before the
  next rows. The guest can neither read nor write it. Every start of a
  packaged application writes its start decisions, so the per-artifact
  directory exists after any start. A failed write ends the session with an
  error (fail closed). The worker syncs once more on every exit through
  `Consent::end` (a closed window, a failed turn, a host error; after a
  failure the failure is reported, not a sync error). Once the event loop ends, the worker runs no
  new turn, any open prompt is dismissed, and the window waits up to
  `WORKER_EXIT_WAIT` (1 s) for that final sync; a turn still running after
  it is not waited for, and its entries are then lost.
- **Open points (owner decisions, not implemented).** "Allow for this
  session", a cool-down after refusals and its value, how a refused required
  permission is presented beyond the stderr message, and the identity key
  before C3 provenance. (`consent::PROMPT_INPUT_DELAY` = 500 ms was
  confirmed by the owner on 2026-11-05.) The prompt window has no
  AccessKit tree, follows no dark appearance and draws only printable ASCII
  (other characters as escapes); `PermissionPrompt` does not say whether a
  `ui.open_url` prompt is a one-time activation, so the native prompt uses
  the same wording for both. Only the macOS prompt window has been run.

## Developer compatibility inventory

`varta-conformance` is an outer development-tool consumer of public common,
compiler and runtime APIs. It has no dependency on project packaging or the CLI
and adds no dependency, import, source profile or budget to the execution-only
runtime. Workspace dependency-boundary tests classify it as tooling. SHA-256
uses the already locked sha2 0.10.9 dependency in this tool alone.

The [runner contract](../conformance/README.md) pins edition 2025, the profile named in its manifest and
checked-ts-main-v1 programs. Original corpus files are mandatory manifest entries
with exact SHA-256; duplicate/unknown metadata, escapes, symlinks, omissions and
byte/count limits fail before launch. Source bytes are snapshotted before workers
and passed on stdin without compiler filesystem loading or upstream rewriting.
The report includes inventory/source/dependency-lock fingerprints and host target
identity. ECMAScript-derived feature rows and Varta-specific contracts have
separate origins and map to CORE IDs; feature case counts do not assert complete
feature semantics or produce a global completion percentage.

A child process compiles each source, validates it through the runtime API and
runs with empty grants/host ceiling and ordinary fuel/memory/deadline limits,
unless the case's manifest row lists reviewed `grants`; those are then both the
requested grants and the host ceiling, and only `time.timer` is admitted (any
other grant fails inventory loading).
The parent clears the worker environment, writes and drains bounded protocol
pipes on independent threads, polls a bounded wall deadline, and kills/reaps failed
workers. Internal compiler, transport, output, process and timeout faults are
infrastructure failures. Runtime faults and changed observations are regressions;
a documented exact compile diagnostic may match a known-unsupported baseline but
never increments the passed count. Unexpected support requires baseline review.
Strict mode also rejects known gaps and untested feature rows. CI stores the
baseline report in logs while preserving these categories.

This is partial CORE-15 verification of the checked execution model. Script/global
realms, full module/strict/non-strict modes, upstream harness bindings, complete
edition/profile matrices and independent platform/readiness evidence remain open.
Current feature and case counts are reported by the runner and recorded in
[conformance/README.md](../conformance/README.md). An explicit union-typed JSON case and separate
uncontextual inference/peer/reference cases retain independent observations;
v27 closes the formerly unsupported inference case. Existing
regression tests, public APIs, artifacts, fuzzing and readiness acceptance work
remain part of the full core objective.

## Runtime internals (non-normative)

These sections describe runtime and common-crate mechanisms that no source profile
admits yet. They are implementation notes, not language contracts.

### Managed closure envelope views (transport preparation)

Common function views independently validate the existing v12+ closure cell,
its optional environment and each captured binding envelope without allocating
or invoking guest code. Count/mask validation is bounded by MAX_CAPTURES; payload
bits stay opaque, preserving legitimate recursive captures and scalar bits that
resemble pointers. Binding type IDs are private per-module metadata. Native
result pairs retain their two-slot physical shape and a root bit only for their
first slot. Legacy v11 cells and public structured value tags remain distinct.

This is envelope validation, not proof of module code membership or typed captured
payload validity. A future public function-value transport must supply those
proofs and version its tags, schemas and native operations before source admission.
Current v30 value13 cannot represent function-valued properties, arrays or unions.

### Typed private capture catalog

Optional v30 `varta.functions` metadata describes private binding IDs, result
widths, value schema DAGs and code/signature capture layouts. The compiler builds
it from its binding and checked dispatch tables. Preflight validates catalog
version/profile, bounded references/counts, acyclic type depths and uniqueness;
missing optional metadata remains compatible with earlier v30 artifacts.

A typed inspector consumes immutable catalog data plus a borrowed guest memory
snapshot. It validates exact binding masks/types/widths/status, primitive payloads,
canonical BigInt/Error objects and typed aggregate/union children. Record fields
must match their compiler slot identities as well as names/kinds/optionality;
serialized descriptor entry order may vary. A v32 `class` node is a record-tagged
leaf validated as a record aggregate; it counts as the record member of a
reference union and cannot appear in a primitive union. Sparse arrays preserve holes and
validate their exact element type. Code/signature catalog membership is checked
before function memoization so aliases cannot bypass a type mismatch. Recursive
closures are legal and work/node/depth allowances remain bounded. Actual callable
invocation still uses the guest's checked dispatch; this API supplies no call
permission and does not invoke code. A public function tag and versioned native
transport remain a separate required step.

### Function tag12 in value14

Value14 reuses the existing physical closure but makes Function tag12 an explicit
reference kind. Legacy tag support stays exact. Reference-cell function reads
require a module-owned catalog; header-only envelope inspection is separate from
payload validation. V14 catalog schemas can describe function-valued record fields,
array elements and a single signature in a reference union. Data validation keeps
recursive private closure graphs bounded and checks signature membership before
memoization. A Rust codec entry point supplies immutable catalog data and a shared
function work allowance; it cannot invoke guest code.

JSON resolution validates each function before mapping it to Undefined, allowing
existing object omission, array-null and top-level-Undefined rules to apply. This
mapping does not expose private capture cycles as JSON cycles. Callable toJSON
properties fail explicitly until invocation can happen in guest code. Schema14
inherits JSON input types/layout generation without a callable JSON constructor.
Host-operation registration and source admission remain future versioned work;
current v30 modules still use value13/ABI28.

### Prepared module capture ownership
