`VartaRuntime::prepare_module` and `prepare_module_and_tools` retain the validated
Wasm module together with an optional immutable `VerifiedFunctionCatalog`.
Metadata is verified once during portable-module preflight. The sealed common
catalog exposes shared schema reads and bounded capture proofs, without mutable
schema access or repeated metadata-DAG validation. The raw `FunctionCatalog`
API still verifies metadata on each proof because its fields remain mutable.

Normal startup, tool invocation and fresh HTTP request instances use the prepared
module path. Each Store receives its module's catalog before instantiation and
owns an Arc independently of the prepared module's lifetime. Execution allows
one instantiation attempt, matching its existing one-instance resource ceiling.
A second attempt cannot replace a live instance's schema; a failed first attempt
clears the schema and cannot be retried in that Store. No process-wide catalog
registry or guest-memory metadata lookup is involved.

The existing `validate_module`/`validate_module_and_tools` APIs continue returning
backend modules for compatibility and inspection. A backend module alone carries
no capture owner. Missing optional catalogs remain accepted for older v30 code.
This ownership layer does not admit value14 source operations or grant indirect
call authority; versioned host handlers and source admission are still pending.
Continuation-frame layouts extend this module-owned metadata in the frame catalog
described next; the design is in the
[development plan](development-plan.md#k44--suspension-scheduling-and-async-planned).

### Suspension foundation (K4.4 block 1)

This is the implemented foundation of the agreed K4.4 design. No profile admits
suspension syntax: the only producer of a suspension point is a test-only
lowering hook in the compiler. No host import, capability or value tag changes;
runtime preflight admits the resulting frame surface only under v33
([runtime admission](#runtime-admission-resumable_frames)). Modules without
suspension points compile exactly as before (the passes below find nothing to
do).

**IR and normalization.** `Expression::Suspend { value, state }` yields `value`
and evaluates to the resume input, whose type is the node's type. After lowering
and literal erasure, `lower::suspension` normalizes every function that contains
one. Operands evaluated before a suspension point (callees, ignored receivers,
arguments, binary operands, record/array elements, member bases and indices) move
into hidden locals in their original order; later operands stay in place. `&&`,
`||`, `??` and `?:` become explicit branches assigning one result local, so the
suspending operand runs only on its branch. Loop tests that suspend move to the
top of the body as `if (!test) break`. Lowering-produced value blocks split into
ordinary statements only for the constructs whose preparation has been reviewed:
simple, compound and logical assignments, updates and `&&`/`||`/`??`/`?:`. Then
the prepared receiver, key and old value are evaluated before the suspension.
Every other value block and the remaining positions are rejected with
`unsupported suspension point inside <construct>`. The construct is named from
the source node at the block's span, for example `call to Math.hypot`,
`` `repeat` method call ``, `switch case test`, `do-while condition`,
`a closure` or `an entry function`. The canonical form is
`Init(t, Suspend { value })` with a suspension-free `value` and a fresh `t`.

**State machine.** Suspension points are numbered 1..n in statement order, so
each structured statement covers one contiguous state range. State 0 means
"created, not started". Every list member is guarded: suspension-free runs execute
only while running (state 0), and compound statements are entered while running
or when the target state lies in their range. An `if` records its branch choice in
a hidden local; a loop re-checks its test only while running. Resumption restores
all saved locals, then re-enters the structured code, so the emitter rebuilds the
`try` handler, label and root bookkeeping of the target state itself. The handler
context is therefore static per state, and the frame's handler field stays zero.
At the target state the delivery clears the state, raises a `Throw` input as a
Number exception at that point, performs a `Return` input as `return` (running
enclosing `finally` blocks) or binds a `Normal` input. Suspension inside `catch`
and `finally` bodies and `switch` case bodies, first rejected in this block, is
admitted with the v33 rules in
[completions in handlers](#synchronous-generators-generators).

**Frames.** A frame is a separate managed kind, heap flag **4096**, with a
48-byte body: `[layout-id:u32, fields=5:u32, control:i64, status:i64,
environment:i64, completion:i64, handler:i64]`. Control is `resume-code:u32 |
state:u32`, status is `status:u32 | generation:u32` (suspended 1, running 2,
completed 3), and the exact edge mask is **28** (environment, completion and
handler). The environment is an environment block (flag 256) of kind **1** whose
entries are segments of kind **2**. Each segment holds at most 32 binding handles
(the 32-bit edge mask), and a frame holds at most 8 segments. Kinds 1 and 2 are
rejected by closure validators, which expect kind 0. Saved bindings reuse binding
cells (flag 512) with their private type ids, widths and reference bits. A
captured local stores its closure cell, so closures and the continuation share
one binding; that entry is zero until the cell exists. Every other local owns a
frame cell that the creator allocates. The state, completion and input locals are
re-initialized on each entry and are not saved. Budgets: 256 saved bindings per
frame (independent of the 32-capture closure limit), 256 suspension states per
function, and 64 live frames. Live frames are permanent root-table slots placed
after module-constant roots in the reserved root region.

**Creator, resume body and dispatcher.** A suspendable function's own index
becomes its creator: it allocates and registers the frame (rooted before the next
allocation), binds the arguments into cells and returns a resume token `frame:u32
| generation:u32 << 32` without running the body. Generations come from one
instance-wide counter; exhausting it is fatal. The resume body takes
`(frame:i64, completion:i32, value:i64)`. The exported dispatcher
`varta_resume(token:i64, completion:i32, value:i64) -> i32` performs closed direct
calls by layout id; it uses no table or indirect call. Before any effect it traps
when:

- the exception channel is not empty;
- the frame is not live in this instance's root table (ownership);
- the envelope is not exact (length, flags, mask, field count, zero handler);
- the frame is running (reentrancy) or completed, or the generation is stale;
- the completion kind is not Normal 0, Throw 1 or Return 2;
- the layout, resume code and state do not agree;
- the input is not admissible.

Admissible inputs are scalars only. Float64 accepts any bits, Boolean only 0 or
1, and Undefined only 0. A Throw input is a Number, and a Return input must match
a Float64, Boolean, undefined or void result; other results admit no Return.
Host-supplied references need a validated transport and are outside this block.
The dispatcher reports Suspended 0, Returned 1 or Threw 2. It moves an uncaught
exception from the channel into an exception-union completion cell and clears the
channel. The completion type is the profile's catch union; in a v32 program
that declares an Error class it holds the Error root class, so an uncaught
Error-class instance is a Record member of the completion with its descriptor,
`message` and `name` intact, and saved class instances are traced through the
frame like any other reference binding. Suspension points inside methods,
constructors (including Error-root `super(...)`), `instanceof` tests and the
other value blocks of the new v32 forms are rejected by construct name, and a
generic instance can contain one only behind a rejected reference. A completed
frame leaves the root table. Its completion stays readable
until the next guest call that may collect it. The dispatcher has effects and is
never a pure helper; JSON helper purity validation is unchanged.

**Exception and GC invariants.** The exception channel is empty whenever the
scheduler holds control. A suspension point asserts this fatally before
returning, and the dispatcher requires it on entry. Fatal traps and resource
exhaustion are never converted into completions. In frame-bearing modules the
collector additionally traces the frame flag through the exact mask; segment and
cell tracing reuses the environment/binding path. Restoration checks every saved
cell before use: allocation bounds, flags, reference mask, private type id, width
and canonical Boolean/null/undefined payloads.

**Metadata and versioning.** Frame-bearing modules emit function catalog version
**2** with `frames` rows: resume code, saved binding ids and sharing, per-state
input class and yielded binding, result and Return-input class, and exception
binding. `FunctionCatalog::from_bytes` still accepts only version 1 and rejects
version 2; `from_frame_bytes` reads both. Runtime preflight selects the reader
by profile, so only v33 and v34 read version 2; v35 frames use liveness
layouts and catalog version 3 instead
([frame liveness](#frame-liveness-frame_liveness)).
Modules without frames keep emitting version 1 unchanged. Test builds also export
frame creators (`varta.test.frame.<layout>`) and the collector
(`varta.test.collect`); release builds export only `varta_resume`.

Profile v33 and its host ABI declare the `varta_resume` export, the frame flag
and layout and frame catalog version 2 validation in preflight
([runtime admission](#runtime-admission-resumable_frames)). Profile v34 adds the
scheduler-owned token, root and generation policy that lets suspended frames
outlive the guest call that created them
([microtask scheduler](#microtask-scheduler-promises)).


### Review corrections (2026-11-01)

Generated checked casts can contain conditional spines much deeper than the
bounded source AST (a 180-member literal union is sufficient). The emitter uses
an explicit work stack for conditional branches and their root-scope epilogues;
it preserves instruction order, root marks, branch result roots and fuel without
requiring a larger native thread stack. The CLI regression checks, executes and
builds the cast, then runs its artifact after the source has been removed. The
UARP console remains an external integration workload, not an engine dependency.

Thenable rejection is enforced both statically and at dynamic resolution sites,
including constructor/withResolvers resolvers, reaction results and async returns.
Six v37 programs include the changed resolution helpers: the network abort,
basics, denial, redirects and streams cases, and the SSE integration case. Their
corrected aggregate baseline was checked by comparing all 133 programs with
`b2a36e0`; the other 127 programs are byte-identical. V36 and legacy aggregate
baselines and fuel golden numbers remain unchanged. Existing portable artifacts, host signatures and
capability grants keep their ABI. Timer imports in both native and JavaScript
hosts now implement the stated Node integer-delay normalization; the previous
fraction-preserving description was erroneous.


<a id="http-contract-v2--server-integration-in-progress"></a>

### HTTP contract v2 — native server

V38 synchronous and async HTTP adapters use `http::UTF16_VERSION` (2). Contract v1 remains
unchanged for legacy i32 profiles; v2 is rejected outside v38 and v1 is rejected
for v38. The host verifies contract/profile/value layout before starting a
listener. Both versions use the same bounded UTF-8 JSON wire envelopes and fixed
listener limits; v2 copy/retain/handler strings contain UTF-16LE guest bytes.
The host checks input-copy identity after transcoding, roots it before calling,
checks pending exceptions, validates the response range/even UTF-16 byte length,
decodes without replacement and enforces the UTF-8 output limit and response
schema. Binary64 statuses must still serialize as valid integer HTTP statuses.
Each request owns a fresh bounded Store; a handler failure does not terminate the
listener. In v2, module initializers run once per request Store before the adapter;
main remains startup-only. Mutable module state is isolated between requests.

An optional `asynchronous: true` field (v2 only) means `handle(i64)->i64` returns
a Promise<string> handle. The host retains it, drains microtasks and drives the
normal bounded timer/network loop until the response settles. The additional
`varta.http_abi.state(i64)->f64` and `varta.http_abi.value(i64)->i64` exports read
its state and fulfilled string. Both must be guest-defined and transitively
host-free; unexpected exports and flag/version/signature mismatches are rejected.
Pending with no runnable work fails the request, as does an unhandled rejection;
a successful response drops its request Store, cancelling background timers and
owned transfers. Sync v2 responses are rooted through their microtask checkpoint.
Neither path renews request budgets. V2 effects are computed from the emitted
closed direct-call graph and independently recomputed by validation. V1 omits the
new flag and exports and retains its previous encoding and execution behavior.

**Streaming responses and the connection pool (v2).** A v38 handler may also
return a Web `Response` (or a promise of one), as with `Deno.serve`; its body,
text, bytes or a `ReadableStream`, reaches the client as chunked transfer
encoding while the guest produces it. The contract then sets `streaming`
(with `asynchronous`): `handle` resolves to a record holding the pull function
the fetch prelude makes of the `Response` (`httpResponseBody`, unnameable by
programs), and the additional `varta.http_abi.pull(i64)->i64` calls it and
returns its `Promise<string>`, read through the pure
`varta.http_abi.chunk_state(i64)->f64` and `chunk_value(i64)->i64`. The record
keeps the current chunk promise, so the host roots it once, not per chunk.
The first pull yields the head envelope (the v2 response schema with an empty
body); every later one a record whose first code unit is `http::STREAM_DATA`
followed by at most `http::STREAM_CHUNK_BYTES` bytes as a byte string (one
code unit 0..=0xFF per byte; the prelude splits a larger chunk) or
`http::STREAM_END`. The head is validated as a whole response's (status,
headers, no framing headers) but has no `content-length`; HEAD and bodyless
statuses pull nothing more. Validation requires exactly these exports, their
signatures and the chunk accessors to be host-free, and counts the effects of
`pull`'s graph with the handler's in `required_effects`.

The head runs as the first turn under the request budgets, as an async
handler does. Each later pull is one `stream` turn with fresh fuel, host calls
and microtasks and `http::STREAM_IDLE_SECONDS` as its deadline (its timer and
network sub-turns share that allowance); the whole response lives at most
`http::STREAM_LIFETIME_SECONDS`, after which its pull fails and the body is
aborted, and an SSE client reconnects with `Last-Event-ID`. The worker sends
chunks through a one-chunk channel, so it never runs ahead of the client. A
client that leaves drops the body, which cancels the worker (it stops at its
next cancellation check); a service shutdown cancels every streaming worker;
a failure after the head aborts the body (no terminating chunk). A streaming
service's connection lifetime adds the stream lifetime.

V2 services keep HTTP/1.1 connections alive: up to `http::MAX_OPEN_CONNECTIONS`
open connections, which cost no worker while idle, and up to
`http::MAX_CONCURRENT_REQUESTS` requests running at once, each a task with its
own Store, while the memory budgets of the running requests fit
`http::SERVER_MEMORY_BYTES` (see async execution below). A request
waits at most `http::WORKER_WAIT_SECONDS` for a slot and its memory, else it gets 503 with
`Retry-After: http::BUSY_RETRY_AFTER_SECONDS`; the wait is bounded by the open
connections, never an unbounded queue. A connection's idle time between
requests is also its client's deadline for a request head
(`http::KEEP_ALIVE_IDLE_SECONDS`, Node's keep-alive default); its
`http::MAX_KEEP_ALIVE_REQUESTS`-th answer, or the end of its lifetime
(`http::CONNECTION_LIFETIME_SECONDS`, plus the stream lifetime for a streaming
service), finishes the current response and closes it (`connection: close`).
A further connection waits in the listener's backlog. Shutdown stops
accepting and waits for the open connections. HTTP contract v1 keeps one
connection per request and its immediate 503. The limits travel in the
contract metadata (`HttpLimits::for_version`: `connections`, `pool`,
`stream`, `transport`), so a v38 service built before them must be rebuilt.
A v2 connection whose response write (or flush) makes no progress for
`http::WRITE_IDLE_SECONDS` closes, so a client that stops reading holds its
connection no longer than that. The same bound applies to each streamed
body on its own: a chunk the transport does not take within it (an HTTP/2
stream whose client keeps its window closed while the connection still
moves other streams) aborts the stream, so its worker and admission are
released then; the client sees the stream reset once it reads again. A
failure after the head reaches the body through a flag set before its chunks
close, never through its full chunk buffer.

**Web `Request` handlers (v2).** A v38 handler may take a Web `Request`
instead of a `VartaHttpRequest`, with any of the four result forms, as
`Deno.serve` handlers do. The contract then sets `webRequest` (with
`asynchronous`; v2 only), and the adapter makes the argument of a
`WebRequestHead` envelope: the method; the absolute URL of the cleartext
scheme, the authority the request names (an absolute-form target, an HTTP/2
`:authority`, else the `Host` header, which must be a valid authority, else
the listener's address) and the target's path and query; the headers as
received; and `body`, the id of the transfer its body streams through, or 0
for a request without one. The fetch prelude's `httpRequest` (unnameable by
programs) builds the `Request`; its body is a `ReadableStream` whose reads
are the network reads of a response body (`net_body_read*`), so the host
holds at most one received frame and a slow guest applies backpressure to
the client. `Request` gained `body`, `bodyUsed`, `text()`, `json()`,
`arrayBuffer()`, `bytes()` and `blob()`; a `Request` made of a received one
takes its stream over, and `fetch` of it reads the body whole (within the
received bound) and sends it as bytes. A declared `content-length` above
`http::MAX_REQUEST_BODY_BYTES` gets 413 before dispatch; a body that grows
beyond it, or whose next frame takes longer than
`http::REQUEST_BODY_IDLE_SECONDS` once the guest asked for it, fails the
guest's read (a catchable `TypeError: terminated`). Such a request is a
sequence of turns: the handler's first turn, then every timer, network or
body completion begins a turn with fresh fuel, host calls, microtasks and
the per-turn deadline (capped by the fixed handler deadline), and the waits
between turns use no turn deadline. The request lives at most
`http::REQUEST_LIFETIME_SECONDS` to its response head (plus the stream
lifetime for a streaming response, whose pulls keep the stream idle bound),
and a connection whose lifetime ends lets its current request finish within
that bound. `VartaHttpRequest` handlers keep their whole-body envelope and
budgets unchanged.

**Host limits (v2).** A host policy's `http.limits`
([embedding contract](embedding.md#manifest)) lowers server limits of a v2
service: connections, workers, worker wait, keep-alive idle, requests and
lifetime, stream idle and lifetime, request body bytes, body idle, request
lifetime and write idle. Each value must lie between 1 and the registry's
(`HttpLimits::lowered`); a larger one, 0, or any limit for a v1 service
fails the run before a socket is bound. A package never carries the
member, and the application can change no limit.

Timer/Unicode, mutable-state, forced-GC, outbound-body/denial and hostile metadata
cases have focused verification. Every request now receives a shareable snapshot
of startup's effective budgets/caps and artifact-scoped headless broker inputs,
with fresh counters and no allowance renewal across tasks. The fixed HTTP deadline
caps a larger application deadline. A fresh headless broker applies required and
optional consents/stored decisions within the original grants/ceiling; its states
also authorize bind before socket creation. V2 workers deliver bounded logs even
before failure, and report errors once independently of transport-result delivery.
Lower package/host fuel, memory, host-call/output budgets, aggregate async bounds,
listener consent and artifact/ceiling decisions have focused server verification.
V1 still ignores v38-only budget/consent requests.

**Async execution (H2).** The native server is a multi-threaded Tokio
runtime with one worker thread per available CPU, and every v2 request is a
task of it, never a thread of its own. Its engine shares the runtime's
compilation settings (`engine_config`, so fuel is the embedding engine's),
uses a pooling allocator of `http::MAX_CONCURRENT_REQUESTS` instance slots of
`http::REQUEST_MEMORY_BYTES` each, and links the module once into an
`InstancePre`; each request still instantiates its own Store from it. Guest
calls are asynchronous (`call_async`) and yield to the executor at every
epoch tick (one ticker thread per server advances the epoch every
`server::engine::TICK`, which also meets per-turn deadlines without a
deadline thread per Store). The fair call charge is taken around libcalls
too, so the epoch callback refunds it: fuel never depends on when epochs
advance, here or when another Store's deadline or cancellation advances a
shared engine's epoch; the server does not yield on fuel intervals, whose
libcalls would count. The scheduler's timer waits, network and request-body
completions and cancellation are awaited (`checkpoint_until_async`,
`Net::wait_async`, `Cancellation::cancelled`), and a request's transfers run
on the server's runtime, so a waiting request or open stream costs no
thread. A blocking host operation (legacy `net.get`/`net.fetch`,
`fs.read`/`fs.print` file reads, KV reads and commits) hands its thread's
other tasks on first (`block_in_place`), within the server's blocking-thread
bound (one per request slot). An operating-system read cannot be
interrupted: it is bounded by the result size limit, and the request's
deadline and cancellation take effect as soon as it returns.
A v2 request is admitted once a slot is free and its memory budget fits the
server memory ceiling less the budgets of the running requests; the
admission ends with its task, after its Store is dropped. A host policy may
lower slots and ceiling (`workers`, `memoryBytes`); a ceiling below one
request's budget fails before bind. Fuel, turn order, budgets, deadlines and
cancellation keep their contracts. Contract v1 (frozen) keeps one blocking
worker: its checked JSON parsing calls back into the guest from a host
import, which an asynchronous call cannot.

**TLS 1.3 and HTTP/2 (H3).** A host policy's `http.tls` names the absolute
paths of a PEM certificate chain and private key
([embedding contract](embedding.md#manifest)); every contract v2 service of
that host then serves TLS 1.3 only (rustls with the ring provider, no TLS
1.2, no 0-RTT data) and offers ALPN `h2` before `http/1.1`. The host reads
the files (at most `http::MAX_TLS_FILE_BYTES` each) before the listener
exists; a missing, oversized or malformed file, a relative path, or TLS for
a contract v1 service fails the run before bind, and neither file nor key
ever reaches a package or guest. The `net.listen` grant names whether an
endpoint serves TLS: `"https://127.0.0.1:8443"` for TLS, the bare
`"127.0.0.1:8080"` for cleartext, each canonical; the package and the host
ceiling must both grant the form the host serves, so a cleartext grant
never authorizes a TLS listener or the reverse, and `http_stop` checks the
same form. A Web `Request`'s URL then has the `https` scheme, and the
readiness event (`RuntimeEvent::Listening`) names the scheme.

A client has `http::TLS_HANDSHAKE_SECONDS` to finish its handshake; one that
negotiated `h2` gets HTTP/2, any other HTTP/1.1. HTTP/2 announces at most
`http::MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` concurrent streams and a header list of
`http::MAX_HEADER_LIST_BYTES` (the request header bounds still apply to each
request), uses receive windows of `http::STREAM_WINDOW_BYTES` per stream and
`http::CONNECTION_WINDOW_BYTES` per connection and a send buffer of one
stream chunk, pings its peer every `http::PING_INTERVAL_SECONDS` (closing it
without an answer within `http::PING_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`), and ends a
connection with `GOAWAY` after `http::MAX_PENDING_RESET_STREAMS` resets of
streams not yet accepted or reset by the server (the rapid-reset bounds of
`h2`). Each stream is a request of its own, with the same admission,
budgets and reports; an HTTP/2 request's `VartaHttpRequest` target is its
path and query. A connection whose clients abandon more than
`http::MAX_ABANDONED_REQUESTS` requests (resets that reached the
application) is retired with `GOAWAY` and closed within a second; its
keep-alive request count, idle bound and lifetime retire it with `GOAWAY`
(HTTP/2 has no `connection` header), and the write idle bound covers its
TLS records. A request counts as running for the idle bound until its
response body ends (streamed, aborted, or reset by its client), not only
until its head is sent, and the bound measures quiet since the last request
or body started or ended.

**Hardening (H4).** Seeded fuzz tests cover the contract metadata and host
policies, the response envelope's framing and every adapter form with
random requests; flood and slow-client tests cover slow heads, slow bodies,
connection and request floods and HTTP/2 rapid resets. The load
benchmarks (`server_tests::bench`, ignored) and their recorded acceptance
numbers are in the [development plan](development-plan.md#k7--modern-http-server-agreed-design-2026-11-05).

The v2 service future owns a cancellation guard for its request task.
Disconnect or connection timeout drops that owner and signals its execution;
epoch checks interrupt guest loops, while timer/network waits await the same
token without advancing guest time or delivering extra guest events.
Other Stores sharing the engine remain live. A completed worker disarms the guard
and releases guest/network resources before invoking trusted output observers.
A cancelled worker keeps its admission (slot and memory) until it stops (its
next cancellation check, then its report and output delivery). A v2 request
that finds no admission waits for one within the worker wait, so a request
sent right after a client disconnected is served instead of being refused
with the transport's `503 request failed`; the wait is bounded by the
worker's cancellation checks and its own request deadline, and shutdown
ends it. HTTP contract v1 is frozen: its workers are not cancelled, and its
transport keeps the immediate 503 while the worker is busy; only v2 waits for
the worker permit.
Shutdown stops acceptance, immediately closes idle/partial-header connections and
drains the active response under its original connection and request deadlines.
These paths have real loopback/disconnect, guest-loop and timer verification.

Native async name resolution uses a process-owned bounded system DNS pool, with
limits in the [embedding registry](embedding.md#network-request-limits-v37).
Only owned host names, deadlines and result channels cross into DNS workers;
request runtime destruction never joins an OS lookup. Cancelled/expired queued
jobs are skipped, late results cannot open sockets, and oversized answers fail
explicitly. System address order remains unchanged. These native resource bounds
also apply to earlier async fetch profiles without changing their guest ABI.
Already running OS lookups may finish later within the fixed process pool.

V2 workers close one non-renewing execution usage entry on both success and
failure, including cancellation. After releasing their Store they emit
`RuntimeEvent::HttpRequest(Box<HttpRequestReport>)`, with a server-local completion
sequence, invocation outcome, effective budget/caps, actual fuel/host-call/
microtask/wall/memory/output usage and their broker audit log. Setup failures have
no budget record. `Returned { status }` describes a guest envelope returned to
the transport; framing validation or delivery can still fail. Connections rejected
before a worker starts have no request record. Audit entry sequences/timestamps
remain local to each fresh request broker.

`RunReport::http` holds HTTP worker totals and a bounded prefix of request details,
separate from its original startup budget/audit fields. The shared
[entry limits](embedding.md#entry-point-limits) bound retained request records and
the aggregate audit prefix. Totals keep counting every worker; omitted detail and
audit entries are counted explicitly. A trusted observer receives every completed
worker's bounded report before aggregate truncation, without an unbounded native
event queue. Evidence survives a failed server run and transport disconnect.
Legacy HTTP publishes no v2 request reports. CLI and companion `--budget-report`
stream each v2 worker's usage at completion; startup reporting remains separate.

Inside an owned v2 request, the synchronous `net.get`/`net.fetch` imports drive
the cancellable native transport under the same absolute request deadline.
They remain synchronous guest calls: native polling runs no guest jobs and
renews no allowance. Exact legacy HTTP-only package/host grants are checked before
DNS or sockets. The transport never follows redirects or uses ambient proxies;
`net.fetch` returns the received status without waiting for a body, while
`net.get` collects raw body bytes under `abi::MAX_RESULT_BYTES` before the existing
guest string conversion. Response headers use `net::MAX_RESPONSE_HEADERS` and
`net::MAX_FETCH_HEADER_BYTES`; DNS uses the bounded process pool. Cancellation
and the exhausted execution deadline escape as fatal execution failures before
a host result is published, including through `try/catch` or result capture.
The request closes its socket/runtime before reporting. Calls without an owned
cancellation context retain the previous synchronous transport and behavior.

Bounded `wait_network` steps now drive native scripted view I/O with explicit
wall/virtual clock scope; their contract is in the
[scripted session rules](#v38-view-protocol-and-tsx-view_protocol-tsx).
Native server and source-free/hostile-artifact acceptance passed the full gate
recorded in the [development plan](development-plan.md#status). Broader sustained
native RSS, cross-host and release acceptance remain open.
